### [1] [TabletCraft: Bridging a 4,000-Year Cultural Gap with Bidirectional Akkadian NMT and Cuneiform Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02609)
*Zhaohui Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TabletCraft is the first open-source system for bidirectional interaction with cuneiform, supporting both Akkadian-to-English translation and English-to-Akkadian-to-cuneiform composition, achieving ~49 BLEU in both directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Half a million cuneiform tablets survive in museums, but a 4,000-year cultural barrier persists: existing NLP tools only support one-way (Akkadian→English), scholar-oriented translation, leaving non-specialists as passive consumers unable to compose new cuneiform content.

Method: A ByT5-based translation model trained on 116K bidirectional samples; a cuneiform sign converter with 14,240 mappings (95.3% coverage); a visual tablet renderer; packaged as a pip-installable toolkit with CLI and web demo.

Result: 49.1 BLEU (Akkadian→English) and 48.5 BLEU (English→Akkadian) on the Akkademia validation split (2,812 samples), representing the first published quantitative result for the reverse direction.

Conclusion: TabletCraft successfully bridges the 4,000-year cultural gap by enabling bidirectional cuneiform interaction, empowering non-specialist users to transition from passive consumers to active participants in Mesopotamian writing culture.

Abstract: Half a million cuneiform clay tablets survive in museums worldwide, yet modern users can neither read nor write in the world's oldest writing system, leaving a 4,000-year cultural barrier that existing NLP tools have only partially addressed.
  Prior work enables one-way, scholar-oriented translation from Akkadian to English, but offers no path in the reverse direction: non-specialist users cannot compose new content in cuneiform, and therefore remain passive consumers of ancient culture rather than active participants.
  We present TabletCraft, the first open-source system that enables bidirectional interaction with Mesopotamian writing. Users can read ancient tablets (Akkadian to English) and compose new messages as cuneiform clay tablets (English to Akkadian to cuneiform to rendered tablet).
  The system integrates a ByT5-based translation model trained on 116K bidirectional samples, a cuneiform sign converter with 14,240 mappings (95.3% coverage), and a visual tablet renderer, packaged as a pip-installable toolkit with CLI and web demo.
  On the held-out Akkademia validation split (2,812 samples), we report 49.1 BLEU for Akkadian-to-English and 48.5 BLEU for English-to-Akkadian, the first published quantitative result in the reverse direction.

</details>


### [2] [BBOWP-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Black-Box Optimization Word Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02612)
*Yutaro Yamada,Kei Hiroshima,Nozomu Yoshinari,Kento Uchida,Shinichi Shirakawa*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces BBOWP, a new setting where LLMs must infer both search space design and optimization algorithm selection from natural-language descriptions of black-box optimization problems. Provides BBOWP-Bench, a benchmark dataset with evaluation environments, and shows LLMs can select algorithms but struggle with search space design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for automatically deriving optimization problems from natural language focus on problems with explicit mathematical formulations. However, many practical problems are black-box optimization (BBO) problems where only objective values are observable and the functional form is unknown. In BBO, designing the search space and selecting the right algorithm are both critical and non-trivial, and automating these using LLMs remains an open challenge.

Method: The authors propose the BBOWP (Black-Box Optimization Word Problems) setting and contribute BBOWP-Bench, a benchmark dataset where each instance consists of (1) a natural-language problem description, (2) an executable evaluation environment, and (3) a human-designed baseline formulation. This enables systematic evaluation of both search-space design quality and algorithm selection appropriateness. The benchmark is used to conduct the first evaluation of LLMs on this task.

Result: Current LLMs demonstrate the ability to select suitable optimization algorithms based on the given evaluation budget. However, they struggle with search space design, especially in identifying important variables and properly balancing their ranges when problem descriptions are less informative or when the search space is highly problem-specific.

Conclusion: BBOWP represents a significant new challenge at the intersection of LLM-based reasoning and black-box optimization. While LLMs show promise in algorithm selection, search space design remains a bottleneck, highlighting directions for future improvement.

Abstract: Formulating an optimization problem strongly affects the quality of the final solution, yet good formulations usually require substantial expertise. Recent studies have therefore examined how to automatically derive optimization problems from natural-language descriptions, but existing benchmarks focus on settings where objectives and constraints can be written explicitly as mathematical expressions. Many practically important problems are naturally treated as black-box optimization (BBO) problems, in which only objective values are observable, and the functional form is unavailable. In BBO, the search space design, a part of the problem formulation, and the selection of the optimization algorithm are crucial for problem-solving. Automating these processes with large language models (LLMs) is a significant challenge. This paper introduces Black-Box Optimization Word Problems (BBOWP), a novel problem setting in which a system must infer both a search space and an optimization algorithm from a natural-language description of a black-box optimization task. To support research on this setting, we establish the BBOWP Benchmark Suite (BBOWP-Bench), a dataset and evaluation framework for BBOWP. Each instance combines a natural-language problem description, an executable evaluation environment, and a human-designed baseline formulation, allowing evaluation of both search-space design and algorithm selection. Using this benchmark, we provide the first evaluation of LLMs and show that current LLMs are capable of selecting suitable algorithms based on the given evaluation budget. However, they sometimes struggle with search space design, particularly in identifying important variables and balancing their ranges when the problem description is less informative or the search space is highly problem-specific. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/shiralab/bbowp-bench.

</details>


### [3] [MemArena: An Ego-Centric Benchmark for On-Device Agentic Personal Memory Assistants at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02613)
*Jiadong Zhang,Xiaosong Ma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MemArena is a multi-session conversational benchmark for evaluating on-device personal memory assistants, featuring 50 simulated agents over 15 days with 10.3M tokens, assessing six dimensions including recall, reasoning, and trustworthiness. Key findings: memory backend choice significantly impacts accuracy (outweighing reader scaling), permission-aware access fails universally, and search latency is modest on edge hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge-deployed personal memory assistants need open-weight models to handle private interpersonal conversations on-device, but existing memory benchmarks insufficiently test activity-dense, ego-centric, multi-session scenarios with coherent world states.

Method: MemArena constructs a single-world conversational benchmark using the MASim agent simulator to generate interactions among 50 agents over 15 days, producing 10.3M dialog-text tokens (24.1K ego-observed tokens/agent/day). Ground truth is co-generated across six evaluation dimensions: recall, reasoning, and trustworthiness. Five open-weight readers are evaluated with five memory backends: Vanilla context, BM25-RAG, Oracle retrieval, Memobase, and MemSearch.

Result: (1) Memory backend choice dominates content accuracy: at Qwen3-0.6B, switching from Memobase to MemSearch yields +32.5/+19.2 percentage points, exceeding gains from scaling the reader (+10.6/+6.8 pp). (2) Permission-aware access fails universally — Oracle leaks heavily while other backends are excessively conservative. (3) Search latency adds only 87/7/48 ms (BM25-RAG/Memobase/MemSearch) on a Spark GB10 edge node, a small fraction of total TTFT for most configurations.

Conclusion: Memory backend selection is the dominant factor for content accuracy in on-device memory assistants, surpassing reader model scaling. Permission-aware memory access remains an open challenge. Practical deployment on edge hardware is feasible given modest search latency overhead. Code, MASim, and MemArena-L will be released upon acceptance.

Abstract: Edge-deployed personal memory assistants must handle private interpersonal conversations on-device with open-weight models. Yet, existing memory benchmarks often under-test the combination of activity-dense interaction, ego-centric perspective, and coherent multi-session worlds. MemArena fills these gaps with a single-world conversational benchmark built with its MASim agent simulator, for 50 agents over 15 days (10.3M dialog-text tokens, 24.1K text-only ego-observed tokens/agent/day). With the interaction history, it co-generates ground truth over six recall, reasoning, and trustworthiness evaluation dimensions. We evaluate five open-weight readers with Vanilla context, BM25-RAG, Oracle retrieval, Memobase, and MemSearch as memory backends. Three results stand out: (1) Memory-backend choice matters more for content accuracy: At Qwen3-0.6B, Memobase-to-MemSearch gains +32.5/+19.2 pp, exceeding MemSearch reader scaling (+10.6/+6.8 pp). (2) Permission-aware access fails universally, with Oracle leaking heavily and other backends too timid to disclose. (3) Search latency bites only at very small reader: on a Spark GB10 edge node, memory-search adds a moderate and fixed 87/7/48 ms (BM25-RAG/Memobase/MemSearch) that composes a small part of TTFT for most reader-backend combinations. Code, the MASim simulator, and the MemArena-L benchmark will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [4] [OncoTriad-QA: A Patient-Level Radiology-Pathology-Genomics Benchmark for Pan-Cancer Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02615)
*Ahnaf Munir,Dannong Wang,Michael W. McDonald,Mubarak Shah,Pegah Khosravi,Yu Tian*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OncoTriad-QA is a pan-cancer QA benchmark integrating radiology, pathology, and genomics from 9,281 TCGA patients, and OncoVLM is a multimodal model that surpasses existing medical LLMs on integrated cancer assessment by 10.7 points after fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical LLM/VLM benchmarks focus on isolated modalities or narrow image-text tasks, leaving patient-level, multi-evidence oncology assessment untested. There is a gap in evaluating models that can integrate radiology, pathology, genomics, and clinical metadata for comprehensive cancer diagnosis.

Method: The authors construct OncoTriad-QA, an 86.1k-question benchmark spanning 9,281 TCGA cases across 32 cancer cohorts, using an LLM-assisted annotation pipeline grounded in curated labels, diagnostic reports, molecular profiles, and modality-derived evidence with automated consistency checks and clinician review. They also introduce OncoVLM, a multimodal model that maps radiology, pathology, DNA methylation, and RNA-seq evidence into an LLM interface via learned projectors, and fine-tune it on the benchmark.

Result: Existing general-purpose and medical LLMs perform poorly on pan-cancer QA requiring multi-modal integration. OncoVLM fine-tuned on OncoTriad-QA outperforms MedGemma-4B by an average of 10.7 points (MCQ accuracy + BERTScore-F1), with consistent gains across multiple-choice and open-ended questions in radiology-only, pathology-only, and all-available settings.

Conclusion: OncoTriad-QA provides a valuable resource for training and evaluating integrated cancer QA models, and OncoVLM demonstrates that multi-modal fusion of imaging and molecular data yields substantial improvements in patient-level oncology question answering.

Abstract: Cancer diagnosis and characterization require integrating complementary evidence from radiology, pathology, genomics, and clinical metadata. However, most medical large language model (LLM) and vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks focus on isolated modalities or narrow image-text tasks, leaving patient-level oncology assessment across multiple evidence streams largely untested. We introduce OncoTriad-QA, a patient-level radiology-pathology-genomics benchmark for pan-cancer question answering. OncoTriad-QA contains 86.1k semantic questions across 9,281 TCGA patient cases from 32 cancer cohorts, aligning CT/MRI radiology, whole-slide histopathology, somatic mutations, copy-number alterations, DNA methylation, bulk RNA-seq, and clinical metadata. Case-specific annotations are constructed through a source-grounded LLM-assisted pipeline using curated labels, diagnostic reports, molecular profiles, and modality-derived evidence as primary sources of truth, with automated consistency checks and clinician review. We also introduce OncoVLM, a reference multimodal model that maps modality-native radiology, pathology, DNA methylation, and RNA-seq evidence into an LLM interface through learned projectors. Experiments show that existing general-purpose and medical LLMs remain limited on comprehensive pan-cancer QA, especially when questions require integrating imaging findings, tumor morphology, and molecular evidence. After fine-tuning on OncoTriad-QA, OncoVLM exceeds MedGemma-4B by an average of 10.7 points when using MCQ accuracy and BERTScore-F1, with consistent gains across multiple-choice and open-ended questions under radiology-only, pathology-only, and all-available settings. These results demonstrate the benchmark's value for training and evaluating models for integrated cancer question answering.

</details>


### [5] [Evaluating OpenAI's Privacy Filter: Cross-Lingual, Cross-Domain PII Detection Across 42 Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02616)
*Rohith Uppala*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: First independent systematic evaluation of OpenAI's Privacy Filter (OPF), a 1.5B-parameter bidirectional PII detector, tested across 42 synthetic benchmarks in 22 languages and 5 domains. OPF excels on structured PII but degrades sharply on narrative prose and non-Latin scripts, with strong recall but weak precision globally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite OpenAI releasing their Privacy Filter as a PII detection tool, no independent, systematic, multilingual, and multi-domain evaluation existed. The authors aim to fill this gap by benchmarking OPF against established PII detectors (Presidio, XLM-RoBERTa) and general-purpose LLMs (GPT-4o) across diverse languages, domains, and PII types to characterize its strengths, failure modes, and deployment readiness.

Method: The authors constructed 42 synthetic benchmarks covering 22 languages (including Indic and non-Latin scripts) and 5 domains (medical, legal, financial, customer support, structured synthetic). They evaluated OPF zero-shot alongside Presidio, XLM-RoBERTa, and GPT-4o, measuring F1, precision, and recall across PII types (email, phone, person, address, etc.). Error analysis examined performance as a function of structural regularity, cultural variability, narrative embedding, and script type.

Result: OPF achieved F1=0.855 on AI4Privacy and 0.464 on SPY medical, outperforming Presidio (0.431, 0.273) and XLM-RoBERTa (0.269, 0.111) on PII benchmarks. GPT-4o led on medical/legal/financial PII (SPY: 0.643 avg, Gretel: 0.527); OPF led on structured synthetic PII (0.71 avg) and customer support (0.60). OPF collapsed on narrative prose (F1=0.04–0.57) and non-Latin scripts (Arabic: 0.04, Cyrillic: 0.03). Strongest on email (0.78) and phone (0.76); weakest on person (0.40) and address (0.49). Recall-biased on customer-support and medical/legal PII (P=0.31–0.54, R=0.70–0.85); global precision ranged 0.31–0.86.

Conclusion: OPF is competitive for structured, high-regularity PII in Latin-script domains but is not deployment-ready for narrative text or non-Latin languages. Its systematic recall bias (high recall, low precision) limits reliability in production pipelines. GPT-4o is a stronger generalist for domain-specific PII, while OPF excels only in narrow, structured contexts. The findings caution against unvalidated use of OPF in multilingual or free-text settings.

Abstract: We present the first independent, systematic evaluation of OpenAI's Privacy Filter (OPF), a 1.5B-parameter bidirectional PII detector, across 42 synthetic benchmarks spanning 22 languages and 5 domains. Zero-shot, OPF achieves F1=0.855 on AI4Privacy and 0.464 on SPY medical, outperforming Presidio (0.431, 0.273) and XLM-RoBERTa (0.269, 0.111) on PII-annotated benchmarks; on multilingual NER, XLM-RoBERTa leads OPF on all 13 Indic and non-Latin languages. GPT-4o leads on medical, legal, and financial PII (SPY: 0.643 avg, Gretel: 0.527), while OPF leads on structured synthetic PII (0.71 avg) and customer support (0.60). OPF degrades sharply when PII is embedded in narrative prose: F1=0.04--0.57 on NER benchmarks and collapse for non-Latin scripts (Arabic: 0.04, Cyrillic: 0.03). Error analysis shows OPF is strongest on structurally regular PII types (email: 0.78, phone: 0.76) and weakest on culturally variable ones (person: 0.40, address: 0.49), and is recall-biased on customer-support and medical/legal PII (P=0.31--0.54, R=0.70--0.85); global precision spans 0.31--0.86 across all domains.

</details>


### [6] [Preferred, Not Safer: Pairwise Preference Is a Poor Proxy for Clinical Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02617)
*Fay Elhassan,David Sasu,Alexandra Kulinkina,Lars Henning Klein,Mary-Anne Hartley*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Clinician pairwise preferences are an unreliable proxy for clinical safety in LLM evaluation. Models ranked highly by preference can still exhibit significant safety-critical failures, which are unevenly distributed across medical specialties. The authors propose a clinically adjusted ranking combining preference with rubric-based safety feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluation often relies on pairwise human preferences (e.g., LMSys-style leaderboards), but it is unclear whether clinician preferences reliably signal clinical safety. The authors investigate whether preference-based rankings adequately capture safety-critical failures that could harm patients.

Method: Using 26,804 blinded pairwise judgments from 736+ clinicians across 28+ countries on the MOOVE platform, the authors evaluate 13 LLMs. Clinicians provide both pairwise preferences and rubric ratings on a [-2, +2] scale (negative = unsafe). They analyze failure rates on Harmlessness and Accuracy, examine prompt length, refusal/escalation behavior, decompose preference variance into safety-critical vs. surface-level features, and introduce a clinically adjusted ranking that merges Bradley-Terry preference strength with rubric-derived safety feedback.

Result: Preference rankings poorly reflect safety: high-preference models still exhibit substantial clinically meaningful failure rates (≤ -1). Failures are specialty-specific, creating domain "no-go zones" invisible in aggregate leaderboards. Surface-level features explain slightly more preference variance than safety-critical rubric differences. A substantial fraction of preference votes carry no positive safety signal.

Conclusion: Evaluation practices should separate preference from safety, report safety-critical failure rates directly rather than relying on aggregate rankings, and incorporate clinically grounded adjustments when ranking LLMs for clinical use.

Abstract: We evaluate whether clinician pairwise preferences provide a reliable signal of clinical safety in large language model (LLM) evaluation using expert feedback from MOOVE (Massive Open Online Validation and Evaluation), a clinician-led platform collecting blinded pairwise preferences alongside multi-criterion rubric ratings. Clinicians assign scores on a discrete $[-2, +2]$ scale, where negative values indicate clinically unsafe or misleading content. Using 26{,}804 pairwise judgments across outputs from 13 LLMs, contributed by more than 736 clinicians across 28+ countries, we find that clinician preference is a poor proxy for safety-critical performance. Models ranking highly under pairwise preference can still exhibit substantial rates of clinically meaningful failures ($\leq -1$) on dimensions such as \emph{Harmlessness} and \emph{Accuracy}. These failures are unevenly distributed across specialties, creating domain-specific ``no-go zones'' not visible in aggregate rankings or single-number leaderboards. We further analyze contributing factors including prompt length, refusal and escalation behavior, and the relative contributions of safety-critical versus surface-level features. A substantial fraction of preference votes carry no positive safety signal, while feature decomposition shows that surface-level characteristics explain slightly more preference variation than safety-critical rubric differences. Finally, we introduce a clinically adjusted preference ranking combining pairwise preference with rubric-derived feedback, producing a more safety-aware ordering than raw Bradley--Terry strength alone. Our findings support evaluation practices that separate preference from safety, report safety-critical failure rates directly, and incorporate clinically grounded adjustments when ranking LLMs for clinical decision making.

</details>


### [7] [JudgeArena: A Unified Framework for Reproducible LLM-Judge Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02620)
*Erlis Lushtaku,Bora Kargi,Ali Elganzory,Fabio Ferreira,Alejandro R. Salamanca,Julia Kreutzer,David Salinas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: JudgeArena is an open-source framework that unifies major LLM-judge benchmarks under a single interface with swappable judges, enabling systematic study of how design choices affect model quality conclusions. It provides tuned open-model judge configurations that rival closed-model judges and can accurately simulate LMArena Elo scores without large-scale human annotation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The LLM-as-a-judge evaluation ecosystem is fragmented: each benchmark uses its own codebase, hardcodes specific closed-model judges (e.g., GPT-4), and supports only a single evaluation protocol. This makes it difficult to systematically study how choices of benchmark, judge model, prompt, and inference backend affect conclusions about model quality. There is also over-reliance on opaque closed models as judges and costly human annotation campaigns.

Method: JudgeArena unifies four major benchmarks (AlpacaEval, Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, m-Arena-Hard) into a single interface with modular, swappable judges and comprehensive metadata logging. Any model accessible via vLLM, llama.cpp, or OpenRouter can serve as candidate or judge. The framework includes tuned judge configurations for open models, validated against human preference datasets in English and multilingual settings. It also combines existing human annotations with LLM-judge evaluations to simulate LMArena Elo scores.

Result: Tuned open-model judge configurations match or outperform closed-model judges on human preference datasets in both English and multilingual settings. The framework successfully simulates LMArena Elo scores with high accuracy using a combination of existing human annotations and LLM-judge evaluations, providing a practical, low-cost alternative to large-scale human annotation.

Conclusion: JudgeArena addresses fragmentation in LLM evaluation by providing a unified, transparent, and reproducible framework. It demonstrates that open models can serve as effective judges, reducing reliance on closed-model APIs, and that Elo scores can be accurately simulated without expensive human annotation, making rigorous model evaluation more accessible and systematic.

Abstract: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation has become a dominant paradigm for ranking language models, yet the ecosystem remains fragmented: most benchmarks ship their own code base, hardcode a specific closed-model judge, and support a single evaluation protocol. This fragmentation makes it difficult to study how design choices--the benchmark, the judge model, the prompt, the inference backend--affect the conclusions we draw about model quality. We introduce JudgeArena, an open-source framework that unifies major LLM-judge benchmarks (AlpacaEval, Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, and m-Arena-Hard) under a single interface with swappable judges and comprehensive metadata logging for increased transparency in reporting and reproducibility. It enables systematic studies of judge choices, as any model accessible via vLLM, llama.cpp, or OpenRouter can serve as both candidate and judge. Furthermore, JudgeArena ships with tuned judge configurations for open models that match or outperform closed-model judges, validated on human preference datasets in both English and multilingual settings, reducing the reliance on opaque closed models. Finally, by combining existing human annotations with LLM-judge evaluations of a target model, JudgeArena can simulate LMArena Elo scores with high accuracy offering a practical, open, and low-cost alternative to large-scale human annotation campaigns.

</details>


### [8] [Knowing the Form, Not the Function: Automatically Auditing Answer--Authority Decoupling in Legal Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02621)
*Hsien-Jyh Liao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs spontaneously cite legal authority even when not prompted, but answer correctness and authority grounding frequently dissociate. The paper proposes jointly evaluating both dimensions rather than using answer-only scoring, which masks authority-grounding failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal benchmarks typically score only final answers, ignoring whether models correctly ground responses in statutory authority. The authors investigate whether answer correctness can serve as a proxy for authority grounding, motivated by the observation that LLMs spontaneously cite legal provisions even without prompting.

Method: The authors tested four LLMs on 238 Taiwan bar-examination items under ordinary reasoning prompts that did not request citations. Each item has a verified governing statutory provision, enabling automatic joint auditing of answer correctness and authority grounding. They also conducted a statutory-retrieval probe and a permissive citation-abstention intervention to test output-level separability, plus a preliminary extension to PRC civil law.

Result: Answer correctness and authority grounding dissociate bidirectionally. In criminal law, 24.0–42.4% of valid responses were answer-correct but missed the gold authority; 15.2–21.7% were answer-incorrect but cited it. The retrieval probe and abstention intervention confirmed that answer and citation behavior can move independently at the output level. This mismatch occurs without adversarial prompting, meaning answer-only scoring treats gold-authority misses as complete successes.

Conclusion: Because authority grounding failures are structurally extractable and externally verifiable, they can be measured automatically. The authors propose joint answer–authority evaluation for all statute-grounded legal benchmarks and motivate cross-jurisdictional extension of this audit framework.

Abstract: Legal benchmarks typically score final answers even when models also state legal authority. We test whether answer correctness can serve as a proxy for authority grounding. Under ordinary reasoning prompts that did not request statutory citations, four LLMs spontaneously produced authority markers across 238 Taiwan bar-examination items. Because each item has a verified governing provision, we automatically audit answer correctness and authority grounding jointly. The two dimensions dissociate in both directions. In criminal law, 24.0--42.4\% of valid responses were answer-correct but missed the gold authority, while 15.2--21.7\% were answer-incorrect but cited it. A separate statutory-retrieval probe and a permissive citation-abstention intervention further show that answer and citation behavior can move separately at the output level. Because this mismatch arises without adversarial or inconsistency-inducing prompting, answer-only scoring treats naturally occurring gold-authority misses as complete benchmark successes. Because statutory authority is structurally extractable and externally verifiable, the failure can be measured automatically. A preliminary PRC civil-law extension also observes citation-unrequested authority marking, motivating a full cross-jurisdictional joint audit. We therefore propose joint answer--authority evaluation for statute-grounded legal benchmarks.

</details>


### [9] [Speculative Correction: Draft-then-Refine Decoding for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02625)
*Brian K Chen,Chong Wu,Kenji Kawaguchi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DLMs can self-improve by generating a complete draft via block-autoregressive decoding, then refining it bidirectionally. Same-model draft-and-refine (Flash-Flash) boosts GSM8K accuracy from 0.848→0.899 and MBPP from 0.545→0.693 with 1.20× speedup. Speculative correction (Mini-Flash) offers quality-latency trade-offs, e.g., MATH 0.294 vs. 0.300 at 2.17× speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard DLM decoding is typically adapted to left-to-right block-autoregressive generation, underutilizing DLMs' inherent bidirectional revision capability. The authors investigate whether bidirectional refinement can serve as a simple, plug-and-play post-hoc improvement over block-autoregressive outputs, and whether a smaller drafter can provide a training-free fast-generation route via speculative correction.

Method: Two configurations are evaluated: (1) Flash-Flash — the same Flash model drafts a complete response block-autoregressively, then refines it via full bidirectional diffusion; (2) Mini-Flash — a smaller Mini model drafts a full response, which Flash revises as an editable initialization (speculative correction). Causal ablations test fully masked spans, full global vs. local refinement. Latency-window-matched controls isolate gains from mere decoding hyperparameter tuning.

Result: Flash-Flash improves GSM8K-384 from 0.848→0.899 (1.20× faster than baseline) and MBPP-384 from 0.545→0.693. Gains persist against latency-matched controls. Causal ablations: refinement from fully masked spans performs poorly; full global refinement adds clear gain on GSM8K; local refinement captures most gain on MBPP and MATH. Mini-Flash achieves MATH-384 0.294 vs. Flash 0.300 at 2.17× speedup, supporting a Pareto-frontier interpretation.

Conclusion: Same-model draft-and-refine demonstrates that bidirectional refinement is a useful decoding primitive for DLMs. Speculative correction provides a training-free route to fast DLM generation. The heterogeneous cascade does not uniformly match Flash quality but offers favorable quality-latency trade-offs along a Pareto frontier.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can revise tokens bidirectionally, but standard decoding procedures often adapt them to left-to-right generation by producing text block by block. We study a simple plug-and-play inference pattern: first generate a complete draft, then refine the full response using bidirectional diffusion. Using LLaDA2.1-Flash and LLaDA2.1-Mini, we evaluate two configurations. In Flash-Flash, the same Flash model serves as both drafter and refiner, testing whether an existing model can improve its own block-autoregressive output through global refinement. In Mini-Flash, inspired by speculative decoding, we introduce speculative correction: Mini drafts a full response, and Flash revises it as an editable initialization. Flash-Flash improves GSM8K-384 accuracy from 0.848 to 0.899 while running 1.20 times faster than the selected Flash block-autoregressive baseline, and improves MBPP-384 from 0.545 to 0.693. Latency-window-matched Flash-only controls indicate that these gains persist after targeted tuning of block-autoregressive decoding. Causal ablations indicate that completed drafts provide useful initializations: refinement from a fully masked span performs poorly, full global refinement provides a clear additional gain on GSM8K, and local refinement captures much of the gain on MBPP and MATH. Mini-Flash provides useful quality-latency trade-offs, including MATH-384 performance of 0.294 versus 0.300 for Flash while running 2.17 times faster. These results support a Pareto-frontier interpretation rather than the claim that the heterogeneous cascade uniformly matches Flash quality. Overall, same-model draft-and-refine provides evidence that bidirectional refinement is a useful decoding primitive for DLMs, while speculative correction demonstrates a training-free route to fast DLM generation.

</details>


### [10] [Stuck on "A": Diagnosing and Repairing Interface Injury in Attention-to-KDA Linearization of a 0.6B Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02689)
*Ronglong Bao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Converting 21 of 28 attention layers in Qwen3-0.6B-Base to KDA linear-attention yields good perplexity but catastrophic collapse in multiple-choice accuracy. The root cause is an "interface injury" where the model fixates on answer labels (predicting "A" 81% of the time) rather than content. A targeted format-repair stage restores performance, and subsequent SFT/DPO preserves it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Linear-attention models promise efficiency gains, but converting full-attention pretrained models to linear-attention (rather than training from scratch) introduces subtle behavioral degradations that standard perplexity and distillation metrics fail to capture. The authors aim to rigorously diagnose what breaks during such conversion, particularly on multiple-choice benchmarks.

Method: 21 of 28 full-attention layers of Qwen3-0.6B-Base are surgically replaced with KDA linear-attention layers on a consumer GPU budget. The student is trained via hidden-state alignment and end-to-end KL distillation. A novel four-permutation diagnostic rotates multiple-choice answer option labels while keeping content fixed to detect label-stickiness. A 1,000-step format-targeted completion-only KL stage is introduced to repair the interface, followed by persona SFT and on-policy DPO. An FP32-master training workaround is described for stable bf16 convergence.

Result: The converted model matches the teacher closely in perplexity but drops to near-random accuracy (25-29% vs. 50.6%) on C-Eval. The permutation diagnostic reveals the model predicts "A" 81% of the time, with 106/161 questions keeping the same label across all four rotations. The format-targeted repair stage adds +12.48 C-Eval points and roughly halves label-stickiness. Persona SFT and DPO preserve scores within noise. The FP32-master failure mode (bf16 updates silently swallowed) is documented as a critical engineering lesson.

Conclusion: Standard distillation metrics (perplexity, KL divergence) are blind to "interface injuries" — format-level behavioral failures in downstream task interaction. A dedicated format-alignment stage is necessary and sufficient to repair such injuries in attention-converted models. The work provides open-source recipes, weights, and engineering insights for budget-constrained linear-attention model conversion.

Abstract: We convert 21 of 28 full-attention layers of Qwen3-0.6B-Base into KDA (Kimi Delta Attention) linear-attention layers on a single consumer-grade GPU budget, and ask a simple question: what exactly does the conversion break? After surgery, hidden-state alignment and end-to-end KL distillation drive the student close to its teacher in perplexity, yet multiple-choice accuracy stays near random chance (25-29% vs. the teacher's 50.6% on C-Eval). Using a four-permutation diagnostic that rotates answer options while holding content fixed, we show the model sticks to option labels (predicting "A" 81% of the time; 106/161 questions keep the same label under all four rotations) rather than following answer content -- an interface injury that standard distillation metrics cannot see. A 1,000-step format-targeted completion-only KL stage repairs the interface (+12.48 points on C-Eval, label-stickiness roughly halved), after which persona SFT and one round of on-policy DPO preserve benchmark scores within noise. We release code, weights, recipes, and the full audit trail, and distill the engineering lessons -- including an FP32-master failure mode in which bf16 optimizer updates are silently swallowed -- that made convergence possible at this budget.

</details>


### [11] [Crayotter: Learning Long-Horizon Video Editing Agents via Group-Relative Preference Backpropagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02694)
*Lecheng Yan,Jianze Lin,Yichong Zhang,Ben Pan,Wenxi Li,Chenyang Lyu,Liting Zhou,Cathal Gurrin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GRPB transforms subjective, long-horizon video editing feedback into ordinal same-task comparisons, redistributing zero-sum advantages as bounded credit over segments. The 9B Crayotter model trained with GRPB surpasses proprietary systems on AgenticVBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon video editing agents suffer from sparse, subjective, and temporally uninformative feedback — a single scalar reward cannot meaningfully guide hundreds of interdependent decisions across heterogeneous editing requests.

Method: GRPB converts same-task rankings into zero-sum advantages and backpropagates them as bounded credit over semantic editing segments. A lagged allocator and guarded transmission mechanism prevent current judgments from contaminating the rollout group, enabling stable learning from ordinal preferences.

Result: The 9B Crayotter model, trained with GRPB, outperforms matched baselines across credit interventions, external benchmarks, and blinded human evaluation, surpassing several proprietary systems on AgenticVBench.

Conclusion: Task-local preference reduction via ordinal comparisons is a practical and effective paradigm for learning from subjective, delayed outcomes in long-horizon agentic video editing.

Abstract: Long-horizon video editing agents receive final-product feedback only after many interdependent decisions. Yet editing quality is subjective, admits multiple valid solutions, and is not meaningfully calibrated across heterogeneous requests, making a global scalar objective both ambiguous and temporally uninformative. Our key observation is that fixing the request, materials, and production constraints converts this subjective objective into an ordinal comparison among directly comparable alternatives. We introduce Group-Relative Preference Backpropagation (GRPB), which transforms same-task rankings into zero-sum advantages and redistributes them as bounded credit over semantic editing segments. A lagged allocator and guarded transmission prevent current judgments or unreliable estimates from directly shaping the same rollout group. We manually construct a project-disjoint, horizon-stratified suite of realistic editing tasks for training and controlled evaluation. Across matched baselines, credit interventions, external benchmarking, and blinded human evaluation, GRPB improves both editing behavior and rendered products. The resulting 9B Crayotter model surpasses several proprietary systems on AgenticVBench, supporting task-local preference reduction as a practical approach to learning from subjective, delayed outcomes. Code and all supporting materials are publicly available at https://github.com/idwts/Crayotter.

</details>


### [12] [ARCHead: Activation-Metric Residual Correction for Large Language Model Output Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02703)
*Şuayp Talha Kocabay,Talha Rüzgar Akkuş,Kamer Ali Yuksel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ARCHead compresses the LM-head of LLMs using a quantized low-rank core, group-wise INT4 residuals, and activation-aware low-rank correction, achieving 3.7-3.9× storage reduction with minimal perplexity degradation, complementing existing block quantizers like AWQ and bitsandbytes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing weight-only quantization methods reduce transformer block storage but leave the LM-head in BF16/FP16. Naively quantizing the LM-head severely distorts vocabulary-logit distributions. There is a need for a specialized compression technique targeting this large, often-untouched output projection.

Method: ARCHead uses a three-component packed compressor: (1) a quantized low-rank core, (2) group-wise INT4 residuals for preserving fine-grained structure, and (3) a low-rank correction matrix fitted using an activation-derived metric to minimize distortion in logit space.

Result: On Qwen3-8B-Base, ARCHead uses 25.6% of BF16 head storage, achieving 1.007 relative perplexity vs. 1.14–1.16 for storage-matched naive INT4 quantization. When replacing the BF16 head from AWQ or bitsandbytes, it adds only 0.006–0.007 cross-entropy with under 2% throughput change.

Conclusion: ARCHead effectively complements block-level weight-only quantizers by compressing the LM-head they leave untouched, enabling substantial end-to-end storage reduction with negligible quality loss and throughput impact.

Abstract: Weight-only quantization substantially reduces the storage of large language model (LLM) transformer blocks, but practical backends often retain the final language-modeling head (LM-head) in BF16 or FP16. Quantizing this projection naively can strongly perturb the vocabulary-logit distribution. We present ARCHead, a packed LM-head compressor that combines a quantized low-rank core, group-wise INT4 residuals, and a low-rank correction fitted in an activation-derived metric. ARCHead stores no dense BF16 head and reduces persistent LM-head storage by 3.7-3.9x. On Qwen3-8B-Base, it uses 25.6% of BF16 head storage while attaining 1.007 relative perplexity; storage-matched naive INT4 yields 1.14-1.16. Replacing the BF16 head left by AWQ or bitsandbytes adds only 0.006-0.007 cross-entropy, with less than 2% throughput change in our measurements. ARCHead therefore complements block quantizers by compressing the large output projection they can leave untouched. Code is available at https://github.com/suayptalha/archead.

</details>


### [13] [Learning a Vector-Symbolic Model for Socio-Cultural Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02807)
*Meera Ray,Swapnika Dulam,Christopher L. Dancy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a multi-level declarative memory system for the ACT-R cognitive architecture that uses a vector-symbolic autoencoder to represent semantic associations across different levels, incorporating self-representations to model how sociocultural structures influence decision-making. The system is tested on cognitive models of a racially contextualized implicit association test (IAT).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current computational cognitive models lack a principled way to represent how sociocultural structures impact decision-making. The challenge lies in determining which levels of semantic representation are most salient for a given situation. While LLMs and corpus-based models capture broad semantic co-occurrences, they do not account for the role of self-representations in memory, which is crucial for understanding how cultural associations shape decisions.

Method: The authors propose a declarative memory system within the ACT-R cognitive architecture that uses a vector-symbolic autoencoder to represent semantic associations at multiple levels of representation. A simple holographic reduced representation (HRR) operation encodes episodic memories separately from semantic memory vectors extracted from text, producing a final chunk activation when a memory request is made. The system is validated using ACT-R cognitive models of a racially contextualized implicit association test (IAT).

Result: The paper presents the design and implementation of the declarative memory system, but the abstract does not report specific quantitative results from the IAT modeling experiments. It implies that the system offers a viable mechanism for integrating multi-level semantic representations with self-representations in memory to capture culturally shaped decision-making.

Conclusion: Incorporating self-representations and multi-level semantic encoding via vector-symbolic architectures into declarative memory systems can improve the ecological validity of cognitive models when accounting for sociocultural influences on decision-making, as demonstrated through IAT modeling.

Abstract: How can we better represent the impact of sociocultural structures on decision making in computational cognitive models? Modeling this impact requires traversing multiple levels of semantic representation, however it is not immediately clear to a modeler which levels of representation are most salient to a given situation. Though large language models and cognitively grounded corpus models can represent broad semantic associations through co-occurences, the role of self representations in memory should be accounted for to determine how cultural associations shape decision making. We propose a declarative memory system to be used in the ACT-R cognitive architecture that represents semantic associations at multiple levels via a vector-symbolic autoencoder. We use a simple HRR operation to encode episodic memories differently from semantic memory vectors extracted from text to produce a final chunk activation for a memory request. We use ACT-R cognitive models of a racially contextualized implicit association test (IAT) to test this new declarative memory system.

</details>


### [14] [SciRet: A Compute-Aware Empirical Study of Retrieval and Reranking for Scientific RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03860)
*Kaysarul Anas Apurba,Md. Hasibul Hasan,Rofiqul Alam Shehab,Asab Azad*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SciRet evaluates a fixed retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for scientific QA on CORD-19 across three corpus scales (1K, 5K, 15K papers). It finds hybrid retrieval (BM25 + BGE-M3 + RRF) most robust, while an MS MARCO-trained cross-encoder reranker hurts precision due to domain mismatch. RAGAS faithfulness improves with corpus scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To conduct a compute-aware empirical study of RAG for scientific question answering, focusing on how retrieval and generation components behave across different corpus scales, rather than proposing a new model. The work aims to provide controlled comparative evidence about design choices in scientific RAG pipelines.

Method: A fixed RAG pipeline is evaluated across three corpus sizes (1,034 / 5,160 / 15,480 chunks). The pipeline uses: sentence-window chunking, BM25 sparse retrieval, BGE-M3 dense retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) for hybrid retrieval, optional cross-encoder reranking (MS MARCO-trained), and grounded answer generation. Evaluation uses pseudo-relevance labels derived from the hybrid system's own output, and faithfulness is measured with RAGAS.

Result: Hybrid retrieval achieves Recall@10 of 1.000 at both 1K and 15K scales, outperforming sparse-only and dense-only retrieval. The MS MARCO-trained cross-encoder reranker reduces precision on the scientific corpus, indicating domain mismatch. Generation faithfulness (RAGAS) increases with larger corpus scale.

Conclusion: Hybrid retrieval is the most robust strategy for scientific RAG. Cross-encoder rerankers trained on general-domain data (MS MARCO) can harm scientific retrieval due to domain mismatch. Corpus scale positively affects generation faithfulness. Results are presented as controlled comparative evidence rather than benchmark claims, with code and data released for reproducibility.

Abstract: We introduce SciRet, a compute-aware empirical study of retrieval-augmented generation for scientific question answering over CORD-19. Rather than proposing a new model, we evaluate a fixed scientific RAG pipeline across three corpus scales: 1,034 chunks (1K papers), 5,160 chunks (5K papers), and 15,480 chunks (15K papers). The pipeline combines sentence-window chunking, BM25, BGE-M3 dense retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, optional cross-encoder reranking, and grounded answer generation. Across these settings, hybrid retrieval is more robust than either sparse-only or dense-only retrieval in our setting, reaching Recall@10 of 1.000 at 1K and 15K. In contrast, an MS MARCO-trained cross-encoder reranker reduces precision on the scientific corpus, suggesting that domain mismatch can outweigh the benefits of stronger query-passage interaction. Generation faithfulness measured with RAGAS increases with corpus scale in our setup. Retrieval evaluation uses pseudo-relevance labels derived from the hybrid system, so we treat the results as controlled comparative evidence rather than a benchmark claim. We release code, indexes, and evaluation outputs to support replication and follow-up studies.

</details>


### [15] [BODHI: Do LLMs Branch Out and Discover Heterogeneous Inferences?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02867)
*Soumadeep Saha,Krish Sharma,Akshay Chaturvedi,Nicholas Asher*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RLVR improves LLM sample efficiency by collapsing semantic branching entropy, not just syntactic variation, at the cost of genuine inferential diversity during test-time exploration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Debate exists over whether RLVR expands reasoning capability boundaries or merely boosts sampling efficiency. The authors aim to disentangle this by investigating the nature of test-time exploration in RLVR-trained LLMs, specifically whether entropy reduction is syntactic or semantic.

Method: Controlled maze-solving experiments combined with a novel tree-structured representation (BODHI-Trees) extracted from mathematical reasoning traces based on semantic equivalence, to separate stylistic entropy from genuine inferential branching.

Result: Policy entropy collapse in RLVR models is both syntactic and semantic — RLVR significantly reduces semantic branching entropy. While it improves environmental constraint adherence and backtracking, it narrows the continuation space, likely explaining sample efficiency gains at the cost of rollout diversity.

Conclusion: RLVR does not expand the reasoning boundary; it trades off inferential diversity for efficiency by constricting semantic exploration, suggesting sample efficiency improvements come from reduced branching rather than deeper reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Although reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has improved the performance of large language models (LLMs) across a variety of reasoning tasks, there is significant debate as to whether RLVR expands the reasoning capability boundary, or just improves sampling efficiency. In this paper, we investigate the nature of test-time exploration in RLVR-trained LLMs by employing controlled maze-solving experiments and extracting a tree structure from mathematical reasoning traces (BODHI-Trees) based on semantic equivalence. This helps us delineate between entropy arising from stylistic variations and genuine inferential branching. Our findings demonstrate that the policy entropy collapse observed in RLVR models is not merely syntactic, and is accompanied by a significant reduction in semantic branching entropy. While RLVR improves adherence to environmental constraints and backtracking capabilities, it constricts the space of continuations; we provide evidence suggesting that this might be responsible for the sample efficiency gains of RLVR, albeit at the cost of genuine rollout diversity.

</details>


### [16] [MultiGlobeQA: A Multilingual and Globally Diverse Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03882)
*Martin Böckling,Elizaveta Nosova,Heiko Paulheim,Andreea Iana*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MultiGlobeQA is a large multilingual benchmark with 46,060 QA pairs testing LLMs on 14 spatial reasoning function families over real-world geographic knowledge graphs. LLMs fail on grid indexing and shape computation, excel at topological relations and directions, and plateau below 66% even with gold facts — revealing computation (not knowledge access) as the bottleneck, with worse performance on low-income regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing geospatial reasoning benchmarks are synthetic, small-scale, largely monolingual, and offer limited geographic coverage control. This masks the true nature of LLM failures in spatial computation versus knowledge recall, and fails to capture performance disparities across languages and regions.

Method: The authors construct MultiGlobeQA with 46,060 QA pairs across 14 spatial-function families (e.g., distance, containment, direction, shape computation, grid indexing) and 15 answer formats. Ground truth is execution-based over three knowledge graphs (OpenStreetMap, GeoNames, Wikidata). Sampling covers 201 countries/territories stratified by income and population density, with parallel questions in English and 16 additional languages. Evaluation spans parametric (zero-shot), reasoning (chain-of-thought), and agentic (retrieval/tool-use) settings, including an oracle condition where gold facts are supplied directly.

Result: LLMs perform worst on grid indexing and shape computation tasks; topological relations and cardinal directions are handled best. Retrieval and tool use yield substantial gains, but performance saturates below 66% even when gold facts are provided — indicating computation, not knowledge access, is the bottleneck. Models systematically underperform on low-income regions, and providing gold facts widens rather than closes this gap.

Conclusion: Geospatial reasoning failures in LLMs stem primarily from computational limitations rather than knowledge gaps. Multilingual coverage and region-stratified sampling reveal persistent disparities that additional factual knowledge cannot resolve, pointing to fundamental architectural shortcomings in spatial computation that future work must address.

Abstract: Geospatial reasoning, i.e., computing distances, containment, and other spatial relations over real-world entities, is central to navigation and logistics, yet large language models (LLMs) struggle with the required geometric and topological computation despite storing considerable geographic knowledge. Existing benchmarks localize these failures only partially: they are synthetic or smallscale, largely monolingual, and offer limited control over geographic coverage. We introduce MultiGlobeQA, a multilingual benchmark of 46,060 question-answer pairs spanning 14 spatial-function families and 15 answer formats, with execution-based ground truth over three knowledge graphs. It covers 201 countries and territories via income- and density-stratified sampling, with parallel questions in English and 16 additional high- and low-resource languages. Across parametric, reasoning, and agentic settings, LLMs collapse on tasks requiring grid indexing and shape computation, while topological relations and directions fare best. Retrieval and tool use yield considerable gains, yet performance plateaus below two thirds even when gold facts are supplied, indicating that computation, not access to knowledge, is the bottleneck. Models also underperform on low-income regions, a gap that gold facts widen rather than close.

</details>


### [17] [FLARE: Few-shot Learning-based Adaptive Reflective Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02919)
*Dhanasekar Sundararaman,Bharat Gandhi,Aashna Garg,Minjie Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FLARE introduces few-shot learning-based reflective instruction optimization that consistently outperforms GEPA across diverse benchmarks (HotPotQA, tool calling, GoEmotions) using GPT-5 models, achieving up to +14.2 point gains while being more data-efficient and stable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent optimizers like GEPA claim reflective instruction evolution surpasses traditional reinforcement learning and few-shot optimization. The authors challenge this by arguing that strategic optimization of few-shot learning, combined with reflective mechanisms, remains an underexplored and critical frontier for maximizing LLM performance in compound AI systems.

Method: FLARE (Few-shot Learning-based Adaptive Reflective Engine) combines advanced reflective mechanisms with a small set of few-shot reference examples to optimize prompts/instructions. It is evaluated against GEPA across retrieval-augmented reasoning (HotPotQA, MedQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA), tool calling, and multi-label emotion classification (GoEmotions) using GPT-5 series models.

Result: FLARE outperforms GEPA on every task-model pair: +14.2 points on HotPotQA (52.2 vs. 42.2), 87.0% vs. 81.0% on tool calling, and +15.3 micro-F1 gain on GoEmotions (52.7%) vs. GEPA's +5.7 gain. FLARE reaches peak performance with only 100 validation examples on GoEmotions and demonstrates superior stability across random seeds.

Conclusion: Reflective instructions are powerful, but strategic few-shot optimization remains essential. FLARE demonstrates that combining reflective mechanisms with few-shot reference examples yields superior, data-efficient, and stable instruction optimization for next-generation LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in complex, compound AI systems where performance hinges on the quality of prompts. Recent state-of-the-art optimizers like GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) have argued that reflective instruction evolution can outperform traditional reinforcement learning and few-shot optimization. In this work, we challenge this shift by introducing FLARE (Few-shot Learning-based Adaptive Reflective Engine), a framework that leverages advanced reflective mechanisms and a small set of few-shot reference examples to optimize instructions. We evaluate our method across a diverse suite of benchmarks -- spanning retrieval-augmented reasoning (HotPotQA, MedQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA), tool calling, and multi-label emotion classification (GoEmotions) -- using the GPT-5 series of models. Our results demonstrate that FLARE consistently outperforms GEPA, winning on every task-model pair: it achieves gains of up to +14.2 points on HotPotQA (52.2 vs. GEPA's 42.2 with GPT-5-Chat), reaches 87.0% on tool calling (vs. 81.0% for GEPA), and lifts GoEmotions micro-F1 to 52.7% (+15.3) with GPT-5.1 on the full 5408-example test split, more than doubling GEPA's +5.7 gain. Beyond raw accuracy, FLARE is also strikingly data-efficient: on GoEmotions it reaches its peak performance using as few as 100 validation examples, while remaining markedly more stable across random seeds than GEPA. Our findings suggest that while reflective instructions are powerful, the strategic optimization of few-shot learning remains a critical frontier for maximizing the potential of next-generation LLMs.

</details>


### [18] [Character Iconicity vs. Arbitrariness: An Arabic NLP Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02935)
*Dorieh Alomari,Irfan Ahmad,Maged S. Al-shaibani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Arabic NLP models do not require original character distinctions or traditional rasm-based groupings; arbitrary but consistent character remappings to 19 undotted rasms achieve competitive performance across multiple NLP tasks while reducing vocabulary size, OOV rates, and training costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether the success of dotless Arabic in NLP depends on preserving original rasm groupings, or whether arbitrary remappings to the same reduced rasm set can achieve comparable performance, testing the functional necessity of Arabic character-form distinctions.

Method: Generated 2,000 random character remappings constrained to 19 undotted rasms under word- and character-level tokenization; selected four representative mappings by entropy (highest/lowest); evaluated across language modeling, text classification, sequence labeling, machine translation, and restoration tasks.

Result: Random remappings achieve competitive performance with standard dotted and dotless Arabic. Neither preserving original character distinctions nor traditional rasm-based groupings is necessary. Remappings reduce vocabulary size, OOV rates, model size, and training cost.

Conclusion: From an NLP perspective, Arabic character form-function relationships are largely arbitrary; models rely on stable distributional structure rather than the visual iconicity of letter forms.

Abstract: Arabic script uses 28 letters, many of which share a common base shape (rasm) and are distinguished only by dot placement. Because early Arabic manuscripts were written without dots yet remained interpretable, dot removal offers a natural test of whether these visual distinctions are functionally necessary. Prior work has shown that dotless Arabic can remain readable and effective for natural language processing (NLP), but it remains unclear whether this success depends on preserving the original rasm groupings or whether arbitrary but consistent remappings to the same reduced rasm set can achieve comparable performance. We address this question by comparing standard dotted and dotless Arabic with arbitrary character remappings constrained to the same 19 undotted rasms. We generated 2,000 random remappings under word- and character-level tokenization and selected four representative mappings with the highest and lowest entropy values. These representations were evaluated across language modeling, text classification, sequence labeling, machine translation, and restoration to the original script. The results show that neither preserving original character distinctions nor retaining traditional rasm-based groupings is necessary for strong NLP performance. Random remappings achieve competitive performance while reducing vocabulary size, out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rates, model size, and training cost. These findings suggest that, from an NLP perspective, Arabic character form-function relationships are largely arbitrary: models rely more on stable distributional structure than on the visual iconicity of letter forms.

</details>


### [19] [Aligned in Form, Not in Meaning: The Comprehension - Containment Decoupling of LLM Safety in Low-Resource Bangla Derogatory Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02941)
*Shadab Bin Habib,A K M Ferdous Reza Habib,Subarno Neel,Adib Sakhawat*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper audits five frontier LLMs on Bangla hate speech, demonstrating that safety alignment depends on high-resource surface forms rather than harmful meaning. This "Comprehension-Containment Decoupling" means models can contain slurs without understanding them, and containment collapses under adversarial prompts, exposing a fundamental flaw in low-resource language safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM safety alignment is evaluated primarily on high-resource languages (e.g., English), creating a blind spot: models may appear safe on low-resource languages like Bangla not because they understand and refuse harmful content, but because they fail to comprehend it at all. The authors hypothesize that comprehension and containment operate independently for low-resource derogatory speech, meaning safety benchmarks in English cannot certify safety in Bangla or similar languages.

Method: The authors audit five frontier LLMs on native Bangla derogatory speech (gali) across six experimental protocols, using a human-calibrated baseline (kappa = 0.84). The protocols include: (1) baseline comprehension vs. token leakage measurement across Bangla and English; (2) severity calibration tracking surface anatomical cues vs. compositional harm; (3) orthographic perturbation to test for tokenizer-driven "containment mirages"; (4) Chain-of-Thought reasoning to isolate comprehension from containment; (5) expert-persona framing to probe keyword-based filter robustness; and (6) evaluation of dehumanizing communal slurs. Each protocol systematically tests the Comprehension-Containment Decoupling hypothesis.

Result: All six protocols corroborated the decoupling hypothesis. Key findings: (1) Models showed a 7.92 pp comprehension deficit in Bangla versus English, yet identical token leakage (~92.83%) across both languages. (2) Severity calibration tracked surface cues rather than compositional harm (over-penalizing mild slang by +4.00 error, under-penalizing threats by -2.00). (3) Apparent containment gains from orthographic perturbation were illusory — a tokenizer-driven "containment mirage." (4) Chain-of-Thought reasoning rescued comprehension to 94.72% but simultaneously dismantled containment to 96.23% leakage. (5) Expert-persona framing collapsed refusal rates to 6.57%. (6) Keyword-based filters completely ignored dehumanizing communal slurs.

Conclusion: High-resource benchmarks cannot certify low-resource safety. The decoupling of comprehension from containment reveals that current alignment techniques are superficial, relying on surface-form pattern matching rather than meaning-grounded understanding of harm. The authors call for meaning-grounded containment mechanisms that function across languages regardless of resource level, particularly given that adversarial prompting (CoT, persona framing) easily dismantles existing safeguards.

Abstract: We audit five frontier large language models on native Bangla derogatory speech (gali) across six protocols to test a single hypothesis: Comprehension-Containment Decoupling. We propose that contemporary safety alignment is bound to high-resource surface forms rather than harmful meaning, causing a model's capacity to comprehend a low-resource slur and its capacity to contain it to operate independently. Every protocol corroborates this hypothesis against a human-calibrated baseline (kappa = 0.84). At baseline, models exhibit a 7.92 percentage point comprehension deficit in Bangla while maintaining an identical 92.83% token leakage rate across both languages. Severity calibration tracks surface anatomical cues over compositional harm (+4.00 error on mild slang; -2.00 on threats), while apparent containment gains under orthographic perturbation prove to be a tokenizer-driven "containment mirage." Crucially, explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning rescues comprehension (94.72% Pass) while systematically dismantling containment (96.23% Use). Furthermore, expert-persona framing collapses refusal to 6.57%, revealing that keyword-based filters ignore dehumanizing communal slurs entirely. Our findings demonstrate that high-resource benchmarks cannot certify low-resource safety, necessitating meaning-grounded containment.

</details>


### [20] [OPTD: On-Policy Transition Distillation with Consistency-Guided Adaptive Compression for Few-Step Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02942)
*Xiaocheng Lu,Hualei Zhang,Shuhan Guo,Jie Zhang,Xiaoyi Pang,Jian Liu,Haoxi Li,Bohai Gu,Haoxuan Che,Jingcai Guo,Song Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OPTD is an on-policy distillation method for diffusion language models that uses a frozen teacher to verify which future tokens a student can safely commit to in parallel, selecting the longest consistent prefix to maximize compression without degrading output quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing few-step distillation for diffusion LMs uses off-policy supervision, creating a train-test mismatch where the student's early parallel commitments shift later context, causing drift that is most severe under aggressive step compression. On-policy distillation fixes the mismatch but lacks a principled way to determine how far each transition should advance—conservatively matching only the teacher's next action limits compression, while indiscriminately merging future actions can break intermediate dependencies.

Method: OPTD operates on-policy by sampling partial states from the student's own few-step trajectories. A frozen, question-only teacher identifies future candidate tokens consistent with the teacher's eventual rollout outcome, ordered by current-state confidence. The method selects the longest prefix whose joint commitment preserves that outcome. A set-bottleneck objective pushes verified candidates to the decoder's release threshold, while a frozen-teacher KL anchor regularizes all other active positions. No gold response is used for target construction or training.

Result: Across four mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, OPTD consistently improves the quality–efficiency trade-off and achieves the strongest overall quality-constrained AUP (Area Under the Pareto frontier) among evaluated few-step baselines.

Conclusion: On-policy distillation with consistency-guided adaptive compression effectively resolves the off-policy drift problem in few-step diffusion LM distillation, enabling aggressive step compression without sacrificing output quality by dynamically determining how many future tokens can be safely committed at each transition.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) can predict many tokens in parallel, but accurate generation still requires many iterative denoising steps. Few-step distillation accelerates decoding by compressing multiple teacher steps into a single student transition. However, existing methods construct supervision on off-policy trajectories. At inference, the student's early parallel commitments alter the context of later predictions, so the states it actually visits drift away from the supervised ones--precisely when step compression is most aggressive. On-policy distillation is a natural remedy for this mismatch, but it leaves open how far each transition should advance: matching only the teacher's next action limits compression, while indiscriminately merging future actions can violate intermediate dependencies. To address this limitation, we propose OPTD, On-Policy Transition Distillation with consistency-guided adaptive compression. It samples partial states from the few-step student's own trajectories, uses a frozen, question-only teacher to identify outcome-aligned future candidates, and orders them by current-state confidence. The method then selects the longest prefix whose joint commitment preserves the teacher's rollout outcome. A set-bottleneck objective promotes every verified future candidate to the decoder's release threshold, while a frozen-teacher KL anchor regularizes all other active positions. Neither target construction nor training uses a gold response. Across four mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, OPTD consistently improves the quality--efficiency trade-off and attains the strongest overall quality-constrained AUP among the evaluated few-step baselines.

</details>


### [21] [Every Wrong Answer Counts: Option-Level Psychometrics for LLM Multiple-Choice Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02966)
*Xiao Fei,Yang Zhang,Sarah Almeida Carneiro,Michalis Vazirgiannis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LLM-NRM, a psychometric framework that models the full distribution over MCQ answer choices rather than binary correct/incorrect scoring. It extracts systematic information from LLMs' distractor preferences to improve ability estimation, achieving state-of-the-art correlation with human preference rankings and enabling efficient benchmark reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MCQ benchmarks for LLMs use binary scoring (correct/incorrect), treating all wrong answers as equivalent. This discards potentially systematic and informative patterns in how LLMs distribute their responses among incorrect options. The authors argue that distractor preferences carry meaningful measurement information about model behavior and ability.

Method: The authors propose the LLM Nominal Response Model (LLM-NRM), an option-aware psychometric model extending Item Response Theory to polytomous (multi-category) outcomes. It jointly estimates LLM ability and option-level item characteristics while separating three model-specific parameters: response calibration sharpness (discrimination), positional preference (tendency to favor certain answer positions), and difficulty-dependent fallback behavior (how models guess when uncertain). Evaluated across 189 LLMs and 31,554 items from 14 benchmarks.

Result: LLM-NRM predicts held-out LLM-item interactions better than binary IRT and nominal-response baselines. Ability estimates achieve Spearman correlation of 0.920 with Arena.ai Elo (human preference leaderboard). Distractor identity contributes +101% additional Fisher Information beyond correctness alone. Incorrect responses alone can recover ability estimates with Spearman 0.943. Using 41 selected items preserves full-bank ranking with Kendall's τ = 0.85 (770× reduction).

Conclusion: Incorrect answers are not equivalent mistakes; they carry distinct, systematic, and useful measurement information. Modeling the full nominal response distribution yields superior LLM evaluation, more efficient benchmarks, and richer psychometric characterization of model behavior.

Abstract: Most multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) only by whether they select the correct answers. This binary scoring treats all incorrect responses alike, even though an LLM's preferences among incorrect options may contain systematic and useful information about its behavior and ability. We introduce the LLM Nominal Response Model (LLM-NRM), an option-aware psychometric framework that models the full distribution over answer choices to jointly estimate LLM ability and option-level item characteristics, while separating model-specific response calibration sharpness, positional preference, and difficulty-dependent fallback behavior. Across 189 LLMs and 31,554 items from 14 benchmarks, LLM-NRM predicts held-out LLM-item interactions more accurately than binary Item Response models and conventional nominal-response baselines, and its ability estimates achieve the strongest Spearman correlation of 0.920 with the external human-preference Arena.ai Elo leaderboard. Distractor identity contributes +101% additional Fisher Information per item beyond correctness, and incorrect responses alone recover full-information ability estimates with Spearman 0.943. The learned item parameters also enable efficient benchmarking, where 41 selected items preserve the full-bank ranking with Kendall's correlation 0.85, corresponding to a 770 times reduction. In conclusion, we show that incorrect answers carry distinct and useful measurement information rather than representing equivalent mistakes.

</details>


### [22] [Mapping the City Through the Lens of Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02971)
*Wanqi Liu,Rong Zhao,Zhizhou Sha,Qinyu Cui,Yecheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Language models harbor implicit, measurable assumptions about what constitutes a "typical" city. By analyzing model ratings of anonymized urban profiles across 40 indicators, the study reveals a shared preference for larger, faster-growing, denser, and infrastructure-rich cities, with typicality and desirability closely aligned. This framework makes the models' otherwise vague urban biases empirically traceable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models frequently complete underspecified references to cities (e.g., "the city has...") with unstated assumptions. These implicit priors about urban size, form, infrastructure, and function are consequential but poorly understood. The authors aim to measure these assumptions systematically without relying on named places, thereby making an otherwise vague notion of what models regard as an "ordinary city" empirically traceable.

Method: Ten open-weight language model checkpoints rate anonymized profiles derived from real morphological urban centres across 40 audited indicators spanning seven domains. The design employs constrained probability-based ratings, prespecified reliability screens, lineage-aware aggregation, multiple population weightings, an independent replication sample, and whole-profile validation to ensure robust measurement.

Result: The clearest shared tendency across models favours urban profiles with larger developed area, faster recent growth, greater mapped infrastructure and non-residential capacity, and less sparse form. Most eligible directions recur in replication data. Direct ratings of complete profiles show moderate agreement with the indicator-wise construction. Geographic differences shrink after accounting for city scale and development. Reliably measured paired tasks indicate that typicality and desirability are often closely aligned.

Conclusion: The framework successfully delineates a shared yet model-dependent portrait of the city through the lens of language models. The evidence demonstrates that language models carry systematic, measurable urban priors that are neither random nor purely reflective of training data prominence, but rather constitute a distinct, traceable construct of what a "typical" city looks like.

Abstract: Language models often complete an underspecified reference to a city with unstated assumptions about urban size, form, infrastructure, environment, and function. We measure those assumptions without naming places. Ten open-weight checkpoints rate anonymized profiles derived from real morphological urban centres across 40 audited indicators and seven domains. The design combines constrained probability-based ratings, prespecified reliability screens, lineage-aware aggregation, multiple population weightings, an independent replication sample, and whole-profile validation. The clearest shared tendency favours urban profiles with larger developed area, faster recent growth, greater mapped infrastructure and non-residential capacity, and less sparse form. Most eligible directions recur in the replication data, and direct ratings of complete profiles show moderate agreement with the indicator-wise construction. Geographic differences shrink after accounting for city scale and development, while reliably measured paired tasks indicate that typicality and desirability are often closely aligned. The framework makes an otherwise vague notion of what models regard as an ordinary city empirically traceable. The resulting evidence delineates a shared yet model-dependent portrait of the city through the lens of language models.

</details>


### [23] [TQLite: Multi-LLM Jury Guided Distillation for Real-time MQM Translation Quality Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02975)
*Bhavin Jawade,Cameron R. Wolfe*

Main category: cs.CL
