TL;DR: The paper benchmarks SLMs, LLMs, and LRMs on MQM translation quality evaluation, then introduces TQLite, a distillation framework using a multi-LRM jury to train SLMs that approach LRM-level evaluation performance at lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs and LRMs achieve strong MQM translation quality evaluation but are computationally expensive at scale. SLMs are efficient but lack the complex reasoning needed for evaluation tasks. A cost-effective solution bridging this gap is needed.

Method: The authors conduct an extensive empirical benchmark of SLMs, LLMs, and LRMs across various TQ evaluation setups. They then propose TQLite, a distillation framework that uses a multi-LRM jury to generate high-quality synthetic training data through data curation techniques and aggregation of evaluation responses from a diverse model panel, training SLMs to mimic LRM-level evaluation.

Result: SLMs trained via TQLite achieve MQM evaluation performance far exceeding off-the-shelf SLM capabilities, offering a scalable and cost-effective alternative to LLM- and LRM-based evaluators.

Conclusion: Distillation from a multi-LRM jury via the TQLite framework effectively transfers complex evaluation reasoning to SLMs, making high-quality MQM translation quality evaluation both scalable and cost-efficient.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in MQM-based translation quality (TQ) evaluation, and recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) promise even greater improvements. However, both LLMs and LRMs are computationally expensive to deploy at scale, while small language models (SLMs)---though much more efficient---struggle with the complex reasoning required for evaluation tasks. In this work, we present an extensive empirical study benchmarking SLMs, LLMs, and LRMs across a wide range of TQ evaluation setups, providing a comprehensive view of the current landscape and establishing best practices. To address the scalability challenge, we introduce TQLite, a novel distillation framework that enables SLMs to approach the MQM evaluation performance of the best LRM-based evaluators. Our approach leverages a multi-LRM jury to generate high-quality synthetic training data via practical data curation techniques and aggregation of evaluation responses across a diverse panel of models. Our results demonstrate that SLMs trained via TQLite achieve strong MQM evaluation performance that far exceeds off-the-shelf evaluation capabilities of standard SLMs, offering a scalable and cost-effective alternative to LLM- and LRM-based evaluators.

</details>


### [24] [On the Non-Specificity of Statistical Measures Used in Script Decipherment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02999)
*Nikhil Raghavendra*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SIGIL, a generative emblem system with no phonological values, reproduces all Indus-script-like statistical signatures on 54 literature-derived measures, demonstrating that these measures detect organization but cannot distinguish language from structured non-language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Statistical regularities are commonly cited as evidence that undeciphered sign systems (e.g., Indus script) encode language. The paper challenges this inference by testing whether such regularities are truly specific to language, or whether they can be replicated by a purpose-built non-linguistic structured system.

Method: The authors construct SIGIL, a generative emblem system with 3,000 texts carrying explicit compositional meanings but no phonological values. They compile a literature registry of 54 methods, reproduce published Indus outcomes with source-defined decision rules, and compare SIGIL against the Indus corpus on repetition, directional-asymmetry, lexical-distribution, entropy, frequency, positional, predictive, classifier, and network measures. A sequential decipherment stress test is also applied using English, Sanskrit, and Tamil.

Result: SIGIL receives the same category as the Indus corpus on every scored criterion. It reproduces familiar Indus-like signatures across all declared measures. The decipherment stress test achieves high dictionary coverage for English, Sanskrit, and Tamil on the same corpus, but grouped held-out declines and unstable keys reveal that coverage does not indicate true decipherment.

Conclusion: The evaluated statistical measures detect organization without being specific to language and therefore cannot, on their own, establish that a sign system encodes speech. Claims about the Indus script's linguistic status based solely on such measures are unfounded.

Abstract: Statistical regularities are routinely offered as evidence that undeciphered sign systems encode language; the Indus script debate is the canonical example. Any such inference rests on specificity: the reported outcome must be unusual among plausible structured non-languages. We test that premise constructively with SIGIL, a purpose-built generative emblem system whose 3,000-text core corpus carries explicit compositional meanings although no sign has a phonological value. A literature registry compiled in advance of evaluation records 54 methods and admits a method to exact scoring when both the published Indus outcome and a source-defined decision rule can be reproduced. SIGIL receives the same category as the Indus corpus on every criterion scored this way, across repetition, directional-asymmetry, and lexical-distribution tests. Declared reconstructions of entropy, frequency, positional, predictive, classifier, and network measures reproduce the familiar Indus-like signatures as well. A sequential decipherment stress test then reaches high dictionary coverage for English, Sanskrit, and Tamil on the same corpus, while grouped held-out declines and unstable keys reveal how little that coverage identifies. The construction does not decide what the Indus signs encode: it shows that the evaluated measures detect organization without being specific to language, and therefore cannot, on their own, establish encoded speech.

</details>


### [25] [Language Models Encode the Contextual Truth of Propositions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03035)
*Rupak Sarkar,Pritika Ramu,Rachel Rudinger*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs encode contextual truth (truth determined by in-context evidence) along linear directions in activation space, distinct from world-knowledge truth. These representations persist across different output policies and can be causally manipulated. In collaborative multi-agent settings, partner assertions can sway truth representations, especially near decision boundaries. The authors identify two forms of sycophancy distinguishable only through representation analysis: accommodating false claims while internally representing them as false, versus actually shifting internal representations—the latter being 2.59x more common with explicit restatement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on linear truth representations in LLMs focused on factual propositions grounded in world knowledge. It was unclear whether and how these representations extend to contextual truth—propositions whose truth depends on in-context evidence. Additionally, behavioral measures alone cannot distinguish between superficial accommodation and genuine belief shift in sycophantic behavior.

Method: The authors probe LLM activation spaces for linear directions encoding contextual truth. They use steering experiments to establish causal links. They analyze transcripts from a collaborative vision-language task where two LLMs maintain common ground, measuring how partner assertions shift truth representations of propositions, particularly near decision boundaries. They separate internal representation from output behavior to distinguish two sycophancy types.

Result: (1) Linear representations of contextual truth exist and persist across structurally different output policies, even when output does not require truth evaluation. (2) Steering experiments confirm causal influence. (3) Partner assertions significantly sway truth representations, especially for propositions near the decision boundary. (4) Two sycophancy forms identified: accommodating false claims while internally representing them as false, versus shifting internal representations across the boundary. The latter occurs 2.59x more often when agreement involves explicit restatement rather than implicit agreement.

Conclusion: Linear representations extend from factual to contextual truth in LLMs. Distinguishing internal representation from output reveals nuances in sycophancy that behavioral analysis alone misses—models may outwardly agree while internally maintaining correct representations, or genuinely shift their representations, with explicit restatement driving deeper representational change.

Abstract: Prior work has shown that LLMs encode the truth of factual propositions along linear directions in activation space. It's unclear how these representations extend to contextual truth: propositions whose truth is determined by in-context evidence rather than world knowledge. We show that LLMs maintain a linear representation of contextual truth that persists across structurally different output policies, even when the output doesn't require the model to determine a proposition's truth, and show causal evidence via steering experiments. Using the transcripts from a collaborative vision-language task that requires two LLMs to maintain a shared common ground, we show that truth representations of a proposition are significantly swayed by partner assertions about that proposition, even when the LLM has enough evidence to determine its truth. We find evidence that propositions near the decision boundary are more susceptible to having their truth shifted through partner assertions. Separating representation from output distinguish two forms of sycophancy that output behavior alone cannot: the model may accommodate a false proposition while continuing to represent it as false, or shift its representation across the boundary. The latter is 2.59x more common when the model agrees by restating the false claim explicitly than when it agrees implicitly.

</details>


### [26] [Beyond Accuracy: A Multidimensional Evaluation of Statistical Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03038)
*Monnie McGee,Mateo Langston Smith,Julian Cabrera*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Current LLM evaluations for statistical reasoning focus narrowly on accuracy, ignoring how models construct explanations. This study proposes a multidimensional framework combining accuracy, response behavior, structural topic modeling, and lexical similarity to analyze 15 LLMs on 90 statistics exam questions. Results show accuracy ranges from 55-78%, a shared conceptual organization across all models, and modest vendor-specific stylistic differences in explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Statistical reasoning is multidimensional, but LLM evaluations overwhelmingly emphasize response accuracy while neglecting how models construct and communicate statistical explanations. A more comprehensive evaluation framework is needed to capture both the substantive correctness and the explanatory quality of LLM-generated statistical reasoning.

Method: The authors applied a multidimensional evaluation framework to explanations from 15 current-generation LLMs responding to 90 questions drawn from four statistics examinations (high school, undergraduate, and graduate levels). The framework integrates four complementary analyses: (1) response accuracy, (2) response behavior analysis, (3) structural topic modeling to uncover conceptual organization, and (4) lexical similarity analysis to detect stylistic patterns and vendor-specific differences.

Result: Accuracy varied substantially across models (55% to 78%). Structural topic modeling revealed a shared conceptual organization of statistical reasoning common to all models. Lexical similarity analysis identified modest but consistent vendor-specific stylistic differences — models from the same vendor (e.g., Anthropic, OpenAI) produced more lexically similar explanations than those from different vendors.

Conclusion: Statistical reasoning in contemporary LLMs cannot be characterized by accuracy alone. Complementary analyses of response behavior and model-generated explanations provide a richer, more comprehensive evaluation. The shared conceptual structure suggests convergent reasoning patterns, while vendor-specific lexical differences point to stylistic influences from training processes.

Abstract: Statistical reasoning is multidimensional, yet evaluations of large language models (LLMs) typically emphasize response accuracy while overlooking how models construct and communicate statistical explanations. This study demonstrates the value of a multidimensional evaluation by combining response accuracy, response behavior, structural topic modeling, and lexical similarity analysis. The framework is applied to explanations generated by 15 current-generation LLMs responding to 90 questions drawn from four statistics examinations spanning high school, undergraduate, and graduate levels. Accuracy varied substantially across models, ranging from 55\% to 78\%. In contrast, structural topic modeling revealed a common conceptual organization of statistical reasoning across all models, while lexical similarity analysis identified modest but consistent vendor-specific differences in explanatory style. Models developed by the same vendor (e.g. Anthropic, OpenAI) produced explanations that were slightly more similar than models from different vendors. These findings demonstrate that statistical reasoning in contemporary LLMs cannot be characterized by accuracy alone and illustrate how complementary analyses of response behavior and model-generated explanations provide a more comprehensive evaluation of statistical reasoning in generative AI.

</details>


### [27] [Emulate or Estimate? The Divergent Strengths of Base and Post-Trained Language Models for Opinion Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03044)
*Seth Grief-Albert,Jessica Bo,Difan Jiao,Ashton Anderson*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper resolves conflicting findings in LLM-based human simulation by distinguishing two tasks: emulation (generating individual responses that aggregate into distributions) and estimation (directly predicting population distributions). Base models excel at emulation; post-trained models excel at estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on using LLMs to simulate human opinions yields contradictory results — some studies show strong alignment with surveys, others reveal persona collapse and weak demographic sensitivity. The authors identify that this conflict arises from conflating two distinct tasks: emulation and estimation.

Method: The authors define two tasks: (1) emulation — generating individual-level responses that aggregate into a population distribution, and (2) estimation — directly predicting the population-level distribution. They evaluate six matched base and post-trained (instruction-tuned/RLHF) models on the Pew American Trends Panel, comparing response distributions to human ground truth and assessing demographic structure preservation.

Result: Base models are stronger emulators, producing response distributions closer to human ground truth and better preserving demographic structure. Post-trained models are stronger estimators, yielding more accurate distributional predictions when asked directly for aggregate distributions.

Conclusion: Model selection for human simulation should be guided by task type: base models for emulation tasks requiring text generation from individual personas, and post-trained models for estimation tasks requiring direct distributional prediction.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate human opinions, but prior work reports conflicting results: some studies find promising alignment with human survey data, while others find persona collapse and weak demographic sensitivity. We show that much of this conflict stems from conflating two distinct tasks. We call the first task emulation, in which models generate individual responses that aggregate into a population distribution. We call the second task estimation, in which models directly predict the population distribution. Evaluating six matched base and post-trained models on the Pew American Trends Panel, we find that base models are stronger emulators: they produce response distributions closer to human ground truth and better preserve demographic structure. Post-trained models are stronger estimators, producing more accurate distributional predictions when asked directly. We propose that model selection for human simulation should be guided by whether the task requires generating text or predicting distributions.

</details>


### [28] [PI-Mem: Pushing Long-Context Reasoning to 3.6M Tokens with Parallel-Iterative Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03048)
*Dawei Liu,Haixu Song,Shuang Cheng,Shijie Wang,Haozheng Hou,Kaifeng Liu,Ermo Hua,Zhonghang Yuan,Zhijie Zhong,Yuchen Fan,Biqing Qi,Bowen Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PI-Mem proposes a parallel-iterative memory mechanism that processes all chunks simultaneously and refines a shared memory over bounded turns, using reinforcement learning with turn-efficiency rewards for adaptive early exit. It outperforms recurrent-memory baselines on HotpotQA by +6–8 points with up to 6.1× inference speedup at context lengths up to 3.6M tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context reasoning in LLMs is bottlenecked by recurrent-memory approaches that suffer from two issues: (1) sequential chunk-wise updates can overwrite early critical evidence with later irrelevant content, and (2) serial inter-chunk dependencies limit parallelism, causing inference latency to grow with context length.

Method: PI-Mem processes all chunks in parallel each turn, conditioned on a shared memory state. In each iteration, the model reads all chunks, selects new or complementary evidence, and merges it into a compact shared memory. The workflow is optimized via reinforcement learning with an auxiliary turn-efficiency reward, enabling adaptive early exit when sufficient evidence is accumulated.

Result: Evaluated with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Qwen2.5-7B on HotpotQA at up to 3.6M tokens, PI-Mem outperforms the recurrent-memory baseline by +6.25 and +7.81 absolute points, with 6.1× and 2.1× inference speedups respectively.

Conclusion: PI-Mem breaks the accuracy–efficiency trade-off in long-context reasoning, offering a scalable approach to complex multi-hop question answering over extremely long documents.

Abstract: Long-context reasoning remains a critical bottleneck for large language models, as recent recurrent-memory approaches face two inherent challenges: sequential chunk-wise updates can overwrite early critical evidence with later irrelevant content, and serial inter-chunk dependencies limit parallelism and cause latency to increase with context length. To address these issues, we propose PI-Mem (Parallel-Iterative Memory), a mechanism that processes all chunks in parallel and iteratively refines a shared memory over a bounded number of turns. In each turn, PI-Mem reads all chunks in parallel conditioned on the current memory, selects new or complementary evidence from each chunk, and merges the selected evidence into a compact shared memory for the next turn. To discourage redundant turns, we optimize the workflow through reinforcement learning with an auxiliary turn-efficiency reward, enabling the model to adaptively exit once sufficient evidence has been accumulated. We evaluate PI-Mem with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Qwen2.5-7B on the HotpotQA benchmark across context lengths up to 3.6 million tokens and find that it outperforms the recurrent-memory baseline by +6.25 and +7.81 absolute points while achieving 6.1$\times$ and 2.1$\times$ inference speedups, respectively. These results demonstrate that PI-Mem breaks the accuracy--efficiency trade-off in long-context reasoning and provides a scalable approach to complex multi-hop question answering over extremely long documents.

</details>


### [29] [SeqLLM: Augmenting LLMs with Behavioral-Sequence Modeling for High-Stakes Decisions at WeChat Pay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03063)
*Guilin Li,Jiaxing Zhang,Matthias Hwai Yong Tan,Bo Wang,Weiran Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SeqLLM integrates behavioral-sequence modeling into a pretrained LLM via discrete behavior tokens, a two-stage alignment projector, and task-prefixed supervised fine-tuning, achieving significant improvements in payment risk control and recommendation benchmarks while preserving language ability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale merchant risk control requires jointly modeling textual profiles and long behavioral sequences. LLMs excel at text but cannot natively handle behavioral sequences, and naive adaptation often causes catastrophic forgetting of language capabilities.

Method: SeqLLM uses three components: (1) a compact discrete vocabulary mapping behavioral events to native tokens; (2) a lightweight projector trained with a two-stage alignment curriculum to ground behavior tokens in the LLM's semantic space; and (3) prefix-guided capability injection via task-prefixed supervised fine-tuning (rather than continual pre-training) to acquire sequence-modeling ability while preserving language skills.

Result: At WeChat Pay, SeqLLM improved screening precision from 92.0% to 97.5% over a production DeepSeek-based LLM, and pretrained behavior-token embeddings boosted Precision@Top-0.01% by 26.8 pp in a billion-scale fraud detector. On MovieLens and Amazon, it achieved up to 32% relative Recall@5 improvement over User-LLM. On RecIF, it improved Pass@32 by 14.2% over the full OneRec-8B pipeline using only one-fifth of the GPU-days.

Conclusion: SeqLLM demonstrates that behavioral-sequence modeling can be effectively integrated into pretrained LLMs without sacrificing language ability, yielding state-of-the-art performance in both industrial payment risk control and public recommendation benchmarks.

Abstract: Merchant risk control at large payment platforms screens tens of millions of merchants daily, where false positives harm legitimate merchants and false negatives leave harmful activity undetected. The hardest cases require jointly understanding a merchant's textual profile and long behavioral sequence. Large language models (LLMs) excel at text but cannot natively model such sequences, while adapting them often causes catastrophic forgetting. We present SeqLLM, a framework that adds behavioral-sequence modeling to a pretrained LLM while preserving its language ability. SeqLLM combines three components: a compact discrete vocabulary that represents behavioral events as native tokens; a lightweight projector, trained with a two-stage alignment curriculum, that grounds these tokens in the LLM's semantic space; and prefix-guided capability injection, which acquires sequence-modeling ability through task-prefixed supervised fine-tuning rather than continual pre-training. SeqLLM is deployed at WeChat Pay, screening millions of merchants daily. Against the production DeepSeek-based LLM baseline, it raises screening precision from 92.0% to 97.5%. Its pretrained behavior-token embeddings also improve Precision@Top-0.01% by 26.8 percentage points in a production fraud detector serving billion-scale transaction traffic. Beyond payments, SeqLLM achieves state-of-the-art results on public recommendation benchmarks. On MovieLens and Amazon, it surpasses the strong User-LLM baseline by up to 32% relative Recall@5 while retaining markedly stronger language ability. On RecIF, it improves Pass@32 by 14.2% over the full OneRec-8B pipeline using only one-fifth of its GPU-days.

</details>


### [30] [Activation-Guided Neuron Intervention to Induce Alzheimer's-Related Computational Language Phenotypes in a Large Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03067)
*Rui He,Ercong Nie,Hong Jiang,Iris E. Sommer,Philipp Homan,Wolfram Hinzen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Researchers used an LLM (Qwen3-8B) to identify neurons that activate differently for Alzheimer's disease speech vs. controls. By amplifying those neurons, they induced graded cognitive impairments across multiple domains (story recall, verbal fluency, working memory, etc.) mirroring human AD speech patterns, establishing a causal link between model representations and behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work shows LLMs can detect AD from speech, but detection alone does not demonstrate that the underlying neural representations causally contribute to behavior. The authors sought to establish whether AD-associated internal representations in LLMs are functionally implicated in producing the cognitive-linguistic deficits characteristic of AD.

Method: An activation-guided intervention framework was applied to Qwen3-8B: (1) feed-forward neurons with higher activation rates for AD vs. control transcripts were identified; (2) their down-projection weights were scaled to either amplify or attenuate contributions; (3) nine edited model variants were created varying in direction, magnitude, and scope; (4) all models completed a 12-turn neuropsychological battery evaluated via blinded human ratings and computational linguistic measures.

Result: Amplifying AD-associated neurons produced graded impairments in story recall, verbal fluency, working memory, procedural discourse, scene construction, and coreference resolution. Attenuation largely preserved or selectively improved performance. Amplification also reduced lexical surprisal, idea density, syntactic complexity, and discourse quantity — mirroring known AD speech patterns.

Conclusion: Neurons identified solely from clinical language differences can causally influence behavior across multiple cognitive domains, providing proof of concept for an AD-related computational phenotype and a controlled experimental framework for studying links between language and broader cognitive dysfunction.

Abstract: Changes in spontaneous speech provide an early signal of cognitive dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD) that large language models (LLMs) can detect. However, detection alone cannot establish whether the underlying model representations contribute functionally to behavior. We introduce an activation-guided intervention framework using Qwen3-8B. The framework identifies feed-forward neurons with higher activation rates for AD than control transcripts and modulates their output contributions during generation by scaling the corresponding down-projection weights. This yielded nine edited variants differing in intervention direction, magnitude, and scope. The original and edited models completed the same 12-turn neuropsychological battery, assessed through blinded human ratings and computational linguistic measures. Amplifying AD-associated neurons produced graded impairments in story recall, verbal fluency, working memory, procedural discourse, scene construction, and coreference resolution. Attenuation largely preserved performance and selectively improved several outcomes. Amplification also reduced lexical surprisal, idea density, syntactic complexity, and discourse quantity, broadly paralleling changes reported in human AD speech. These findings show that neurons identified solely from clinical language differences can influence behavior across multiple cognitive domains, providing proof of concept for an AD-related computational phenotype and a controlled framework for experimentally examining links between language and broader cognitive dysfunction.

</details>


### [31] [CVPO: Enhancing LLM Reinforcement Learning Reasoning via Value-Variance Adaptation and Dynamic Curriculum Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03068)
*Ziqi Jia,Yalu Ouyang,Bo Pang,Panpan Li,Hangfei Xu,Shengzhao Wen,Shiyong Li,Yanpeng Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CVPO proposes curriculum-guided value-variance policy optimization for LLM reasoning, using token-level value-variance to bound policy updates and dynamically weight questions by difficulty, outperforming VAPO on math tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods for LLM reasoning suffer from imprecise feedback on generated answer trajectories and problem difficulty drift, where the model's training distribution shifts away from appropriately challenging tasks.

Method: CVPO operates at two levels: (1) trajectory level — token-level value-variance is shown to correlate with exploration intensity and theoretically bounds policy update magnitude; this is used to design a variance-aware advantage adjustment mechanism for different reward types; (2) question level — a dynamic curriculum weighting method adapts to question difficulty, steering the model toward tasks matched to its current capability at each training stage.

Result: CVPO outperforms strong value-based baselines including VAPO, achieving better performance and stronger exploration, yielding more accurate and robust reasoning across various math tasks.

Conclusion: By integrating token-level value-variance for advantage adjustment and curriculum-based difficulty weighting, CVPO addresses core limitations in RL-based LLM reasoning training, demonstrating superior performance and enhanced exploration capabilities.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as an effective method for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods suffer from insufficient precision in feedback on generated answer trajectories and exhibit the phenomenon of problem difficulty drift. To address these challenges, we propose CVPO - Curriculum-guided Value-Variance Policy Optimization. At the response trajectory level, we find that token-level value-variance correlates with exploration intensity. Our theoretical analysis shows this variance bounds policy update magnitude. We then use the estimated trajectory value-variance to quantify the intrinsic randomness in generation. Based on this, we design a variance-aware advantage adjustment mechanism for different reward types. At the question level, we introduce a dynamic curriculum weighting method that adapts to question difficulty. This helps the model focus on tasks matched to its current ability during each training stage. Experimental results show our method outperforms strong value-based baselines like VAPO. It achieves better performance and stronger exploration, enabling more accurate and robust reasoning in language models across various math tasks.

</details>


### [32] [PAMT: Process-Aligned Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Domain Machine Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03077)
*Yongshi Ye,Biao Fu,Chongxuan Huang,Yidong Chen,Xiaodong Shi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PAMT addresses multi-domain machine translation by aligning explicit reasoning steps with reference translations via process rewards, improving domain-sensitive translation but revealing a credit-assignment bottleneck where existing methods cannot identify which intermediate steps actually help.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large reasoning models (LRMs) use explicit intermediate translation steps for domain-sensitive decisions (disambiguation, terminology, style), but these steps exhibit a double-edged nature: beneficial for long-form/hard translations, yet unreliable in terminology-intensive and stylistically constrained settings. The root cause is a credit-assignment bottleneck—current optimization methods cannot pinpoint which reasoning steps genuinely contribute to translation quality.

Method: PAMT (Process-Aligned Machine Translation), a training framework combining: (1) cold-start domain-aware Long Chain-of-Thought (Long-CoT) supervision to seed reasoning behavior, (2) sequence-level format and outcome rewards for final translations, and (3) a novel step-level process reward measuring how much each explicit translation step increases reference-translation likelihood. Training uses reinforcement learning across two backbones.

Result: PAMT outperforms base models and MT-specialized baselines on average across 15 domains and four translation directions, while remaining competitive with strong LLMs and LRMs in in-domain, out-of-domain (OOD), and multilingual settings.

Conclusion: Explicit reasoning in MDMT is double-edged; the credit-assignment bottleneck is a critical failure mode. Process-aligned training with step-level process rewards effectively mitigates this issue, yielding robust domain-sensitive translation.

Abstract: Multi-domain machine translation (MDMT) requires more than fluent generation: it demands domain-sensitive translation decisions such as domain disambiguation, terminology control, and stylistic adaptation. Large reasoning models (LRMs) make such decisions explicit through intermediate translation steps, but our analysis across 15 domains and four translation directions shows that this explicit reasoning is double-edged: it improves long-form and high-difficulty translation, yet often drifts in terminology-intensive and stylistically constrained settings. We trace this failure to a credit-assignment bottleneck: existing methods optimize final outputs or coarse trajectories, but cannot identify which translation steps actually help the final translation. To address this, we propose PAMT, a process-aligned training framework that combines cold-start domain-aware Long-CoT supervision with reinforcement learning. PAMT uses sequence-level format and outcome rewards for the final translation, together with a step-level process reward that measures how much each explicit translation step increases the likelihood of the reference translation. Across two backbones, PAMT improves over base models, outperforms MT-specialized baselines on average, and remains competitive with strong LLMs/LRMs across in-domain, OOD, and multilingual settings.

</details>


### [33] [Scalable Frequency- and Length-Aware Subdocument Deduplication for Large Language Model Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03089)
*Hai Wang,Chenhao Wang,Qifeng Cai,Yixiu Liu,Miao Peng,Nuo Chen,Yuanlin Tu,Chengcheng Xu,Feng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a scalable subdocument deduplication framework that decouples duplicate detection from copy retention, using natural-boundary segmentation, normalized hashing, distributed aggregation, and an adaptive frequency- and length-aware retention policy. Experiments show models trained on this data outperform other deduplication settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale pretraining corpora contain substantial duplicate content at the subdocument level. Existing suffix-array-based methods operate within shards, missing cross-shard duplicates and being sensitive to sharding configuration. Hash-based methods allow global counting but rely on rigid, fixed copy-retention policies ill-suited to heterogeneous repetition patterns. There is a need for a method that achieves global subdocument deduplication with flexible, adaptive retention control.

Method: A scalable two-stage framework: (1) Duplicate detection via natural-boundary segmentation, normalized exact hashing, and distributed aggregation to identify global duplicate groups; (2) An explicit frequency- and length-aware retention policy that assigns an adaptive copy budget per group — retaining more copies of low-frequency or short repetitions while more aggressively pruning high-frequency or long ones.

Result: Models trained on data processed by the proposed method achieve the best overall performance among all evaluated settings on FineWeb-Edu and a code-containing web corpus.

Conclusion: Explicit, adaptive copy-retention control is critical for effective subdocument deduplication, and decoupling detection from retention enables scalable, globally-aware deduplication that improves downstream model performance.

Abstract: Large-scale pretraining corpora contain substantial duplicate content. Although document-level deduplication is widely used, removing subdocument-level redundancy remains challenging. At corpus scale, suffix-array-based methods are commonly applied independently within shards, leaving cross-shard duplicates undetected and making the resulting retention behavior sensitive to the sharding configuration. Hash-based methods enable global exact duplicate counting, but often rely on fixed copy-retention policies that cannot accommodate heterogeneous repetition patterns. We propose a scalable subdocument deduplication framework that decouples duplicate detection from copy retention. It identifies duplicate groups through natural-boundary segmentation, normalized exact hashing, and distributed aggregation, and then applies an explicit frequency- and length-aware retention policy that allocates an adaptive copy budget to each group, retaining more copies of low-frequency or short repetitions while more aggressively deleting high-frequency or long ones. Experiments on FineWeb-Edu and a code-containing web corpus show that models trained on data processed by our method achieve the best overall performance among the evaluated settings. These results underscore the importance of explicit copy-retention control.

</details>


### [34] [VIVID: A Culturally Grounded Benchmark Exposing the Figurative Language Gap in Vietnamese NLP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03095)
*Tu Tran Do,Nhat Ngoc Nguyen,Khanh-Tung Tran,Hoang D. Nguyen,Tu Minh Phuong,Long Hoang Dang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: VIVID is the first benchmark for Vietnamese figurative language understanding, comprising 1,636 idioms/proverbs annotated with complexity traits and themes. Evaluation of 8 models reveals significant cultural competence gaps, with even top models scoring below 50% maximum, and few-shot prompting sometimes degrading performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current NLP models lack robust evaluation for culturally grounded figurative language in low-resource languages like Vietnamese. Existing benchmarks fail to capture the nuanced interplay of literal, pragmatic, Sino-Vietnamese, and folk knowledge dimensions that characterize Vietnamese idioms and proverbs.

Method: The authors construct VIVID, a benchmark of 1,636 Vietnamese idioms and proverbs annotated with five complexity traits and seven semantic themes. They design a dual-task evaluation framework: generative (explanation generation) and discriminative (multiple-choice interpretation). An LLM-as-a-Judge approach with aspect-based prompting is validated against human judgments (Cohen's κ = 0.792). Eight SOTA models are evaluated, including both Vietnamese-specialized and multilingual systems, under zero-shot and few-shot settings.

Result: Vietnamese-specialized models severely underperform multilingual systems (VinaLLaMA-7B: 0.13 vs. GPT-4o: 2.46 on a 0–5 scale). Top models achieve less than 50% of maximum scores. Few-shot prompting does not universally improve performance; GPT-4o shows degradation due to stylistic overfitting. Systematic failure modes identified include literal over-interpretation, lexical gaps, and pragmatic flattening.

Conclusion: Current LLMs lack the cultural competence required for nuanced figurative interpretation in Vietnamese. VIVID serves as a critical diagnostic tool for evaluating and advancing figurative language understanding in culturally rich, low-resource contexts. The findings highlight the inadequacy of monolingual specialization alone and the need for culturally informed model development.

Abstract: We present VIVID (Vietnamese Idioms for Validation and Interpretation Depth), the first systematic benchmark for evaluating culturally grounded figurative language understanding in Vietnamese. VIVID comprises 1,636 idioms and proverbs annotated with five complexity traits (literal expressions, pragmatic nuances, Sino-Vietnamese terms, uncommon vocabulary, folk knowledge) and seven semantic themes. We establish an evaluation framework combining generative and discriminative tasks, proposing an LLM-as-a-Judge approach with aspect-based prompting validated against human judgment (Cohen's kappa = 0.792). Evaluating eight state-of-the-art models reveals critical gaps: Vietnamese-specialized models drastically underperform multilingual systems (VinaLLaMA-7B: 0.13 vs. GPT-4o: 2.46), and even top models achieve less than 50% of maximum scores. Notably, few-shot prompting does not universally improve performance, with GPT-4o exhibiting degradation due to stylistic overfitting. Our analysis exposes systematic failures including literal over-interpretation, lexical gaps, and pragmatic flattening, demonstrating that current models lack cultural competence for nuanced figurative interpretation. VIVID provides an essential tool for advancing figurative language understanding in culturally rich contexts.

</details>


### [35] [What Language Does and What the Evidence Supports: A Functional Role Taxonomy and Evidence Audit of Language Grounding in Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03099)
*Yifan Guo,Chenghao Li,Zhu Wang,Wei Xu,Yu Li,Yulong Zhu,Zhuo Sun,Bin Guo,Zhiwen Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This survey disentangles what language contributes in embodied agents from how well that contribution is empirically grounded, proposing a five-role taxonomy and a claim-by-claim evaluation framework that reveals a persistent gap between functional claims and evidential support in the literature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models increasingly embed language into embodied agents, but the mere presence of language does not clarify its actual functional contribution or the strength of evidence backing that contribution. The authors aim to separate these two questions—what language does versus whether the evidence supports that claim—to bring rigor to evaluating language's role in embodied systems.

Method: The paper defines five non-exclusive functional roles for language in embodied agents: (1) Specification, (2) Embodied Representation, (3) Action Orchestration, (4) Grounding Regulation, and (5) Execution Coupling. For each role, the authors trace the path from linguistic content to its embodied consumer and identify the observations or interventions required to test causal responsibility. They then apply this framework to the existing literature, evaluating grounding claim by claim—using role claims rather than system architectures as the unit of comparison.

Result: The analysis reveals a recurring gap: interpretable or revised linguistic intermediates may be incorrect, unused, or fail to influence downstream behavior. Even when actions are directly conditioned on language, system-level success alone does not isolate language's specific contribution. The claim-by-claim evaluation shows that evidence often falls short of supporting the particular functional responsibility attributed to language.

Conclusion: Using functional roles rather than architectures as the unit of comparison enables fair cross-paradigm evaluation between modular and end-to-end agents without overextending conclusions. The framework exposes where empirical grounding is lacking and provides a structured basis for more rigorous future work on language in embodied agents.

Abstract: Foundation models place language throughout embodied agents, but its presence does not show what it contributes or how well that contribution is grounded. This survey separates these two questions. We define five non-exclusive functional roles for language: Specification, Embodied Representation, Action Orchestration, Grounding Regulation, and Execution Coupling. For each role, we trace the path from linguistic content to its embodied consumer and identify the observations or interventions that can test the claimed responsibility. Applying this framework to the reviewed literature reveals a recurring gap between functional use and evidential support. Interpretable or revised linguistic intermediates may be incorrect, go unused, or fail to affect later behavior. Even when actions are directly conditioned on language, system-level success does not by itself isolate language's contribution. We therefore evaluate grounding claim by claim, asking whether the reported evidence supports the specific responsibility assigned to language. Using role claims rather than architectures as the unit of comparison allows us to compare modular and end-to-end embodied agents without extending conclusions beyond the reported evidence.

</details>


### [36] [HomoEnsNER: Does Language Alignment Outperform Architectural Complexity in Gujarati Named Entity Recognition?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03105)
*Chandrakant K. Bhogayata*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HomoEnsNER, a homogeneous ensemble of five fine-tuned GujaratiBERT models with majority voting, outperforms both a single GujaratiBERT baseline and six architecturally diverse heterogeneous ensembles on Gujarati NER, demonstrating that monolingual language alignment trumps architectural complexity for low-resource morphologically rich languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gujarati NER is underexplored due to lack of capitalization, rich morphology, lexical ambiguity, and free word order. Prior ensemble approaches emphasize architectural diversity (heterogeneous classifiers, multilingual encoders, classical sequence models) but neglect the potential of monolingual pretraining. The paper asks whether a homogeneous ensemble of a single monolingual encoder can outperform architecturally diverse ensembles.

Method: HomoEnsNER: a homogeneous ensemble of five independently fine-tuned GujaratiBERT models combined via majority voting. Compared against (1) a single GujaratiBERT baseline and (2) six heterogeneous alternatives incorporating MuRIL-base, MuRIL-large, IndicBERT, mBERT, BiLSTM, CRF, and a stacked BiLSTM-CRF-GujaratiBERT architecture. All eight models trained under a consistent budget, evaluated by entity-level F1 on the Naamapadam Gujarati test split.

Result: HomoEnsNER achieved the highest entity-level F1 of 0.8442, surpassing the single GujaratiBERT baseline (0.8347) and all heterogeneous alternatives (lowest F1: 0.7855).

Conclusion: Language-aligned monolingual pretraining is a more effective and budget-conscious ensembling strategy than architectural diversity for low-resource Indian language NER. Homogeneous ensembles of a well-aligned monolingual encoder should be preferred over architecturally complex heterogeneous combinations.

Abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) for Gujarati remains underexplored, hindered by the absence of capitalization cues, rich morphology, lexical ambiguity, and free word order. Prior ensemble work has emphasized architectural diversity by combining heterogeneous classifiers, multilingual encoders, or classical sequence models, rather than exploiting language-aligned monolingual pretraining. This study asks whether, for a low-resource, morphologically rich language like Gujarati, a homogeneous ensemble of a single monolingual encoder outperforms such architectural diversity. We propose HomoEnsNER, a homogeneous ensemble of five independently fine-tuned GujaratiBERT models combined via majority voting, evaluated against a single GujaratiBERT baseline and six heterogeneous alternatives, including combinations with MuRIL-base, MuRIL-large, IndicBERT, mBERT, BiLSTM, CRF, and a stacked BiLSTM-CRF-GujaratiBERT architecture. All eight models were trained under a consistent budget and evaluated using entity-level F1 on the Naamapadam Gujarati test split. HomoEnsNER achieved the highest F1 (0.8442), surpassing the baseline (0.8347) and every heterogeneous alternative (lowest: 0.7855), indicating that language alignment is a more effective, budget-conscious ensembling strategy than architectural complexity for low-resource Indian language NER.

</details>


### [37] [From SQL Errors to Concept Gaps: An AI-Powered Knowledge Graph Analytics Platform for Personalized Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03118)
*Abdulrahman AlRabah,Weijian Zhou,Xing Gao,Abdussalam Alawini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: An AI-powered knowledge graph platform that links SQL errors in student submissions to specific course concepts, enabling concept-level diagnostic feedback beyond traditional autograding. Evaluated across two universities, 95.7% of extracted concept nodes were rated valid, and 63.8% of concept-relation triplets were fully correct.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Students learning SQL struggle with semantic errors reflecting conceptual misunderstandings (e.g., misusing NATURAL JOIN due to intertwined gaps in JOIN, GROUP BY, and HAVING). Existing autograding systems only detect correctness and provide surface-level feedback without connecting errors to the conceptual structure of the course. While educational knowledge graphs have been used for curriculum analysis, they have not been applied to diagnosing SQL misconceptions from student submissions.

Method: The authors developed a platform that (1) automatically extracts course concepts and their relations from instructional materials, (2) links these concepts to student submission traces via a graph database, and (3) classifies errors at the concept level. Evaluation was conducted across two database systems courses at two universities — one using real student submissions and one using simulated submissions — through an expert study (five participants) and automated evaluation using an LLM as a judge.

Result: 95.7% of extracted knowledge graph nodes were rated as at least somewhat valid, and 63.8% of triplets were rated as fully correct by expert evaluation. Experts confirmed that generated graphs align with instructor mental models and that mapping errors to course concepts provides actionable diagnostic insight.

Conclusion: The AI-powered knowledge graph platform successfully connects SQL errors to course concepts, producing concept-level diagnostic feedback that aligns with instructor mental models. However, evaluating the actual impact on student learning outcomes remains as future work.

Abstract: This innovative practice full paper describes an AI-powered knowledge graph platform that connects SQL errors to conceptual gaps in undergraduate and graduate database systems courses. Students learning Structured Query Language (SQL) frequently struggle with semantic errors that reflect conceptual misunderstandings rather than syntax mistakes. A query may execute yet return incorrect results due to gaps spanning related concepts; misusing NATURAL JOIN in place of an explicit subquery reflects intertwined misunderstandings of JOIN, GROUP BY, and HAVING. Autograding systems detect correctness but provide surface-level feedback without connecting errors to the conceptual structure of the course. Educational knowledge graph research has shown the value of structured concept representations for curriculum analysis and adaptive learning, but these approaches have not been applied to diagnosing SQL misconceptions from student submissions. We present a platform that automatically extracts course concepts and relations from instructional materials, links them to student submission traces through a graph database, and classifies errors at the concept level. We evaluate the platform across two database systems courses at two universities, one using real student submissions and one using simulated submissions, through an expert study with five participants and an automated evaluation using an LLM as a judge. Results show that 95.7% of extracted nodes were rated as at least somewhat valid and 63.8% of triplets were rated fully correct. Expert feedback confirmed that the generated graphs align with instructor mental models and that mapping errors to course concepts provides actionable diagnostic insight; evaluating impact on student learning remains future work.

</details>


### [38] [Internalizing Academic Writing Workflows for Introduction Generation via Struct-Aware Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03138)
*Meicong Zhang,Tiancheng Su,Jiahao Cheng,Guoxiu He,Xinqi Tao,Dejia Song*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: StructPO internalizes multi-stage paper introduction writing into a single-pass LLM policy using stage tokens, struct-aware credit assignment, and refinement-guided optimization, outperforming workflow baselines and matching GPT-5.1 at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based paper introduction generation relies on expensive multi-stage prompts or agent workflows that suffer from cross-stage drift, where errors propagate across stages. There is a need for a more efficient, coherent single-pass alternative.

Method: StructPO is a struct-aware policy learning framework that: (1) uses explicit stage tokens to control a single-pass generation policy; (2) employs struct-aware credit assignment to decouple per-stage quality from global coherence; and (3) uses refinement-guided optimization to internalize iterative revision into the first-pass policy.

Result: StructPO improves semantic alignment, structural rationality, and inference efficiency over workflow-based baselines. It generalizes to out-of-domain settings and matches GPT-5.1 in human evaluation when scaled to Qwen3-32B.

Conclusion: Internalizing academic writing workflows via fine-grained policy optimization is a viable and cost-effective alternative to external multi-stage orchestration for structured long-form generation.

Abstract: Generating a rigorous paper introduction with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging, since it requires coordinating background, gap identification, method and contribution within a coherent narrative. Existing solutions externalize this process as multi-stage prompts or agent workflows which are expensive and vulnerable to cross-stage drift. We propose StructPO, a struct-aware policy learning framework that internalizes the entire multi-stage writing workflow into a single-pass policy controlled by explicit stage tokens. StructPO introduces struct-aware credit assignment to decouple local stage quality from global coherence and refinement-guided optimization to internalize revision behavior into the first-pass policy. Experiments show that StructPO improves semantic alignment, structural rationality and inference efficiency over workflow-based baselines, generalizes to out-of-domain settings, and remains competitive with GPT-5.1 in human evaluation when scaled to Qwen3-32B. These results show that internalizing academic writing workflows through fine-grained policy optimization offers a viable alternative to costly external orchestration.

</details>


### [39] [ANCHOR-RE: An Agentic Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Grounded Biomedical Relation Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03154)
*Shufan Ming,Yikun Han,Gibong Hong,Rui Zhang,Halil Kilicoglu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ANCHOR-RE is a neuro-symbolic framework that enhances LLM-based biomedical relation extraction by integrating ontology-guided reasoning, external knowledge grounding, and data-driven verification rules, achieving improved F1 scores across multiple benchmarks without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional systems like SemRep offer high precision but low recall, while LLMs provide stronger reasoning but suffer from false positives. The authors seek to combine the strengths of both paradigms — symbolic precision with neural flexibility — to improve BioRE reliability without requiring parameter updates.

Method: ANCHOR-RE integrates three components into LLM inference: (1) ontology-guided reasoning, (2) external knowledge grounding, and (3) data-driven verification rules. Evaluated on SemRepGS, DDI, and ChemProt benchmarks using both proprietary and open-weight LLMs. A temporal evaluation on 100 articles published in 2026 (post-training-cutoff) assessed generalizability and mitigated pretraining contamination bias.

Result: With the proprietary backbone, micro-F1 improved from 0.654→0.676 (SemRepGS), 0.769→0.872 (DDI), 0.939→0.941 (ChemProt). On DDI and ChemProt, ANCHOR-RE outperformed prior inference-only methods and approached fine-tuned systems. Gains held with open-weight LLMs. Post-cutoff evaluation yielded 69% precision on manual assessment of 500 predictions.

Conclusion: Neuro-symbolic reasoning improves LLM-based BioRE reliability without fine-tuning. ANCHOR-RE is a practical, training-free approach validated across benchmarks, model families, and temporally unseen literature.

Abstract: Biomedical relation extraction (BioRE) extracts structured knowledge from biomedical literature for applications such as knowledge base construction and hypothesis generation. Traditional symbolic systems such as SemRep provide high precision but limited recall, while large language models (LLMs) offer stronger contextual reasoning but remain prone to false-positive predictions. We developed ANCHOR-RE, a framework that integrates ontology-guided reasoning, external knowledge grounding, and data-driven verification rules into LLM inference. We evaluated it on three BioRE benchmarks (SemRepGS, DDI, and ChemProt) using both proprietary and open-weight LLMs. To assess generalizability beyond benchmark datasets while reducing potential evaluation bias from LLM pretraining contamination, we conducted a temporal evaluation using 100 biomedical articles published in 2026. With the proprietary backbone, ANCHOR-RE outperformed direct LLM prompting, improving micro-F1 from 0.654 to 0.676 on SemRepGS, from 0.769 to 0.872 on DDI, and from 0.939 to 0.941 on ChemProt. On DDI and ChemProt, it also outperformed previously reported inference-only methods and approached fine-tuned or instruction-tuned systems without parameter updates. Similar performance gains observed with open-weight LLMs indicate that the benefits were not limited to the proprietary backbone. On the post-cutoff set, manual assessment of 500 randomly sampled predictions yielded a precision of 69%, maintaining consistent precision on previously unseen biomedical literature. Neuro-symbolic reasoning can improve the reliability of LLM-based BioRE without fine-tuning. Results across multiple benchmarks, model families, and post-cutoff literature support ANCHOR-RE as a practical training-free approach to biomedical literature mining.

</details>


### [40] [Aligning Large Vision-Language Models at Test Time: A Trajectory-Guided Structured Sampling Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03204)
*Tianbao Jiang,Weicong Ni,Gerard de Melo,Linlin Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a test-time alignment approach for LVLMs using trajectory-guided structured sampling with MCMC refinement, avoiding costly post-training RL while improving visual reasoning accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL-based post-training alignment for large vision-language models (LVLMs) is resource-intensive and suffers from distribution mismatches between training objectives and inference-time requirements, motivating a more efficient test-time alternative.

Method: The method consists of two stages: (1) a trajectory learning algorithm builds a reasoning memory bank by decomposing complex questions into ordered sequences of predefined reasoning patterns; (2) at inference time, trajectories are collected from this memory bank to establish a global structural prior, followed by iterative Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling for localized multi-objective refinement of the reasoning trace.

Result: Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning datasets show significant accuracy improvements without prohibitive inference overhead.

Conclusion: Trajectory-guided test-time sampling is a scalable, effective alternative to traditional post-training alignment, especially for complex visual reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Post-training reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are commonly used to align large vision-language models (LVLMs) with human intent and the requirements of visual reasoning tasks. However, existing RL-based alignment methods are often resource-intensive and encounter mismatches between training objectives and inference-time distributions. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel test-time alignment approach that leverages trajectory-guided structured sampling for dynamic inference-time refinement, achieving better alignment with visual grounding and ensuring logical consistency. Our approach begins with curating a reasoning memory bank via a trajectory learning algorithm, which decomposes complex question solving into ordered sequences of predefined reasoning patterns. It subsequently accomplishes inference-time alignment by first collecting trajectories from reasoning memory bank to establish a global structural reasoning prior, and then using an iterative Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm for localized multi-objective refinement of the reasoning trace. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves accuracy without incurring prohibitive inference overhead. These results establish trajectory-guided test-time sampling as a scalable and effective alternative to traditional post-training alignment, particularly for complex visual reasoning tasks.

</details>


### [41] [ICO: Enhancing Semantic-Shift Jailbreaks via Iterative Context Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03210)
*Hujian Zhu,Yihao Huang,Felix Juefei-Xu,Xinfeng Li,Peng Zeng,Simeng Qin,Qing Guo,Geguang Pu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Semantic-shift jailbreaks bypass model safety by replacing harmful terms with benign ones and using context to induce harmful reinterpretation. The authors find that context effectiveness varies greatly, distill characteristics of effective contexts, and propose ICO—a black-box iterative context optimization framework that achieves a 74.6% average attack success rate across 8 models, outperforming 8 SOTA baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing semantic-shift jailbreak attacks achieve limited effectiveness because they overlook that contexts differ substantially in their semantic-shift capability—i.e., their ability to induce models to reinterpret benign terms as harmful concepts. This capability gap has not been systematically studied or exploited.

Method: The authors systematically analyze context semantic-shift capabilities, distill characteristics of effective contexts, and propose a black-box framework called Iterative Context Optimization (ICO). ICO iteratively optimizes contexts by leveraging identified characteristics and target model feedback, using semantic-shift to transform benign-substituted harmful questions into successful jailbreaks.

Result: ICO consistently outperforms eight state-of-the-art baselines across three datasets and eight target foundation models, achieving an average attack success rate of 74.6%.

Conclusion: The limited effectiveness of prior semantic-shift jailbreaks stems from ignoring the varying semantic-shift capability of contexts. By identifying what makes contexts effective and optimizing them iteratively with model feedback, ICO significantly advances jailbreak attack performance, revealing a critical vulnerability in foundation model safety mechanisms.

Abstract: Foundation models have achieved remarkable success across diverse tasks, but they remain vulnerable. To investigate such vulnerabilities, semantic-shift jailbreaks have recently emerged as a promising attack paradigm. They bypass explicit safety mechanisms by replacing harmful terms in original harmful questions with benign alternatives and leveraging contextual information to induce the target model to reinterpret these alternatives as their corresponding harmful concepts. However, existing semantic-shift jailbreaks often achieve limited effectiveness. In this work, we reveal that this limitation arises from overlooking the semantic-shift capability of contexts. Through systematic analysis, we find that contexts exhibit substantially different abilities in inducing semantic shifts: contexts with stronger semantic-shift capabilities are more likely to guide models toward recovering harmful meanings and achieving successful jailbreaks. Based on this finding, we systematically identify and distill the characteristics of effective contexts and propose a black-box context-aware semantic-shift jailbreak framework with Iterative Context Optimization (ICO). In each iteration, ICO leverages these characteristics and feedback from the target model to optimize contexts. Extensive experiments on three datasets and eight target foundation models demonstrate that ICO consistently outperforms eight state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average attack success rate of 74.6%.

</details>


### [42] [On the Diversity of Analogy Making in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03233)
*Yuanhao Shen,Daniel Xavier de Sousa,Caio César Sifuentes Barcelos,Hongyu Guo,Xiaodan Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A systematic evaluation of analogy-making diversity across 10 LLMs reveals pervasive domain homogeneity (narrow target domains), a fundamental diversity-quality trade-off in existing enhancement methods, and distinct model-sensitive regions governing diversity via causal information flow analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs show strong analogy-making capabilities, output diversity—critical for cross-domain creativity and scientific discovery—has been largely unexplored. Prior work focused on applications and mechanisms, neglecting whether LLMs can generate analogies spanning diverse domains rather than clustering in narrow sets.

Method: The authors evaluate analogy diversity across 10 state-of-the-art open- and closed-source LLMs using both inter-query and intra-model diversity metrics. They assess existing diversity-enhancement methods against output quality, and conduct causal information flow analysis to identify model-sensitive regions governing analogy diversity across different LLMs.

Result: Key findings: (1) Domain homogeneity is prevalent—LLMs generate analogies from a narrow set of target domains. (2) A fundamental trade-off exists: diversity-enhancement methods that increase output diversity simultaneously degrade output quality. (3) Causal analysis reveals substantial differences in model-sensitive regions governing analogy diversity across LLMs, suggesting a mechanistic basis for the diversity-quality trade-off.

Conclusion: This is among the first systematic investigations of output diversity in LLM-based analogy making. The identified domain homogeneity problem and diversity-quality trade-off highlight critical limitations in current LLMs for creative tasks, and the causal analysis provides mechanistic insights that may guide future improvements in balancing diverse yet high-quality analogical outputs.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential for analogy making, a core cognitive capability that drives novelty and creativity. While prior research has extensively investigated the applications and underlying mechanisms of LLM-based analogy making, its output diversity remains largely unexplored, despite being essential for broadening cross-domain connections and fostering scientific innovation. In this work, we present a comprehensive evaluation of analogy diversity across ten state-of-the-art open- and closed-source LLMs. Our findings highlight a concerning issue of domain homogeneity, a prevalent tendency for LLMs to generate analogies from a narrow set of target domains, limiting both inter-query and intra-model diversity. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a fundamental trade-off in existing LLM diversity-enhancement methods: increasing output diversity often comes at the expense of output quality. Finally, our causal analysis of LLM information flow reveals substantial differences in the model-sensitive regions governing analogy diversity across LLMs, suggesting a potential mechanism for the observed diversity-quality trade-off. To our knowledge, this is among the first studies to systematically investigate output diversity in LLM-based analogy making.

</details>


### [43] [Relational Priors as Convergence Pressure in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03239)
*Ming Shen,Chao Shang,Sadat Shahriar,Devang Kulshreshtha,Yi Zhang,Sandesh Swamy,Yanjun Qi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Explicitly encoding inter-agent relational semantics (e.g., trust, challenge, defer) as signed-network priors in LLM-MAS prompts creates convergence pressure that increases agreement but does not reliably improve accuracy. Relational priors should be used diagnostically and only when task-validated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-MAS designs implicitly embed social expectations between agents, but the effects of making these relational semantics explicit and formalized are not well understood. The authors aim to systematically investigate whether injecting relational priors improves or harms multi-agent system performance.

Method: The authors use a minimal signed-network formulation to encode relational priors (positive/negative/neutral ties) and render them as natural-language prompts injected into agent system prompts, holding the task protocol constant. They evaluate across two task domains: a commons-governance simulation and multi-agent debate, measuring agreement, coordination, and accuracy metrics, including correctness-conditioned agreement.

Result: Relational priors primarily act as convergence pressure: increasing positivity leads to higher agreement/coordination. This benefits tasks where alignment is rewarded (sustainable resource governance, subjective consensus) but does not reliably improve accuracy. In objective QA debates, higher positivity can inflate agreement without improving correctness-conditioned agreement, and may even reduce it. Effects vary by model backbone, relation type, and topology. Explicit neutrality differs from omitting relational framing entirely.

Conclusion: Relational priors should not be a default add-on in LLM-MAS. Safer use is diagnostic and task-specific: compare against a no-prior baseline, monitor correctness-conditioned metrics when truth matters, and omit the relational layer when validation does not justify it.

Abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) are designed through roles, debate protocols, and aggregation rules. These choices create implicit social expectations: agents may be expected to trust, challenge, defer to, or collaborate with peers. We study the effects of making inter-agent relation semantics explicit. We use a minimal signed-network formulation of relational priors and inject natural-language renderings into agent system prompts while holding the task protocol fixed. Across a commons-governance simulation and multi-agent debate, relational priors primarily act as convergence pressure: increasing relational positivity tends to make agents coordinate or agree more readily. This pressure can help when utility rewards behavioral alignment, as in sustainable resource governance and subjective consensus. It does not, however, reliably improve accuracy. In objective QA debates, higher positivity can increase agreement even when correctness-conditioned agreement does not improve and may decline in some settings. Effects vary by model backbone, relation type, and topology; explicit neutrality is not equivalent to omitting relational framing. We argue that relational priors should not be a default add-on for LLM-MAS. Their safer use is diagnostic and task-specific: compare against a no-prior baseline, monitor correctness-conditioned metrics when truth matters, and omit the relational layer when validation does not justify it.

</details>


### [44] [MoEGen: Mixture-of-Experts for Instance-Adaptive LoRA Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03275)
*Yiming Zeng,Lei Lu,Zexin Li,Zhuochun Li,Shuoqiu Li,Shuyi Liao,Xidong Wu,Zeyu Zhang,Minmei Wang,Yu Zhao,Tingting Yu,Shangqian Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MoEGen proposes a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework that replaces storing full LoRA experts with small expert-code vectors. A hypernetwork generates instance-specific low-rank updates conditioned on a weighted combination of routed expert codes, decoupling capacity from storage while enabling input-conditional adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MoE-based PEFT methods store multiple full LoRA adapters, causing storage to scale linearly with expert count and limiting adaptation to a fixed expert pool. The authors aim to achieve instance-specific adaptation without explicitly storing a separate LoRA module per expert.

Method: MoEGen represents each expert as a small learnable vector (expert code). Inputs are routed over these codes, and their weighted combination conditions a lightweight hypernetwork that dynamically generates input-specific low-rank update matrices (A and B), avoiding explicit per-expert LoRA storage.

Result: MoEGen achieves consistent improvements over strong static and MoE-based PEFT baselines on eight commonsense reasoning benchmarks across three backbone models. It also performs strongly in joint medical and legal-domain adaptation tasks.

Conclusion: Shifting from expert selection to expert-conditioned parameter generation enables effective instance-specific adaptation with decoupled storage and capacity, offering a more scalable and flexible alternative to conventional MoE-based PEFT.

Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of large language models, but existing MoE-based PEFT methods typically improve capacity by storing multiple full LoRA experts, causing adapter storage to grow linearly with the number of experts and restricting adaptation to a fixed expert pool. We ask whether MoE-based PEFT can produce instance-specific adaptations without explicitly storing a separate LoRA module for each expert. To address this gap, we propose MoEGen, an adaptation framework that shifts MoE-based PEFT from expert selection to expert-conditioned parameter generation. Instead of storing each expert as a full LoRA adapter, MoEGen represents each expert as a small learnable vector, termed an expert code. It routes each input over these vectors and uses their weighted combination to condition a lightweight hypernetwork that generates input-specific low-rank updates. This design decouples expert capacity from adapter storage while enabling instance-conditioned adaptation. Experiments on eight commonsense reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong static and MoE-based PEFT baselines across three backbones. MoEGen also performs strongly in joint medical and legal-domain adaptation.

</details>


### [45] [Benchmarking the Benchmarks: Testing the Predictive Validity of Commonsense Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03340)
*Ine Gevers,Walter Daelemans*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether standard commonsense reasoning benchmarks reliably predict LLM performance on downstream real-world tasks, finding that they offer only narrow, task-dependent predictive validity rather than broad evidence of commonsense competence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The extent to which performance on widely adopted commonsense benchmarks predicts downstream, real-world task performance remains underspecified. The authors aim to empirically establish the practical usability and criterion validity of these benchmarks.

Method: The authors evaluate 23 models from six model families on four established commonsense benchmarks, four reworked variants, three non-commonsense controls, and eight downstream tasks requiring implicit social, pragmatic, temporal, or physical reasoning. They compare model rankings, compute controlled correlations, and employ leave-one-family-out cross-validation to assess criterion validity.

Result: Revised benchmarks largely preserve original model rankings and do not improve downstream predictive power. Commonsense benchmarks show consistent cross-family predictive validity only for a narrow subset of downstream tasks, with smaller or metric-specific gains elsewhere.

Conclusion: Standardized commonsense benchmarks provide task-dependent rather than broad evidence of downstream commonsense competence, cautioning against overgeneralizing benchmark performance to real-world reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Predicting LLM's capabilities on real-world tasks is essential, yet the extent to which performance on commonsense benchmarks predicts downstream performance remains underspecified. To establish the practical usability of widely adopted commonsense benchmarks, we evaluate 23 models from six families on four established commonsense benchmarks, four reworked variants, three non-commonsense controls, and eight downstream tasks requiring implicit social, pragmatic, temporal, or physical reasoning. We compare model rankings, compute controlled correlations, and use leave-one-family-out cross-validation to assess the criterion validity of commonsense benchmarks. Our results show that revised benchmarks largely preserve original model rankings and do not improve downstream predictive power. Commonsense benchmarks show consistent cross-family predictive validity for only a narrow subset of downstream tasks, with smaller or metric-specific gains elsewhere. Overall, standardized commonsense benchmarks provide task-dependent rather than broad evidence of downstream commonsense competence.

</details>


### [46] [ArtECulture: Benchmarking Culture-Conditioned Visual Emotion Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03358)
*Xiaolin Chen,Xuemeng Song,Wenhao Shi,Xianjing Han,Mong-Li Lee,Wynne Hsu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ArtECulture is a benchmark for culture-conditioned visual emotion understanding, evaluating how well MLLMs predict and explain culture-specific emotional reactions to artworks across English, Chinese, and Arabic cultures. A retrieval-augmented framework using a cultural emotion knowledge base is proposed to improve MLLM performance without additional training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual emotion understanding methods ignore cultural variations in emotional perception. Current benchmarks suffer from inconsistent individual annotations (hindering majority-supported culture-level labels) and imbalanced cultural coverage, motivating the need for a well-structured, culturally balanced benchmark.

Method: The authors construct ArtECulture, a benchmark of 6,792 artworks with culture-specific emotion labels and explanations across English, Chinese, and Arabic cultures, balanced between Western and non-Western content. They evaluate 16 open- and closed-source MLLMs in a zero-shot setting. To improve performance, they propose a retrieval-augmented framework that uses a concept-based cultural emotion knowledge base to inject explicit cultural knowledge into MLLMs without additional training.
