Result: Zero-shot evaluation of 16 MLLMs reveals that culture-conditioned visual emotion understanding remains highly challenging, with the best model achieving below 50% accuracy. The proposed retrieval-augmented framework improves both culturally aligned emotion prediction and grounded explanation generation.

Conclusion: Culture-conditioned visual emotion understanding is a difficult open problem for current MLLMs. Injecting explicit cultural knowledge via retrieval augmentation offers a promising direction for improving cross-cultural emotional alignment in vision-language models.

Abstract: Existing visual emotion understanding methods typically ignore cultural variations in emotional perception. We introduce culture-conditioned visual emotion understanding, a task that predicts the culture-specific emotional perception of a given image and explains the underlying rationale. Although related benchmarks exist, they are limited by inconsistent individual annotations, which hinder the derivation of majority-supported culture-level emotion labels, and imbalanced cultural coverage. Thus, we present ArtECulture, a benchmark containing 6,792 artworks with culture-specific emotion labels and explanations across English, Chinese, and Arabic cultures, with balanced Western and non-Western content. Evaluations of 16 open- and closed-source Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) under a zero-shot setting reveal that the task remains challenging, with the best model achieving below 50\% accuracy. To address this limitation, we introduce a retrieval-augmented culture-conditioned emotion understanding framework, which leverages a concept-based cultural emotion knowledge base to inject explicit cultural knowledge into MLLMs without additional training. The framework improves both culturally aligned emotion prediction and grounded explanation generation. Our benchmark and code will be publicly released.

</details>


### [47] [FACTWASH: Catching AI Rewrites That Wash Hearsay into Fact](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03372)
*Alex Kwon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces "factwashing" — when AI rewrites strip checkability metadata from claims — and presents factwash, an open-source gate using word lists for bounded cues (negation, 0.91 F1) and a precision-only LLM witness for open-ended cues (hedging/attribution, +17/+15 recall). Analysis of 105K+ annotated sentences shows factwashing concentrates in conversational hearsay (55%) vs. business email (7%), reframing deployment as a triage problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI systems routinely transform information (e.g., conversations to stored memories, documents to answers), but this rewriting process can strip away crucial metadata — who said it, how certain they were, when it was true — while preserving the claim itself. The authors term this failure "factwashing." The motivation is to build a deterministic, open-source detection gate that catches factwashing at write-time using named flags and evidence, rather than relying on an opaque LLM judge.

Method: The paper proposes a dual-approach detection system based on the nature of the linguistic property being checked. For properties with a bounded, enumerable surface-cue inventory (e.g., explicit negation cues), a simple word-list suffices and achieves strong performance (0.91 F1). For properties with open-ended realizations (hedging and attribution), where vocabulary-based methods plateau at ~50% recall, the system employs a one-question LLM witness that recovers +17 and +15 points of cue-detection recall at equal precision. The LLM witness is deployed conservatively: it can only lower a verdict, buying precision rather than coverage. Evaluation uses 105,596 independently annotated sentences for cue detection, plus a blind-labeled corpus of memory writes to locate failure modes.

Result: The word-list approach achieves 0.91 F1 for negation cues on untuned text. For hedging and attribution, vocabulary methods plateau near half recall; the LLM witness recovers +17 and +15 recall points respectively at equal precision. Deployment analysis on memory writes reveals that 55% of bad writes occur in conversational hearsay versus 7% in business email (p < 0.001), suggesting the first deployment question is whether the failure mode occurs at all, not which detector to use. On unmodified mem0 2.0.7, the gate flags 5 of 8 hedged-hearsay writes.

Conclusion: The key insight is that the choice between cheap (word-list) and expensive (LLM) checks depends on whether the target property has a bounded surface-cue inventory. When cues are enumerable, cheap methods suffice and transfer well; when open-ended, an LLM witness becomes necessary but can be deployed strategically to prioritize precision. The deployment finding that factwashing is heavily domain-concentrated (dominated by conversational hearsay) reframes the practical question from detector selection to failure-mode triage.

Abstract: AI systems rewrite information constantly: conversations become stored memories, documents become answers. The rewrite can keep a claim while washing away what made it checkable, who said it, how sure they were, when it held. We call that failure factwashing, and release factwash, an open-source write-time gate that catches it deterministically, with named flags and evidence rather than an LLM judge. Building it answers a practical question: when does a cheap check suffice, and when do you need a model? What decides is whether the property has a bounded surface-cue inventory. Explicit negation cues are close to enumerable, so a word list finishes and transfers, reaching 0.91 F1 on untuned text. Hedging and attribution have open-ended realizations, so vocabulary plateaus near half recall, and a one-question LLM witness recovers +17 and +15 points of cue-detection recall at equal precision. Deployed, that witness may only lower a verdict, so it buys precision rather than coverage. We measure cue detection on 105,596 independently annotated sentences. A blind-labelled corpus of memory writes then locates the failure: 55% of bad writes in conversational hearsay, 7% in business email (p < 0.001), so the first deployment question is not which detector to use but whether the failure occurs at all. On unmodified mem0 2.0.7, the gate flags 5 of 8 hedged-hearsay writes.

</details>


### [48] [Don't Let Me Ask for It: LLMs Show Deficiencies in Active Multi-Turn Information Acquisition for Abductive Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03388)
*Shahrukh Mohiuddin,Chalamalasetti Kranti,Sherzod Hakimov,David Schlangen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Alien Abduction game to probe how LLMs perform abductive reasoning under varying interaction modes. Key findings: upfront evidence yields higher success than distributed evidence; models either commit prematurely or fail to converge in multi-turn settings; oracle-provided examples outperform self-selected queries, though self-selected evidence produces more internally consistent hypotheses, suggesting models may overfit to their own queries without adequately considering alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs are frequently benchmarked on abductive reasoning accuracy, little is known about the underlying behavioral dynamics — specifically how models acquire evidence, update hypotheses, and determine when to stop. The authors aim to study these process-level aspects rather than just outcome correctness.

Method: The authors introduce the Alien Abduction game, an interactive probing environment with varying interaction modes: (1) evidence provided upfront vs. distributed across turns, and (2) model-selected queries vs. oracle-provided examples. Multiple LLMs are evaluated across these conditions on both success rate and behavioral metrics such as hypothesis consistency and stopping behavior.

Result: Three main findings: (1) Upfront evidence yields higher success rates than turn-distributed evidence. (2) In multi-turn settings, models exhibit maladaptive behaviors — either committing to hypotheses before exhausting available evidence or exhausting the turn budget without converging. (3) Oracle-provided examples lead to higher success rates than self-selected queries, yet self-selected evidence produces hypotheses that are more internally consistent with the evidence chosen — suggesting models may form hypotheses that fit their own queries while failing to rule out alternatives.

Conclusion: LLMs exhibit notable weaknesses in the process of abductive reasoning: they struggle to validate and refine hypotheses, fail to adequately distinguish between competing explanations, and show poor metacognitive calibration regarding when to stop gathering evidence. These findings highlight that evaluating only final answer correctness obscures important deficiencies in how models reason abductively.

Abstract: Abductive reasoning requires forming hypotheses that explain observed evidence and revising them as new evidence becomes available. While large language models (LLMs) are often evaluated on whether they solve abductive reasoning tasks correctly, less is known about how they acquire evidence, update their hypotheses, and decide when to stop. We introduce Alien Abduction game, an interactive probe for studying these behaviours under different interaction modes. The modes vary in whether evidence is provided upfront or across turns, and whether queries are selected by the model or examples are provided by the oracle. Across models, providing evidence upfront leads to higher success rates than distributing it across turns. In multi-turn settings, some models commit before using the available evidence, while others exhaust the turn budget without converging. Models also achieve higher success rates when examples are provided by the oracle than when they select their own queries, although their final hypotheses are more consistent with the evidence they selected. These findings suggest that models may form hypotheses that fit self-selected evidence without sufficiently distinguishing them from alternatives, and may struggle to validate and refine their hypotheses or determine when to stop.

</details>


### [49] [DUD: Decoupled Update Dynamics for Reliable Uncertainty Quantification in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03411)
*Yixin Bu,Runze Xia,Guanyun Zou,Yupeng Ji,Haodong Liu,Piji Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DUD decouples FFN and Attention contributions in LLM residual streams via noise-induced causal interventions, creating a dual-stream dynamic profile that significantly outperforms existing UQ methods in estimation, calibration, and cross-dataset generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mechanistic UQ approaches aggregate residual stream updates, conflating parametric memory (FFN) and contextual processing (Attention), which obscures fine-grained conflicts like memory-context misalignment that signal uncertainty. The authors argue this conflation prevents accurate epistemic state capture.

Method: DUD uses noise-induced causal interventions to independently quantify FFN and Attention restoration capabilities, then constructs a dual-stream dynamic profile that captures the model's internal fragility by explicitly measuring each module's contribution to state recovery.

Result: DUD significantly outperforms SOTA baselines in uncertainty estimation and calibration, with superior cross-dataset generalization, validating decoupled dynamics as a robust proxy for model faithfulness.

Conclusion: Decoupling residual stream update dynamics into FFN and Attention components provides a more faithful signal of LLM uncertainty than aggregated approaches, establishing DUD as a superior UQ framework.

Abstract: Accurate Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is critical for reliable deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet traditional probability-based metrics often fail to capture the model's true epistemic state. While recent mechanistic approaches leverage hidden state dynamics, they typically aggregate residual stream updates, conflating the distinct roles of parametric memory (Feed-Forward Networks) and contextual processing (Attention). We argue that this aggregation obscures fine-grained mechanistic conflicts, such as memory-context misalignment, that are fundamental indicators of uncertainty. To address this, we introduce \textbf{D}ecoupled \textbf{U}pdate \textbf{D}ynamics \textbf{(DUD)}, a framework that explicitly decouples FFN and Attention contributions via noise-induced causal interventions. By quantifying the independent restoration capabilities of each module, we construct a dual-stream dynamic profile that captures the model's internal fragility. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both uncertainty estimation and calibration, while exhibiting superior cross-dataset generalization, validating decoupled dynamics as a robust proxy for model faithfulness.

</details>


### [50] [Dynamically Allocating Evaluation Effort for Model Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03437)
*Vilém Zouhar,Julia Kreutzer,Alon Lavie,Tom Kocmi,Matt Post,Ondřej Bojar,Mrinmaya Sachan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper formalizes multi-model human evaluation as a best-arm identification problem in a correlated multi-armed bandit framework, enabling adaptive sampling that focuses annotation budget on competitive models, thereby reducing evaluation costs while improving discrimination among top performers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human evaluation is costly and poorly scalable. Standard evaluation protocols exhaustively evaluate all models on entire benchmarks, which is inefficient when the primary goal is identifying the best-performing models. The key insight is that annotation effort should be concentrated where it matters most — distinguishing among top contenders.

Method: The authors cast multi-model human evaluation as a best-arm identification problem in a multi-armed bandit with correlated arms. Each "arm pull" corresponds to a human evaluation of a model on a test instance. By adaptively allocating evaluation samples based on intermediate model rankings, the method concentrates the annotation budget on the most competitive models. The paper proves the optimality of the proposed adaptive sampling algorithms.

Result: The proposed algorithms are proven to be optimal and demonstrate improved discrimination between top-performing models compared to exhaustive evaluation, making evaluations faster, cheaper, and better aligned with the goals of large-scale competition settings.

Conclusion: Adaptive sampling via correlated multi-armed bandits offers a principled and efficient alternative to exhaustive human evaluation, enabling more scalable and cost-effective model benchmarking without sacrificing the ability to reliably identify the best models.

Abstract: While human evaluation is the gold standard in many NLP tasks, it suffers from prohibitive costs and poor scalability. When identifying top-performing models, typical evaluation protocols waste effort by exhaustively evaluating all models on the entire benchmark, a safe but inefficient approach. In this work, we formalize multi-model human evaluation as a best-arm identification problem in a multi-armed bandit setup with correlated arms, where pulling an arm corresponds to human-evaluating a model. By sampling adaptively based on the intermediate model rankings obtained on the samples so far, we can focus the annotation budget on the most competitive models. We prove the optimality of the proposed algorithms and show that it improves discrimination between top-performing models. This makes evaluations faster, cheaper and more aligned with large-scale competition evaluation goals.

</details>


### [51] [Predicting Multilingual Classification and Translation Performance of LLMs with Cross-Lingual Alignment $\unicode{x2013}$ Is English Enough?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03446)
*Adnan Al Ali,Kathy Hämmerl,Jindřich Libovický,Alexander Fraser*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A comparative analysis of 27 cross-lingual alignment (CLA) score variants reveals that alignment with English predicts both classification and translation performance in multilingual LLMs, supporting the hypothesis that English serves as an internal pivot language. The authors also introduce a PMI-based translation metric that correlates well with chrF while being less target-language-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on CLA scores has focused almost exclusively on classification tasks, despite LLMs being widely used for generative tasks like machine translation. The authors aim to (1) systematically compare CLA score variants and (2) determine whether CLA scores also predict translation quality, which would shed light on whether LLMs use English as an internal pivot.

Method: The authors compare 27 CLA score variants derived from different alignment formulas and embedding extraction methods. For classification, they correlate CLA scores with downstream task performance. For translation, they propose a PMI-based translation metric that is less dependent on the target language and correlates strongly with chrF, then compute correlations between CLA scores and translation quality across target languages.

Result: CLA with English predicts translation quality comparably to or better than source-target CLA, providing new evidence that multilingual LLMs use English as an internal pivot language. The proposed PMI-based translation metric shows strong correlation with chrF while reducing target-language dependence.

Conclusion: English-alignment is a strong predictor of both classification and generative (translation) performance in multilingual LLMs. The findings support the internal pivot language hypothesis and highlight the need for evaluating CLA beyond classification tasks.

Abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) have been shown to perform better on non-English classification tasks when the representations of the given language are more aligned to English within the model. Several cross-lingual alignment (CLA) scores have been proposed for use with LLMs, along with multiple approaches for extracting embeddings from the models. We provide a comparative analysis of 27 CLA score variants, examining how they differ and how well each predicts downstream performance across three tasks. Crucially, while LLMs are widely used for generative tasks such as machine translation, prior work has focused almost exclusively on classification. We therefore investigate whether CLA scores are similarly predictive of translation performance. To enable computing correlations across target languages, we propose a PMI-based translation metric, which is less dependent on the target language and correlates strongly with chrF. We find that CLA with English predicts translation quality comparably to or better than source-target CLA, providing new evidence that LLMs use English as an internal pivot language.

</details>


### [52] [Probing Character-level Transformers for the Spanish L-shaped Morphome](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03452)
*Akhilesh Kakolu Ramarao,Kevin Tang,Wiebke Petersen,Dinah Baer-Henney*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Character-level transformers encode the Spanish L-shaped morphome as an item-specific lexical abstraction localized at the stem-final position in the middle decoder, decodable even when surface alternations are absent, but the representation supports reproduction rather than human-like generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed transformers can reproduce the Spanish L-shaped morphome, but it was unknown whether models learn the abstract morphomic class itself or merely memorize visible stem alternations. The authors aim to distinguish these possibilities through representational probing.

Method: Five architectures (transformer, LSTM, GRU, CNN, and a baseline) with 12 trained models each were probed under lemma-disjoint cross-validation. Probes classified L-shaped vs. non-L-shaped verbs at every token position across all decoder layers. Controls included surface baselines (identity of the stem alternant), ablation of alternating forms, and testing on non-alternating instances after training on alternating ones.

Result: The L-shaped class is decodable above every surface baseline. Encoding persists even when all forms of a verb share the same stem. Probes trained on alternating instances generalize to non-alternating ones. The information is localized at the stem-final consonant position in the middle decoder layer, before the alternant is read. Item-specific learning dominates: which verbs are learned matters far more than architectural choice.

Conclusion: Transformers store the L-shaped morphome as an item-specific lexical abstraction — sufficient for pattern reproduction but insufficient for the productivity and generalization characteristic of human morphological knowledge.

Abstract: When a transformer learns an irregular morphological pattern, what has it learned? Our test case is the Spanish \emph{L-shaped morphome}, a complex irregular pattern in which the verb's stem alternates in exactly the first-person singular indicative and all subjunctive forms, and whose membership no phonological, semantic, or syntactic feature predicts. Prior studies have shown that character-level transformers can reproduce this pattern, but that evidence describes what models produce, not what they represent. Probing five architectures, twelve trained models each, under lemma-disjoint cross-validation with controls and surface baselines, we show that the models encode the L-shaped class itself, not just its visible alternations. It is decodable above every surface baseline, survives instances in which every form shows the same stem, and probes trained on alternating instances still classify non-alternating ones. The encoding is localized where the stem choice is made, at the stem-final consonant position of the middle decoder, before the alternant is read. And it is item-specific: which verbs a model learned matters far more than which architecture it is. The models store the morphome as an item-specific lexical abstraction, sufficient to reproduce the pattern but not to generalize it as humans do.

</details>


### [53] [Efficient Multilingual Neural Machine Translation via Corpus-Driven Vocabulary Pruning: An English-Arabic Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03480)
*Ahmed Amine Aliane,Nasredine Semmar,Hassina Aliane*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes a vocabulary pruning + fine-tuning framework for multilingual NMT models, reducing vocabulary from 128K+ to ~10K tokens, achieving 60% memory savings with no performance loss. The pruned M2M100 model achieves BLEU 42.04 and surpasses a dedicated bilingual baseline on COMET (0.8730 vs 0.7911).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large pre-trained multilingual NMT models suffer from excessive memory and computational costs due to oversized vocabularies and embedding layers. Existing compression methods (pruning, quantization, distillation) retain the original vocabulary structure, leaving a core source of inefficiency unaddressed.

Method: A general optimization framework combining (1) a vocabulary pruning method that drastically reduces the token vocabulary (from ~128K to ~10K) and (2) a targeted fine-tuning protocol designed specifically for multilingual NMT models. Evaluated on the English–Arabic language pair using three models: M2M100, NLLB-200, and mBART-50.

Result: Vocabulary reduction from >128K to ~10K tokens yields ~60% memory savings with no performance degradation. The pruned and fine-tuned M2M100 achieves a BLEU of 42.04 (vs. 44.59 for the bilingual OPUS-MT baseline) and significantly outperforms it on COMET (0.8730 vs. 0.7911), indicating better semantic adequacy and fluency.

Conclusion: Optimized multilingual models can match or exceed dedicated bilingual baselines, especially in semantic quality (COMET). Vocabulary pruning combined with targeted fine-tuning is a viable and effective strategy for deploying efficient multilingual NMT without sacrificing translation quality.

Abstract: The adoption of large pre-trained multilingual models for neural machine translation (MNMT) faces a major challenge: excessive memory and computational consumption due to overly large vocabularies and embedding layers. Although existing compression methods like pruning, quantization and knowledge distillation reduce parameter redundancy, they mainly preserve the structure of the original vocabulary, thereby leaving a major source of inefficiency unresolved. We propose in this paper a general optimization framework that combines a vocabulary pruning method with a targeted fine-tuning protocol for MNMT models. We evaluate the proposed framework using three models (M2M100, NLLB-200, mBART-50) on the English-Arabic language pair. Our approach reduces the vocabulary size from over 128,000 to approximately 10,000 tokens, enabling a 60% memory saving without any loss in performance. Results show that optimized multilingual models can match or exceed the performance of dedicated bilingual baselines. In particular, the pruned and fine-tuned M2M100 model achieves a competitive BLEU score of 42.04 (against 44.59 for the OPUS-MTen- ar bilingual model) while it significantly outperforms it on the COMET metric (0.8730 vs 0.7911) revealing superior semantic adequacy and fluency.

</details>


### [54] [Beyond Initialization Loss: A Systematic Study of Token Embedding Initialization Strategies for LLM Vocabulary Extension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03494)
*Raviraj Joshi,Utkarsh Vaidya,Sanjay Singh Chauhan,Niranjan Wartikar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Over 20 vocabulary extension initialization strategies for Hindi in a large LLM are compared. Subword composition methods, especially asymmetric variants with norm calibration, substantially outperform baselines, achieving over 6x reduction in continued pre-training steps to reach comparable loss. Lightweight CPT (≥50 steps) is shown to be a reliable, cost-effective predictor of downstream convergence, unlike static initialization metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vocabulary extension is an efficient approach for adapting LLMs to new languages, but the initialization of newly added token embeddings critically affects continued pre-training efficiency. A systematic, large-scale comparison of initialization strategies is lacking.

Method: The authors systematically compare 20+ initialization strategies for Hindi vocabulary extension using Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B. Methods include: vocabulary-averaging baselines (Mean-all, Mean-unique, Mean-partial), external/learned approaches (FOCUS, top-k semantic retrieval, residual MLP mappings), subword composition (uniform, frequency-weighted, character-length-weighted, with symmetric and asymmetric input-output variants), norm calibration (original or Hindi-specific), and input-output asymmetry. Evaluation uses validation loss, downstream MILU-Hindi accuracy, initialization loss, and Init BPB, with lightweight CPT probes (50–500 steps) as a selection signal.

Result: Subword composition methods outperform both vocabulary averaging and external/learned approaches. Asymmetric subword composition variants yield the lowest early validation loss. The best configuration uses uniform subword averaging + Hindi-specific norm calibration for input embeddings, and character-length-weighted subword averaging for the output head. This pipeline reaches comparable validation loss with >6x reduction in CPT steps versus Mean-all, and matches the baseline's 3,500-step MILU-Hindi accuracy after only 500 steps. Initialization loss and Init BPB are unreliable convergence predictors; lightweight CPT (as few as 50 steps) provides a reliable, cost-effective signal for strategy selection.

Conclusion: Subword composition with asymmetric input-output initialization and language-specific norm calibration is the most effective approach for vocabulary extension. Lightweight CPT should be used over static initialization metrics to select the best initialization strategy.

Abstract: Vocabulary extension is an efficient way to adapt pretrained large language models (LLMs) to new languages, but the initialization of newly added token embeddings can strongly affect continued pre-training (CPT) efficiency. We present a systematic study of more than 20 initialization strategies for Hindi vocabulary extension in Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B. Our comparison spans vocabulary-averaging baselines; external and learned initialization methods, including FOCUS, top-k semantic retrieval, and residual MLP mappings; subword composition; norm calibration; and input-output asymmetry. We find that subword composition methods outperform both vocabulary averaging and external/learned initialization approaches. Within subword composition, asymmetric variants achieve the lowest observed early validation loss and reveal distinct preferences for input and output embedding initialization. The best observed configuration initializes the input embedding matrix with uniform subword averaging and Hindi-specific norm calibration, and the output language modeling head with character-length-weighted subword averaging. Relative to the standard Mean-all baseline, this full initialization pipeline reaches comparable validation loss with over a 6x reduction in CPT steps and exceeds the baseline's 3,500-step MILU-Hindi accuracy after only 500 steps. Finally, we show that initialization loss and initialization bits-per-byte (Init BPB) are unreliable predictors of downstream convergence, whereas lightweight CPT, as few as 50 steps, provides a cost-effective and reliable signal for selecting the best initialization strategy.

</details>


### [55] [ConlangBench: Exploring Language Knowledge and Learning in LLMs through Diverse Constructed Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03505)
*Jinhong Jeong,Seungyeop Yi,Sangah Lee,Youngjae Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ConlangBench is a large-scale benchmark of 21 constructed languages with 21M parallel sentence pairs and 321K vocabulary entries, used to evaluate and train LLMs. Models perform better on a posteriori conlangs (derived from natural languages), and training on sufficient parallel data enables learning of all tested conlangs, with learning curves varying by conlang design type.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constructed languages (conlangs) are underexplored in LLM research despite offering a unique opportunity to study language learning. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a systematic benchmark for evaluating how LLMs acquire and translate low-resource, intentionally designed languages.

Method: The authors introduce ConlangBench, comprising 21 conlangs with over 21M conlang-English parallel sentence pairs and 321K vocabulary entries. They conduct bidirectional translation experiments to evaluate LLM performance and perform training on the benchmark data to analyze learning curves across conlangs with sufficient parallel corpora.

Result: LLMs perform better on a posteriori conlangs (vocabulary derived from natural languages) than on a priori ones. Training on ConlangBench enables models to learn all eight conlangs with sufficient parallel data, but learning curves differ based on how each conlang was created, reflecting their design characteristics.

Conclusion: Conlangs serve as a valuable testbed for studying how LLMs acquire low-resource languages. The varying learnability across conlang types highlights the impact of linguistic design principles on model acquisition, offering insights for both conlang research and low-resource NLP.

Abstract: Constructed languages (conlangs) are intentionally created human languages with a rich tradition of linguistic creativity. Despite their potential for studying language learning in large language models (LLMs), existing conlangs remain largely underexplored in LLM research. We present ConlangBench, the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating and training LLMs on 21 existing conlangs. We collect over 21M conlang-English parallel sentence pairs (including 430K pairs across the 20 non-Esperanto conlangs) and 321K vocabulary entries. In bidirectional translation experiments, we find that models perform better on a posteriori conlangs, whose vocabularies are derived from natural languages, reflecting the design characteristics of conlangs. Training on ConlangBench also shows that models can learn all eight conlangs for which sufficient parallel corpora are available, while their learning curves vary depending on how the conlangs were created. Our findings suggest that conlangs provide a unique testbed for investigating how LLMs acquire low-resource languages.

</details>

### [56] [ISEE: Interactive Semantic Enrichment for Database Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02604)
*Yuan Tian,Yiru Chen,Rakesh R. Menon,Zifan Liu,Ting Cai,Fei Wu,Anudeep Chimakurthi,Prashanthi Ramamurthy,Sridevi Aishwariya Ganesan,Kun Qian,Yunyao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ISEE is an interactive semantic enrichment system that collaborates with users to improve data field descriptions, thereby enhancing LLM-based agent performance on downstream tasks like entity linking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with data tasks when field descriptions are ambiguous or incomplete, because critical domain knowledge resides in users' minds and is rarely documented. This semantic gap directly limits agent performance on tasks such as entity linking.

Method: ISEE employs a scoring system to measure semantic quality of field descriptions, then interactively gathers domain knowledge from users to collaboratively enrich the semantics. The approach is evaluated through four methods: a user study, automated user simulation, quantitative evaluation, and a case study.

Result: ISEE significantly reduces cognitive load on users, improves the quality of data field descriptions, and enhances downstream task performance (specifically entity linking).

Conclusion: Interactive semantic enrichment via ISEE effectively bridges the gap between undocumented domain knowledge and agent-usable data semantics, yielding measurable improvements in both user experience and task outcomes.

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly being deployed for data-related tasks, including data sense-making, exploration, and retrieval. However, their performance heavily depends on the clarity and completeness of data semantics. In practice, many field descriptions remain ambiguous or incomplete, as much of the essential context (e.g., the meaning of a customized field) originates from users' domain knowledge and is rarely documented publicly. This gap restricts the agents' task performance in downstream tasks, such as entity-linking. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel and comprehensive Interactive SEmantic Enrichment system (ISEE). Given a data field description, ISEE measures its quality through a scoring system, gathers domain knowledge, and collaboratively enriches the semantics with users. Through a user study, automated user simulation, quantitative evaluation, and case study, we demonstrate that ISEE significantly reduces cognitive load, improves description quality, and enhances downstream task performance.

</details>


### [57] [Self-Organising Digital Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02606)
*Marcello Barylli,Gabriel Béna,Alexander Mordvintsev,Eleni Nisioti,Sebastian Risi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A Transformer-based architecture inspired by biological self-organisation learns to configure Lookup Tables (LUTs) of Boolean gates, enabling digital circuits to self-assemble from scratch and adaptively re-route logic around hardware faults with near-perfect recovery, while generalising to larger circuit scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical fault tolerance relies on static strategies (hardware redundancy, error-correcting codes), whereas biological systems demonstrate adaptive plasticity — dynamically re-organising around damage to maintain function. This gap motivates a biologically inspired approach to digital circuit resilience.

Method: The authors frame functional logic generation and maintenance as a meta-learning problem on graphs. Their architecture uses a topology-masked Transformer to configure the Lookup Tables (LUTs) of Boolean gates, extending Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) principles. Rather than regenerating a fixed target state, the system navigates the degenerate Boolean search space to satisfy a computational task.

Result: The system self-assembles functional circuits from scratch and rapidly re-routes logic around permanent, previously unseen hardware faults. For soft errors, it achieves >99.99% recovery accuracy from damage sizes far exceeding training conditions. It also exhibits generalisation: accuracy improves on circuit graphs substantially wider than those seen during training.

Conclusion: This work successfully bridges biological self-organisation principles with digital hardware, offering a dynamic, adaptive alternative to traditional static fault-tolerance strategies.

Abstract: Fault tolerance in classical computing has traditionally relied on static strategies like hardware redundancy and error-correcting codes. Biological systems, in contrast, exhibit adaptive plasticity, maintaining function through dynamic re-organisation around damage. Inspired by this principle, we introduce Self-Organising Digital Circuits, framing functional logic generation and maintenance as a meta-learning problem on graphs. Our architecture employs a topology-masked Transformer that configures the Lookup Tables (LUT) of a circuit's Boolean gates. Extending the pattern-generation paradigm of Neural Cellular Automata (NCA), it navigates the degenerate Boolean search space to satisfy a computational task, rather than regenerating a fixed target state. We demonstrate that it can self-assemble functional circuits from scratch and rapidly re-route logic around permanent, previously unseen hardware faults. For soft errors, the policy achieves near-perfect recovery (>99.99\% accuracy) from damage sizes far exceeding training conditions. We further observe generalisation across circuit scales: accuracy improves on graphs substantially wider than those seen during training. This work bridges the principles of biological self-organisation with the practical domain of digital hardware.

</details>


### [58] [Beyond the Hivemind: Escaping LLM Homogeneity via Meta-Persona Anchoring and Sequential Temperature Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02618)
*Tairan Fu,Javier Conde,Carlos Arriaga,Gonzalo Martínez,Pedro Reviriego,Javier Coronado-Blázquez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Meta-Persona Anchoring + Filtered Temperature Scaling to combat LLM "Artificial Hivemind" (semantic collapse), reducing inter-response cosine similarity from ~0.85 to ~0.65 under ~20B parameter models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit an "Artificial Hivemind" effect where outputs converge to a narrow, homogenized consensus even on open questions, yielding inter-response similarity of 0.80–0.90 even at high temperature. This semantic collapse severely limits response diversity and creativity in AI systems.

Method: A two-stage generation framework: (1) Meta-Persona Anchoring — the model self-selects a unique, idiosyncratic persona to anchor its generation starting point; (2) Filtered Temperature Scaling (FTS) — a dual-stage sampling sieve using Top-p filtering to preserve grammatical validity, followed by extreme temperature scaling (T ≥ 4.0) on surviving candidates to explore the broadened probability distribution.

Result: On the INFINITY-CHAT dataset with open-weight models under ~20B parameters, average pairwise cosine similarity dropped from ~0.85 to ~0.65, with a majority of questions falling below the 0.7 threshold — substantially reducing the gap between artificial mode collapse and human-level typological diversity.

Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively mitigates semantic convergence in LLMs, enabling more diverse and creative outputs. Released as open-source to facilitate broader adoption in diverse AI deployments.

Abstract: Recent studies have identified an ``Artificial Hivemind'' effect in Large Language Models (LLMs) causing models to converge on a narrow, homogenized consensus even for open questions. This semantic collapse limits the diversity of AI, resulting in high inter-response similarity ($\approx 0.80-0.90$) even under high-temperature sampling. In this paper, we propose a novel mitigation framework to increase diversity: Meta-Persona Anchoring combined with Filtered Temperature Scaling (FTS). Our approach utilizes a two-stage generation process: first, the model is prompted to self-select a unique, idiosyncratic persona to anchor its starting point; second, we apply a dual-stage sampling sieve, utilizing Top-$p$ filtering to preserve grammatical validity followed by extreme temperature scaling ($T \ge 4.0$) on the surviving candidates to explore the broadened probability distribution. We evaluate our method using the INFINITY-CHAT dataset on state-of-the-art open weight models under $\sim$20B parameters. Our results demonstrate a significant reduction in semantic convergence, with average pairwise cosine similarity dropping from ($\approx 0.85$) to ($\approx 0.65$). Our scheme achieves a majority of questions below the 0.7 threshold, effectively reducing the gap between artificial mode collapse and human-level typological diversity. We provide our implementation as an open-source framework to enable more diverse and creative AI deployments.

</details>


### [59] [PULSE: An Executable Contract Language for Spatiotemporal Knowledge Graph Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02630)
*Dongxu Yang,Ziyi Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PULSE is an OPM-inspired language that localizes operational roles (modes) and their write effects into a single typed runtime with a fixed execution contract. It enforces safety properties like evidence non-overwrite, branch isolation, and guarded state changes, while generating GeoSPARQL, SOSA, and SHACL views. The paper provides a core calculus with safety lemmas, Lean 4 formal verification, and extensive empirical validation against standards, statecharts, and NOAA hurricane data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Knowledge graph engineering distributes operational state, observations, constraints, processes, and hypothetical scenarios across separate artifacts (ontologies, SHACL shapes, rule engines), leaving their combined execution contract implicit and external. This fragmentation makes it difficult to reason about safety properties, side effects, and temporal behavior holistically.

Method: The authors design PULSE, a typed language with four operational roles (modes) localized in one runtime. A core calculus establishes an effect-confinement lemma and six safety properties. Lean 4 formally checks kernel analogues for positions, evidence, clocks, monitors, atomicity, and branch source retention. Validation uses 88 tests, 3,534 bounded checks, 32 Lean/Python runtime-kernel cases, standards composition (GeoSPARQL/SOSA/SHACL), a Sismic statechart reproduction, 37,440 temporal traces with mutant analysis, and the NOAA IBTrACS hurricane dataset (since 1980, 1,476,290 transition-zone pairs).

Result: PULSE matches a separate workflow across 37,440 generated temporal traces and distinguishes ten single-field mutants. On NOAA IBTrACS, it agrees with GEOS and an event sweep on 1,476,290 transition-zone pairs, including 4,800 sampled and 12,831 duration-qualified events. The Lean 4 formalization holds for the checked cases. Project-specific GeoSPARQL probes measure interface coverage, supporting contract localization, safety arguments, and trace parity for the tested fragment.

Conclusion: The results support contract localization, safety arguments, and trace parity for the tested fragment. However, the authors explicitly note that language superiority and usability remain outside the evaluation scope.

Abstract: Knowledge graph engineering often distributes accepted state, observations, constraints, processes, and hypothetical scenarios across artifacts whose combined execution contract remains external. We present PULSE, an Object-Process-Methodology-inspired language that localizes four operational roles and their write effects in one typed runtime. Here, modes denote operational roles rather than modal or deontic logic. The implemented contract fixes evidence non-overwrite, branch isolation, grounded multi-subject timers, guarded state change, and declaration-ranked event ordering over time and space; an external runner still decides whether evidence becomes an authoritative move. GeoSPARQL, SOSA, and SHACL remain generated views. A core calculus gives an effect-confinement lemma and six safety properties. Lean 4 checks kernel analogues for positions, evidence, clocks, monitors, atomicity, and branch source retention; 88 tests, 3,534 bounded checks, and 32 Lean/Python runtime-kernel cases bound the implementation claim to the checked cases. First-author implementations of a standards composition and a separate Sismic statechart reproduce the tested cold-chain trace. Across 37,440 generated temporal traces, PULSE matches a separate workflow and distinguishes ten single-field mutants. On the complete NOAA IBTrACS since1980 subset it agrees with GEOS and an event sweep on 1,476,290 transition-zone pairs, including 4,800 sampled and 12,831 duration-qualified events. Project-specific GeoSPARQL probes measure interface coverage. Overall, the results support contract localization, safety arguments, and trace parity for the tested fragment; language superiority and usability remain outside the evaluation.

</details>


### [60] [HyperAgent: Planning and Acting over Tool-Schema Hypergraphs for Tool-Use LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02650)
*Zian Zhai,Xingyu Tan,Gaowang Zou,Xiaoyang Wang,Wenjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyperAgent models tool relationships via a directed Tool-Schema Hypergraph and uses it to guide dynamic tool-use planning. It constructs a schema-aware Task DAG and performs deficit-oriented expansion during execution, improving task completion while reducing API calls, LLM interactions, and token consumption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM tool-use agents rely on implicit reasoning from textual descriptions to infer tool compositions, which is inefficient and unreliable for complex, evolving real-world tasks. There is a need for explicit, structured modeling of tool relationships to enable more robust planning.

Method: The authors model tool relations at the schema level as a directed Tool-Schema Hypergraph, where tools are hyperedges connecting required input-schema nodes to output-schema nodes. HyperAgent first extracts a task-relevant tool context graph from the hypergraph, then constructs a schema-aware Task DAG. During execution, it dynamically realizes subtasks via state-conditioned tool support graphs using deficit-oriented expansion, which identifies unresolved requirements and retrieves supporting producer tools based on the current agent state.

Result: Experiments on the AppWorld benchmark show that HyperAgent improves task completion performance while reducing redundant API calls, LLM interactions, and token consumption compared to existing agent baselines.

Conclusion: Explicit schema-level modeling of tool relations via a hypergraph, combined with deficit-oriented dynamic planning, provides a more efficient and reliable approach to tool-use planning for LLM agents.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external tools to complete complex real-world tasks. However, reliable tool-use planning remains challenging due to the limitations of implicit reasoning and the evolving nature of real-world execution environments. Existing tool-use agents typically rely on LLMs to infer tool compositions from textual descriptions, which can lead to inefficient exploration and unreliable execution in complex tasks. To address these challenges, we model tool relations at the schema level and construct a directed Tool--Schema Hypergraph, in which tools are represented as hyperedges from their required input-schema nodes to their output-schema nodes. Furthermore, we propose HyperAgent, a Tool--Schema Hypergraph-guided framework for dynamic planning and execution. Given a task, HyperAgent first extracts a task-relevant tool context graph and uses it to guide the construction of a schema-aware Task DAG. During execution, HyperAgent dynamically realizes each subtask by constructing a state-conditioned tool support graph through deficit-oriented expansion, which identifies unresolved requirements and retrieves supporting producer tools according to the current agent state. Experiments on AppWorld demonstrate that HyperAgent improves task completion performance while reducing redundant API calls, LLM interactions, and token consumption compared with existing agent baselines.

</details>


### [61] [Hybrid LLM-Augmented Reinforcement Learning Agents for Complex Sequential Decision Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03502)
*Christophe D. Hounwanou,John Emeka Eze,Yaé Ulrich Gaba*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hybrid agent architecture that combines LLM-driven planning (subgoal generation, structured plans) with RL-based action optimization for long-horizon sequential decision tasks, achieving improved sample efficiency, success rates, and action coherence over single-paradigm baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents excel at high-level reasoning and task decomposition but struggle with precise action optimization in long-horizon sequential tasks. Conversely, RL excels at sequential control but lacks the abstraction and planning capabilities needed for complex scenarios. This complementarity motivates a hybrid approach that bridges the gap.

Method: An architecture where an LLM generates subgoals, structured plans, and contextual guidance, while a downstream RL agent refines low-level actions through environment interaction. The LLM provides hierarchical decomposition; the RL component handles fine-grained action optimization based on environmental feedback.

Result: Experiments on sequential decision tasks show that the hybrid LLM-RL agent achieves improved sample efficiency, higher success rates, and more coherent action trajectories compared to both RL-only and LLM-only baselines.

Conclusion: The LLM-augmented RL paradigm represents a promising direction for building more capable autonomous systems by combining the complementary strengths of language model reasoning and reinforcement learning control.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown strong capabilities in reasoning, planning, and tool-use, enabling new forms of autonomous agents. However, LLM-based agents struggle with long-horizon sequential decision tasks that require precise action optimization and environment interaction. Reinforcement Learning (RL), while effective for sequential control, often lacks the high-level abstraction and task decomposition abilities needed for complex scenarios. This paper introduces an LLM-Augmented Reinforcement Learning Agent that integrates LLM-driven planning with RL-based action optimization. The proposed architecture leverages the LLM to generate subgoals, structured plans, and contextual guidance, while the RL agent refines low-level actions through interaction with the environment. Experiments on sequential decision tasks demonstrate improved sample efficiency, higher success rates, and more coherent action trajectories compared to RL-only and LLM-only baselines. This hybrid paradigm highlights a promising direction for building more capable autonomous systems.

</details>


### [62] [RF-HOI: Recognize Human-Object Interaction with Radio Frequency Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00289)
*Lihao Wang,Linlu Gao,Jiacan Yu,Yanyu Lin,Yifan Yin,Jianxin Wang,Tianmin Shu,Renjie Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RF-HOI is the first framework that uses only multimodal RF signals (mmWave radar + RFID) for Human-Object Interaction recognition, leveraging a simulator to generate large-scale synthetic RF data, achieving near-vision performance while preserving privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-based HOI recognition suffers from privacy concerns and poor lighting conditions. Existing solutions rely on cameras, which are intrusive and fail in darkness. The authors aim to achieve robust HOI recognition using only RF signals, which are privacy-preserving and illumination-invariant.

Method: RF-HOI fuses mmWave radar (for action/motion sensing) and RFID (for object identification) into a single recognition pipeline. To address data scarcity, the authors build a simulator that synthesizes multimodal RF data for diverse HOI scenarios at scale, and then fine-tune the model with a small amount of real-world data.

Result: RF-HOI outperforms all RF-based baselines and approaches the performance of vision-based models. The synthetic training data significantly boosts real-world performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of the RF synthesis pipeline.

Conclusion: Multimodal RF sensing is a viable, privacy-preserving alternative to vision for HOI recognition. The combination of radar-RFID fusion and scalable RF data synthesis effectively overcomes single-modality limitations and data scarcity, paving the way for deployment in real-world intelligent systems.

Abstract: Recognizing Human-Object Interactions (HOI) is essential for intelligent systems, underpinning applications in virtual and augmented reality, embodied AI, and assistive robotics. However, vision-based HOI methods face challenges in privacy concerns and poor light conditions. In this work, we introduce RF-HOI, the first framework that only uses radio frequency (RF) signals for HOI recognition. A key challenge of RF-HOI is that single-modality RF sensing is insufficient to recognize both actions and the objects being interacted with. RF-HOI addresses this through a novel modality fusion that combines mmWave radar and RFID, enabling simultaneous action recognition and target identification. Another challenge is limited training data across diverse setups, which impairs the generalizability of the recognition model. To overcome this, we develop a simulator that synthesizes multimodal RF data for diverse HOIs at scale, allowing us to fine-tune with only a small amount of real-world data. Experiment results show that RF-HOI outperforms all baselines, approaching vision model performance, and that our diverse synthetic training data can significantly boost our system's performance on real-world scenarios. These results highlight the potential of multimodal RF sensing for robust and privacy-preserving HOI recognition as well as the effectiveness of our RF data synthesis.

</details>


### [63] [Explainable AI for the EU Right to Explanation: A Systematic Review of the Law-XAI Translation Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02699)
*Benjamin Fresz,Elena Dubovitskaya,Marco F. Huber*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic review of XAI literature (2024+) in the context of the EU Right to Explanation reveals widespread misinterpretation of legal frameworks, conflation of explanation form and content, and lack of interdisciplinary rigor. The authors propose an Addressee/Purpose Framework and a four-phase operationalization blueprint to bridge the gap between legal mandates and technical feasibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The EU grants individuals a Right to Explanation for consequential automated decisions (GDPR Art. 15(1)(h), AIA Art. 86), but whether XAI can satisfy this right in practice is poorly understood. Without clarity, individuals cannot effectively contest automated decisions affecting their lives, and the right risks becoming a hollow formality.

Method: Systematic literature review following a deliberately broad search strategy across 2643 initial records, narrowed to 57 full texts, of which only 19 demonstrated substantive integration of both legal and technical perspectives. Papers were limited to 2024 onward, coinciding with the final AIA publication. Analysis focused on identifying patterns of legal misinterpretation and conceptual gaps.

Result: Three problematic patterns emerged: (1) most papers misidentify the GDPR legal basis for the Right to Explanation; (2) few engage with the CJEU's Dun & Bradstreet judgment; (3) the distinction between explanation form (governed by addressee) and content (governed by legal purpose) is routinely conflated. Only 19 of 57 papers achieved substantive legal-technical integration.

Conclusion: The field lacks adequate interdisciplinary synthesis. The authors propose the Addressee/Purpose Framework to disentangle form and content, a four-phase blueprint for operationalizing the Right to Explanation, and six open research questions. Without progress, the right risks remaining a formal obligation without a technically realizable compliance pathway.

Abstract: When algorithms make or influence consequential decisions---about loan eligibility, hiring, or healthcare---EU law grants affected individuals a Right to Explanation. Yet whether (and how) Explainable AI (XAI) can satisfy this right in practice remains poorly understood, with direct implications for individuals' ability to contest automated decisions that affect their lives. This paper presents a systematic literature review of XAI in the context of the EU Right to Explanation, with particular focus on Art. 15(1)(h) GDPR, Art. 86 AI Act (AIA), and related instruments. We consider papers published from 2024 onwards, as the final version of the AIA was published in July 2024---with Art. 86 being added late. From 2643 initial records identified by a deliberately broad search, we review 57 full texts, of which only 19 papers demonstrate substantive integration of both legal and technical perspectives, showing gaps in the interdisciplinary synthesis of the current regulatory framework. We document three problematic patterns across the corpus: Most misidentify the GDPR legal basis; few engage with the CJEU's Dun & Bradstreet judgment (likely due to publication timing); and the distinction between explanation form (governed by addressee) and content (governed by legal purpose) is often conflated. We conceptualize this as the Addressee/Purpose Framework, propose a four-phase blueprint for operationalization, and identify six concrete open research questions. Without further progress, the Right to Explanation risks remaining a formal obligation without a technically realizable path to compliance.

</details>


### [64] [Adversarial Fast-Moving Real-World Domains as Test Beds for Benchmarking AI Scientist Capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03569)
*William Bolton,Philip Torr*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes using complex, adversarial, fast-moving real-world domains (Formula 1 car design and Magic: The Gathering deck building) as benchmarks for evaluating AI scientists' ability to generate novel ideas. While models can produce plausible outputs, they struggle with filtering and prioritization — the best GPT-5.2 matched only 10/40 real F1 innovations, and decks rarely aligned with expert Pro Tour solutions, though card selection correlated with expert choices (Spearman ρ=0.74).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for AI scientific reasoning rely on synthetic tasks or retrospective targets confounded by prior exposure. The authors argue that real-world, fast-moving, adversarial domains where experts independently produce observable outputs provide a more authentic testbed for evaluating novelty, reasoning, and hypothesis formulation in AI scientists — addressing the gap in assessing genuine scientific ideation rather than recall or replication.

Method: The framework is instantiated in two structurally distinct domains: (1) Formula 1, where models generate car design concepts for the upcoming 2026 season and are evaluated against real pre-season innovations as ground truth; (2) Magic: The Gathering, where models propose competitive decks from a recently updated card pool and are benchmarked against 19 Pro Tour decklists. Multiple frontier models are tested, with outputs compared to expert-generated ground truth using metrics like match counts and Spearman rank correlation.

Result: In F1, GPT-5.2 matched 10 out of 40 real innovations across 166 generated ideas. In MTG, the best deck (Gemini 3 Flash) recovered 5 of 7 new-set cards from the third-place Pro Tour deck. Across all 108 model-generated decks, the cards most frequently selected by models were also those most widely adopted by Pro Tour decks (Spearman ρ=0.74, p=0.0003), indicating models identify individually valuable components but fail to synthesize them into coherent, winning strategies.

Conclusion: The key capability gap for AI scientists lies not in idea generation per se, but in filtering, prioritization, and producing coherent novelty. Models can identify relevant components but cannot reliably assemble them into expert-quality solutions, suggesting that future advances should focus on evaluation and integration capabilities rather than raw ideation.

Abstract: Benchmarking the ability of AI scientists to generate novel ideas is notoriously difficult. Existing benchmarks in this field have made progress in evaluating scientific reasoning and research replication, but often rely on synthetic tasks or retrospective targets, which may be confounded by prior exposure. We hypothesize that complex, adversarial, fast-moving real-world domains where expert practitioners independently generate observable outputs can provide a practical solution to fill this gap and evaluate the capabilities needed for AI scientists, including reasoning, novelty, and hypothesis formulation. We instantiate this framework in two structurally different domains, Formula 1 (F1), where models ideate around car design concepts for the 2026 season, and real pre-season innovations provide a ground truth, and Magic: The Gathering (MTG), where models propose decks from a recently updated card pool and are evaluated against 19 Pro Tour (PT) decklists. Across both domains, models produce plausible outputs, but few align with real-world expert solutions. In F1, the best model, GPT-5.2 matched 10 of 40 real innovations with 166 ideas proposed across runs. In MTG, the best deck from Gemini 3 Flash recovered 5 of 7 new-set cards from the third-place PT deck, and across all 108 decks, the cards models selected most often were also the cards most widely adopted by PT decks (Spearman $ρ= 0.74$, $p = 0.0003$). These results suggest that a key capability gap for AI scientists is not idea generation, but filtering, prioritization, and coherent novelty.

</details>


### [65] [Predictive Set Theory: A Generative Framework for Cognitive Architecture with Operationalized Core Mechanisms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02704)
*Yiyang Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Predictive Set Theory (PST) is introduced as a formal generative framework that reconstructs cognitive architecture from first principles using minimal set-theoretic operations, offering a design specification for systems maintaining internal consistency under incomplete information and resolving classical problems like Russell's paradox and the grounding of negative feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing predictive processing theories lack operational definitions for the structure of a prediction, standardized responses to prediction error, and mechanisms for consistency across updates. Bayesian cognitive science presupposes a closed hypothesis space and fails to explain how objects become discrete, identifiable referents. PST aims to fill these gaps by providing a rigorous, generative foundation for cognition.

Method: PST builds cognition from a minimal set of operations: a sensor formalized as an identity function, set-theoretic state refresh, and three fundamental reference chains (reference, counter-reference, and semi-reference). From these primitives, it formally derives core cognitive functions including state sequences, demand, comparison, efficiency, and finite-horizon probabilistic planning.

Result: The framework yields novel resolutions to Russell's paradox, the cognitive status of Gödelian incompleteness, the grounding of negative feedback, and the comprehension of film editing. It constitutes a design specification for any system that must maintain internal consistency while acting under incomplete information and irreversible risk.

Conclusion: The primary purpose is to establish, through the public academic record, the originality and completeness of the Predictive Set Theory framework as a foundational alternative to both predictive processing and Bayesian cognitive science.

Abstract: Predictive processing theories portray the brain as a hierarchical prediction engine that minimizes prediction error, yet they lack operational definitions for the structure of a "prediction," the standardized response to a prediction error, and the mechanism that maintains consistency across successive updates. Bayesian cognitive science attempts to subsume all uncertainty under probabilistic belief updating, but it presupposes a closed hypothesis space and provides no generative account of how the objects over which probabilities are distributed become discrete, identifiable referents in the first place. This paper introduces Predictive Set Theory (PST), a formal generative framework that reconstructs cognitive architecture from first principles. PST anchors cognition in a minimal set of operations---a sensor formalized as an identity function, set-theoretic state refresh, and three fundamental forms of reference chains (reference, counter-reference, and semi-reference)---and rigorously derives core cognitive functions including state sequences, demand, comparison, efficiency, and finite-horizon probabilistic planning. Rather than modeling neural mechanisms, PST constitutes a design specification for any system that must maintain internal consistency while acting under incomplete information and irreversible risk. The framework offers novel resolutions to classical problems such as Russell's paradox, the cognitive status of Gödelian incompleteness, the grounding of negative feedback, and the comprehension of film editing. The primary purpose of this paper is to establish, through the public academic record, the originality and completeness of the Predictive Set Theory framework.

</details>


### [66] [Is Inter-Seed Cross-Play Enough? Evaluating the Robustness of Zero-Shot Coordination Algorithms to Implementation Details](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03644)
*Maksymilian Wolski,Nicholas Hoernle,Johannes Forkel,Jakob Foerster*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates the robustness of Zero-Shot Coordination (ZSC) algorithms to implementation variations by introducing a new "cross-implementation cross-play" evaluation scheme. Testing the popular Other-Play algorithm, the authors find that standard single-implementation ZSC evaluation serves as a reasonable proxy for cross-implementation robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ZSC algorithms are evaluated almost exclusively using a single implementation with different random seeds, rarely varying implementation details like neural architecture. This leaves open questions about whether ZSC methods are robust to specification ambiguities and implementation variations that naturally arise when independent parties independently implement the same algorithm. The paper aims to fill this evaluation gap.

Method: The authors introduce a "cross-implementation cross-play" evaluation scheme that systematically varies implementation details known to affect MARL performance. They apply this scheme to evaluate Other-Play, a prominent ZSC algorithm, across multiple independent implementations to test robustness to real-world specification ambiguity.

Result: The findings are encouraging: for Other-Play, the standard ZSC evaluation protocol (single implementation, varying random seeds) proves to be a reasonable proxy for the more rigorous cross-implementation evaluation, suggesting robustness to the tested implementation variations.

Conclusion: The standard ZSC evaluation practice appears to be a valid approximation of cross-implementation robustness for Other-Play, though the authors establish a new methodological benchmark for more thorough ZSC evaluation going forward.

Abstract: AI agents deployed in real-world settings must be capable of coordinating with humans and other AI agents they have not encountered before. Zero-shot coordination (ZSC) algorithms aim to achieve this by specifying high-level learning rules such that independently engineered agents can coordinate with each other at test time. Rigorous evaluation of ZSC algorithms remains difficult: ideally, multiple independent implementations of each proposed algorithm must be used, reflecting the variation that arises when independent parties interpret and implement the same specification. In practice, however, ZSC algorithms have almost exclusively been evaluated using a single implementation trained across different random seeds, with only a handful of works additionally varying the neural network architecture. This leaves open questions about robustness to specification ambiguities and implementation details. In this work, we provide the first systematic evaluation of this robustness. We introduce a new evaluation scheme, cross-implementation cross-play, varying implementation details that prior work has shown to affect the performance of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms, and we evaluate Other-Play, a popular ZSC algorithm, with this scheme. Our findings are encouraging and suggest that, for Other-Play, the standard ZSC evaluation is, in fact, a reasonable proxy for this more thorough cross-implementation evaluation.

</details>


### [67] [Towards a new paradigm of scientific discovery with socialized artificial intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02775)
*Xinjie Yao,Xingxin Xu,Xiyuan Gao,Zhoupeng Guo,Kunlong Yang,Dengyu Zhao,Siqi Zhao,Zhihe Fan,Yichen Dong,Xin Li,Jiekang Feng,Jiahe Wu,Sen Wang,Beiming Yu,Kejia Zhao,Ruipu Zhao,Jiaqi Zhou,Heyang Li,Jianjun Chen,Anbo Dai,Xin Liu,Zhengtao Yu,Qinghua Hu,Pengfei Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BLAZE proposes a paradigm shift from AI-as-assistant to AI-as-organizational-infrastructure for science, integrating persistent knowledge, collective reasoning, empirical validation, and human judgment into a continuous, cumulative discovery lifecycle.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Science now faces a bottleneck where producing more information is insufficient; the core challenge is organizing expanding knowledge, reasoning, and evidence into a coherent, traceable, and cumulative discovery process rather than leaving research fragmented across isolated tasks.

Method: BLAZE (Bridging Literature, Agents, and Zero-gap Experimentation) is introduced as a paradigm of "socialized scientific intelligence" that connects persistent knowledge bases, AI agents for collective reasoning, empirical validation loops, and human judgment within an integrated, continuous research lifecycle — enabling iteration among inquiry, criticism, and revision.

Result: The paradigm is presented as a conceptual framework rather than an empirical study; the key claim is that scientific intelligence emerges from sustained interaction among knowledge, hypotheses, experiments, and collective verification — not from computation alone.

Conclusion: Socialized scientific intelligence may underpin the next era of science by extending the scale, depth, and continuity of collective inquiry while preserving human creativity, judgment, and responsibility, rather than replacing human discovery.

Abstract: Scientific discovery has advanced through successive transformations in the organization of knowledge. Observation and experimentation established the empirical foundations of science. Theory made it possible to derive general principles from particular phenomena. Computation extended inquiry into systems beyond direct observation, while data-intensive methods opened new spaces of pattern and prediction. Science now confronts a different frontier. The central challenge is no longer simply to produce more information, but to organize expanding knowledge, reasoning, and evidence into a coherent process of discovery. Here, we introduce Bridging Literature, Agents, and Zero-gap Experimentation (BLAZE), a paradigm of socialized scientific intelligence. BLAZE conceives AI not as an assistant for isolated research tasks, but as an organizational infrastructure for scientific discovery. It connects persistent knowledge, collective reasoning, empirical validation, and human judgment within a continuous research lifecycle, transforming fragmented activities into a cumulative process of inquiry, criticism, and revision. The central premise of BLAZE is that scientific intelligence does not arise from computation alone. It emerges from the sustained interaction among knowledge, hypotheses, experiments, and collective verification. By organizing humans and machines within a shared scientific process, BLAZE makes discovery more traceable, reproducible, and cumulative while preserving human creativity, judgment, and responsibility. Socialized scientific intelligence may provide a foundation for the next era of science. Its purpose is not to replace human discovery, but to extend the scale, depth, and continuity of collective scientific inquiry.

</details>


### [68] [BAP-SQL: Budget-Aware Observation Planning for Agentic Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02876)
*Chong Peng,Pin Qian,Su Wang,Yihang Chen,Varun Sah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BAP-SQL introduces budget-aware planning for agentic text-to-SQL, treating observation formation as a budget-control stage that estimates query risk, rewrites SQL when beneficial, and enforces hard limits via a runtime shield. It improves tight-budget success across multiple backbones while using fewer tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In agentic text-to-SQL, broad queries can waste context window space and database work before useful evidence appears. Post-hoc compression cannot recover already-omitted rows or expended computational work, motivating a proactive budget-control approach rather than reactive compression.

Method: BAP-SQL introduces observation formation as a budget-control stage with three components: (1) query risk estimation to predict whether a query will be wasteful, (2) SQL rewriting when the risk estimate suggests modification would be beneficial, and (3) an independent runtime shield that enforces hard budget limits during execution. The approach is evaluated across general 4B, specialized FINER-SQL 4B, and 7B backbone models.

Result: On the primary BIRD-derived benchmark, BAP-SQL achieves 3.4–3.6 percentage point gains over matched supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines while consuming 4.5–5.0% fewer tokens. Matched retraining and task-level transfer experiments attribute gains to policy-visible planning and budget-sensitive rescue behavior. Benefits attenuate as model capability and budget increase, and reverse at the loosest budget setting. Database work is not reduced.

Conclusion: BAP-SQL demonstrates that proactive budget-aware observation formation is more effective than post-hoc compression for agentic text-to-SQL under tight budget constraints. The approach's effectiveness diminishes with larger models and budgets, and it does not address database work reduction, suggesting complementary directions for future work.

Abstract: Tool-using agents do not merely consume observations: their actions determine what arrives next. In agentic text-to-SQL, a broad query can spend context and database work before useful evidence appears, while post-hoc compression cannot recover omitted rows or expended work. We present BAP-SQL, which treats observation formation as a budget-control stage: it estimates query risk, rewrites SQL when useful, and delegates hard limits to an independent runtime shield. Across general 4B, specialized FINER-SQL 4B, and 7B backbones, BAP-SQL improves tight-budget success. On the primary BIRD-derived setting, it gains 3.4/3.6 percentage points over matched SFT while using 4.5/5.0% fewer tokens. Matched retraining and task-level transfer associate the gain with policy-visible planning and budget-sensitive rescue. The benefit attenuates as model capability and budget increase, reverses at the loosest setting, and does not reduce database work.

</details>


### [69] [Socially Grounded Agentic AI: Coordinating Plural Perspectives through Social Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03910)
*Matt Ratto,Abhishek Moturu,Daniel Silver*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper argues that pluralistic AI alignment should be reframed through social theory, moving from output diversification to socially grounded coordination. It translates sociological concepts—roles, interaction, and fields of power—into concrete design implications for building AI systems that can recognize, represent, and respond to multiple legitimate perspectives in structured and accountable ways.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems are deployed across diverse social contexts, alignment cannot rely on a single unified value set. Current pluralistic alignment approaches lack a clear theoretical account of how values are socially organized, contested, and coordinated. The paper addresses this gap by drawing on social theory to provide conceptual and design resources for pluralistic alignment.

Method: The paper draws on established sociological traditions to reconceptualize perspectives as structured by roles, shaped through interaction, and distributed across fields of power and expertise. It then translates these theoretical insights into concrete design implications, including role-based representations, structured coordination among perspectives, and context-sensitive evaluation. For agentic systems, it extends alignment requirements to role activations, deliberative traces, aggregation rules, and feedback loops—not merely final outputs.

Result: The paper outlines a design space for pluralistically aligned systems organized around socially grounded coordination rather than output diversification. It identifies the need to align role activations, deliberative traces, aggregation rules, and feedback loops in agentic systems, and proposes directions for future empirical evaluation in real-world settings.

Conclusion: Pluralistic alignment should be repositioned as a problem of socially grounded coordination informed by social theory, rather than mere output diversification.
