This reframing enables the design of systems that engage multiple perspectives in structured and accountable ways, with concrete directions identified for future implementation and empirical evaluation.

Abstract: As AI systems are deployed across increasingly diverse social contexts, alignment can no longer be framed as the optimization of a single, unified set of values. Instead, systems must be able to recognize, represent, and respond to multiple legitimate perspectives. This has led to growing interest in pluralistic alignment, which seeks to move beyond one-size-fits-all models of appropriate behaviour. However, current approaches often lack a clear account of how values are socially organized, contested, and coordinated in practice. In this paper, we argue that social theory provides essential conceptual and design resources for addressing these challenges. Drawing on established traditions in sociology, we show how perspectives can be understood as structured by roles, shaped through interaction, and distributed across fields of power and expertise. We translate these insights into concrete implications for AI system design, including role-based representations, structured coordination among perspectives, and context-sensitive evaluation. For agentic systems, this requires aligning not only final outputs, but also the role activations, deliberative traces, aggregation rules, and feedback loops through which those outputs are produced. Our contribution is to reposition pluralistic alignment as a problem of socially grounded coordination rather than output diversification. We outline a design space for systems that engage multiple perspectives in structured and accountable ways, and we identify directions for future work to implement and empirically evaluate these approaches in real-world settings.

</details>


### [70] [ChartAnno: Evaluating MLLMs for Chart Annotation Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03464)
*Zhenghan Chen,Zekai Shao,Lidan Tan,Xin Lin,Xingchen Zeng,Yi Shan,Ziyue Lin,Xiaoliang Fu,Xinyuan Liu,Yuetong Guo,Fen Wang,Bongshin Lee,Siming Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ChartAnno is a benchmark of 1,200 real-world charts for evaluating MLLMs on chart annotation generation. Evaluating 10 models reveals that proprietary models lead, specific instructions help, abstract intent inference is hardest, and chart images provide only limited gains (mainly in design metrics).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While MLLMs have advanced in chart understanding, generation, and editing, their ability to annotate existing charts—a common communicative task requiring semantic interpretation and appropriate placement of textual/graphical elements—remains underexplored.

Method: The authors introduce ChartAnno, a benchmark comprising 1,200 real-world charts with paired code and annotation instructions across three levels of instruction specificity. Ten representative MLLMs are evaluated under three input settings: (1) chart code alone, (2) chart code + chart image, and (3) chart image-only (ablation).

Result: Proprietary models outperform overall, though large open-source models are narrowing the gap. More specific instructions improve annotation quality. Inferring abstract intent remains the hardest task. Providing chart images yields limited overall gains, with improvements mainly in design-related metrics.

Conclusion: Chart annotation generation is a challenging task requiring both semantic grounding and effective annotation design. Current MLLMs struggle most with abstract intent inference, and multimodal input (code + image) provides only modest benefits over code alone.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in chart understanding, generation, and editing, but their ability to annotate existing charts remains underexplored. Annotating charts is a common yet challenging communicative task, requiring models to infer intended messages, interpret chart semantics, and place appropriate textual or graphical elements. To address this gap, we introduce ChartAnno, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on chart annotation generation. It contains 1,200 real-world charts with paired code and annotation instructions across three levels of instruction specificity. We evaluate 10 representative MLLMs under two primary input settings: (1) chart code alone and (2) both chart code and chart image, and further include a chart image-only ablation study. Results show that proprietary models remain stronger overall, although large-scale open-source models narrow the gap. More specific instructions improve annotation quality, while inferring abstract intent remains most difficult for current MLLMs. Providing chart images brings limited overall gains, with improvements mainly appearing in design-related metrics. These findings highlight chart annotation generation as a challenging task requiring semantic grounding and effective annotation design. Code and data will be released in a future version.

</details>


### [71] [VeriTrace: Human-Like Temporal Exploration Completes Agentic Action Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02878)
*Yu-Tung Liu,Cunxi Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriTrace introduces a multi-agent Verilog generation system with a complete debugging action space, enabling hypothesis-driven waveform exploration. It achieves 100% Pass@1 on VerilogEval-V2, outperforming prior systems that plateau at ~95% due to restricted debugging capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-of-the-art multi-agent Verilog RTL generation systems plateau at ~95% accuracy because their debugging action space is incomplete — they restrict signal inspection, time-window querying, or both, reducing debugging to pattern matching rather than true root-cause analysis.

Method: VeriTrace employs a multi-agent architecture with an Inspector agent that has independent control over signal selection, time-window bounds, and iteration depth — a capability termed Agentic Temporal Exploration. This mirrors how human verification engineers form hypotheses, query waveforms for evidence, and iteratively refine their understanding.

Result: VeriTrace achieves 100% Pass@1 on VerilogEval-V2, making it the first system to attain perfect functional correctness on this benchmark. On a shared Claude Sonnet 4.0 backbone, it outperforms the strongest reproduced baseline by +5.1%.

Conclusion: Debugging agency — providing agents with a complete, unrestricted debugging action space — is the critical factor that closes the final accuracy gap in automated Verilog RTL generation, pushing performance from ~95% to 100%.

Abstract: Large language models have shown promise for automated Verilog RTL generation, yet state-of-the-art multi-agent systems plateau at ~95% accuracy on standard benchmarks. We trace this ceiling to an incomplete debugging action space: existing systems restrict which signals the agent can inspect, which time windows it can query, or both, reducing debugging to pattern matching on a narrow, predetermined view of circuit behavior rather than hypothesis-driven root-cause analysis. We present VeriTrace, a multi-agent system whose Inspector agent operates over a complete debugging action space, with independent control over signal selection, time-window bounds, and iteration depth. This capability, which we term Agentic Temporal Exploration, enables the agent to form hypotheses about failure causes, query the waveform for evidence, and refine its understanding iteratively, mirroring the exploratory process of human verification engineers. VeriTrace achieves 100\% Pass@1 on VerilogEval-V2, the first system to attain perfect functional correctness on this benchmark. On a shared Claude Sonnet 4.0 backbone, VeriTrace outperforms the strongest reproduced baseline by +5.1%, demonstrating that debugging agency closes the final accuracy gap.

</details>


### [72] [Interpreting Black-Box Large Language Models with Sentence-Level Energy Landscapes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02879)
*Maryam Rezaee,Pooriya Safaei,Maryam Asgarinezhad,Fatemeh Seyyedsalehi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A post-hoc, sentence-level attribution interpreter for proprietary LLMs is proposed, using an Energy-Based Model surrogate to quantify prompt sentence influence on target outputs without additional API calls after training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proprietary LLMs accessed via closed APIs lack interpretability, creating a barrier to responsible deployment. Existing attribution methods require repeated API queries or internal access, which is costly or infeasible.

Method: An Energy-Based Model (EBM) is trained as a surrogate to capture conceptual consistency between prompts and responses. This energy landscape then guides training of a lightweight interpreter network. The interpreter operates standalone post-training, quantifying sentence-level influence on user-specified target outputs without further API queries. Training globally across diverse inputs captures broader generation patterns and reduces instance-specific biases.

Result: The EBM accurately simulates the target LLM, and the trained interpreter effectively identifies which prompt sentences most influence the generation of specific target outputs.

Conclusion: The proposed model-agnostic, post-hoc framework enables practical interpretability for black-box proprietary LLMs, offering efficient sentence-level attribution without ongoing API dependency.

Abstract: The widespread adoption of proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs) accessed strictly through closed APIs has created a critical challenge for responsible deployment: a fundamental lack of interpretability. To address this, we propose a model-agnostic, post-hoc attribution interpreter operating at the sentence level. Our approach trains an Energy-Based Model (EBM) as a surrogate to capture the LLM's internal conceptual consistency between prompts and responses. This energy landscape guides the training of a lightweight interpreter network. Uniquely, our interpreter operates as a standalone tool; once trained, it quantifies the influence of prompt sentences on a user-specified target output without requiring further API queries to the LLM. By globally training a local interpreter across diverse inputs, our framework captures broader generation patterns and mitigates instance-specific biases. Experiments demonstrate that our EBM accurately simulates the target LLM, allowing the interpreter to effectively identify the prompt sentences most influential in generating specific target outputs.

</details>


### [73] [Hypercubes, Hyperplanes, and Constraint-Induced Complexity Collapse in Atomic Concept Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02930)
*Irene Tsapara*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reexamines higher-arity atomic concept learning through the geometry of hypercubes and hyperplanes of ground instances, revealing that logical complexity is not uniformly distributed but concentrated along the full diagonal hyperplane, while all other hyperplanes collapse into finitely many elementary-equivalence classes bounded independently of term depth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand where logical complexity is concentrated in atomic concept learning by analyzing the structural asymmetry of the ambient hypercube of ground atoms, and to explain why the full diagonal behaves exceptionally compared to other hyperplanes.

Method: Uses a geometric-logical framework mapping ground instances onto an r-dimensional hypercube, analyzes hyperplane elementary-equivalence classes, and employs reduction-theoretic machinery — canonical simple concepts, minimal orderings, and representative reductions — to characterize hyperplane behavior. The binary case, ternary hypercube, and higher-dimensional generalizations are treated explicitly.

Result: Every hyperplane except the full diagonal collapses into finitely many elementary-equivalence classes with a bound independent of term depth; the full diagonal's class count grows unboundedly. The ternary case reveals orthogonal families, partial diagonals, and the exceptional full diagonal as the core phenomena.

Conclusion: Complexity in atomic concept learning is localized rather than uniform, with the full diagonal serving as the unique locus of unbounded complexity. This suggests modern interpretations in constrained hypothesis spaces and structured classification.

Abstract: We revisit higher-arity atomic concept learning through the geometry of hypercubes and hyperplanes of ground instances. Our starting point is the observation that the ambient r-dimensional hypercube of ground atoms is not structurally uniform. Its logical complexity is organized by hyperplanes: every hyperplane other than the full diagonal collapses into finitely many elementary-equivalence classes, with a bound independent of the term depth, while the full diagonal is exceptional and its class count grows without bound. This asymmetry is not merely geometric. It reflects the reduction-theoretic structure of the concepts themselves. Building on a higher-dimensional framework developed in the author's earlier work, we reinterpret these results through canonical simple concepts, minimal orderings, and representative reductions. This yields a taxonomy of hyperplane behavior in higher dimensions and shows that complexity is localized rather than spread uniformly through the instance space. The paper includes a fully worked binary case, an explicit treatment of the ternary hypercube, and an unpacked account of the reduction machinery that drives the collapse. The three-dimensional case already exhibits the essential phenomenon of orthogonal families, partial diagonals, and the exceptional full diagonal. This geometric-logical perspective clarifies where complexity is concentrated in atomic concept learning and suggests a modern interpretation in terms of constrained hypothesis spaces and structured classification.

</details>


### [74] [When Compression Scores Cannot Decide: Information Boundaries for Group-Robust LLM Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02940)
*Andrew Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates why statistically reliable compression metrics can still select suboptimal model configurations, formalizes the problem through "information interfaces" and conic pricing laws, and proposes group-resolved and endpoint-based selection methods that outperform standard approaches across dense LLMs and mixture-of-experts architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A reproducible compression statistic (0.906 split-half reliability) can nonetheless select endpoints 6–7.7% worse than controls, revealing a fundamental gap between statistical reproducibility and decision quality. This motivates a formal framework for understanding what information a statistic preserves and what it discards, particularly regarding group-level structure and second-moment interactions.

Method: The authors introduce "information interfaces" to delimit which distinctions a statistic supports. For equal-weight groups, a conic law provides the exact pooling price for positive linear fixed-candidate damage, encompassing diagonal and full PSD second moments. Three two-world constructions and an exact observation-fiber radius characterize what pooled moments, group-local moments, and reference-path curvature leave unresolved. A group-resolved diagonal is tested for damage-order recovery. Practical allocation (coarse depth) and model-specific complete-mask endpoint selection are evaluated on dense LLMs. In OLMoE, router traces predict singleton direction, and finite-menu decisions on one layer yield held-out KL reductions.

Result: A group-resolved diagonal recovers broad damage order (Spearman ρ = 0.9239) while fine order remains weak. Coarse depth allocation reduces worst-group perplexity inflation by 12.6–20.9% across three dense LLMs versus balanced uniform allocation. Model-specific complete-mask endpoint selection improves over references by 2.7–8.0%. In OLMoE, router traces predict singleton direction (114/192 vs. 81/192 under strongest relabeling). Finite-menu decisions on one layer yield held-out worst-group KL reductions of 13.7% and 7.2%.

Conclusion: Local measurements can construct candidates, but selection must be licensed by complete candidate endpoints or a validated uniform guarantee, with uncertainty calibrated to every comparison. The gap between reproducibility and decision quality can be systematically characterized and mitigated through group-resolved methods and endpoint-aware selection protocols.

Abstract: A reproducible compression statistic can still select the wrong candidate. A dense pruning score with 0.906 split-half reliability predicted a 16.1% gain. Its selected endpoint was 6.0% and 7.7% worse than two controls. We model the gap through information interfaces that delimit which distinctions each statistic supports. For equal-weight groups, a conic law gives the exact pooling price for positive linear fixed-candidate damage, including diagonal and full PSD second moments. Three two-world constructions and an exact observation-fiber radius characterize what pooled moments, group-local moments, and reference-path curvature leave unresolved. A group-resolved diagonal recovers broad damage order (Spearman 0.9239) while fine order remains weak. Relative to balanced uniform allocation, a coarse depth allocation cuts worst-group perplexity inflation by 12.6--20.9% across three dense LLMs. Model-specific complete-mask endpoint selection improves over those references by 2.7--8.0%. In OLMoE, router traces predict singleton direction (114/192 versus 81/192 under the strongest relabeling). Finite-menu decisions on one layer yield held-out worst-group KL reductions of 13.7% and 7.2%. Local measurements construct candidates. Selection is licensed by complete candidate endpoints or a validated uniform guarantee, with uncertainty calibrated to every comparison.

</details>


### [75] [On the missing data layer and a potential solution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02949)
*Francis F Daniel,Mauro Ibañez,Francis Perelman,Marian Basti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DataHub is a proposed task-first data infrastructure for Latin America that organizes AI datasets through a hierarchical ontology (task/domain/language) with mechanisms for discovery, metadata, contribution, licensing, and reuse, addressing the region's missing dataset layer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latin America lacks foundational AI infrastructure, specifically the dataset and benchmark layers. Existing Latin American AI datasets are scattered across platforms with no unified index (discovery problem), and even with perfect indexing, the total volume is insufficient for frontier AI development (supply problem).

Method: The authors propose DataHub, a task-first data infrastructure organized through the ontology pattern "/<task?>/<domain?>/<language?>". It incorporates structured mechanisms for dataset discovery, metadata standardization, contribution workflows, licensing frameworks, and reuse protocols.

Result: The paper presents the architectural design and rationale for DataHub. Specific empirical results or implementation outcomes are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: A task-first, ontology-driven data infrastructure like DataHub is necessary to address the compounding problems of dataset discovery and supply in Latin America, laying the groundwork for a functional AI ecosystem in the region.

Abstract: Latin America is missing two foundational layers of AI infrastructure: the dataset layer and the benchmark layer. This paper targets the dataset layer. The dataset layer faces two compounding problems: discovery and supply. Latin American AI datasets exist but are scattered across platforms with no shared index. Even with perfect indexing, the total volume would remain far below what frontier AI development requires. We propose DataHub: a task-first data infrastructure organized through the ontology /<task?>/<domain?>/<language?>, with mechanisms for dataset discovery, metadata, contribution, licensing, and reuse.

</details>


### [76] [Neurosymbolic Reasoning with Incremental Knowledge for Sample Efficient Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02993)
*Subrat Prasad Panda,Blaise Genest,Arvind Easwaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes neurosymbolic hierarchical RL with Incremental Knowledge (InK), where symbolic high-level planning uses an updatable knowledge representation and low-level neural modules learn motion primitives, significantly improving sample efficiency in sparse-reward, long-horizon navigation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard HRL encodes knowledge in fixed, non-updatable forms (e.g., architecture), making reasoning with incrementally learned knowledge impractical before sufficient environmental exposure. This leads to poor sample efficiency in sparse-reward, long-horizon settings.

Method: The method combines: (1) symbolic high-level components that perform planning (e.g., D*) on an updatable Incremental Knowledge representation, (2) low-level goal-conditioned neural modules trained via reward shaping to learn motion primitives, and (3) Belief World Tree Search for optimal symbolic planning given prior world knowledge.

Result: Experiments on navigation tasks demonstrate that incorporating Incremental Knowledge substantially improves sample efficiency compared to fixed HRL baselines.

Conclusion: Neurosymbolic HRL with updatable incremental knowledge bridges the gap between symbolic planning and neural learning, enabling effective long-horizon reasoning and improved sample efficiency in sparse-reward environments.

Abstract: (Flat) Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents face significant challenges in environments with sparse rewards that require long-horizon reasoning. A compelling approach to improve sample efficiency is to incorporate knowledge into learning and decision-making. In standard Hierarchical RL (HRL), knowledge is encoded in a fixed, non-updatable form, such as architectural choices, and remains unchanged throughout learning. With fixed HRL, reasoning with incremental knowledge learned during exploration is impractical before sufficient environmental knowledge is acquired, leading to poor sample efficiency. In this work, we propose neurosymbolic HRL with {\em Incremental Knowledge (InK)}: symbolic high-level components perform {\em symbolic planning} (e.g. using $D^*$) on an updatable representation of current InK, while low-level goal-conditioned neural modules learn motion primitives through experience using reward shaping. Experiments on navigation tasks demonstrate that incorporating InK substantially improves sample efficiency. Additionally, to perform {\em optimal} symbolic planning given {\em prior} knowledge about the world, we develop Belief World Tree Search. The code is available at https://github.com/CPS-research-group/ink_bwts.

</details>


### [77] [On the missing benchmarks layer and a potential solution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02996)
*Francis F Daniel,Mauro Ibañez,Francis Perelman,Marian Basti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Latin America lacks a regional AI benchmark infrastructure, causing losses in auditability and optimization direction. The authors propose EvalsHub, with LatamBoard as its first instance—an open, task-first platform for publishing and comparing AI evaluations across models, workflows, and agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latin America lacks a foundational benchmark layer for native AI development, which prevents public institutions from independently auditing foreign AI systems and stops companies from optimizing AI for local problems with state-of-the-art performance. This gap results in a dual loss: loss of auditability and loss of optimization direction over critical AI infrastructure.

Method: Proposes EvalsHub, an open, task-first benchmark infrastructure. LatamBoard serves as its first regional instance, enabling universities, public institutions, professional communities, and companies to publish, execute, compare, and maintain evaluations across models, workflows, and agents. The system follows an open-by-design, incentive-driven construction approach and supports re-execution as new AI systems ship or after system changes.

Result: The paper presents a proposal rather than empirical results. The expected outcomes include restored auditability of foreign AI systems by regional institutions and improved optimization direction for companies building AI solutions tailored to Latin American contexts.

Conclusion: Establishing a regional benchmark layer via EvalsHub/LatamBoard is essential for Latin America to achieve sovereign AI evaluation capability and to direct AI optimization toward locally relevant, economically meaningful environments.

Abstract: Latin America is missing a foundational layer for native AI development: the benchmark layer. The benchmark layer does two things no other layer can - it audits AI systems against regional social requirements and it directs AI optimization in economically relevant environments. Without it, public institutions cannot independently evaluate foreign AI systems, and companies cannot optimize AI systems to solve local problems with SOTA performance. The cost of the missing layer is dual: a loss of auditability and a loss of optimization direction over a technology that is increasingly critical infrastructure. We propose an EvalsHub, with LatamBoard as its first regional instance - an open, task-first benchmark infrastructure where universities, public institutions, professional communities, and companies can publish, execute, compare, and maintain evaluations across models, workflows, and agents. Built once, measured forever - re-run by institutions as new AI systems ship and by industry teams after every system change. Open by design and incentive-driven by construction.

</details>


### [78] [ProPRL: Property-Aware Prerequisite Relation Learning in Educational Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03006)
*Xinghe Cheng,Jiapu Wang,Chaobo He,Ruihai Dong,Quanlong Guan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProPRL is a property-aware prerequisite relation learning framework that combines multi-view concept representations from hypergraphs and directed behavior graphs, adaptively fuses them via a pair-conditioned gate, and enforces an irreversibility constraint to penalize symmetric predictions, achieving SOTA on educational datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prerequisite relation learning methods treat the task as conventional link prediction, which fails to (1) adaptively integrate complementary educational evidence tailored to individual concept pairs, and (2) discourage contradictory reverse predictions where both directions of a pair are predicted as prerequisites.

Method: ProPRL consists of three key components: (1) dual-view concept representation learning from a concept-resource hypergraph and a directed learning-behavior graph with direction-preserving personalized propagation for multi-hop behavioral evidence; (2) a Pair-conditioned Gate that adaptively weights and fuses the two views for each candidate ordered concept pair; and (3) an Irreversibility Constraint, an anti-symmetry regularizer that penalizes high confidence in both directions of the same concept pair simultaneously.

Result: Experiments on multiple real-world educational datasets demonstrate that ProPRL achieves state-of-the-art performance on prerequisite relation learning.

Conclusion: The proposed ProPRL framework effectively addresses key limitations of prior work by enabling adaptive, pair-specific evidence fusion and enforcing directional consistency, leading to superior prerequisite relation prediction in educational settings.

Abstract: Prerequisite relation learning is central to adaptive instruction, yet existing methods often formulate it as conventional link prediction, limiting their ability to adaptively integrate complementary educational evidence for individual candidate pairs and to discourage contradictory reverse predictions. We propose ProPRL, a Property-aware Prerequisite Relation Learning framework. ProPRL first learns complementary concept representations from a concept-resource hypergraph and a directed learning-behavior graph, where direction-preserving personalized propagation aggregates multi-hop behavioral evidence. It then employs a Pair-conditioned Gate to adaptively weight and fuse the two views for each candidate ordered concept pair. Finally, an \textit{Irreversibility Constraint} introduces an anti-symmetry regularizer that penalizes simultaneously high confidence in both directions of the same concept pair. Experiments on multiple real-world educational datasets show that ProPRL achieves state-of-the-art performance on prerequisite relation learning.

</details>


### [79] [UrbanAgent: A Tool-Augmented Agent for Cross-System Urban Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03018)
*Jiayu Cao,Xingyuan Zeng,feiyu Li,Zhijing Huang,Xujie Yuan,Rongxiang Chen,Shimin Di,Libin Zheng,Jian Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Urban-Agent is an LLM-based agent framework that translates complex natural-language urban requests into executable cross-system workflows. It outperforms baselines by 10 points (71% task success rate) on a new benchmark, Urban-Eval, which evaluates both task results and execution quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern digital city services are fragmented with poor interoperability, forcing residents to manually navigate disconnected systems. Existing solutions — digital platforms, urban foundation models, and intelligent assistants — each tackle only isolated aspects and cannot reliably convert complex natural-language requests into executable, cross-system workflows.

Method: Urban-Agent couples an LLM's reasoning with a tool-set supporting code execution, API calls, and the Model Context Protocol. It uses an adaptive closed loop to: (1) clarify missing information before acting, (2) ground tool use in live observations, and (3) align final responses with observed evidence and task constraints. Urban-Eval, a new benchmark, assesses cross-system urban requests by evaluating task results and execution quality (tool coverage, dependency validity, evidence traceability).

Result: Urban-Agent achieves a 71% task success rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 10 percentage points. This performance advantage persists across multiple LLM backends: GPT-5-mini, Gemini-2.5-flash, DeepSeek-V4-flash, and Qwen3-235B-A22B.

Conclusion: A tool-augmented agent framework with adaptive closed-loop reasoning, combined with a purpose-built evaluation benchmark addressing both outcome and process quality, significantly advances the state of automated cross-system urban task execution.

Abstract: Modern cities rely on an increasing number of digital services to operate, but residents' daily needs are still difficult to meet. Services are fragmented and have little interoperability, placing a heavy operational burden on users. Existing digital platforms, urban foundation models, and intelligent assistants each address only isolated aspects of an urban task. But they struggle to reliably convert complex natural-language requests into executable cross-system workflows. We propose Urban-Agent, a tool-augmented agent framework for cross-system urban tasks. It couples the cognitive and reasoning capabilities of a large language model with a tool-set supporting code execution, API calls, and Model Context Protocol. Through one adaptive closed loop, it clarifies missing information before acting, grounds tool use in live observations, and aligns the final response with observed evidence and task constraints. To address the evaluation gap, we introduce Urban-Eval, a benchmark specifically designed for cross-system urban request. Unlike prior benchmarks that assess either general tool use or urban knowledge and reasoning, Urban-Eval evaluates both task results and execution quality, including required tool coverage, dependency validity, and evidence traceability. Experimental results indicate that Urban-Agent reaches a 71% task success rate, 10 points above the strongest baseline. This lead holds across GPT-5-mini, Gemini-2.5-flash, DeepSeek-V4-flash, and Qwen3-235B-A22B.

</details>


### [80] [LoCA: Forward-Only LLM Tuning after One-Shot Calibration with Local Credit Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03020)
*Linhan Xia,Rui Liu,Zhaofeng Zhang,Yihao Wang,Binrui Shen,Shengxin Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LoCA replaces repeated backpropagation in parameter-efficient fine-tuning with a one-time calibration pass. It computes local credit assignment maps from prediction errors to hidden-state corrections, then uses closed-form ridge regression to fit low-rank adapters — enabling forward-only tuning afterward with significant reductions in memory, time, and GPU requirements compared to LoRA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA still require repeated end-to-end backpropagation through the frozen backbone, demanding backward-capable hardware and activation storage/recomputation. The authors ask whether this costly backward chain can be replaced by a single calibration step, enabling forward-only adaptation on hardware without backward support.

Method: LoCA is a two-stage method. Stage 1 (calibration): one backward pass fits a low-rank linear map at each transformer block, projecting the final prediction error to a local hidden-state correction (local credit assignment). Stage 2 (adaptation): these maps are reused to generate blockwise regression targets from forward activations; low-rank adapters are then fitted via closed-form ridge regression, requiring no further backpropagation.

Result: Evaluated on five discriminative benchmarks with Qwen2.5 (0.5B–14B) and SmolLM2-1.7B. LoCA achieves lower cross-entropy than LoRA in 16/25 task–scale comparisons. Full-run GPU peak memory is 26–29% lower than LoRA. After calibration, CPU steady-state memory is 36–52% lower and per-pass time is 43–48% lower. A shared scale-normalized candidate set transfers across all tested model sizes.

Conclusion: LoCA amortizes global credit assignment into a single calibration pass, enabling subsequent forward-only tuning. This makes parameter-efficient adaptation viable in settings where repeated backpropagation is impractical, such as edge devices or inference-only hardware, while maintaining competitive or superior performance to LoRA.

Abstract: Parameter-efficient post-training reduces the number of trainable parameters, but still requires repeated end-to-end backpropagation through the frozen backbone. Every adaptation step therefore needs backward-capable hardware and must store or recompute activations. We ask whether this repeated backward chain can be replaced by a one-time calibration. We introduce Local Credit Assignment (LoCA), a two-stage method for small-shift adaptation. One probe backward pass fits a low-rank map at each transformer block from the final prediction error to a local hidden-state correction. LoCA then reuses these maps to form blockwise regression targets from forward activations and fits low-rank adapters with closed-form ridge solves. No further backbone backward pass is required. We evaluate LoCA on five discriminative benchmarks with Qwen2.5 models from 0.5B to 14B. In 16 of 25 reported task--scale comparisons, LoCA yields lower evaluation cross-entropy than the corresponding LoRA run. Its measured full-run GPU peak, including calibration, is 26--29\% lower than LoRA's. After calibration, its CPU steady-state memory is 36--52\% lower and its per-pass time is 43--48\% lower. A shared scale-normalized candidate set is reused across all tested Qwen2.5 sizes and on SmolLM2-1.7B. LoCA thus amortizes global credit assignment into one calibration and enables later forward-only tuning when repeated backpropagation is impractical. The code associated with this paper is available \href{https://github.com/Xia12121/LoCA}{here}.

</details>


### [81] [DiffImaginE: Imagine to Verify Entity Types with Diffusio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03025)
*Feng Zhang,Feiyu Han,Rongxin Yang,Yang Liu,Yancheng Chen,Rui Wang,Yingguang Yang,Tian Xueyun,Chongyang Zhang,Hao Zheng,Xu Kefu,Congjing Ran,Fuhai Chen,Bin Chong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DiffImaginE reformulates multimodal NER type verification as conditional latent diffusion inference, where a type-conditioned denoiser scores (span, type) pairs via denoising error, serving as an ELBO-consistent surrogate for type-conditional negative log-likelihood. Classifier-free guidance sharpens the type posterior, and antithetic sampling reduces comparison variance, yielding consistent gains over deterministic verifiers on Twitter benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MNER verifiers (e.g., ImaginE) map each (span, type) pair to a single predicted visual prototype, collapsing diverse visual realizations into one deterministic feature and producing compatibility scores without explicit probabilistic semantics. This lacks a principled way to quantify how well a type hypothesis explains the observed visual evidence.

Method: DiffImaginE models MNER type verification as conditional latent diffusion inference. A type-conditioned denoiser predicts noise injected into the standardized latent of span-localized visual features; the denoising error serves as an ELBO-consistent surrogate for type-conditional NLL. The framework retains a standard multimodal encoder and replaces the deterministic verifier with a classifier-free-guided diffusion scorer trained with Min-SNR weighting. Per-type diffusion scores are directly supervised as classification logits, aggregated across noise levels, and antithetic sampling is employed to reduce Monte Carlo comparison variance.

Result: DiffImaginE achieves consistent gains over a matched deterministic ImaginE baseline on Twitter-2015 and Twitter-2017 datasets under identical encoder, auxiliary objectives, and evaluation protocol. Ablations and paired significance tests confirm the contributions of classifier-free guidance, Min-SNR weighting, and antithetic sampling.

Conclusion: Casting MNER type verification as diffusion-based inference provides a probabilistically grounded alternative to deterministic verifiers. Classifier-free guidance sharpens the induced type posterior, and antithetic sampling efficiently reduces comparison variance, together yielding reliable improvements in multimodal NER accuracy.

Abstract: Multimodal named entity recognition (MNER) determines whether each candidate span and entity-type hypothesis is supported by joint textual and visual evidence. Existing imagine-and-compare verifiers map each (span, type) pair to one predicted visual feature, compressing diverse visual realisations into a single prototype and providing a compatibility score without explicit probabilistic semantics. We introduce DiffImaginE, which formulates MNER type verification as conditional latent diffusion inference. Given span-localised visual evidence, a type-conditioned denoiser predicts noise injected into its standardised latent. The resulting denoising error provides an ELBO-consistent surrogate for type-conditional negative log-likelihood, allowing competing type hypotheses to be ranked by how well they explain the observation. DiffImaginE retains a standard multimodal encoder stack and replaces the deterministic verifier with a classifier-free-guided diffusion scorer trained using Min-SNR weighting. We directly supervise per-type diffusion scores as classification logits, learn aggregation across noise levels, and use antithetic sampling to reduce Monte Carlo comparison variance. Our analysis shows that classifier-free guidance sharpens the induced type posterior and characterises when antithetic pairing reduces variance at equal denoiser cost. Experiments on Twitter-2015 and Twitter-2017 show consistent gains over a matched deterministic ImaginE control under the same encoder, auxiliary objectives, and evaluation protocol, supported by ablations and paired significance tests.

</details>


### [82] [Evaluating Counterfactual Sensitivity to Patient Information in Medication-Safety Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03028)
*Zhitian Hou,Yuhang Liu,Pengkai Wang,Zeyu Liu,Guanghao Zhu,Zheng Liu,Shuo Cai,Congkai Xie,Zhijie Sang,Kun Zeng,Hongxia Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces MedPIC-Bench, a benchmark testing whether LLMs can conditionally apply medication-safety rules based on patient-specific information using counterfactual questions; finds all models struggle when patient context changes rule applicability, with accuracy dropping from 63.6% to 45.1%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical evaluations use isolated, fixed scenarios where models can succeed by recalling drug-risk associations without genuinely using patient information. There is no benchmark that tests whether a model can recognize when a safety rule's conditions are met or not met based on patient-specific factors.

Method: The authors create MedPIC-Bench with 467 questions combining guideline-following questions and paired counterfactual questions. In counterfactual pairs, a controlled change in patient information alters whether a medication-safety rule applies. Questions are annotated along six clinical and reasoning dimensions, and 28 LLMs (medical-specific, general, and proprietary) are evaluated.

Result: All models perform worse on counterfactual questions — mean accuracy drops from 63.6% to 45.1%. Models succeed when explicit patient attributes directly signal familiar contraindications but fail when patient information should narrow or withdraw a safety warning. Model rationales often acknowledge changed patient information yet retain the previous safety judgment. Medical-specific LLMs underperform general LLMs on counterfactual questions.

Conclusion: MedPIC-Bench makes conditional rule application measurable and reveals that static medication-safety accuracy is insufficient for assessing patient-specific reliability. Conditional reasoning about when rules apply remains a significant vulnerability across all model types.

Abstract: Applying a valid medication-safety rule when its patient-specific conditions are not met can produce an incorrect decision. Existing medical evaluations largely use isolated and fixed scenarios. A model may therefore answer correctly by recalling a drug-risk association without showing that it used patient information to decide whether the rule applies. To address this gap, we introduce MedPIC-Bench, a benchmark of source-verifiable recommendations and expert-validated questions for patient-specific medication-safety reasoning. It combines guideline-following questions with paired counterfactual questions in which a controlled change in patient information changes whether a rule applies. The benchmark contains 467 questions annotated along six clinical and reasoning dimensions. Across 28 medical-specific, general, and proprietary LLMs, every model performs worse on counterfactual questions, with mean accuracy falling from 63.6\% to 45.1\%. Models perform well when an explicit patient attribute directly signals a familiar contraindication, but struggle when patient information must narrow or withdraw a safety warning. Model rationales often acknowledge the changed patient information, yet the final answers retain the previous safety judgment. This vulnerability persists among medical-specific LLMs, whose average CF performance trails that of general LLMs. MedPIC-Bench therefore makes conditional rule application measurable and highlights the limitations of static medication-safety accuracy for assessing patient-specific reliability.

</details>


### [83] [CastFSR: A Fast--Slow--Reflect Agentic Reasoning Framework for Context-Aware Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03031)
*Xiaoyu Tao,Mingyue Cheng,Bokai Pan,Chuang Jiang,Huanjian Zhang,Tian Gao,Yaguo Liu,Qi Liu,Enhong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CastFSR is an agentic framework for time series forecasting that uses a Fast-Slow-Reflect workflow, leveraging LLMs to reason about contextual features, retrieve evidence, and iteratively refine forecasts for improved accuracy and consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based time series forecasting methods lack explicit mechanisms to identify relevant contexts, reason about their impacts, and validate forecasts against temporal and domain constraints. This limits their ability to go beyond numerical extrapolation toward truly context-aware reasoning.

Method: CastFSR formulates context-aware forecasting as a three-stage agentic workflow: (1) Fast thinking — profiles observations and selects lightweight forecasters to construct a data-driven prior; (2) Slow deliberation — retrieves contextual evidence, adaptively determines informative look-back windows, and reasons about how contexts reshape future dynamics; (3) Reflection — iteratively refines forecasts to ensure temporal, contextual, and domain consistency. The framework supports both training-free inference with off-the-shelf LLMs and efficient deployment via a two-stage SFT plus reinforcement learning strategy to transfer orchestration capability to compact LLMs.

Result: Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that CastFSR consistently outperforms representative baselines.

Conclusion: CastFSR effectively integrates data-driven forecasting with LLM-based contextual reasoning through a structured Fast-Slow-Reflect workflow, achieving superior performance. Its flexible deployment (training-free or fine-tuned compact models) makes it practical for real-world context-aware forecasting tasks.

Abstract: Time series forecasting is fundamental to decision-making in complex systems, where future dynamics are influenced not only by historical observations but also by evolving contextual features. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have extended forecasting beyond numerical extrapolation toward context-aware reasoning. However, existing approaches often lack explicit mechanisms to identify relevant contexts, reason about their impacts, and validate forecasts against temporal and domain constraints. In this work, we propose CastFSR, an agentic framework that formulates context-aware forecasting as a Fast--Slow--Reflect workflow. In fast thinking, CastFSR profiles observations and selects lightweight forecasters to construct a data-driven forecast prior. In slow deliberation, it retrieves contextual evidence, adaptively determines informative look-back windows, and reasons about how contexts reshape future dynamics. In reflection, it iteratively refines forecasts to ensure temporal, contextual, and domain consistency. CastFSR supports both training-free inference with off-the-shelf LLMs and efficient deployment through a two-stage SFT and reinforcement learning strategy that transfers its orchestration capability to compact LLMs. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that CastFSR consistently outperforms representative baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xiaoyu-Tao/CastFSR.

</details>


### [84] [TraceCAD: Trace-Guided Repair for Agentic CAD Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03062)
*Fengxiao Fan,Jingzhe Ni,Fan Sang,Xiaolong Yin,Yu Liu,Ruofeng Tong,Min Tang,Peng Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TraceCAD introduces a persistent recovery layer for LLM-based CAD agents that retains requirement evidence, failure diagnostics, and repair outcomes across correction loops. It uses localized dependency-region edits, execution validation, and reusable skill memory to improve CAD quality and repair reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-generated CAD programs require iterative correction loops, but these loops discard valuable information about satisfied requirements, faulty operations, and prior repair attempts. This loss of evidence leads to inefficient re-exploration and degraded repair quality.

Method: TraceCAD is a recovery layer with four components: (1) persistent state linking requested features, modeling steps, failure evidence, and candidate outcomes; (2) diagnosis of likely faulty operations within dependency regions; (3) bounded local search for edits validated through execution and preservation checks; and (4) a reusable skill memory that stores both successful and failed repair outcomes for future reuse.

Result: On DeepCAD-derived benchmarks (200-model ablations, 1K-model comparison), TraceCAD matches competitive geometric quality (IoU, Chamfer, Hausdorff). Ablations show: removing persistent state nearly halves recovery score; removing localized search doubles geometric regression and code-agent invocations. Initializing the skill store on disjoint training models further reduces retries, token cost, and latency.

Conclusion: Persistent, localized, and reusable recovery mechanisms significantly improve final CAD quality and repair reliability, validating TraceCAD's design as an effective recovery layer for LLM-based CAD agents.

Abstract: LLM-based CAD agents produce executable parametric programs, but their correction loops may lose evidence about satisfied requirements, faulty operations, and prior repairs. We introduce TraceCAD, a recovery layer that links requested features, modeling steps, failure evidence, and candidate outcomes as persistent state. TraceCAD diagnoses likely faulty operations, searches bounded edits in their dependency regions, validates candidates through execution and preservation checks, and retains successful and failed repair outcomes in reusable skill memory. On DeepCAD-derived benchmarks with 200-model ablations and a 1K-model comparison, TraceCAD achieves competitive geometric quality in terms of IoU, Chamfer distance, and Hausdorff distance. Removing persistent state nearly halves recovery score; removing localized search more than doubles geometric regression and doubles code-agent invocations. Initializing the skill store on disjoint training models further reduces retries, token cost, and latency. These results demonstrate that persistent, localized, and reusable recovery improves final CAD quality and repair reliability.

</details>


### [85] [Getting the Parameters Right: A Difficulty-Graded Benchmark and Probe-Guided Training for LLM Tool Calls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03071)
*Guoyao Yu,Xiaoqing Sun,Ziqi Huang,Shaojing Fan,Zhongyi Zhang,Xiaomeng Hu,Xiaobo Xue,Yangyang Shi,Xiong Xiao,Yang Song,Biao Lyu,Rong Wen,Xing Li,Qinming He,Shunming Zhu,Zhenguang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs often fail at filling tool-call parameters correctly. The authors discover that hidden states contain a correctness signal detectable by a linear probe. They propose a probe-guided framework with two methods—probe-filtered bootstrapped training (PBT) for fine-tuning and probe-guided reranking (PGR) for inference—along with ParamBench, a new benchmark. Experiments show exact match improves from 19.7% to 59.6%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tool-use research focuses on tool selection and call orchestration, but correctly filling tool parameters is equally critical and severely understudied. In domains like cloud networking, even frontier models achieve <50% correctness on parameter filling. There is a need for methods that specifically improve parameter generation accuracy.

Method: The authors first discover that LLM hidden states encode a strong correctness signal for parameter values—verifiable via a simple linear probe. They then propose a unified probe-guided framework with: (1) Probe-Filtered Bootstrapped Training (PBT): the probe filters reliable self-generated tool calls used as training data for fine-tuning; (2) Probe-Guided Reranking (PGR): at inference, the probe scores multiple candidate parameter values and selects the best one. They also release ParamBench, a benchmark of real cloud-network APIs with five difficulty levels based on parameter nesting depth, cross-parameter dependencies, and reasoning complexity.

Result: Experiments across 5 open models on ParamBench and 6 external benchmarks show substantial improvement: average exact match rises from 19.7% to 59.6%. Both PBT and PGR contribute to these gains.

Conclusion: Probing LLM hidden states for correctness signals is an effective and lightweight strategy for improving tool-call parameter generation. The probe-guided framework (PBT + PGR) substantially boosts accuracy, and ParamBench provides a rigorous, multi-level benchmark for future research in this area.

Abstract: Large language model agents derive much of their capability from tool use. Existing research on tool use has largely focused on selecting the right tool and orchestrating the order of calls. However, correctly filling the parameters of a tool call is equally critical for successful execution and has received far less attention. In domains such as cloud networking, even frontier models correctly complete fewer than half of tool calls. Inspired by recent analyses showing that LLM hidden states encode rich information about model predictions, we discover that while the model generates a parameter value, its hidden state contains a strong correctness signal: a simple linear probe can accurately predict whether the value will be correct. Based on this observation, we propose a unified probe-guided framework with two complementary approaches: probe-filtered bootstrapped training (PBT), which uses the probe to filter reliable self-generated calls for fine-tuning, and probe-guided reranking (PGR), which uses the probe to select better candidates during inference. To support systematic evaluation, we release ParamBench, a benchmark built from real cloud-network APIs that categorizes every instance into five difficulty levels according to parameter nesting depth, cross-parameter dependencies, and the reasoning required to derive values from earlier calls. Extensive experiments across 5 open models on ParamBench and 6 external benchmarks demonstrate that our method substantially improves parameter generation, raising the average exact match from 19.7% to 59.6%.

</details>


### [86] [AI Agent Economics: Can Autonomous Economic Behavior Emerge among AI Agents under Minimal External Conditions?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03076)
*Lingyun Zhang,Shang Shang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI agents without prescribed roles develop economic organization (transfers, loans, vote-for-access, allocation strategies) only when executable mechanisms involve productive tasks with scarce access and real resource consequences. Symbolic stakes eliminate redistribution, confirming that economic structure follows executable rights, not role labels or prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior multi-agent research embeds agents in predefined economic scenarios, confounding endogenous emergent behavior with inherited structure. The authors seek to isolate whether economic relations—production, allocation, exchange, institutions—spontaneously arise when agents are given only executable mechanisms without prescribed social or economic strategies.

Method: A two-stage framework: (1) a no-production boundary test where agents can communicate and govern resource provision; (2) 24 independent six-agent worlds across GPT and DeepSeek with verified work, scarce task access, and executable mechanisms for transfers, elections, and allocation. Conditions are systematically varied, including replacing energy stakes with symbolic tokens to test whether organization depends on resource consequences.

Result: Without productive tasks, only communication and resource-provision governance emerge, with no substantive transfers. With verified work and scarce access, transfers, loans, access promises, vote-for-access exchanges, and allocation strategies emerge. Executable allocation authority increases differentiation but reduces failed allocations and prolonged exclusion. Under symbolic energy, continuation support vanishes while task-access competition persists.

Conclusion: Economic organization follows executable rights and resource consequences rather than role labels or prompt language. This motivates governance audits focused on the actual mechanisms constraining agents' future actions, rather than surface-level designations of roles or scenarios.

Abstract: Multi-agent studies commonly place AI agents in predefined games, markets, or roles, making it difficult to distinguish endogenous economic organization from behavior inherited from the scenario. We ask whether economic relations emerge when agents receive executable mechanisms for work, transfer, elections, and allocation but no prescribed social or economic strategy. We define AI Agent Economics as systems of production, allocation, consumption, exchange, and institutions that alter agents' future feasible actions. We develop a two-stage framework comprising a no-production boundary test and 24 independent six-agent worlds across GPT and DeepSeek. Without productive tasks, agents communicate and govern resource provision but show no substantive inter-agent transfer activity. With verified work and scarce task access, transfers, loans, access promises, vote-for-access exchanges, and allocation strategies emerge. Holding the election interface fixed, executable allocation authority increases differentiation while reducing failed allocation and prolonged exclusion. When energy becomes symbolic, continuation support disappears, yet competition over task access persists. These findings show that organization follows executable rights and resource consequences rather than role labels or prompt language, and motivate governance audits of the mechanisms that actually constrain agents' future actions.

</details>


### [87] [Don't Peek at the Answer: Outcome-Masked Group Relative Policy Optimization for Label-Free RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03119)
*Yongshi Ye,Liang Zhang,Yidong Chen,Xiaodong Shi,Biao Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OM-GRPO is a label-free RLVR framework that prevents training collapse by masking answer-token gradients during optimization while using soft consensus for reward estimation, augmented with contrastive pairwise comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RLVR requires ground-truth answers, limiting scalability. Voting-based label-free methods suffer from collapse because the same answer-level signal drives both reward estimation and token-level policy optimization, causing the model to reinforce answer tokens rather than reasoning chains.

Method: OM-GRPO introduces two components: (1) gradient masking on answer spans to decouple reward estimation from policy optimization, shifting pressure away from answer tokens; (2) Contrast-Augmented Reward, which refines the soft consensus reward via low-cost pairwise comparisons over existing trajectories without extra rollouts.

Result: Across diverse reasoning benchmarks and three LLM backbones, OM-GRPO consistently outperforms existing label-free RLVR methods and matches supervised GT-reward training. In Test-Time Training, it surpasses majority voting by 4.24 points.

Conclusion: Decoupling reward estimation from policy optimization via gradient masking on answer tokens resolves the collapse problem in label-free RLVR, enabling stable training that rivals supervised methods and yields substantial gains in test-time adaptation.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves LLM reasoning but typically relies on ground-truth (GT) answers, limiting scalability. Voting-based label-free RLVR replace gold supervision with answer-level consensus from model samples. However, collapse arises when the same answer-level signal is used both to estimate rewards and to drive token-level policy optimization, encouraging the model to directly reinforce answer tokens rather than improve reasoning. We propose OM-GRPO, a label-free RLVR framework that decouples reward estimation from policy optimization. OM-GRPO masks gradients on the answer span while retaining answer-level rewards through a soft consensus signal, shifting optimization pressure away from answer tokens. We further introduce Contrast-Augmented Reward, which refines reward estimation via low-cost pairwise comparisons over existing trajectories without additional rollouts. Across diverse reasoning benchmarks and three LLM backbones, OM-GRPO consistently outperforms existing label-free RLVR methods and matches supervised GT-reward training with stable optimization. This stability is particularly beneficial in the Test-Time Training setting, where OM-GRPO surpasses majority voting by 4.24 points.

</details>


### [88] [Beyond Average Performance: Dynamic Instance Clustering and Specialized Algorithm Design in LLM-Assisted Evolutionary Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03129)
*Qinglong Hu,Qingfu Zhang,Fei Liu,Xialiang Tong,Kun Mao,Mingxuan Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DyCA proposes a co-evolving instance clustering mechanism within LES that uses accumulated evaluation data as feature-free signals to dynamically partition heterogeneous instances, enabling specialized algorithm design that improves tail robustness by 15.2% and overall performance by 7.1%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LES methods optimize for average performance, which biases search toward dominant instances and neglects others, resulting in poor tail robustness and limited real-world reliability under heterogeneous instance distributions.

Method: DyCA integrates dynamic instance clustering as a co-evolving component within the LES search process. It reuses accumulated evaluation data (feature-free signals) to progressively partition instances based on similar algorithmic response patterns. The discovered clusters decompose the mixed objective into structure-aware sub-objectives, providing finer-grained, adaptive guidance for evolving specialized algorithm portfolios.

Result: Across four algorithm design tasks with heterogeneous instances, DyCA outperforms state-of-the-art LES baselines, achieving 15.2% improvement in tail robustness, 7.1% improvement in overall performance, while maintaining competitive head performance.

Conclusion: DyCA demonstrates that co-evolving instance clustering within LES effectively addresses the tail robustness limitation of average-performance-oriented methods, yielding more reliable algorithm portfolios through structure-aware, specialized design without requiring explicit instance features.

Abstract: Large Language Model-assisted Evolutionary Search (LES) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for automated algorithm design. However, existing LES methods primarily optimize for average performance, inherently directing search effort toward instances that contribute most to this metric while leaving others poorly served, resulting in weak tail robustness and limited real-world reliability. To address this limitation, we propose Dynamic Instance Clustering and Specialized Algorithm Design (DyCA), an LES framework with a feature-free, structure-aware mechanism for constructing reliable algorithm portfolios under heterogeneous instance distributions. DyCA treats instance clustering as a co-evolving component within the search process, reusing accumulated evaluation data as feature-free signals to progressively partition instances with similar algorithmic response patterns. The uncovered clusters decompose the mixed objective into a set of structure-aware sub-objectives, thereby enabling finer-grained and more adaptive guidance for specialized algorithm design. Experimental results across four algorithm design tasks with heterogeneous instances demonstrate that DyCA outperforms state-of-the-art LES baselines, improving tail robustness by an average of 15.2\% and overall performance by 7.1\% while maintaining competitive head performance.

</details>


### [89] [Verifiable Memory: Learning Unified Memory Management with Local and Global Verifiers for Large Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03137)
*Xiaolong Sun,Qichao Wang,Hangyu Li,Liang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VerMem is a memory management framework for LLM agents that unifies long-term, short-term, and episodic memory under a single policy with seven atomic operations, trained via a three-stage RL curriculum with local and global verifiers for hierarchical credit assignment, achieving SOTA across five benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems treat long-term and short-term memory separately, and unified approaches rely on weak trajectory-level feedback that poorly credits individual memory decisions. There is a need for a unified memory policy with fine-grained, verifiable credit assignment.

Method: VerMem represents LTM, active context, and episodic history as distinct states controlled by a single memory operation policy with seven atomic operations (add, revise, soft-delete LTM entries; retrieve LTM into context; filter/summarize context; restore episodic fragments). Training uses SFT initialization followed by a three-stage RL curriculum. Credit assignment combines: (1) a local verifier that scores executable memory transitions, (2) a global verifier that assesses evidence coherence and terminal-memory consistency post-task, and (3) programmatically computed task, evidence-recall, efficiency, and constraint signals — all combined via hierarchical credit assignment. Verifiers are used only during training.

Result: VerMem achieved the best results on the vast majority of reported metrics across five benchmarks and two LLM backbones, consistently outperforming strong memory baselines. Under controlled online-token budgets on three interactive benchmarks, it achieved the strongest efficiency–performance frontier among compared methods.

Conclusion: A unified memory operation policy with verifier-guided hierarchical credit assignment significantly improves LLM agent performance and efficiency in long-horizon interactive tasks compared to separately optimized or weakly-credited memory approaches.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents must retain reusable information, control a bounded active context, and recover earlier evidence during long-horizon interaction. Existing methods commonly optimize long-term memory (LTM) and short-term memory (STM) separately, while unified policies are often trained primarily with trajectory-level feedback, which provides weak credit for individual memory decisions. We present Verifiable Memory (VerMem), a framework that represents LTM, active context, and episodic history as distinct states and controls them with one memory operation policy. Seven atomic operations let the policy add, revise, or soft-delete LTM entries; retrieve LTM into the active context; filter or summarize the active context; and restore selected episodic fragments. VerMem is initialized by supervised fine-tuning and trained with a three-stage reinforcement-learning curriculum. The local verifier scores executable memory transitions, and a global verifier assesses evidence coherence and terminal-memory consistency after task completion. These scores are combined with programmatically computed task, evidence-recall, efficiency, and constraint signals through hierarchical credit assignment. The verifiers are used only during training. Across five benchmarks and two LLM backbones, VerMem achieves the best result on the vast majority of reported metrics and consistently outperforms strong memory baselines. Under controlled online-token budgets on three interactive benchmarks, it also achieves the strongest efficiency--performance frontier among the compared methods. Code is available at https://github.com/Sun-SYSU-24/VerMem.

</details>


### [90] [Spatial proteomics guided by H&E-based AI reveals recurrence-risk niches in triple-negative breast cancer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03145)
*Yesung Cho,Ji Hwan Park,Chanil Kim,Hyewon Kim,Honglan Li,Yumin Lee,Geongyu Lee,Sujeong Hong,Seong Min Park,Yoonyoung Lee,Hee Sool Rho,Sumin Lee,Amos Chungwon Lee,Changhwan Lee,Hwanyoung Shim,Hyunwook Kim,Hyeji Shin,Sanha Park,Jihoon Yu,Yoon Hee Shin,Sooheon Kim,Hyunjin Park,Seung Min Park,Sangwan Kim,Yujung Kim,Sung-Im Do,Eun-Young Kim,Dongmyung Shin,Jongbae Park,In-Gu Do*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Researchers developed a framework integrating AI-based recurrence risk heatmaps from H&E slides with spatial proteomics in TNBC. AI risk scores correlated with distinct molecular programs (cell cycle vs. immune). Using AI heatmaps as spatial guides, they physically isolated and profiled high/low risk tumor regions, revealing concordant proteomic contrasts. Integrating protein and image-based scores improved prognostic accuracy (C-index 0.679→0.739).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While deep learning models can predict cancer recurrence from H&E histology, the underlying localized molecular states driving these predictions remain obscure. There is a need to connect prognostic morphology with spatially resolved molecular programs to advance biologically interpretable biomarker discovery in TNBC.

Method: The authors developed an outcome-informed spatial pathology framework for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Key steps: (1) Training an AI model to generate recurrence risk heatmaps from H&E stained slides in a 156-patient cohort (AUC 0.77, C-index 0.77). (2) Associating high/low image-derived risk with bulk proteomics. (3) Using AI heatmaps as coordinate-level guides to physically isolate 46 tumor regions from two recurrence patients. (4) Performing mass spectrometry-based spatial proteomics on these regions. (5) Deriving a 13-protein composite and integrating it with H&E risk scores for improved prognostication, validated in an expanded cohort and the METABRIC TNBC cohort.

Result: High AI-derived risk correlated with cell cycle and genome maintenance programs; low risk correlated with immune activation. High/low risk patches coexisted within the same tumor compartment, revealing intratumoral heterogeneity. Spatial proteomics confirmed mitotic enrichment in high-risk regions and immune/antigen presentation enrichment in low-risk regions across both patients. The 13-protein composite showed a trend toward poorer recurrence-free survival. Integrating the protein composite with H&E risk improved the out-of-bag C-index from 0.679 to 0.739 and enhanced time-dependent discrimination at 3 and 5 years. The transcript-based counterpart stratified survival in METABRIC.

Conclusion: Outcome-trained AI models can serve as spatially explicit experimental guides linking prognostic morphology with localized molecular states. This integration of AI-derived spatial heatmaps with proteomics enables biologically grounded, multiscale biomarker discovery in TNBC and reveals intratumoral heterogeneity beyond conventional tissue compartment classification.

Abstract: Deep learning models can predict cancer recurrence from H&E stained slides, but the localized molecular states underlying these predictions remain largely obscured. Here, we developed an outcome informed spatial pathology framework in TNBC that integrates AI generated recurrence risk heatmaps with mass spectrometry based spatial proteomics. In a cohort of 156 patients, distribution based aggregation of high scoring patches achieved an AUC of 0.77 and a C-index of 0.77 in an independent test cohort. Bulk proteomics associated high image derived risk with cell cycle and genome maintenance programs and low risk with immune activation. High and low risk patches coexisted within the same tumor compartment and displayed distinct nuclear and architectural features, revealing intratumoral heterogeneity beyond tissue compartment identity. We then used the heatmaps as coordinate level guides to physically isolate and profile 46 AI defined tumor regions from two recurrence patients. Spatial proteomic profiling revealed a concordant molecular contrast across both patients: mitotic programs were enriched in high risk regions and immune and antigen presentation programs in low risk regions. A 13 protein composite derived from these spatial contrasts showed a trend toward poorer recurrence-free survival with increasing scores in an expanded cohort, while the corresponding transcript based composite stratified recurrence free survival in the independent METABRIC TNBC cohort. Integrating the protein composite with the H&E derived risk score improved the out of bag C-index from 0.679 to 0.739 and enhanced time dependent discrimination at 3 and 5 years. Together, these findings define a new role for outcome trained AI models as spatially explicit experimental guides that connect prognostic morphology with localized molecular states and advance biologically grounded, multiscale biomarker discovery in TNBC.

</details>


### [91] [UniGD: A Unified Generative-Discriminative Framework for Industrial Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03150)
*Shujie Ji,Yawei Kong,Yilin Zhao,Li Wang,Xialong Liu,Peng Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UniGD unifies generative retrieval and relevance scoring into a single model for search advertising, using conflict-aware gradient enhancement, codebook-anchored semantics, and heterogeneous ad modeling to improve revenue (+5.78%), reduce latency (-33%), and boost recall on public benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing industrial generative retrieval systems cascade a GR model with an independent relevance model, creating a mismatch between the generative likelihood training objective and the discriminative query-ad relevance task. This decoupling harms effectiveness and inflates serving costs. The authors aim to unify both objectives in a single model to meet strict industrial relevance and latency requirements.

Method: UniGD integrates retrieval and relevance scoring within one model. Three key technical components are proposed: (1) Conflict-Aware Gradient Enhancement (CAGE) to adaptively resolve gradient interference between the generative and discriminative objectives during joint training; (2) Codebook-Anchored Representation Module (CAM), which anchors item representations to frozen hierarchical codebooks distilled from a multimodal pretrained model for rich semantic priors; (3) Heterogeneous Ad-material Modeling (HAM), which uses a shared backbone to capture cross-type semantic commonality while preserving type-specific capacity for short-video, product, and live-stream ads.

Result: Online A/B tests on the Kuaishou search advertising platform demonstrate a 5.78% increase in ad revenue, a 33% reduction in inference latency, and improved discriminative relevance estimation. On public benchmarks NQ320K and MS300K, UniGD improves Recall@10 over the strongest reproduced GR baseline by 8.44% and 3.19%, respectively.

Conclusion: UniGD successfully unifies generative retrieval and relevance discrimination in a single model for industrial search advertising, overcoming gradient interference and semantic representation challenges. The framework delivers significant gains in both commercial metrics (revenue, latency) and academic benchmarks, establishing a viable path for deploying unified GR systems at scale.

Abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) is a promising paradigm for industrial search advertising, yet its deployment is constrained by strict relevance and latency requirements. Existing systems cascade GR with an independent relevance model, decoupling the generative likelihood objective from query-ad relevance discrimination, which compromises effectiveness and increases serving costs. We propose a Unified Generative-Discriminative framework (UniGD) that integrates retrieval and relevance scoring within a single model. To mitigate gradient interference in joint optimization, UniGD introduces Conflict-Aware Gradient Enhancement (CAGE) to adaptively coordinate the two objectives. UniGD further designs a Codebook-Anchored Representation Module (CAM) that anchors item representations to frozen hierarchical codebooks distilled from a multimodal pretrained model, thereby endowing them with rich and generalizable semantic priors. For heterogeneous short-video, product, and live-stream ads, UniGD proposes Heterogeneous Ad-material Modeling (HAM), which captures cross-type semantic commonality over a shared backbone while preserving type-specific modeling capacity. Online AB tests on Kuaishou search advertising platform show that UniGD raises ad revenue by 5.78%, reduces inference latency by 33%, and improves discriminative relevance estimation. On NQ320K and MS300K, UniGD improves Recall@10 over the strongest reproduced GR baseline by 8.44% and 3.19%, respectively.

</details>


### [92] [Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03161)
*Sahil Al Farib,Momota Ahsana Meem,Sheikh Redwanul Islam,Md. Tanvir Raihan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multimodal pipeline converts lecture videos into provenance-rich knowledge graphs by grounding extracted concepts and relationships in transcript, OCR, or visual evidence, achieving high retrieval accuracy on a small test set.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transcript-only retrieval fails to preserve the full multimodal richness of lecture videos—speech, slide text, diagrams, equations, and presentation order. There is a need for an auditable, evidence-grounded method to construct structured knowledge representations from lecture videos.

Method: An evidence-grounded multimodal pipeline that: (1) transcribes lecture audio; (2) selects semantic anchors from frames; (3) applies OCR to slide text; (4) uses a vision-language model to extract concepts and typed relationships, retaining only those supported by transcript, OCR, or visual evidence; and (5) validates and canonicalizes mentions into a knowledge graph with provenance tracking.

Result: On three neural-network lectures (3,118 frames, 756 transcript segments, 559 anchors), the pipeline retained 1,022 concept mentions and 312 relationship mentions, yielding 172 canonical concepts and 282 relationships with 90.38% endpoint coverage. A three-question retrieval test achieved 100% top-1 accuracy, 100% top-3 accuracy, and 100% mean top-5 recall.

Conclusion: The paper's primary contribution is an auditable, evidence-grounded construction methodology for building provenance-rich knowledge graphs from lecture videos, rather than claiming state-of-the-art performance. The high retrieval accuracy on a preliminary test suggests promise for the approach.

Abstract: Lecture videos distribute knowledge across speech, slide text, diagrams, equations, and presentation order, which transcript-only retrieval does not fully preserve. This paper presents an evidence-grounded multimodal pipeline that transcribes lectures, selects semantic anchors, applies optical character recognition (OCR), and uses a vision-language model to extract only concepts and typed relationships supported by transcript, OCR, or visual evidence.
