Mentions are validated and canonicalized into a provenance-rich knowledge graph. On three neural-network lectures, the pipeline processed 3,118 frames, 756 transcript segments, and 559 anchors. It retained 1,022 concept and 312 relationship mentions, yielding 172 canonical concepts and 282 relationships with 90.38% endpoint coverage. A preliminary three question retrieval test achieved 100% top-1 and top-3 accuracy and 100% mean top-5 recall. The contribution is an auditable construction method rather than a state-of-the-art performance claim.

</details>


### [93] [Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03166)
*Saqib Shouqi,Abdullah Nazly,Januki Wanniarachchi,Ravisha De Alwis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multi-agent platform adversarially stress-tests Role-Playing Language Agents (RPLAs) through multi-turn dialogue using six progressive attack strategies, revealing failure modes missed by single-strategy testing. Authority Challenge and Emotional Manipulation are the most effective attacks. Automated judging aligns strongly with human evaluation (r=0.82).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RPLA evaluation methods rely on static benchmarks or isolated single-turn prompts, which fail to capture cumulative behavioral failures (persona drift, ethical violations, consistency breakdowns) that emerge over extended, adversarial multi-turn interactions in high-stakes domains like healthcare, customer support, and education.

Method: A modular multi-agent platform with three coordinated components: (1) a strategy-driven Interrogator Agent applying six progressive adversarial strategies, (2) a Target Agent representing the RPLA under test, and (3) an automated Judging Agent scoring four dimensions — role fidelity, drift, ethical deviation, and consistency. Evaluated across three personas and three LLM families (Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Haiku).

Result: Multi-strategy adversarial evaluation reduced robustness scores by 0.17–0.20 points vs. single-strategy baselines. Authority Challenge and Emotional Manipulation were the most effective attack strategies. Automated judging achieved strong human alignment: Pearson r = 0.82 and Fleiss' κ = 0.71.

Conclusion: Multi-turn, multi-strategy adversarial stress-testing systematically uncovers RPLA failure modes that static/single-turn methods miss. The framework is released as open-source to advance AI safety and reproducible benchmarking, though the authors caution about ethical risks of adversarial testing methodologies.

Abstract: Role-Playing Language Agents (RPLAs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications such as healthcare assistance, customer support, and education, where maintaining consistent personas, ethical constraints, and behavioral coherence under adversarial pressure is critical. Existing evaluation approaches rely on static benchmarks or isolated single-turn prompts that fail to capture cumulative behavioral failures emerging over extended interactions.
  We present a modular multi-agent platform for adversarially stress-testing RPLAs through structured, multi-turn dialogue. The system coordinates three agents: a strategy-driven Interrogator Agent that applies six progressive adversarial strategies, a Target Agent representing the RPLA under evaluation, and an automated Judging Agent that scores behavior across role fidelity, drift, ethical deviation, and consistency dimensions.
  Through experiments across three personas and three LLM families, we demonstrate that multi-strategy adversarial evaluation reveals failure modes invisible to single-strategy testing, reducing overall robustness scores by 0.17--0.20 points on average. Cross-model validation confirms consistent degradation patterns across Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-4o-mini, and Claude-3.5-Haiku, with Authority Challenge and Emotional Manipulation emerging as the most effective attack strategies. Automated judging achieves strong human alignment ($r = 0.82$, Fleiss' $κ= 0.71$). This work is released as an open-source platform to support AI safety and reproducible RPLA benchmarking. While the framework enables systematic discovery of failure modes, we acknowledge potential ethical risks associated with adversarial testing methodologies and emphasize responsible usage for improving AI safety.

</details>


### [94] [Surrogate Substitution Preserves PHI Detectability: A Multi-Detector Equivalence Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03172)
*Qiming Bao,Sherry J. H. Feng,Kim Chester Eugenio,Meng Fon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether structure-preserving de-identification (replacing PHI with realistic surrogates) corrupts downstream PHI detection. Using a paired, multi-detector protocol with equivalence testing on 57k masked spans across 11 detectors, 7 benchmarks, and 7 languages, the authors find recall drops only 1.2 percentage points (76.1%→74.9%), which is statistically equivalent to zero within ±2 points. Residual failures stem from malformed/out-of-distribution surrogates, not detector degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structure-preserving de-identification is widely used to maintain clinical text fluency and tool compatibility, but no prior work rigorously tests whether surrogate substitution itself corrupts the signal that downstream PHI detectors rely on. Existing evaluations conflate coverage and utility, use inappropriate significance testing, and lack a taxonomy of failure modes.

Method: The authors introduce a three-part evaluation protocol: (1) utility scoring restricted to only the spans a de-identifier actually masks, decoupling coverage from utility; (2) TOST (Two One-Sided Tests) equivalence testing instead of null-hypothesis significance testing, appropriate for large samples (57k paired spans) where NHST would detect trivial differences; and (3) a surrogate-failure typology that separates fixable generator defects (truncation, salience loss) from intrinsic detector limits. Experiments span 11 PHI detectors, 7 benchmarks, and 7 languages across 1,750 documents.

Result: Recall on masked spans drops from 76.1% to 74.9%, a change TOST confirms as statistically equivalent to zero within a ±2-point margin (p ≈ 3e-9). Detector ranking is preserved. The residual loss concentrates in malformed surrogates (e.g., "Chicago" truncated to "Illino") and out-of-distribution replacements (e.g., "Cedars-Sinai" → "Vidant"), not in detectors losing PHI sensitivity. A redaction floor and open-source surrogate baseline confirm the effect is a property of well-formed substitution, not of any single tool.

Conclusion: Well-formed structure-preserving de-identification does not meaningfully degrade downstream PHI detection performance. The evaluation protocol and typology provide a reusable audit framework for any structure-preserving transform, and all artifacts (evaluation subsets, scoring code, interactive dashboard) are released publicly.

Abstract: Structure-preserving de-identification replaces protected health information (PHI) with realistic same-type surrogates -- "Anna S." becomes "Maria S.", not [NAME] -- so that clinical text stays fluent and downstream tools keep working. But this only helps if the substitution does not itself corrupt the signal those tools rely on. We ask a narrow, testable question: on the spans a de-identifier actually masks, can downstream PHI detectors still find the surrogate? We introduce a paired, multi-detector evaluation protocol that (i) scores utility only on masked spans, decoupling coverage from utility; (ii) uses equivalence testing (TOST) rather than null-hypothesis significance testing, which is uninformative at our sample size (57k paired spans); and (iii) builds a surrogate-failure typology separating fixable generator defects from intrinsic detector limits. Across 11 detectors, 7 benchmarks, and 7 languages (1,750 documents), recall on masked spans moves from 76.1% to 74.9% -- a change our equivalence test shows is statistically equivalent to zero within a +/-2-point margin (p ~ 3e-9), with detector ranking preserved. The residual loss does not reflect detectors getting worse at PHI: it concentrates in malformed and out-of-distribution surrogates (truncation Chicago -> Illino, salience loss Cedars-Sinai -> Vidant). A redaction floor and an open-source surrogate baseline indicate the effect is a property of well-formed substitution, not of one tool. We release the evaluation subsets, scoring code, and an interactive dashboard at https://custodianai.pages.dev so the protocol can audit any structure-preserving transform.

</details>


### [95] [Diversity is Not Ambiguity: Toward Accurate and Efficient Ambiguity Detection for Open-Domain QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03177)
*Jiwon Lee,Yong-chan Park,Jungin Hong,U Kang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ARCHIVE is a fast, accurate ambiguity detection framework for QA systems that identifies ambiguous queries via logical conflict: a query is ambiguous if its valid answers cannot all be true under a single interpretation. It combines an early-exit encoder with a conflict reasoning module and achieves up to 10.4% F1-amb improvement while being 16× faster than competitors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ambiguity detection methods conflate answer diversity with ambiguity, causing inaccurate predictions, and process all queries uniformly, wasting computation. A more principled approach is needed that properly distinguishes ambiguity from mere answer diversity while maintaining efficiency.

Method: ARCHIVE uses two components: (1) a lightweight early-exit encoder that handles surface-detectable ambiguity cases efficiently, and (2) a conflict reasoning module that models logical relations among answers, determining ambiguity by checking whether all valid answers can be simultaneously true under a single interpretation. An invariance objective reinforces robustness to noisy answer sets. The authors also introduce QuireQA, a 4,703-query benchmark covering factoid, non-factoid, and ill-formed queries.

Result: ARCHIVE outperforms all competitors, improving F1-amb (ambiguous) by up to 10.4% and F1-unamb (unambiguous) by up to 21.6%, while operating 16× faster than the best competitor.

Conclusion: Logical conflict is a superior criterion for ambiguity detection compared to answer diversity. The cascaded architecture of ARCHIVE provides both accuracy gains and significant computational efficiency, making it practical for real-world open-domain QA systems.

Abstract: How can question answering (QA) systems determine whether a query is ambiguous? Ambiguity detection is essential in open-domain QA, as misclassification leads to answering the wrong interpretation or unnecessary clarification. However, existing methods conflate answer diversity with ambiguity, leading to inaccurate predictions. They also process queries uniformly, resulting in wasteful computation. We propose ARCHIVE (Ambiguity Recognition via Cascaded Hypothesis Inspection and Conflict Verification), an accurate and efficient framework that detects ambiguity via logical conflict: a query is ambiguous when its valid answers cannot all be true under a single interpretation. ARCHIVE combines a lightweight early-exit encoder for surface-detectable cases with a conflict reasoning module that models logical relations among answers, reinforced by an invariance objective for robustness to noisy answer sets. We present QuireQA, a 4,703-query benchmark spanning factoid, non-factoid, and ill-formed queries. Experiments show ARCHIVE outperforms competitors, improving F1-amb by up to 10.4% and F1-unamb by up to 21.6%, while operating 16$\times$ faster than the best competitor.

</details>


### [96] [TumorBoard: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent Decision Support for Longitudinal Neuro-Oncology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03190)
*Yantong Liu,Zheyu Zhang,Runpeng Liu,Mu Xitang,Seong-Yoon Shin,Hyun-Ae Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TumorBoard is a multi-agent neuro-oncology decision-support system that coordinates specialist agents via a shared case state and claim-evidence ledger, with an adversarial critic and safety governor. It achieved strong performance on a 360-case benchmark (F1: 0.772, evidence entailment: 0.914) and outperformed baselines while maintaining safety through evidence-gated recommendation release.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neuro-oncology decisions require integrating heterogeneous, longitudinal data (serial MRI, pathology, molecular markers, treatment history, guidelines), which is error-prone and cognitively demanding. Existing single-model or simple ensemble approaches lack structured coordination, auditability, and safety mechanisms for this high-stakes domain.

Method: TumorBoard employs a multi-agent architecture with (1) specialist agents (radiology, neuropathology, molecular diagnosis, guidelines, therapy planning) that produce atomic, provenance-tracked claims; (2) a shared longitudinal case state; (3) an auditable claim-evidence ledger; (4) an adversarial critic that exposes contradictions; and (5) a safety governor that releases, qualifies, or defers recommendations based on evidence sufficiency and temporal validity. Evaluated on a 360-case hidden benchmark with matched token budgets against typed-council baselines, with ablation studies and evidence-deletion stress testing.

Result: TumorBoard achieved an action F1 of 0.772 and evidence entailment of 0.914, exceeding the strongest typed-council baseline by 3.1 pp (95% CI: 1.6–4.7, adjusted p=0.0012). Recommendation-to-evidence coverage reached 0.927. Under evidence deletion, it deferred 84.2% of unsafe cases with only 5.8% harmful recommendations. The safety governor reduced harmful release by 7.8 pp at a false-deferral cost of 4.3 pp. Ablation of the ledger, critic, and governor produced predicted failure patterns.

Conclusion: Structured coordination — via the shared state, claim-evidence ledger, adversarial critic, and safety governor — is the key source of TumorBoard's multi-agent advantage, enabling both high performance and calibrated safety in neuro-oncology decision support.

Abstract: Neuro-oncology decisions require coordinated interpretation of serial MRI, pathology, molecular markers, treatment history, performance status, and evolving guidelines. We present TumorBoard, a multi-agent decision-support system built around a shared longitudinal case state and an auditable claim-evidence ledger. Specialist agents for radiology, neuropathology, molecular diagnosis, guidelines, and therapy planning produce atomic claims with provenance. An adversarial critic exposes contradictions, and a safety governor releases, qualifies, or defers recommendations according to evidence sufficiency and temporal validity. On a 360-case hidden benchmark at a matched token budget, TumorBoard achieved an action F1 of 0.772 and evidence entailment of 0.914. It exceeded the strongest typed-council baseline by 3.1 percentage points (95% CI: 1.6 to 4.7, adjusted p = 0.0012), while recommendation-to-evidence coverage reached 0.927. Under evidence deletion, the system deferred 84.2% of unsafe cases and limited harmful recommendations to 5.8%. The safety governor reduced harmful release by 7.8 percentage points at a false-deferral cost of 4.3 percentage points. Ablation studies of the ledger, critic, and governor produced the predicted failure patterns, establishing structured coordination as the source of the measured multi-agent advantage.

</details>


### [97] [When Refusal Looks Safe: The Refusal-Cue Shortcut in Safety Guard Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03201)
*Yu Feng,Chunting Zang,Chen Shen,Rui Miao,Ge Teng,Weidong Cai,Jieping Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Safety guards trained on imbalanced datasets learn a "refusal-cue shortcut," where inserting refusal expressions into harmful responses fools the guard. The authors propose a post-hoc sparse complementary masking intervention that suppresses shortcut-associated attention heads and MLP neurons, achieving ~79% relative reduction in these failures without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Auditing reveals that in popular safety-guard training datasets (WildGuardMix, GR-Train), refusal expressions almost exclusively co-occur with "unharmful" labels. This dataset imbalance causes models to learn a spurious shortcut: the mere presence of refusal language flips harmful classifications to unharmful, undermining the guard's reliability against adversarial rewording of harmful content.

Method: The authors (1) audit training datasets to establish the refusal-cue co-occurrence imbalance, (2) demonstrate the shortcut's effect across multiple models (LlamaGuard3, Qwen3Guard) and response positions, (3) adapt sparse complementary masking — a post-hoc, retraining-free intervention that identifies and suppresses a small subset of attention heads and MLP neurons associated with the shortcut, and (4) evaluate on two benchmarks, testing generalization across unseen positions and datasets.

Result: The refusal-cue shortcut is pervasive: it affects both openly trained guards and undisclosed models, persists across response positions, and is stronger in smaller model variants. The proposed intervention achieves ~79% relative reduction in response-initial detection failures caused by refusal cues while preserving standard detection performance. Suppression effects transfer to unseen positions and datasets, and shortcut reliance is shown to be partially functionally separable from legitimate refusal recognition.

Conclusion: Dataset-induced refusal-cue shortcuts represent a significant vulnerability in safety guards. Sparse complementary masking offers an effective, lightweight mitigation that surgically removes shortcut reliance without sacrificing genuine refusal detection, and the functional separability suggests safe intervention is possible without degrading legitimate safety behavior.

Abstract: Safety guards are widely used to filter harmful content and are typically trained via supervised fine-tuning on labeled prompt-response pairs. We audit two widely used safety-guard training datasets, WildGuardMix and GR-Train, and find that among responses to harmful prompts, refusal expressions co-occur almost exclusively with unharmful labels. This imbalance motivates what we term the refusal-cue shortcut: inserting a refusal cue into a harmful response could flip the guard's verdict from harmful to unharmful. The shortcut affects not only guards trained on these datasets but also officially released models such as LlamaGuard3 and Qwen3Guard whose training data is undisclosed. It persists across response positions and is generally stronger in smaller variants within a family. To mitigate it, we adapt sparse complementary masking as a lightweight post-hoc intervention that identifies and suppresses a small set of shortcut-associated attention heads and MLP neurons without retraining. On two primary benchmarks, the intervention achieves an approximately 79% relative reduction in response-initial detection failures induced by refusal cues, while preserving standard detection performance. Although optimized using cues at a single response position, the suppression effect transfers to unseen positions and datasets, suggesting that shortcut manifestations across positions are partly mediated by shared internal components. Further analysis provides evidence that shortcut reliance and legitimate refusal recognition are partially functionally separable, as suppressing the shortcut broadly preserves the guard's ability to recognize genuine refusals.

</details>


### [98] [LiveEvalBench: Toward Open-World Evaluation for Web Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03689)
*Yiyao Wang,Zhen Wen,Yinghao Tang,Yixiao Fu,Lin Yuan,Xiaolau Zhang,Jun Zhou,Wei Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LiveEvalBench introduces an agentic, adaptive, and extensible evaluation framework for web frontend generation that uses a collaborative multi-agent workflow (Build Engineer, Code Engineer, UI Tester) to assess projects across their full lifecycle, achieving high alignment with human expert judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks treat web generation as a static evaluation problem, which is fundamentally misaligned with the nature of frontend artifacts. Frontend projects are interactive (not static), admit diverse yet equally valid implementations, and evolve faster than rigid evaluation pipelines can accommodate. These gaps motivate a new evaluation paradigm.

Method: LiveEvalBench reformulates evaluation as an agentic, adaptive, and extensible process with three key components: (1) a collaborative multi-agent review workflow with three specialized roles — Build Engineer, Code Engineer, and UI Tester — that collectively gather evidence across deployment, code inspection, and browser-based interaction; (2) an adaptive protocol that combines shared rubrics (for cross-model comparability) with implementation-grounded criteria (tailored to each artifact) to handle implementation diversity; and (3) an extensible architecture supporting incremental integration of new evaluator roles and assessment dimensions without pipeline redesign.

Result: Experiments across diverse real-world web-generation scenarios demonstrate that LiveEvalBench closely aligns with human expert judgment and provides fine-grained insights into frontier models' web generation capabilities.

Conclusion: Shifting from static to agentic, lifecycle-based evaluation yields assessment that better matches human judgment and captures the interactive, diverse, and rapidly evolving nature of frontend development, offering a more robust benchmark for LLM-driven web generation.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable of synthesizing executable frontend projects, yet existing benchmarks still treat web generation as a static evaluation problem. We argue that frontend artifacts demand a different paradigm: they are interactive rather than static, admit diverse yet equally valid implementations, and evolve faster than rigid pipelines can accommodate. To address these gaps, we present LiveEvalBench, an automated framework that reformulates web-generation evaluation as an agentic, adaptive, and extensible process. LiveEvalBench instantiates evaluation as a collaborative review workflow, in which a Build Engineer, a Code Engineer, and a UI Tester collectively gather evidence across the full lifecycle of a frontend project, from deployment and code inspection to browser-based interaction. To handle implementation diversity, an adaptive protocol couples shared rubrics for cross-model comparability with implementation-grounded criteria tailored to each artifact. The framework further supports incremental integration of new evaluator roles and assessment dimensions without pipeline redesign. Experiments across diverse real-world web-generation scenarios show that LiveEvalBench aligns closely with human expert judgment and provides fine-grained insights into frontier models' web generation capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/wyysteelhead/LiveEvalBench

</details>


### [99] [The Agent Operating System (AOS): A Reference Operating Architecture for Distributed Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03214)
*Ankur Sharma,Deep Shah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes the Agent Operating System (AOS), a vendor-neutral reference operating architecture for distributed agentic systems. AOS defines two planes — Control & Governance and Runtime & Coordination — to enable governable, reliable, observable, and interoperable composition of heterogeneous agent components, without replacing existing frameworks or infrastructure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs have evolved into components of complex, long-running distributed systems that reason, delegate, and act autonomously, the surrounding ecosystem (agent frameworks, workflow engines, model-serving platforms, etc.) lacks a stable, implementation-independent operating architecture for governing intent, preserving authority across delegation, controlling uncertainty, coordinating runtime behavior, and reconstructing consequential decisions.

Method: The paper specifies AOS as a reference architecture with two internal planes: (1) Control & Governance Plane handling intent, policy, trust, authority, confidence, auditability, observability, and human oversight; (2) Runtime & Coordination Plane handling agent lifecycle, workflow coordination, model/tool routing, context/memory coordination, scheduling, traffic management, and runtime assurance. It defines concepts, invariants, interface objects, optimization objectives, deployment profiles, and reliability responsibilities, while explicitly placing platform services, operating systems, container runtimes, and physical infrastructure outside the AOS boundary via explicit interfaces.

Result: The paper does not report empirical results but delivers a conceptual architecture specification. It identifies key tradeoffs and unresolved research questions in building governable, observable, and interoperable agentic systems through the proposed AOS framework.

Conclusion: AOS is not a replacement for existing agent frameworks or infrastructure; rather, it serves as the operating architecture through which heterogeneous components can be composed into governable, reliable, observable, and interoperable agentic systems, addressing critical gaps in authority, uncertainty management, and auditability.

Abstract: Large language models have transformed artificial intelligence from isolated prediction services into components of long-running, distributed systems that reason, invoke tools, retrieve external state, delegate tasks, and act on behalf of users and organizations. The surrounding ecosystem has responded with agent frameworks, workflow engines, model-serving platforms, memory systems, communication protocols, and observability tools. These technologies improve execution, but they do not provide a stable, implementation-independent operating architecture for governing intent, selecting capabilities, preserving authority across delegation, controlling uncertainty, coordinating runtime behavior, and reconstructing why consequential actions occurred. This paper proposes the Agent Operating System (AOS), a vendor-neutral reference operating architecture for distributed agentic systems. AOS contains two internal planes: a Control & Governance Plane responsible for intent, policy, trust, authority, confidence, auditability, observability, and human oversight; and a Runtime & Coordination Plane responsible for agent lifecycle, workflow coordination, model and tool routing, context and memory coordination, scheduling, traffic management, and runtime assurance. Platform services, Linux or Windows, container runtimes, and physical infrastructure remain outside the AOS boundary and are integrated through explicit interfaces. The paper specifies AOS concepts, invariants, interface objects, optimization objectives, deployment profiles, and reliability responsibilities. It also identifies tradeoffs and unresolved research questions. AOS is not presented as a replacement for existing frameworks or infrastructure; it is proposed as the operating architecture through which heterogeneous components can be composed into governable, reliable, observable, and interoperable agentic systems.

</details>


### [100] [Reachability Is Not Realization: Tracing the Sources of LLM Benchmark Gains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03219)
*Yanchao Li,Wanhao Liu,Jiaqing Xie,Ben Gao,Yanbo Wang,Tianfan Fu,Yuqiang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Aggregate benchmark gains conflate two distinct phenomena: new capability (answers previously unreachable) versus improved realization (answers already reachable now appearing). The paper introduces a question-level audit distinguishing "realization" from "reachability," showing that inference-time routing gains require answer access, a single MLP block often blocks reachable answers, and training can raise deployed scores while the reachable ceiling remains flat or falls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmark improvements are routinely interpreted as evidence of expanding LLM capabilities, but aggregate scores obscure whether models are genuinely acquiring new capacities or simply surfacing answers that were already latent. This conflation undermines claims about capability expansion and calls for a more granular, question-level audit framework.

Method: The authors define "realization" (correct answer produced under default deployment) and "reachability" (correct answer found by a probe under fixed budget). Three experiments are conducted: (1) testing whether inference-time layer routing expands reachability under matched budgets; (2) identifying specific MLP blocks whose silencing repairs failure; (3) evaluating whether training (e.g., DAPO) changes both deployed performance and the reachable ceiling across six matched evaluations spanning 0.5B to 31B models.

Result: Random routing matches or exceeds structured search across all 43 model-task settings; answer-blind procedures retain almost none of this gain. Silencing a single identified MLP block repairs 68–92% of a predefined failure set. In five of six training evaluations, deployed performance rises while the reachable ceiling stays flat or falls (e.g., DAPO: +14.7 deployed, −13.3 reachable ceiling).

Conclusion: Realization and reachability do not always change together. Capability claims should report both realized performance and reachability under matched evaluation conditions to avoid misinterpreting deployment improvements as genuine capability expansion.

Abstract: Benchmark gains are often treated as evidence of greater LLM capability. Yet the same gain can reflect different changes in model behavior. A model may reach new answers, or produce answers that were already within reach. Aggregate scores do not distinguish these changes question by question. We establish a question-level audit under fixed budgets, temperatures, and answer formats. A question is realized when the default deployment procedure produces the correct answer. A question is reachable when a specified probe finds that answer within a fixed budget. We first test whether inference-time layer routing can expand reachability. Under a matched budget, random routes match or exceed structured search in all 43 model and task settings. Answer-blind procedures retain almost none of this gain, which instead requires access to the correct answer. We then ask why reachable answers sometimes fail to appear. Across six cases spanning 0.5B to 31B, silencing one identified MLP block repairs 68 to 92 percent of a predefined failure set. We next test whether training closes the gap by expanding reachability. In five of six matched evaluations, deployed performance rises while the reachable ceiling remains flat or falls. For DAPO, the deployed score rises by 14.7 points while the reachable ceiling falls by 13.3 points. Across the settings we audit, realization and reachability therefore do not always change together. Claims of capability expansion should report both realized performance and reachability under matched evaluation conditions. Code is available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/reachability-not-realization

</details>


### [101] [UniNav: A Unified World-Action Diffusion Model for Visual Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03244)
*Changqing Zhou,Yueru Luo,Zeyu Jiang,Changhao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UniNav is a unified diffusion model that jointly generates future visual observations and waypoint trajectories for image-goal navigation, outperforming baselines while offering a fast variant with 0.1s latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing navigation policies predict trajectories efficiently but lack visual foresight; navigation world models anticipate future observations but require costly planning rollouts. A unified model that combines both strengths is needed.

Method: UniNav uses a single transformer-based diffusion process to jointly denoise visual tokens and waypoint tokens, conditioned on history frames and a goal image. Geometry-aware camera tokens improve spatial grounding. The model trains on both trajectory-labeled navigation data and unlabeled video-only data. Two variants are offered: UniNav-Full (joint prediction of future frames + trajectories) and UniNav-Fast (drops future-image tokens at inference for efficiency).

Result: UniNav outperforms the strongest baseline in ATE (Average Trajectory Error) across all navigation benchmarks. UniNav-Fast achieves 0.1s inference latency with one-step inference without substantial accuracy degradation.

Conclusion: Unifying future observation prediction and action generation within a single diffusion framework yields state-of-the-art navigation performance while enabling flexible efficiency-accuracy trade-offs.

Abstract: Image-goal visual navigation is a fundamental capability for embodied agents. Existing navigation policies efficiently predict waypoint trajectories but lack visual foresight, while navigation world models can anticipate future observations but often require costly planning rollouts. We present UniNav, a unified world-action model that generates future visual observations and continuous waypoint trajectories through a single diffusion process. Given history frames and a goal image, UniNav jointly denoises visual and waypoint tokens within a single transformer, unifying future prediction and action generation in a shared framework. To improve spatial grounding, we incorporate geometry-aware camera tokens. We also train on both trajectory-labeled navigation data and video-only data, enabling the model to benefit from diverse videos without waypoint annotations. Based on this unified framework, we introduce two variants: UniNav-Full jointly predicts interpretable future observations and their corresponding trajectories, while UniNav-Fast removes future-image tokens at inference for efficient trajectory prediction. Experiments on navigation benchmarks show that UniNav outperforms the strongest baseline in ATE across all datasets. With one-step inference, UniNav-Fast achieves a latency of 0.1s without a substantial accuracy drop. Code will be released.

</details>


### [102] [One Knob to Rule Them All: A Unified Optimal Transport View of Cold-Start Active Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03249)
*Ning Zhu,Xiaochuan Ma,Juntao Xu,Jingze Liang,Mengfei Zhao,An Chen,Liang-Jian Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reframes Cold-Start Active Learning (CSAL) through optimal transport, proposing a unified framework that subsumes existing selection heuristics. It introduces entropic regularization with a data-adaptive rule and presents ε-Adaptive Selection (ε-AS), a Sinkhorn-based algorithm that achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks while significantly reducing selection time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CSAL methods rely on diverse heuristics (typicality, coverage, diversity), each with its own inductive bias — excelling on some tasks but failing on others. The core challenge is not designing yet another heuristic, but making CSAL automatically adapt to the data and task without prior knowledge.

Method: (1) A generalized transport selection framework is proposed, revealing the shared allocation structure across existing methods and subsuming representative formulations. (2) A theoretical analysis characterizes the trade-off controlled by entropic regularization and establishes a task-agnostic minimax bound for cold-start selection. (3) A data-adaptive regularization rule is derived, yielding ε-Adaptive Selection (ε-AS), a novel Sinkhorn-based CSAL algorithm.

Result: Extensive experiments on six public datasets with multiple annotation budgets demonstrate that ε-AS consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. On ImageNet-1k, it improves average accuracy over ActiveFT by 1.29% while reducing selection time by 56.2%.

Conclusion: CSAL can be effectively addressed by optimal transport with a data-adaptive regularization rule, eliminating the need for hand-crafted heuristics. The proposed ε-AS algorithm provides both theoretical guarantees and practical efficiency gains, setting a new state of the art across diverse vision tasks.

Abstract: Cold-Start Active Learning (CSAL) aims to select a valuable subset from an unlabeled pool without any prior knowledge or human assistance. Existing methods take diverse routes based on typicality, coverage, or diversity. Each rests on its own inductive bias and therefore performs well on some tasks yet poorly on others. We argue that the real challenge is not to design yet another selection heuristic, but to make CSAL adapt automatically to the data and task at hand. To this end, we revisit CSAL through the lens of optimal transport. First, we propose a generalized transport selection framework that reveals the shared allocation structure of existing methods and exactly subsumes representative formulations. Second, we introduce a theoretical analysis that characterizes the trade-off controlled by entropic regularization and establishes a task-agnostic minimax bound for cold-start selection. These results provide a principled foundation for adapting the regularization strength to the unlabeled data. Third, we derive a data-adaptive regularization rule and present a novel Sinkhorn-based CSAL algorithm, termed $ε$-Adaptive Selection ($ε$-AS). Extensive experiments on six public datasets and multiple annotation budgets show that $ε$-AS consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. On ImageNet-1k, it improves the average accuracy over ActiveFT by 1.29% while reducing selection time by 56.2%. Code will be released at https://github.com/Z-yiwei/OT-CSAL

</details>


### [103] [TaskPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Compression via Task-Guided Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03276)
*Wonpyo Park,Seung-won Hwang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TaskPress introduces a task-guided, query-agnostic KV cache eviction framework that builds a reusable compressed memory using a meta-query during prefill, and employs quantization scale factors as a zero-cost outlier detection signal for token importance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KV cache pruning methods compute query-specific token importance, making the pruned cache non-reusable across different queries. This limits efficiency in multi-query scenarios. There is a need for a query-agnostic approach that produces a compact cache reusable across diverse downstream queries.

Method: TaskPress uses a high-level task guide as a meta-query during the prefill phase to filter irrelevant tokens before any downstream queries arrive. It constructs a reusable memory representation conditioned on this task guide. Additionally, it leverages quantization scale factors as a zero-cost signal to detect influential representation outliers, serving as an efficient proxy for token importance without extra computation.

Result: Experiments across various long-context tasks show that TaskPress efficiently creates a compact, reusable KV cache that maintains performance across diverse queries.

Conclusion: TaskPress demonstrates that task-guided, query-agnostic KV cache eviction is a viable and efficient strategy for long-context LLM inference, enabling cache reuse and reducing memory overhead without sacrificing task performance.

Abstract: Long-context inference with large language models is constrained by the linear growth of the key-value cache to sequence length. While pruning offers mitigation, prevailing methods determine query-specific token importance that cannot be reused across unseen queries. In contrast, we introduce TaskPress, a framework for task-guided, query-agnostic KV cache eviction. Instead of optimizing the cache for a single query, TaskPress constructs a reusable memory representation conditioned on a high-level task guide. The guide functions as a meta-query during prefill to filter irrelevant tokens before downstream queries are issued. In addition, TaskPress leverages quantization scale factors as a zero-cost signal for detecting influential representation outliers, providing an efficient proxy for token importance. Experiments on conducted on various tasks with long context input demonstrate that TaskPress efficiently creates a compact, reusable cache across diverse queries.

</details>


### [104] [AgentPanel: Toward a New Paradigm for Human--AI Collaboration in Exploring Scientific Questions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03283)
*Zhiyao Cui,Qianyi Wang,Haoyang Yan,Yiqun Zhang,Siyue Ren,Hangfan Zhang,Zelin Tan,Hao Li,Chunjiang Mu,Dexian Cai,Shao Zhang,Chen Zhang,Meng Li,Jianan Chai,Yuting Fan,Zichao Ye,Xiaolei Yang,Xinyao Lu,Yuyang Yu,Wenjie Lou,Xiaosong Wang,Fenghua Ling,Shiyang Feng,Mao Su,Qiaosheng Zhang,Bo Zhang,Yang Chen,Lei Bai,Shuyue Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentPanel is a multi-agent forum system where heterogeneous AI agents asynchronously discuss scientific questions, enabling researchers to browse diverse perspectives, interact with agents, and generate summary reports. Offline experiments show it outperforms centralized multi-agent debate, and a human study found 65% of participants preferred it over standard LLM tools for early-stage scientific exploration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches to identifying promising scientific ideas — small-group discussions or one-to-one LLM interactions — expose researchers to only limited perspectives. There is a need for a system that provides broader, more diverse exploration of scientific directions.

Method: AgentPanel implements a forum-style environment where heterogeneous agents asynchronously discuss user-submitted scientific questions. Researchers can browse and organize candidate ideas, engage agents in follow-up interactions, and optionally generate post-hoc summary reports. The system was evaluated through offline experiments comparing against a centralized multi-agent debate baseline, plus a human study with 20 participants assessing idea quality, exploration breadth, interaction effectiveness, candidate-selection efficiency, and practical utility.

Result: Offline experiments demonstrated that AgentPanel outperforms a centralized multi-agent debate baseline. In the human study, 65% of participants favored AgentPanel over commonly used LLM tools for both breadth of research directions and overall suitability for early-stage exploration. Users valued the system for its perspective diversity and exploration support.

Conclusion: AgentPanel offers a promising paradigm for human-AI collaboration in scientific ideation, with its asynchronous multi-agent forum format effectively broadening the range of perspectives and improving early-stage research exploration compared to existing approaches.

Abstract: Identifying promising scientific ideas remains an important challenge in research practice. Researchers commonly rely on small-group discussions or one-to-one interactions with a single large language model, yet these approaches often expose them to only a limited range of perspectives and directions. We present AgentPanel, a multi-agent forum for human--AI collaboration in scientific exploration. Heterogeneous agents asynchronously discuss scientific questions in a forum-style environment, while researchers can submit questions, browse and organize candidate ideas, engage agents in follow-up interactions, and optionally generate post-hoc summary reports. We evaluate AgentPanel in terms of idea quality, exploration breadth, interaction effectiveness, candidate-selection efficiency, and practical utility. Offline experiments show that AgentPanel outperforms a centralized multi-agent debate baseline. A human study with 20 participants further shows that users value AgentPanel for perspective diversity and exploration support. In experience-based comparisons with commonly used LLM tools, 65\% of participants favored AgentPanel for both breadth of research directions and overall suitability for early-stage exploration. The platform is publicly available at https://agentpanel.cc/.

</details>


### [105] [DocTrace: Towards Traceable Long Document VQA via Hierarchical Evidence Graph Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03292)
*Le Xiang,Zhicheng Guan,Hong Chen,Xiaocong Lin,Zhenghua Lei,Teng Hu,Bolei He,Long Zeng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DocTrace reformulates Long Document VQA as explicit evidence graph reasoning, using a hierarchical framework with two-stage training (SFT + GRPO) to progressively localize, parse, and reason over multi-page document elements, achieving significant gains over baselines while providing traceable, verifiable reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLMs, RAG pipelines, and document agents for LongDocVQA lack explicit mechanisms to represent and verify how grounded evidence is progressively composed during reasoning. This limits answer accuracy and traceability. The authors argue for shifting from implicit answer prediction to explicit evidence graph reasoning.

Method: DocTrace is a hierarchical framework with three stages: evidence localization, structured document parsing, and evidence graph reasoning. Training uses a two-stage approach: (1) joint Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) initializes localization and graph reasoning abilities, followed by (2) task-specific Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with dedicated reward functions to further optimize these capabilities.

Result: On MMLongBench-Doc, LongDocURL, and SlideVQA, DocTrace (using Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone) outperforms open-source baselines and proprietary MLLMs, achieving absolute improvements of 14.4, 11.3, and 11.7 points respectively over the backbone model.

Conclusion: DocTrace demonstrates that explicit evidence graph reasoning with traceable, node-level provenance not only improves answer accuracy but also enables transparent and verifiable reasoning for long document understanding, outperforming both open-source and proprietary models.

Abstract: Long Document Visual Question Answering (LongDocVQA) requires Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to locate, integrate, and reason over heterogeneous document elements distributed across multiple pages. Existing approaches, including end-to-end MLLMs, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, and document agents, often lack explicit mechanisms to represent and verify how grounded evidence is progressively composed during reasoning, limiting both answer accuracy and traceability. In this paper, we cast LongDocVQA as an explicit evidence graph reasoning problem rather than implicit answer prediction. To this end, we propose DocTrace, a hierarchical framework that progressively performs evidence localization, structured document parsing, and evidence graph reasoning to enable explicit evidence provenance. To effectively learn these capabilities, we develop a two-stage training framework: joint Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) first initializes evidence localization and graph reasoning abilities, followed by task-specific Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with dedicated rewards to further optimize these capabilities. Extensive experiments on MMLongBench-Doc, LongDocURL, and SlideVQA demonstrate that DocTrace consistently outperforms both existing open-source baselines and proprietary MLLMs. Compared with the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone, DocTrace achieves absolute improvements of 14.4, 11.3, and 11.7 points on the three benchmarks, respectively. Beyond competitive performance, DocTrace constructs traceable evidence graphs with explicit node-level provenance, enabling transparent and verifiable reasoning for long document understanding.

</details>


### [106] [Distractor-Aware Truncation: Disentangling Context-Length Effects from Signal Loss in Long-Context LLM Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03297)
*Mohsen Arjmandi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper challenges the claim that shorter contexts improve LLM performance. It shows that naive middle-truncation causes score collapse simply because it destroys answer-bearing content, not because long contexts are inherently harmful. When only distractors are removed (distractor-aware protocol), performance is preserved or improves, demonstrating that the "shorter is better" finding is largely a methodological artifact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper questions a standard claim in retrieval-augmented and memory-augmented language model research: that shorter context improves performance when relevant information is preserved. The authors suspect this finding may be confounded by truncation methodology rather than reflecting genuine context-length effects.

Method: The authors evaluated two long-context benchmarks (BABILong, GraphWalks BFS) at four context-retention fractions (100%, 75%, 50%, 25%) using two truncation protocols: (1) naive middle-removal, and (2) distractor-aware removal (only non-relevant content dropped). Three Claude model sizes (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) and GPT-5.5 were tested, with replication on MRCR v2 and Oolong benchmarks. Statistical testing used paired Wilcoxon with Holm correction.

Result: Under naive truncation, performance collapsed monotonically across all conditions (p_adj < 0.05 in all cells). Under distractor-aware truncation, performance was preserved or improved: smaller Claude models showed significant gains on BABILong, while larger models remained at ceiling. The naive protocol destroyed answer-bearing content in >99% of samples at 25% retention, explaining the collapse. Results replicated across providers and benchmarks.

Conclusion: The "shorter context is better" finding is primarily an artifact of naive middle-truncation destroying task-relevant content. Future work on context-length effects must explicitly distinguish signal from distractor in their truncation methodology, otherwise results are ambiguous between the hypothesis that long contexts harm performance and the alternative that naive truncation simply removes the answer.

Abstract: A standard claim in the literature on retrieval-augmented and memory-augmented language models is that shorter context is better when the relevant information is preserved. We test this claim by running every sample of two long-context benchmarks -- BABILong and GraphWalks (BFS) -- at four context-retention fractions (100%, 75%, 50%, 25%) under two truncation protocols. The first is the naive protocol implicitly used in much prior work: drop content from the middle of the prompt. The second is distractor-aware: identify the task-relevant content for each sample and drop only the rest. We evaluate three sizes of the Claude family (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7) and, to test cross-provider generality, GPT-5.5 from a different provider; we apply the same protocol to two further benchmarks (MRCR v2, Oolong). Under naive truncation, score collapses monotonically (paired Wilcoxon, Holm-corrected p_adj < 0.05 in all eight BABILong and GraphWalks cells). Under the distractor-aware protocol -- which preserves the signal by construction -- performance is preserved or improves: the two smaller Claude models show statistically significant gains on BABILong, while the larger models (Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5) sit at their full-context ceiling. The naive collapse and its distractor-aware recovery replicate on GPT-5.5, ruling out a single-provider artifact. The mechanism is direct: under the naive protocol the answer-bearing content survives in fewer than 1% of samples at 25% retention; under the distractor-aware protocol it is preserved by construction. The naive protocol is therefore not a measurement of context-window effects; it is a measurement of how often middle-removal happens to spare the answer. We conclude that future studies of context-length effects must specify how they distinguish signal from distractor, or they are at best ambiguous between two opposite hypotheses.

</details>


### [107] [SeaSlides: Semantic Abstraction Layer for Agentic Slide Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03298)
*Shengjun Fang,Chenyang Wu,Zongzhang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SeaSlides introduces a semantic abstraction layer for agentic slide generation that separates content authoring from layout/rendering. Implemented in both HTML and Typst backends, it uses reusable components, capability modules for specialized objects (equations, code, charts), and three-stage feedback. Evaluated on UltraPresent and a new benchmark (SeaSlidesBench-Rich), it outperforms SVG-heavy generation in rich-content macro-average across most models while maintaining overall quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing slide generation systems force a trade-off: templates preserve regularity but limit adaptation, while free-form HTML/SVG gives flexibility at the cost of brittle low-level rendering. This is especially problematic for technical presentations containing formulas, code, or data charts. No existing system simultaneously preserves source fidelity, maintains coherent design, renders specialized objects, and produces usable artifacts.

Method: SeaSlides proposes a semantic abstraction layer where models write structured slide content via reusable components and capability modules, while templates own layout, style, and rendering. Two instantiations are provided: SeaSlides-HTML (template-defined DOM components) and SeaSlides-Typst (template functions and package-backed modules). Capability modules route equations, code, and charts to dedicated renderers. Three feedback stages localize build errors, project-constraint violations, and visual defects before export.

Result: Evaluated on the 128-task UltraPresent setting plus SeaSlidesBench-Rich (32 tasks stressing math, code, pseudocode, tables, charts, diagrams). Across four generation models, both SeaSlides backends produce more readable, content-oriented source than SVG-heavy generation. A SeaSlides backend achieves the highest rich-content macro-average under three of four models while maintaining competitive overall qualitative performance.

Conclusion: Semantic abstraction is a practical and effective authoring principle for agentic slide generation across presentation backends. By decoupling content specification from rendering details, SeaSlides improves source readability, specialized object rendering, and overall robustness in technical presentation generation.

Abstract: Agentic presentation generation must preserve source content, maintain coherent visual design, render specialized objects, and produce usable artifacts. Existing systems meet only part of this requirement: templates preserve regularity but restrict adaptation, whereas free-form HTML or SVG gives models flexibility at the cost of low-level rendering decisions. This mismatch makes long technical decks brittle, especially when slides contain formulas, code, or data graphics. We present SeaSlides, an agentic slide-generation framework built around a semantic abstraction layer. Rather than authoring coordinates, inline styles, or raw SVG geometry, the model writes structured slide content through reusable components and capability modules, while templates own layout, style, and rendering. We instantiate this principle separately in HTML and Typst: SeaSlides-HTML uses template-defined DOM components, whereas SeaSlides-Typst uses template functions and package-backed modules. Capability modules route equations, code, and charts to dedicated renderers, and three feedback stages localize build errors, project-constraint violations, and visual defects before export. The two systems retain backend-specific syntax and contracts while sharing the same authoring boundary. For evaluation, we combine the 128-task UltraPresent validation setting with SeaSlidesBench-Rich, a new 32-task benchmark stressing mathematics, code, pseudocode, tables, charts, and diagrams. Across four generation models, both SeaSlides backends produce more readable, content-oriented source than SVG-heavy generation. A SeaSlides backend attains the highest rich-content macro-average under three of the four models while maintaining competitive overall qualitative performance. These results support semantic abstraction as a practical authoring principle across presentation backends.

</details>


### [108] [Screenshots or Tools? Eliciting Tool Use and Managing Multimodal Context in Hybrid GUI-MCP Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03327)
*Siqi Fan,Minghao Li,Xiaoqian Ma,Wenhui Tan,Xiusheng Huang,Juntong Wu,Liujie Zhang,Shuo Shang,Weihang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid computer-use agents exhibit a "tool adoption gap": reasoning models benefit modestly from GUI tools while non-reasoning models are harmed. The core issue is that models default to cheaper screenshot-based routes and are never trained to use tools effectively. Multi-turn RL with tool bonuses can steer behavior but not competence; the real bottleneck is tool-call semantics. Compressing observation history by dropping redundant screenshots after successful tool calls reduces input cost by ~1/3 while improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current hybrid agents that combine screenshot-based action with text-tool invocation show inconsistent effects from tool availability. The paper aims to diagnose why identical tools can either help or hurt performance, and to characterize and address the systematic underuse of available tools — termed the "adoption gap."

Method: Experiments use the OSWorld-MCP benchmark (309 tasks) with a unified GUI-MCP harness. Two model classes are compared: reasoning models and non-reasoning models, each run 5 times. Analysis focuses on tool-decision behavior (ignoring, misnaming, false termination). Multi-turn RL probes are conducted at two levels: (1) action-level, using dense tool bonuses to incentivize tool adoption; (2) context-level, compressing observation history by dropping redundant post-tool-call screenshots and retraining under the compressed observation rule.

Result: MCP tools improve reasoning models by +4.0pp but degrade non-reasoning models by -5.9pp (both >2 SE). The reasoning model calls tools on only 55/309 tasks (23.9% of tool-reachable ones). Dense tool bonus RL raises spreadsheet tool adoption from 0.03 to 0.33, but held-out accuracy does not improve, indicating behavior is steerable but competence is not. Context compression (dropping redundant screenshots) cuts input tokens by ~1/3 with small accuracy cost; retraining under this rule removes that cost entirely, yielding 37.8% accuracy vs. 33.0% uncompressed at 53% of the input cost, and closing the rich-lean gap on degraded subsets to zero.

Conclusion: Tools help only when the model both chooses and integrates them correctly. The adoption gap arises because models default to cheaper routes and lack training to use tools. While behavior can be steered via RL, competence is bottlenecked by tool-call semantics. Observation compression with retraining eliminates redundancy and closes performance gaps, suggesting a path toward more efficient hybrid agents that actually leverage their available tools.

Abstract: Hybrid computer-use agents can act through screenshots or call text tools. We find that having a tool available does not settle which way the effect goes. Under one identical GUI-MCP harness on the OSWorld-MCP benchmark (309 tasks), the same MCP tools improve a reasoning model by +4.0pp and degrade a non-reasoning model by -5.9pp (5 runs each, both beyond 2 SE). What separates the two is tool-decision behavior. The non-reasoning policy ignores, misnames, or falsely terminates around tools. The reasoning model avoids these failures, yet still calls a tool on only 55/309 tasks, 23.9% of the tool-reachable ones. We call this shortfall the adoption gap. Both levels of the problem share one cause: the model already has a cheaper route and is never trained to take it. Multi-turn RL probes that cause. At the action level, a dense tool bonus raises spreadsheet adoption 0.03 -> 0.33 and carries into greedy decoding, but held-out accuracy does not follow. Behavior is steerable; competence is not. The bottleneck lies in tool-call semantics. At the context level, a successful tool call often makes the next screenshot redundant. Dropping it and halving image history cuts input tokens by about a third, at a small accuracy cost. Retraining under the same observation rule removes that cost. The compressed agent then reaches 37.8% against 33.0% for the uncompressed operating point, at 53% of the input cost, and closes the rich-lean gap on a pre-registered degraded subset to zero. Tools help when the model chooses and integrates them, and current hybrid agents leave many such choices unused.

</details>

### [109] [An Empirical Analysis of the Glob Ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02610)
*Phyllis Lim,Connor Adkins,Mark Marron*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: First empirical study of glob patterns across 6 ecosystems (1,966 projects, 1,355 GitHub issues, 444 CVEs, 361 StackOverflow posts) revealing widespread fragmentation, inconsistent behaviors, and security vulnerabilities. Proposes GlobSpec, a formal specification to resolve ambiguities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Glob patterns are ubiquitous in modern software (build scripts, config files, web routes) but suffer from a fragmented, non-standardized ecosystem that leads to inconsistent behaviors, security vulnerabilities, and portability issues across tools and languages.

Method: Large-scale empirical study analyzing 1,966 open-source projects, 1,355 GitHub issues, 444 CVE reports, and 361 StackOverflow posts to map feature support and real-world usage of globs across six common ecosystems. Systematic comparison of implementations against developer expectations.

Result: Found a stark divide between glob implementations and developer adoption patterns. Documented wide-ranging inconsistencies that harm portability and reliability. Security vulnerabilities dominate developer discussions, comprising nearly 25% of all glob-related discourse. Identified a significant expressiveness gap between current implementations and developer requirements.

Conclusion: The glob ecosystem is fundamentally fractured. The authors propose GlobSpec, a formal specification designed to eliminate semantic ambiguities and bridge the expressiveness gap, charting a path toward standardization and more robust glob implementations.

Abstract: Glob patterns, a domain-specific language for structured string matching, are a foundational yet understudied component of modern software development embedded in everything from build scripts and configuration files to web server routes. However, this widespread use rests on a fragile foundation. Despite their ubiquity across tools and programming languages, a lack of standardization has led to a fragmented ecosystem rife with inconsistent behaviors, security vulnerabilities, and usability pitfalls. This paper presents the first empirical study of the glob ecosystem to quantify these challenges and chart a path toward robust solutions.
  Through an analysis of 1,966 open source projects, 1,355 Github issues, 444 CVE reports, and 361 StackOverflow posts, we systematically map the feature support and real-world usage of globs across six common ecosystems that utilize globs. Our findings reveal a stark divide between various globbing implementations and developer adoption. In addition, we document inconsistencies that hinder portability, reliability, and create security flaws. Our analysis reveals that security vulnerabilities are not corner cases, but a dominant concern, comprising almost a quarter of all developer discussions. We propose a path forward through standardization and introduce a formal specification for globs, GlobSpec, designed to resolve semantic ambiguities and bridge the expressiveness gap between current implementations and developer requirements.

</details>


### [110] [Rethinking Self-Evolving Agent Skills: Feedback Dynamics over Multiple Rounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02636)
*Yuxuan Liu,Zhaochen Su,Yuhao Zhang,Jiahe Guo,Zhongwei Xie,Huihao Jing,Lingyun Xie,Qing Zong,Yauwai Yim,Zhixiong Zhang,Haoran Li,Yangqiu Song*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Skill self-evolution is sparse and feedback-dependent: only failed trajectories consistently drive useful updates; test-time scaling cannot fully replicate these gains, and returns vary significantly across models and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: It is unclear under what conditions self-evolving skill systems produce meaningful improvements, how different types of feedback (successes vs. failures) influence revision quality, and whether additional test-time computation can achieve comparable results without persistent skill updates.

Method: A controlled evaluation framework is applied across five benchmarks and three models, with 42 feedback runs over 14 model-benchmark settings. Within each setting, only the feedback shown to the optimizer is varied: successes and failures (Normal), failures only, or successes only. A broader SearchQA analysis covers eight models, and GPT-5.5 test-time scaling controls (oracle Parallel Sampling and Sequential Refinement) are used to compare against evolved skills.

Result: Only 55 of 388 candidates achieve byte-distinct validation bests. Validation-based selection chooses evolved skills in 11 of 14 settings, with 9 improving released-test performance. All 11 selections come from conditions that include failed trajectories. Feedback views sometimes diverge on validation vs. downstream metrics. On GPT-5.5, oracle Parallel Sampling comes within 0.43 points of the evolved SearchQA skill but trails by 30.96 points on SpreadsheetBench; Sequential Refinement recovers neither gain.

Conclusion: Persistent skill self-evolution is best characterized as sparse, validation-filtered search with model- and benchmark-dependent returns, rather than steady improvement from additional rounds. Failed trajectories are essential for effective revision, and test-time scaling does not fully substitute for persistent skill updates.

Abstract: Self-evolving skill systems promise to improve agents by turning execution feedback into persistent skill updates without changing the underlying model. Yet it remains unclear when further evolution helps, how successful and failed trajectories shape revision, and whether extra test-time computation can recover the same gains. To address these questions, we present a controlled evaluation framework across five benchmarks and three models. Our primary study contains 42 feedback runs across 14 supported model-benchmark settings. Within each setting, we hold the executor and optimizer configuration, revision procedure, validation rule, and round budget fixed, while varying only the feedback shown to the optimizer: successes and failures (Normal), failures only, or successes only. Evolution is sparse: only 55 of 388 candidates establish byte-distinct validation bests. Validation-based selection chooses an evolved skill in 11 of 14 settings, nine of which improve released-test performance. All 11 selections come from feedback conditions that include failed trajectories, although the relative ranking of Normal and Fail-only varies across settings. Validation and downstream evaluations on test, robustness, and transfer sometimes favor different feedback views. A broader SearchQA analysis covering eight models shows similarly sparse, feedback-dependent dynamics. In the GPT-5.5 test-time-scaling controls, oracle Parallel Sampling comes within 0.43 points of the evolved SearchQA skill but remains 30.96 points behind on SpreadsheetBench; Sequential Refinement recovers neither gain. Overall, persistent skill self-evolution is better understood as sparse, validation-filtered search with model- and benchmark-dependent returns, rather than steady improvement from additional rounds. The implementation is available at https://github.com/HKUST-KnowComp/rethinkskill.

</details>


### [111] [Studying, Identifying, and Fixing Hidden Technical Debt in AI-Intensive Cyber-Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02638)
*Beena*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This thesis investigates technical debt (TD) in AI-enabled Cyber-Physical Systems (AI-CPS), aiming to characterize it, and develop identification and repair approaches, culminating in an automated agentic AI tool for TD governance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-CPS, integrating hardware, AI, and conventional software across domains like autonomous vehicles and healthcare, can accumulate unique and more challenging forms of technical debt than traditional systems, necessitating dedicated characterization and mitigation strategies.

Method: A multi-phase approach: first, characterizing AI-CPS TD by analyzing AI ecosystems, mining AI-CPS repositories, and conducting developer interviews; second, defining identification and mitigation approaches based on acquired knowledge; third, developing and validating an automated tool leveraging agentic AI for TD monitoring, governance, and repayment.

Result: The abstract outlines planned research phases rather than completed results, describing a roadmap for TD characterization, approach definition, and automated tool development.

Conclusion: The thesis contributes a characterization framework for AI-CPS technical debt and proposes agentic AI-driven automation for its continuous management, addressing a critical gap in maintaining these complex, heterogeneous systems.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) components are increasingly pervasive in several software systems, including Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs). AI-CPS are used in several domains, including autonomous vehicles, industry, home automation, robotics, and healthcare. Being composed of hardware, AI components, and conventional modules, AI-CPS can exhibit technical debt (TD) that is peculiar and potentially more challenging than that of conventional systems. This thesis aims to characterize AI-CPS TD and propose approaches for its identification and repair. In a first phase, we characterize AI-CPS TD by analyzing AI ecosystems and AI-CPS repositories, as well as interviewing developers. Based on the acquired knowledge, we define approaches to identify and mitigate such TD. Finally, we plan to develop and validate an automated tool that supports agentic AI solutions to monitor, govern, and repay AI-CPS TD.

</details>


### [112] [Instruction Stacking Collapse: A Benchmark and the Capability-Dependent Value of Prompt Compilation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02639)
*Atul Anand,Sourav Chattaraj*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: As constraints in LLM prompts accumulate, instruction-following accuracy degrades non-linearly from ~96% to ~20% due to structured pairwise conflicts. A training-free instruction compiler can recover up to +11 points for weaker models, with gains attributed to rewriting rather than confounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world LLM prompts often contain multiple simultaneous constraints (e.g., JSON output, word limits, citation requirements, tone specifications), yet prior work largely studies instruction-following for single constraints. The authors aim to systematically characterize how performance degrades as constraints accumulate and whether a lightweight remedy exists.

Method: The authors introduce a benchmark stacking 24 verifier-checked instructions (1–20 at a time) and evaluate three production LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash). They analyze degradation patterns and pairwise conflicts, then evaluate a training-free instruction compiler that rewrites stacked prompts in a single LLM call, reused across queries. Rigorous controls include cluster-robust tests, same-baseline comparisons, and within-family scaling ladder experiments.

Result: Instruction-following degrades non-linearly from ~96% (single instruction) to as low as 20% (multiple instructions). A structured set of pairwise conflicts drives the degradation — e.g., a "JSON output" constraint is jointly unsatisfiable with nine others. The instruction compiler recovers up to +11 follow-rate points for weaker models while leaving stronger models unchanged. Gains are attributed to the rewrite itself, not extra tokens, reordering, or measurement headroom.

Conclusion: Instruction-following suffers from predictable, structured pairwise conflicts under constraint accumulation rather than random failure. A simple, training-free prompt rewriting strategy offers capability-graded benefits — most helpful for weaker (and more commonly deployed) models. The benchmark, verifiers, and cached runs are publicly released for reproducibility.

Abstract: Production prompts rarely carry a single instruction. One system message may require valid JSON, a word limit, three citations, and a fixed tone at the same time. We study how instruction-following degrades as such constraints accumulate. We introduce a benchmark that stacks 24 verifier-checked instructions, one to twenty at a time, and evaluate three production-tier LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash). Instruction-following degrades non-linearly: the follow rate falls from ~96% to as low as 20%, driven by a structured and reproducible set of pairwise conflicts. A single "output JSON" constraint, for example, is jointly unsatisfiable with nine others. We then evaluate a training-free remedy: an instruction compiler that rewrites the stacked prompt in a single LLM call and is reused across queries. Its benefit is capability-graded. It recovers up to +11 points of follow rate for weaker models, which are also the models most often deployed at scale, while leaving stronger models, which already internalise the same structure, essentially unchanged. Cluster-robust tests, same-baseline controls, and a within-family scaling ladder attribute the gain to the rewrite itself rather than to additional tokens, reordering, or measurement headroom. We release the benchmark, verifiers, and cached runs for full reproduction.

</details>


### [113] [IR2Solve: Structured Intermediate Representations for Cost-Efficient Optimization Autoformulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02641)
*Penglin Zhu,Linhai Zhang,Jungang Xu,Xinchi Wei,Xiuqi Wu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: IR2Solve introduces a cost-efficient LLM-based autoformulation pipeline that uses a single semantic call to produce a structured intermediate representation (ModelIR), followed by deterministic verification and compilation, achieving competitive accuracy at a fraction of the inference cost compared to multi-call baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct code generation by LLMs for optimization problems is brittle, prone to schema/indexing/semantic errors causing compilation failures or incorrect models. Existing repair, search, and multi-agent methods increase inference cost. The authors aim to achieve reliable autoformulation with minimal LLM calls.

Method: IR2Solve is a three-stage pipeline: (1) a single semantic LLM call produces a schema-constrained ModelIR — an intermediate representation capturing sets, parameters, variables, objectives, and constraints using restricted Python-like expressions; (2) a deterministic verification stage checks correctness; (3) an IR-to-solver compilation stage translates verified ModelIR into solver-ready formulations. A key design is the scalar-constraint convention, which expands per-index constraint families into individual entries, reducing free-index and implicit-quantification errors.

Result: IR2Solve achieves strong objective correctness across six cleaned optimization benchmarks, remaining competitive with recent systems. An ablation on 153 IndustryOR and ComplexLP instances shows sequential gains from the structured IR, scalar-constraint convention, and deterministic verification. On a ten-instance cost panel, IR2Solve uses 1 semantic call per instance versus 8 for Chain-of-Experts and 39 for SAC-Opt, consuming only 1/3.3 and 1/22.9 of the token volume, respectively.

Conclusion: Structured intermediate representations combined with deterministic post-generation processing offer a practical accuracy-cost trade-off for LLM-based optimization autoformulation, dramatically reducing inference cost while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language optimization problems into solver-ready formulations, but direct code generation is brittle: schema, indexing, and semantic errors can cause compilation failures, infeasible models, or incorrect objectives, while iterative repair, search, and multi-agent workflows increase inference cost. We present IR2Solve, an intermediate-representation-first autoformulation pipeline that uses a single semantic LLM call to produce a schema-constrained ModelIR, followed by two deterministic stages: verification and IR-to-solver compilation. ModelIR explicitly represents sets, parameters, variables, objectives, and constraints using restricted Python-like expression strings. A concrete scalar-constraint convention represents finite per-index constraint families as individual entries, reducing free-index and implicit-quantification errors while simplifying downstream verification and compilation. Across six cleaned optimization benchmarks, IR2Solve achieves strong objective correctness and remains competitive with recent optimization-modeling systems. A controlled ablation on 153 IndustryOR and ComplexLP instances shows sequential gains from the structured IR interface, the scalar-constraint instruction, and deterministic verification. On a matched ten-instance cost panel, IR2Solve uses one semantic call per instance, whereas Chain-of-Experts and SAC-Opt use 8 and 39 calls per instance and consume 3.3 and 22.9 times the token volume of IR2Solve, respectively. These results show that structured intermediate representations, combined with deterministic post-generation processing, provide a practical accuracy-cost trade-off for LLM-based optimization autoformulation.

</details>


### [114] [CUADebug: Diagnosing and Repairing Computer-Use Agent Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02643)
*Weijia Zhang,Kunlun Zhu,Zeyi Liu,Yinting Chen,Tianyi Ma,Jiateng Liu,Jiaxun Zhang,Bingxuan Li,Xiangru Tang,Heng Ji,Jiaxuan You*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CUADebug is a framework for diagnosing and repairing failures in computer-use agents (CUAs). It introduces a CUA-specific error taxonomy, a human-annotated benchmark (CUAErrorBench) of 204 failed OSWorld trajectories, and CUADebugger, a tool-augmented debugger that actively inspects suspicious steps with before/after screenshots and action traces to produce structured diagnoses. The framework improves step-level diagnosis accuracy and enables actionable repair, boosting task completion from 12.2% to 25.86% in continual re-execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
