Motivation: CUA failures are difficult to diagnose and repair because they arise from coupled visual perception, spatial grounding, low-level interaction, task reasoning, and environment dynamics — a distinctive multimodal causal localization problem that text-only agent debugging methods cannot address.

Method: CUADebug consists of three components: (1) a CUA-specific error taxonomy covering task reasoning/control, perception, grounding/interaction, external/system errors, and infeasible tasks; (2) CUAErrorBench, a human-annotated benchmark of 204 failed OSWorld trajectories; and (3) CUADebugger, a tool-augmented debugger that actively inspects suspicious steps using paired before/after screenshots and action traces, then outputs a structured diagnosis (root-cause step, error type, grounded evidence, and corrective strategy) for re-execution, rather than prompting over the full trajectory once.

Result: Task reasoning and control is the largest failure family (110/204), followed by perception (36), grounding/interaction (25), external/system (13), and infeasible-task cases (20). CUADebugger with Gemini 2.5 Pro improved joint subtype-and-step diagnosis from 11.2% to 19.6% on the main Claude-agent split. RCA-based single re-execution achieved 28.47–29.90% task completion vs. 13.89% for history-only continuation. Continual re-execution with CUADebugger improved success from 12.2% to 25.86%, approaching human-oracle guidance at 29.21%.

Conclusion: CUA root-cause diagnosis can provide actionable repair signals rather than merely post-hoc explanations. Structured debugging with active inspection of suspicious steps significantly outperforms naive full-trajectory prompting, and the approach generalizes across different debugger backbones.

Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) operate real desktop and web interfaces through screenshots, mouse and keyboard actions, and stateful UI feedback, yet their failures remain difficult to diagnose and repair. Unlike text-only agents, CUA failures arise from coupled visual perception, spatial grounding, low-level interaction, task reasoning, and environment dynamics, making debugging a distinctive multimodal causal localization problem. We introduce CUADebug, a framework for diagnosing and repairing CUA failures. CUADebug includes a CUA-specific error taxonomy, CUAErrorBench, a human-annotated OSWorld failure benchmark, and CUADebugger, a tool-augmented debugger. Instead of prompting over the full trajectory once, CUADebugger actively inspects suspicious steps with paired before/after screenshots and action traces, then submits a structured diagnosis containing the root-cause step, error type, grounded evidence, and corrective strategy for re-execution. Human annotations over 204 failed trajectories show that task reasoning and control is the largest failure family (110/204), followed by perception (36), grounding/interaction (25), external/system (13), and an others category of 20 OSWorld infeasible-task cases. On the main Claude-agent split, CUADebugger improves joint subtype-and-step diagnosis from 11.2% to 19.6% with Gemini 2.5 Pro and improves consistently across debugger backbones. In single re-execution package evaluation, RCA-based conditions achieve higher task completion than history-only continuation (28.47% with machine RCA and 29.90% with our method, versus 13.89%); in continual re-execution, our method improves success from 12.2% to 25.86%, while human-oracle guidance reaches 29.21%. These results show that CUA root-cause diagnosis can provide actionable repair signals rather than merely post-hoc explanations.

</details>


### [115] [A Unified Feature Model for Microservice Identification and Refactoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02644)
*Ana Almeida,António Rito Silva*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a feature model that captures the variation points across microservice identification tools, demonstrating that while no single tool covers the full design space, existing tools collectively span almost all identified variation points — highlighting fragmentation and the need for integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Systematic comparison and experimentation across microservice identification approaches is hindered by the absence of a common conceptual framework. No single optimal method exists, and integrating multiple approaches is necessary to explore design trade-offs.

Method: The authors conducted an extensive analysis of the state of the art to derive a feature model for variant-rich microservice identification tools. They evaluated this model through a systematic mapping of representative literature and by instantiating it within the architecture of an existing microservice identification tool.

Result: The feature model successfully captures the primary variation points of existing methodologies. No individual tool covers more than a fraction of the model, but collectively the analyzed tools span almost all variation points, revealing complementarity and fragmentation across standalone tools.

Conclusion: The design space for microservice identification is populated but fragmented. A unifying feature model enables analysis, comparison, and design of tools, and the observed complementarity motivates future work on integrating multiple approaches into cohesive solutions.

Abstract: Several approaches have been proposed for the automatic identification of microservices within monolithic systems. These methodologies differ in their data collection and analysis techniques, the decomposition algorithms applied, and the mechanisms used to visualize and refine candidate microservices. Despite this diversity, systematic experimentation and comparison across approaches remain limited by the absence of a common conceptual framework. Furthermore, current research indicates that no single optimal method exists; rather, integrating multiple approaches is necessary to fully explore the trade-offs inherent in any design solution.
  To address this gap, this paper proposes a feature model for variant-rich microservice identification tools, grounded in an extensive analysis of the state of the art. We evaluate this feature model through a systematic mapping of representative literature and by analyzing its instantiation within the architecture of an existing microservice identification tool. Our findings are two-fold. First, the proposed feature model successfully captures the primary variation points of existing methodologies, providing a unifying foundation for analyzing, comparing, and designing microservice identification tools. Second, while no individual tool covers more than a fraction of the model, the analyzed tools jointly span almost all of its variation points. This complementarity is the central result: the design space is already populated, but it is fragmented across standalone tools, none of which can compare or integrate the alternatives that the others implement.

</details>


### [116] [Verified Tool Calls Improve LLM Agent Reliability Under Non-Atomic Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02645)
*Isham Kalappurackal Mansoor,Abhishek Phadke,Pratip Rana*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLM agents suffer reliability issues when tools exhibit non-atomic behaviors (timeouts, partial updates). A lightweight wrapper with postcondition verification, verify-before-retry, and idempotency keys reduces duplicate actions while maintaining task success rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent frameworks assume tool calls are atomic with binary success/failure signals, but real-world tools often behave non-atomically — producing timeouts after dispatch, delayed visibility, and partial state updates. These mismatches cause duplicate actions, spurious task failures, and unnecessary tool executions.

Method: A lightweight, verification-aware tool wrapper is introduced, which augments tool calls with three mechanisms: (1) postcondition verification to confirm intended state changes actually occurred, (2) verify-before-retry logic to avoid redundant re-execution, and (3) idempotency keys to safely handle retries. Evaluation is conducted in a controlled simulated environment with injected non-atomic failures across multiple task templates.

Result: The proposed method significantly reduces duplicate actions while maintaining comparable task success rates, without requiring any modification to the underlying LLM.

Conclusion: Strengthening tool interaction semantics via lightweight wrappers is a promising, model-agnostic direction for improving LLM agent reliability in real-world, non-atomic tool environments.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents rely on external tools to perform multistage tasks. Existing agent frameworks typically assume that tool calls are atomic and return binary success or failure signals. However, real-world systems exhibit non-atomic behaviors such as timeouts after dispatch, delayed visibility, and partial state updates. These mismatches lead to reliability issues including duplicate actions, task success, and unnecessary tool executions. A lightweight, verification-aware tool wrapper is introduced that augments tool calls with postcondition verification, verify-before-retry logic, and idempotency keys. The approach is evaluated in a controlled simulated environment with injected non-atomic failures across multiple task templates. The results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces duplicate actions, while maintaining comparable task success rates. Overall, the findings suggest that strengthening tool interaction semantics is a promising direction for improving LLM agent reliability without requiring modifications to the underlying language model.

</details>


### [117] [Intent-Level Quantum Programming with Assertion-Guided Execution and Inspectable Intermediate Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02648)
*Ilesh Vora,Srikanth Thudumu,John Carlson,Harshil Kamdar,Rajesh Vasa*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A QDSL with intent-execution separation, IR introspection, and assertion-guided automatic modality selection enables portable, inspectable, and automatically validated quantum programs. Fault detection is near-perfect (TPR 1.0), cross-framework numerical agreement is achieved after endianness canonicalization, and IR generation is sub-millisecond.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum programming faces multiple challenges: circuits as imperative gate sequences are hard to inspect, execution modalities require manual selection, outputs are probabilistic, and portability across backend frameworks is difficult due to differing internal conventions. These problems compound, making validation of quantum programs especially challenging.

Method: The authors present a quantum domain-specific language (QDSL) with three mechanisms: (1) intent-execution separation, where algorithmic constructs (preparation, superposition, entanglement, measurement) are inspectable objects compiled to backend-specific circuits after IR validation; (2) first-class IR introspection exposing circuit width, wire mapping, operation order, and measurement intent; (3) assertion-guided modality inference that automatically selects sampling, statevector, or dual execution modes based on declared verification properties. Results are logged in structured form for reproducible regression testing.

Result: Fault-injection experiments on Bell and 3-qubit GHZ circuits show a total-variation-distance detector achieves TPR of 1.0 across all shot budgets. False positives (FPR 2.7–3.8%) occur only at 128 shots. Differential testing shows numerical agreement between PennyLane and Qiskit compilation targets after endianness canonicalization. IR generation costs remain sub-millisecond.

Conclusion: The proposed QDSL effectively addresses quantum program validation challenges through declarative intent representation, pre-execution IR inspection, and automated execution modality inference. The approach demonstrates strong fault-detection capability, cross-framework portability, and negligible compilation overhead, supporting reproducible regression testing for quantum software.

Abstract: Quantum programs are difficult to validate: circuits are typically expressed as imperative gate sequences with limited inspectability, execution modalities must be selected manually, and outputs are inherently probabilistic. These challenges are compounded when programs must be portable across backend frameworks with differing internal conventions. We present a quantum domain-specific language (QDSL) that addresses these problems through three mechanisms: (i) intent-execution separation, where algorithmic constructs such as preparation, superposition, entanglement, and measurement are represented as inspectable objects compiled into backend-specific circuits only after pre-execution Intermediate Representation (IR) validation; (ii) first-class IR introspection, exposing circuit width, wire mapping, operation order, and measurement intent for developer inspection prior to execution; and (iii) assertion-guided modality inference, where the engine examines declared verification properties to automatically select sampling, statevector, or dual execution without user intervention. Results are logged in structured form to support reproducible regression testing. We evaluate our prototype on benchmark circuits spanning entanglement, oracle-based, structured-transform, and variational examples. In fault-injection experiments on Bell and 3-qubit GHZ circuits, a total-variation-distance detector identifies the injected faults across all evaluated shot budgets (True Positive Rate 1.0), with observed false positives (False Positive Rate 2.7-3.8%) only at 128 shots. Differential testing demonstrates numerical agreement across PennyLane and Qiskit compilation targets for the evaluated constructs after endianness canonicalization. IR generation costs are sub-millisecond.

</details>


### [118] [When Policies Change Probabilities: Modular Decision-Making for LLM Code Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02677)
*Rasvik Kudum,Max Corbett,Hitansh Paliwal,Romaisa Fatima,Thomas Jiralerspong,Sneheel Sarangi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLM code reviewers conflate risk estimation with decision policy, causing probability estimates to shift when cost structures change. A modular pipeline that separates evidence elicitation, risk scoring, and cost-based action improves both probability accuracy and downstream loss across four deployed reviewer interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM code reviewers bundle patch risk assessment and approval decisions into a single prompt. This violates the normative principle that probability should depend solely on evidence, while actions should follow from combining probabilities with costs. The authors investigate whether deployed interfaces preserve this separation and quantify the consequences when they fail to do so.

Method: The study evaluates 15,792 responses on 720 candidate patches across 360 repository issues, each with one passing and one failing patch verified by an archived test harness. Four deployed reviewer interfaces are tested under matched prompts where only the cost structure changes: equal-cost versus 10:1 false-accept penalty. A separate modular pipeline is introduced that elicits risk without policy information, incorporates an independent monitor score, and applies costs externally in code. Loss and probability accuracy are compared across all conditions.

Result: Switching from equal-cost to 10:1 false-accept policy shifts reported failure probabilities by 13.6–16.9 pp on average, despite identical evidence. Under the high-cost prompt, all reviewers perform worse than simply rejecting every patch. When the 10:1 rule is applied to probabilities elicited under equal costs, loss drops for all four systems, indicating that probability elicitation itself drives excess loss. The modular pipeline improves probability accuracy and reduces mean loss by 0.073 per issue at equal costs while accepting 58–68% of patches; at 10:1 costs, it accepts none — matching the reject-all baseline.

Conclusion: Policy information leaks into probability estimates when risk elicitation and action are conflated in a single prompt. Separation of risk estimation, evidence integration, and cost-based decision-making improves reliability and reduces loss. The authors recommend evaluating these components independently in LLM-based code review systems.

Abstract: LLM code reviewers often estimate patch risk and make approval decisions in one prompt. A probability should depend on evidence; costs should determine the action taken from it. We test whether four deployed reviewer interfaces preserve this separation using 15,792 responses on 720 candidate patches, with one that passed and one that failed an archived test harness for each of 360 repository issues. In matched calls with the patch and monitor evidence fixed, replacing an equal-cost policy with a 10:1 false-accept policy changes reported failure probabilities by 13.6 to 16.9 percentage points on average. For every reviewer, the actions returned under the high-cost prompt are worse than rejecting all patches. Applying the same high-cost rule to probabilities elicited under equal costs reduces loss for all four systems, showing that probability elicitation itself contributes to the excess loss. We also evaluate a modular pipeline that elicits risk without policy information, combines an independent monitor score, and applies costs in code. Relative to calibrated reviewer-only scores, the pipeline improves average probability accuracy and, at equal costs, reduces mean loss by .073 per issue while accepting 58 to 68% of patches. At 10:1, it accepts none and matches reject-all. Downstream policy can therefore change the probability it is meant to use, motivating separate evaluation of risk, outside evidence, and action.

</details>


### [119] [AI Sandbox: Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02679)
*Muhammad Waseem,Md Aidul Islam,Md Nasir Uddin Shuvo,Md Mahade Hasan,Kai-Kristian Kemell,Jussi Rasku,Mika Saari,Vilma Saari,Roope Pajasmaa,Markku Oivo,Pekka Abrahamsson*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Presents the design of a governance-aware, multi-tenant AI sandbox for industry-academia collaboration, featuring separated architecture layers, structured experimentation, reusable evaluation evidence, and integrated approval/audit workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite growing interest in AI sandboxes, there is limited practical guidance on designing platforms that combine rapid experimentation with governance requirements such as tenant separation, controlled access, and transparent workflows in collaborative industry-academia settings.

Method: Iterative requirements refinement with industrial partners; reference architecture separating multi-tenant UI from backend control plane with dedicated execution and data-management layers; implementation of governed onboarding, project-based collaboration, managed AI service access, approval workflows, audit logging, and persistent experiment records.

Result: A functional governance-aware sandbox platform that enables traceable experimentation with persistent storage of configurations, contextual information, and governance decisions, allowing evidence comparison and reuse across projects and stakeholder groups. Practical deployment and extension lessons were derived.

Conclusion: The development process yields actionable lessons for deploying and extending governance-aware AI sandbox platforms in collaborative research and industrial environments, addressing a gap in practical implementation guidance.

Abstract: Collaborative AI experimentation across industry and academia requires platforms that enable rapid prototyping while preserving controlled access, tenant separation, and transparent workflows. Despite growing interest in AI sandboxes, there is still limited practical guidance on how to design and implement platforms that integrate experimentation capabilities with governance requirements. This work presents the design and implementation of a governance-aware, multi-tenant AI sandbox for structured experimentation and the generation of reusable evaluation evidence across projects and stakeholder groups.
  The sandbox was developed within an industry-academia collaboration based on requirements that were iteratively refined with industrial partners. Its reference architecture separates the multi-tenant user interface from the backend control plane and places execution and data-management functions in dedicated layers. The platform supports governed user onboarding, project-centered collaboration, managed access to AI services, approval workflows, audit logging, and traceable experimentation. Experiment configurations, contextual information, and governance decisions are stored as persistent records, allowing evidence and outcomes to be compared and reused across projects.
  The development process provides practical lessons for deploying and extending governance-aware AI sandbox platforms in collaborative research and industrial environments.

</details>


### [120] [TraceCompiler: Skill-Guided Mining and Compilation of LLM Agent Traces into Mostly Deterministic Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02680)
*Salma El Yadouni,Guanyi Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TraceCompiler mines clusters of noisy agent traces to compile them into deterministic, skill-based workflows. It uses a precise dependency rule — only linking consumer arguments to uniquely attributable producer outputs — achieving high precision/recall on dependency recovery, and demonstrates practical intent compilation with call reduction on AppWorld benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents wastefully rediscover procedures, producing noisy traces with repeated lookups, retries, and accidental orderings. Existing trace-mining approaches using adjacency or frequency-thresholded directly-follows relations yield poor dependency recovery. A principled method is needed to extract reusable, deterministic skill workflows from these traces.

Method: TraceCompiler clusters agent traces by intent and applies a strict producer-consumer dependency rule: an inter-tool dependency is admitted only when a consumer argument contains a value uniquely attributable to an earlier producer. Every hard edge carries an auditable evidence tuple; ambiguous relations are labeled "suspected" with no ordering constraint. Bindings are classified as constants, user inputs, copied outputs, transforms, or residual LLM decisions. The system is evaluated on T1 (a mechanized rule variant) and AppWorld (using deterministic replay to recover masked return values).

Result: On T1's training split (15,775 def-use edges), the rule achieves 0.928 precision and 0.943 recall vs. 0.711 F1 for adjacency and 0.712 for frequency-thresholded directly-follows. Blind skill compilation on 250 edges reaches 0.992. On AppWorld's 563 token edges: 0.993 precision. For a Venmo intent: 34 observed API calls reduced to 11 runtime calls; passes 15/21 leave-one-out state tests. A Spotify/Todoist intent is correctly refused due to under-determined irreversible side effects.

Conclusion: TraceCompiler demonstrates that principled, evidence-based dependency mining from noisy agent traces can produce compact, executable skill workflows with high fidelity. The approach explicitly avoids claiming net efficiency gains, since offline compilation cost is not measured against runtime savings.

Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents repeatedly rediscover procedures they have already executed, producing traces that mix reusable structure with retries, exploration, accidental ordering, and repeated lookups. We present TraceCompiler, a skill-guided system that mines clusters of noisy agent traces and compiles them into executable, mostly deterministic workflows. It admits an inter-tool dependency only when a consumer argument contains a value attributable uniquely to an earlier producer; every hard edge carries an auditable evidence tuple, and ambiguous relations are marked suspected and impose no ordering constraint. Bindings are classified as constants, user inputs, copied outputs, transforms, or residual LLM decisions. On T1, a mechanized form of the rule recovers producer-consumer dependencies at 0.928 precision and 0.943 recall over 15,775 def-use edges of its training split, against 0.711 F1 for adjacency and 0.712 for a frequency-thresholded directly-follows measure on identical data; the compiler skill run blind reaches 0.992 on 250 of those edges. On AppWorld we replay released trajectories in the deterministic simulator to recover masked return values and measure the rule against 563 token edges at 0.993 precision - a self-consistency check, since replay injects tokens by a related heuristic. We compile two recurring intents: a Venmo money-request intent reduces 34 observed API calls to 11 runtime calls and, under leave-one-out execution against the benchmark's own state tests, passes 15 of 21, the failing fold escalating rather than acting because its required branch was never observed; and a Spotify/Todoist intent the compiler correctly refuses to compile, because an irreversible side effect is under-determined. We measure call reduction but not offline compilation cost, so we claim no net efficiency result.

</details>


### [121] [Studying Developer Perceptions on the Potential of CI Recommendation Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02682)
*Osamah H. Alaini,Taher A. Ghaleb*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An exploratory survey of ~5,000 GitHub developers examining why they adopt CI services, whether decisions are need-driven or socially influenced, perceived necessity of CI, adoption barriers, and attitudes toward automated CI recommendation systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work identifies barriers to CI adoption but provides minimal empirical evidence on how developers actually select CI services, and whether choices are driven by genuine project requirements versus social influence. This gap limits understanding of CI adoption dynamics in open-source.

Method: An exploratory survey study targeting approximately 5,000 active GitHub developers, encompassing both CI users and non-users, investigating motivations, perceived necessity, barriers, and attitudes toward automated recommendation.

Result: Findings are anticipated but not yet reported. The study will produce empirical data on need-driven vs. socially influenced CI adoption, context-dependent necessity perceptions, adoption barriers, and developer receptiveness to automated CI recommendation systems.

Conclusion: The findings are expected to inform the design of CI recommendation systems for researchers and help practitioners streamline CI adoption in open-source projects.

Abstract: Continuous Integration (CI) is central to modern software development, yet developers often struggle to choose the most suitable CI service. Prior work has identified barriers to CI adoption but offers little empirical evidence on how developers select CI services or whether adoption decisions are driven by genuine project needs versus social influence. This paper presents an exploratory survey study addressing that gap. We aim to contact about 5,000 active GitHub developers, including both CI users and non-users. The study investigates: (1) what drives CI adoption and service selection, distinguishing need-driven from socially influenced motivations; (2) whether developers consider CI universally necessary or context-dependent and what barriers hinder adoption; and (3) developers' perceptions of automated CI recommendation systems. Our findings will inform researchers developing CI recommendation systems and practitioners aiming to streamline CI adoption in open-source projects.

</details>


### [122] [BulkPR-Bench: Benchmarking Queue-Level Governance of Interacting Pull Requests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02685)
*Zetong Xiong,Qiao Zhao,Jun Zhang,Xueying Lyu,Zhi Li,Yixiang Tu,Xiaowen Yang,Yunjie Zhang,Yufeng Wang,Zhe Zhang,Kaize Yu,Hanwen Du,Zhongkai Sun,Zhuoxin Liu,Zekun Lin,Jianwen Yang,Ruining Chen,Ying Zhang,Tingxuan Pan,Ke Chen,Shubin Han,Chuanhao Sun,Yehua Yang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: BulkPR-Bench evaluates coding agents on the relational challenge of merging interdependent pull requests, where agents must infer hidden relations and select a maximal safe subset. Top models achieve 66.6% Relational Delivery Score vs. 53.1% for sequential baselines, but only 8 of 324 runs complete a queue exactly, revealing a large gap between relation-level gains and dependable whole-queue governance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding-agent benchmarks focus on single-outcome or fixed-sequence tasks, ignoring the real-world scenario where multiple queued PRs interact. Sequential merge policies fail when PRs have hidden dependencies or conflicts, necessitating joint decision-making to maximize safe delivery. The benchmark addresses this gap by requiring agents to recover consequential PR relations and select an executable, safe subset under a rolling-release protocol.

Method: The authors introduce BulkPR-Bench, an executable benchmark comprising 581 newly authored candidate PRs across frozen snapshots of 18 real repositories. A registered state-by-state repository execution with hidden safety checks validates a gold relation graph, and an exact oracle computes the largest safe subset. Two primary metrics are introduced: Relational Delivery Score (RDS), which scores safe delivery and correct rejection over relation groups from the realized merge trace, and Global Safety-Gated Yield (Global-SGY), which measures strict delivery of the realized whole-queue plan. The buffered primary protocol uses batch size K=32.

Result: Under the buffered protocol with K=32, the top three RDS estimates among six models are 66.6%, 62.0%, and 57.9%, compared to 53.1% for the strongest sequential baseline. Only 8 out of 324 total model runs complete a queue exactly. Critical-relation recall ranges from 35.2% to 57.7%. Diagnostic runs where models are supplied with gold relations still show substantial remaining headroom, indicating that relation-level improvements do not yet yield dependable whole-queue governance.

Conclusion: Current coding agents struggle with the combinatorial, relational reasoning required for safe multi-PR merge decisions. While models show some ability to recover individual PR relations, this does not translate to reliable end-to-end queue management. The benchmark exposes a critical capability gap and provides headroom for future work on joint merge planning under hidden dependencies.

Abstract: Coding-agent benchmarks increasingly cover long-horizon, end-to-end, and interactive development, but typically retain one requested outcome or a fixed change sequence. Sequential policies can process a pull-request (PR) queue one candidate at a time, but when queued PRs interact, maximizing safe delivery can require jointly deciding which changes to merge and in what order. We introduce BulkPR-Bench, an executable benchmark in which an agent must recover consequential PR relations and return a large safe subset in executable order under a rolling-release protocol. The suite contains 581 newly authored candidate PRs on frozen snapshots of 18 real repositories. Registered state-by-state repository execution, including hidden safety checks, validates the gold relation graph; an exact oracle then computes the largest safe subset. Our primary metric, Relational Delivery Score (RDS), scores safe delivery and correct rejection over relation groups from the realized merge trace; Global Safety-Gated Yield (Global-SGY) separately measures strict delivery of the realized whole-queue plan. Under the buffered primary protocol with batch size $K=32$, the three highest RDS estimates among the six models are 66.6%, 62.0%, and 57.9%, compared with 53.1% for the strongest sequential baseline. Only 8 of 324 model runs complete a queue exactly. Critical-relation recall ranges from 35.2% to 57.7%, and diagnostic runs supplied with the gold relations show substantial remaining headroom. Gains on relation groups therefore do not yet translate into dependable whole-queue governance.

</details>


### [123] [PRWeaver: Evaluating LLM-Based Code Auditors against Long-Horizon Malicious Pull Requests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02693)
*Yuekun Wang,Mingfei Cheng,Xiaofei Xie*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PRWeaver is a benchmark of 208 execution-validated adversarial attacks across 10 real-world repositories (832 renderings), showing that LLM-based code auditors are highly vulnerable when benign and malicious changes are interleaved within the review context — detection drops from 50-60% under per-PR review to 16-22% under whole-window review.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based code auditors are increasingly deployed in pull-request workflows, but their robustness against adversarial changes distributed across repository history is poorly understood. Existing evaluations focus on isolated diffs, failing to capture how attackers can exploit repository evolution and review context to conceal malicious changes.

Method: The authors introduce PRWeaver, a benchmark comprising 208 execution-validated attacks sourced from 10 real-world repositories, each rendered under four matched review configurations (832 total renderings). They evaluate three PR-auditing agents across six auditor-model systems, systematically varying: (1) commit boundary decomposition, (2) per-PR interleaving (N=16), (3) coherent carrier fusion, and (4) whole-window review (N=24) versus per-PR review.

Result: Decomposing attacks across commit boundaries changes detection by at most ±5 percentage points — commit structure alone does not explain evasion. Per-PR interleaving at N=16 and coherent carrier fusion reduce detection by 5-13 and 10-18 percentage points, respectively. Most critically, whole-window review at N=24 drops detection to 16-22%, compared with 50-60% under per-PR review, demonstrating that concealment is most effective when benign and malicious changes jointly occupy the auditor's active review context.

Conclusion: Access to repository history is insufficient for robust auditing. Adversarial effectiveness peaks when benign and malicious changes co-occupy the auditor's review context or when a plausible stated purpose accounts for the attack-bearing diff. This reveals a fundamental vulnerability in current LLM-based code review systems that future defenses must address.

Abstract: LLM-based code auditors are increasingly integrated into pull-request (PR) workflows, yet their reliability against adversarial changes distributed across repository evolution remains poorly understood. We introduce PRWeaver, a benchmark of 208 execution-validated attacks from ten real-world repositories, each instantiated under four matched review renderings (832 renderings in total). We evaluate three PR-auditing agents across six auditor-model systems. Across all systems, decomposing an attack changes detection by at most five percentage points, showing that commit boundaries alone do not explain evasion. In contrast, per-PR interleaving at $N=16$ and coherent carrier fusion reduce detection by 5-13 and 10-18 points, respectively. Under whole-window review at $N=24$, detection falls to 16-22%, compared with 50-60% under per-PR review. These results show that access to repository history is insufficient: concealment becomes most effective when benign and malicious changes jointly occupy the auditor's active review context or when the stated purpose plausibly accounts for the attack-bearing diff.

</details>


### [124] [Don't Regenerate, Debug: A Domain-Specific Agent for Repairing Near-Miss Hardware Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02712)
*Yansong Sun,Shenxiu Wu,Siyuan Chen,Runlin Hou,Junhao Qiu,Junming Cao,Shudi Shao,Zhichao Lu,Qingfu Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a domain-specific debug agent for repairing near-miss GPU/NPU kernel candidates generated by LLMs, rather than discarding and regenerating them. Debugging achieves a Debug Pass@1 of 66.7% vs. Regenerate Pass@1 of 25.9%, while consuming 92.8% fewer tokens per success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based kernel generation pipelines (using reinforcement learning and evolutionary search) generate, compile, and execute large numbers of candidate kernels, but discard most failures—many of which are "near-miss" operators that compile and run yet fail numerical validation. These discarded candidates embody genuine domain knowledge and represent nontrivial investment in LLM inference, cross-compilation, and hardware execution. The authors argue for a paradigm shift: instead of regenerating from scratch, debug these near-miss candidates.

Method: The authors present a domain-specific debug agent that addresses three challenges: (1) mitigating knowledge scarcity via retrieved patterns and diagnostic instrumentation, (2) ensuring integrity through anti-cheat detection and full-coverage evaluation, and (3) controlling cost via convergence guards and bounded iteration. The debugger operates on near-miss candidates that compile and run but fail numerical checks, leveraging a knowledge base of repair patterns to guide fixes within a constrained search space.

Result: Debug Pass@1 achieves 66.7%, compared to Regenerate Avg Pass@1 at 25.9% and Regenerate Pass@3 at 40.7%. The debug approach consumes 92.8% fewer tokens per success than three-trial regeneration. Ablation studies reveal the knowledge base is critical for recovery, while integrity gates reject 12.5–33.3% of successes that the workflow itself had accepted.

Conclusion: Debugging near-miss kernels serves two complementary roles: extending the capability frontier by recovering operators that repeated regeneration fails to produce, and lowering cost per deliverable operator. The paradigm shift from regeneration to debugging is both more effective and more efficient for LLM-driven kernel generation.

Abstract: Kernel generation for hardware accelerators such as GPUs and NPUs has become a proving ground for large language models (LLMs), and state-of-the-art systems raise correctness through pipelines that couple LLMs with agentic reinforcement learning and evolutionary search. Such pipelines generate, compile, and execute large numbers of candidate kernels, discarding most of them and forgoing the opportunity to distill failures into reusable knowledge. Many discarded candidates are near-miss operators that compile and run but fail numerical validation; each embodies genuine domain knowledge and a nontrivial investment in LLM inference, cross-compilation, and hardware execution. We argue for a paradigm shift: rather than regenerate, debug. Debugging is far more constrained than generating from scratch: the search space is small and feedback is dense. We present a domain-specific debug agent that addresses three core challenges in autonomous repair: mitigating knowledge scarcity through retrieved patterns and diagnostic instrumentation, ensuring integrity through anti-cheat detection and full-coverage evaluation, and controlling cost via convergence guards and bounded iteration. Debugging serves two complementary roles: it extends the capability frontier by recovering operators that repeated regeneration fails to produce, and it lowers cost per deliverable operator. Debug Pass@1 achieves 66.7% versus Regenerate Avg Pass@1's 25.9% and Regenerate Pass@3's 40.7%, while consuming 92.8% fewer tokens per success than three-trial regeneration. Component ablations show that the knowledge base drives recovery, while integrity gates reject 12.5-33.3% of the successes the workflow itself accepted.

</details>


### [125] [HyperFL: Query-Adaptive Representation Learning for Software Fault Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02967)
*Shuai Shao,Yiming Zeng,Yu Zhao,Tingting Yu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: HyperFL introduces a query-adaptive representation learning framework for software fault localization that uses a hypernetwork to generate LoRA parameters dynamically for each issue report, yielding up to 13.3% MRR@10 and 16.7% Hit@1 improvement over SweRank.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dense-retrieval fault localization methods encode all issue reports with a fixed query representation, ignoring the substantial diversity of real-world issues in length, structure, and debugging information. This one-size-fits-all approach limits retrieval effectiveness.

Method: HyperFL employs a lightweight hypernetwork that takes the query as input and generates query-specific Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) parameters for the query encoder. This enables dynamic, per-query adaptation while keeping the code encoder fixed and reusable, preserving efficiency and avoiding the need to recompute code embeddings.

Result: On a real-world issue localization benchmark, HyperFL consistently improves retrieval performance across multiple embedding backbones, achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement in function-level MRR@10 and 16.7% relative improvement in Hit@1 over the state-of-the-art method SweRank. Analysis reveals distinct adaptation patterns learned for different issue characteristics.

Conclusion: Query-adaptive representations via hypernetwork-generated LoRA parameters are highly effective for software fault localization, outperforming fixed-representation methods and validating the importance of adapting to the diversity in real-world issue reports.

Abstract: Software fault localization identifies the code locations responsible for reported issues and is a fundamental step toward automated debugging and program repair. Recent retrieval-based approaches formulate fault localization as a dense retrieval task by learning a shared embedding space between issue reports and source code. However, these methods encode all issue reports using a fixed query representation, despite the substantial diversity of real-world issue reports in length, structure, and debugging information. To address this limitation, we propose HyperFL, a query-adaptive representation learning framework for software fault localization. HyperFL employs a lightweight hypernetwork to generate query-specific LoRA parameters for the query encoder, enabling dynamic query adaptation while keeping the code encoder fixed and reusable. Experiments on a real-world issue localization benchmark demonstrate that HyperFL consistently improves retrieval performance across multiple embedding backbones, achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement in function-level MRR@10 and 16.7% relative improvement in Hit@1 over the state-of-the-art method SweRank. Further analysis shows that HyperFL learns distinct adaptation patterns for different issue characteristics, highlighting the effectiveness of query-adaptive representations for software issue localization.

</details>


### [126] [Integration Barriers in Open-Source SSI Frameworks: An Exploratory Developer Experience Probe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03039)
*Breno Cerqueira Reis Nakamura,Arlindo Flavio da Conceição*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A probe study with nine developers reveals critical abstraction gaps in open-source SSI tooling (Walt.id, Traction, MetaMask), where passive credential operations are mature but active schema customization exposes architectural friction, prompting three proposed architectural shifts: web sandboxes, AI-assisted schema generators, and executable documentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite SSI's promise to decentralize digital identity, widespread adoption is hindered by integration complexity and immature tooling. Understanding the developer experience (DX) barriers in open-source SSI frameworks is essential to diagnosing structural impediments that prevent ecosystem maturation.

Method: An exploratory probe study where nine developers with prior decentralized identity knowledge performed core credential lifecycle tasks using Walt.id, Traction, and MetaMask. Data was collected through open-ended developer reports and task-level difficulty ratings, then analyzed via qualitative thematic analysis to surface recurring integration barriers.

Result: A critical abstraction gap was identified: passive operations (e.g., credential receipt) are relatively mature, while active construction tasks — especially schema customization — expose significant architectural friction. Root causes include inadequate API abstractions, brittle environment configurations, and documentation that lags behind rapid ecosystem evolution.

Conclusion: Current SSI frameworks embed structural design decisions that create integration barriers. To bridge the abstraction gap, the authors propose three architectural shifts: web-based sandboxes for lowering entry barriers, AI-assisted schema generators to automate complex customization, and executable documentation strategies to maintain synchrony with evolving codebases.

Abstract: Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) promises to decentralize digital identity, but widespread adoption remains hindered by integration complexity and tooling immaturity. This paper investigates the Developer Experience (DX) of open-source SSI tooling through an exploratory probe study. Nine developers with prior knowledge of decentralized identity concepts, representing early integrators building SSI applications, attempted core credential lifecycle tasks using Walt.id, Traction, and MetaMask. Our goal was to surface recurring integration barriers through qualitative thematic analysis of open-ended developer reports, complemented by task-level difficulty ratings. Our findings reveal a critical abstraction gap: while passive operations like credential receipt are relatively mature, active construction tasks, particularly schema customization, expose significant architectural friction. We identify that these barriers stem from inadequate API abstractions, brittle environment configurations, and documentation that fails to track the ecosystem's rapid evolution. These issues reflect structural design decisions in current frameworks. This study characterizes the structural integration barriers in the current SSI open-source ecosystem. To address the identified gaps, we propose three architectural shifts for developer tooling: web-based sandboxes, AI-assisted schema generators, and executable documentation strategies.

</details>


### [127] [ConFL: Explainable Concurrent Fault Localization via Hierarchy-Guided LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02974)
*Shuai Shao,Dingbang Wang,Yiming Zeng,Tingting Yu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ConFL is an explainable concurrent fault localization framework that couples LLM reasoning with a structured Concurrent Knowledge Base (CKB) and hierarchical retrieval, using an interaction-level DSL to model cross-thread interactions. It significantly outperforms IR-based and LLM-based baselines on real-world Java concurrency bugs, achieving MRR of 0.503 and MAP of 0.486.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based approaches for localizing concurrent bugs from bug reports suffer from unstable reasoning and limited explainability due to incomplete information, misleading program-entity mentions, and complex cross-thread interactions.

Method: ConFL constructs a Concurrent Knowledge Base (CKB) from source code and performs LLM-guided hierarchical retrieval to narrow the search space from components down to interaction-level concurrency contexts. An interaction-level DSL explicitly encodes cross-thread interactions over shared resources, enabling focused reasoning without traversing deep call chains.

Result: Evaluated on real-world concurrent bugs from eight large-scale Java projects, ConFL achieves an MRR of 0.503 and a MAP of 0.486, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art IR-based and LLM-based baselines. It remains robust to noisy bug reports, unseen bugs, and different LLM backbones.

Conclusion: Augmenting LLM reasoning with structured concurrency knowledge via a CKB and interaction-level DSL yields substantial gains in both accuracy and robustness for concurrent fault localization, while also improving explainability.

Abstract: Localizing concurrent bugs from bug reports alone is challenging due to incomplete information, misleading program-entity mentions, and complex cross-thread interactions, causing existing LLM-based approaches to suffer from unstable reasoning and limited explainability. We propose ConFL, an explainable concurrent fault localization framework that augments LLM reasoning with structured concurrency knowledge. ConFL constructs a Concurrent Knowledge Base (CKB) from source code and performs LLM-guided hierarchical retrieval to progressively narrow the search space from components to interaction-level concurrency contexts. An interaction-level DSL explicitly encodes cross-thread interactions over shared resources, enabling focused reasoning without traversing deep call chains. Experiments on real-world concurrent bugs from eight large-scale Java projects show that ConFL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art IR-based and LLM-based baselines, achieving an MRR of 0.503 and a MAP of 0.486, while remaining robust to noisy bug reports, unseen bugs, and different LLM backbones.

</details>


### [128] [The Ground Is Shifting: A Reflection on the Foundations of Software Measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03007)
*Thomas Bock,Audris Mockus,Bogdan Vasilescu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Software measurement has historically assumed traces from version control tools reflect genuine human development. The rise of AI agents using these same tools violates this assumption, potentially invalidating prior findings. The authors propose a systematic AI-assisted replication program to develop methodologies robust to this shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The foundational assumption underlying decades of software measurement research—that traces from version control and related tools originate from professional human developers building real software—is being violated by the growing use of AI agents that generate similar traces. If unaddressed, this threatens the validity and relevance of empirical software engineering findings.

Method: The paper is a position/vision piece rather than an empirical study. It surveys the historical evolution of software measurement data (from manual collection to repurposed tool traces) and identifies the emerging threat of AI-generated traces. The proposed response is a systematic, AI-assisted replication program that uses modern techniques to re-examine key prior findings, detect when foundational assumptions are violated, and develop methodologies that remain valid under changed data-generation circumstances.

Result: The paper does not report empirical results. Its analytical contribution is the identification of a previously unstated assumption in software measurement (human origin of traces) and the articulation of how AI agents now systematically violate it, threatening the validity of established findings about software development, maintenance, and evolution.

Conclusion: Immediate action is needed: the research community must develop detection mechanisms for assumption violations in contemporary trace data and create new methodologies robust to AI-generated traces. The proposed AI-assisted replication program is presented as the path forward to keep software measurement research meaningful.

Abstract: For most of the past six decades, software measurement relied on labor-intensive manual collection of proprietary data, which hampered progress. The shift to repurposing traces from version control and related tools dramatically expanded data availability$\unicode{x2014}$especially with the rise of open-source software$\unicode{x2014}$but hinged on an often unstated assumption: that these tools are used by professional developers to build genuine software systems. However, as trace-generating tools, data types and scale, and empirical methods have all evolved, it has become clear that changes in data generation and analytical approaches affect many prior findings about software development, maintenance, and evolution. With AI agents now actively using these same tools, the resulting traces frequently violate the original assumption of human origin. To preserve the relevance of software measurement research, immediate action is needed: We must detect when foundational assumptions are violated in contemporary data and develop new methodologies that remain valid under changed circumstances. To this end, we propose a systematic AI-assisted replication program that revisits key findings using modern techniques, aiming for methods that yield consistent results on current data to keep software measurement meaningful.

</details>


### [129] [When AI Joins the Team! A Model of How AI Adoption Relates To Social Patterns in Software Engineering Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03462)
*Giusy Annunziata,Rudrajit Choudhuri,Anita Sarma,Gemma Catolino,Filomena Ferrucci*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AI-assisted development tools affect team social dynamics differently depending on collaboration type: in specialization work, AI fosters knowledge-sharing peer interaction that reduces community smells; in coordination work, AI directly improves communication quality, complementing human interaction rather than replacing it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid adoption of AI-assisted development tools is transforming software team collaboration, yet their impact on team social dynamics—specifically community smells (socio-technical anti-patterns indicating coordination/communication breakdowns)—remains unexamined. The authors aim to clarify whether and how AI adoption influences these dynamics.

Method: Using Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) theory, the authors validated instruments for Human-AI and Human-Human interaction along two TMS dimensions (Specialization and Coordination). They tested five PLS-SEM models on survey data from 152 software professionals using AI tools. Community smell constructs were derived from literature and validated via expert surveys and factor analysis.

Result: The AI–community-smell relationship is mechanism-dependent and work-type-contingent. In specialization work, AI is associated with increased knowledge-sharing peer interaction, which in turn correlates with fewer community smells. In coordination work, AI is directly associated with higher communication quality, complementing rather than displacing human interaction.

Conclusion: The study delivers an empirically validated, TMS-grounded model demonstrating that AI's effect on community smells is contingent on collaboration type, along with a reusable instrument and evidence-based implications for both research and practice.

Abstract: Context: The growing adoption of AI-assisted development tools is changing how software teams collaborate, share knowledge, and coordinate, yet its consequences for team social dynamics remain largely unexplored. Gap: It is unclear whether AI adoption is associated with an increase or reduction in community smells,socio-technical anti-patterns reflecting coordination and communication breakdowns,and through which mechanisms. Method: Grounded in Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) theory, we validate instruments for HumanAI and HumanHuman interaction along two TMS dimensions, Specialization and Coordination, and test five PLS-SEM models on survey data from 152 software professionals using AI tools. Community smell constructs were derived from the literature and validated through expert surveys and factor analysis. Results: AI adoption relates to community smells not in a single way, but through mechanisms depending on the work. In specialization work, AI is associated with higher knowledge-sharing peer interaction, which is in turn associated with fewer smells. In coordination work, AI is directly associated with higher communication quality, complementing rather than replacing human interaction. Contributions: We provide an empirically validated, TMS-grounded model showing that the AIcommunity-smell relationship is contingent on the type of collaboration, with a reusable instrument and evidence-based implications for research and practice.

</details>


### [130] [LLM Serving in the Wild: An Empirical Study of Frameworks, Methods, and System Designs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03036)
*Forough Majidi,Mohammad Mehdi Morovati,Foutse Khomh,Heng Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An empirical study analyzing how five major LLM serving frameworks (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, LMDeploy, FlashInfer) are adopted in open-source software, revealing vLLM's dominance, prevalent serving techniques (parallel computation, memory management, network pruning), limited multi-framework usage, and diverse adoption patterns across model families, modalities, and deployment architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite extensive research on LLM inference optimization and serving techniques, there is a gap in understanding how these frameworks and methods are actually adopted in real-world practice. The authors aim to bridge this gap through empirical characterization.

Method: The authors conducted a large-scale empirical study by identifying and analyzing five LLM-specific serving frameworks (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, LMDeploy, FlashInfer) across open-source software repositories. They examined adoption patterns individually and in combination, variation across LLM categories, and repository-level differences in intent, focus, use case, and architectural design.

Result: vLLM is the most visible framework in both popularity and adoption. Parallel computation, memory management, and network pruning are the most frequently used serving-method categories. Multi-framework usage is limited, but combined frameworks connect complementary capabilities. Adoption varies across model families, modalities, model sizes, domain specializations, and deployment settings. LLM serving frameworks support diverse applications including RL-based reasoning, multimodal generation/understanding, microservices, and cloud infrastructure.

Conclusion: This study provides the first large-scale empirical characterization of LLM serving framework adoption in practice, offering actionable insights for researchers, framework maintainers, and practitioners building LLM-based systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are integrated into software systems and AI services, making efficient LLM serving a concern for software engineering. Serving LLMs is challenging because inference requires computation, memory, GPU resources, and execution while maintaining latency and throughput. Although prior research has proposed LLM inference, optimization, and serving techniques and frameworks, little is known about how they are adopted in practice. In this study, we investigate the use of LLM serving frameworks and serving methods in open-source software systems. We identify and analyze five LLM-specific frameworks: vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, LMDeploy, and FlashInfer. We examine how these frameworks and techniques are adopted individually and in combination, how adoption varies across categories of LLMs, and how repositories differ in intent, focus, use case, and architectural design. Our results show that vLLM is the most visible framework in popularity and adoption, while parallel computation, memory management, and network pruning are the most frequently used serving-method categories. Multi-framework usage is limited, suggesting that developers rely on a single serving framework; however, combined frameworks connect complementary capabilities across the serving stack. Framework adoption varies across model families, modalities, model sizes, domain specializations, and deployment settings. Repository-level analysis shows that LLM serving frameworks support applications and architectures, including Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based reasoning, multimodal generation and understanding, microservices, and cloud infrastructure. Overall, this study provides a large-scale empirical characterization of LLM serving framework adoption in practice and offers insights for researchers, framework maintainers, and practitioners working on LLM systems.

</details>


### [131] [Efficient Grammar-Constrained Decoding via Parser Stack Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03065)
*Yongmin Li,Yihong Dong,Jia Li,Ge Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PSC is a grammar-constrained decoding method that reduces per-step masking overhead from O(vocabulary size) to O(1) by precomputing a parser stack classifier, achieving up to 700× faster mask computation and near-unconstrained LLM throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing grammar-constrained decoding (GCD) methods incur online latency that scales linearly with vocabulary size, which bottlenecks LLM throughput — especially for models with large vocabularies and complex grammars like programming languages or JSON schema.

Method: PSC preprocesses the grammar by combining acceptance conditions for all vocabulary tokens into a single classifier over parser stack states. During decoding, the complete vocabulary mask is computed by checking the parser stack exactly once per step, eliminating dependence on vocabulary size. The method also includes a break-even analysis framework to help users decide whether to perform preprocessing themselves or rely on a third-party provider.

Result: PSC computes masks up to 700× faster than baselines on complex programming language grammars and up to 30× faster for schema-conformant JSON. End-to-end LLM throughput with PSC approaches that of unconstrained decoding.

Conclusion: PSC effectively eliminates the vocabulary-size bottleneck in GCD, making grammar-constrained decoding practical at scale. The break-even analysis provides practical guidance for deployment trade-offs between preprocessing cost and decoding latency.

Abstract: LLMs are widely used to generate structured output like source code or JSON. Grammar-constrained decoding (GCD) can guarantee the syntactic validity of the generated output, by masking out tokens that violate rules specified by a context-free grammar. However, the online computational overhead of existing GCD methods, with latency typically scaling linearly with vocabulary size, limits the throughput of LLMs, especially for models with large vocabularies. To address this issue, we propose PSC, a novel grammar-constrained decoding method. By combining acceptance conditions of all vocabulary tokens into a single classifier of the parser stack during preprocessing, PSC can compute the complete vocabulary mask by checking the parser stack exactly once per decoding step, with time complexity independent of the vocabulary size. Experiments show that PSC computes masks up to 700$\times$ faster than baselines on complex programming language grammars, and up to 30$\times$ faster for schema-conformant JSON; end-to-end LLM throughput with PSC approaches that of unconstrained decoding. We analyze the preprocessing overhead for preprocessing providers and decoding users, and provide a break-even point analysis to help users decide whether to do preprocessing by themselves.

</details>


### [132] [Cross-Ecosystem Bug Classification in Quantum Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03173)
*Mir Mohammad Yousuf,Shabir Ahmad Sofi,Bisma Majid*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A comparative study analyzing 17,523 issues across Qiskit, Cirq, PyQuil, and other quantum software repositories reveals that classical bugs dominate (67%), while quantum-specific bugs (27-30%) center on gate/circuit issues. A rule-based classification framework outperforms ML baselines and generalizes across ecosystems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum software engineering is plagued by poorly understood bug patterns arising from the interplay of classical and quantum components. Without systematic characterization of these bugs, testing, debugging, and quality assurance in quantum ecosystems remain underdeveloped. The authors aim to fill this gap with a large-scale, cross-ecosystem empirical study.

Method: The authors collected 12,910 issues from Qiskit repositories and 4,613 issues from 11 additional repositories (including Cirq and PyQuil). They developed a rule-based classification framework to categorize bugs along multiple dimensions: bug type, category, severity, quality attributes, and quantum-specific subtypes. The framework was statistically validated for generalizability and benchmarked against four supervised machine-learning baselines. A longitudinal analysis spanning 2017–2025 was also conducted.

Result: Classical bugs consistently dominate at ~67% across all ecosystems, with quantum-specific bugs comprising 27–30%. Qiskit repositories show more compatibility-related bugs, while non-Qiskit ecosystems exhibit higher rates of syntax and quantum-specific bugs. Gate and circuit issues dominate quantum-specific bugs overall, but non-Qiskit projects display broader diversity (algorithmic, resource, and hybrid-interface issues). Statistical validation confirms the framework generalizes at the bug-type level but reveals significant variations at finer granularity. The rule-based framework consistently outperforms four ML baselines, especially for fine-grained quantum-specific subtypes. Longitudinal analysis shows quantum-specific bug rates remain stable over time rather than increasing.

Conclusion: This study provides the first cross-ecosystem comparison of bug distributions in quantum software and demonstrates that an interpretable, automation-ready, rule-based classification framework can effectively guide testing, debugging, and quality assurance efforts in the quantum software domain.

Abstract: Quantum software engineering faces unique challenges due to the interaction of classical and quantum components, which produce complex and often poorly understood bug patterns. Characterizing these bugs is essential for advancing testing, debugging, and quality assurance in quantum ecosystems. This paper presents a comparative study of 12,910 issues from Qiskit and 4,613 issues from 11 additional repositories, including Cirq and PyQuil. Using a rule-based classification framework, we analyze bugs by type, category, severity, quality attributes, and quantum-specific subtypes. Results show that classical bugs consistently dominate (67%) across ecosystems, while quantum-specific bugs account for 27-30%. Ecosystem-specific trends emerge: Qiskit repositories exhibit more compatibility related bugs, whereas other ecosystems show higher syntax and quantum-specific bug rates. Across both ecosystems, gate and circuit issues dominate quantum-specific bugs, though non-Qiskit projects reveal broader diversity, including algorithmic, resource, and hybrid-interface issues. Statistical validation confirms that the framework generalizes at the bug-type level while detecting significant variations at finer levels. Benchmarking against four supervised machine-learning baselines further shows that the rule-based framework consistently outperforms data-driven models, particularly for fine-grained quantum-specific subtypes, while longitudinal analysis (2017-2025) indicates that quantum- specific bugs remain relatively stable over time rather than exhibiting a steady increase. This study provides the first cross- ecosystem comparison of bug distributions in quantum software, demonstrating the utility of an interpretable, automation-ready, rule-based framework for guiding testing, debugging, and quality assurance.

</details>


### [133] [Fail-Fast, Restart-Smart: Early Failure Prediction and Restart for SWE Agentic Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03222)
*Chenyu Wang,Yunbo Lyu,Junda He,Zhou Yang,Chenxing Zhong,Yaniv Harel,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FailFast-RestartSmart is a two-stage controller that uses a lightweight 0.6B monitor to predict trajectory failure early and, upon alarm, restarts with a fresh rollout while optionally carrying forward the interrupted repository diff. It saves 14.6–20.4% execution tokens at 5% FPR and improves resolution from 66.6% to 71.8% at 25% FPR, outperforming cold restart.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software engineering agents solving repository-level issues produce long, expensive trajectories. Failed runs are often longer with redundant exploration or looping, suggesting failures can be detected before completion. Simple early termination risks killing trajectories that would succeed, and even failed trajectories may contain useful edits worth preserving.

Method: A two-stage controller: (1) FailFast — a lightweight 0.6B monitor trained with both terminal and dense fail-to-pass supervision that predicts failure from observable prefixes without needing policy logits or hidden states; (2) RestartSmart — upon alarm, launches a fresh same-policy rollout with no prior prompt history and offers the interrupted repository diff as an optional overlay the agent can inspect, apply, or discard. The monitor is trained on Qwen3.6-27B trajectories and tested for transfer to three other policies including a closed-API model. Also compared against a per-step AgentStop adaptation.

Result: On SWE-bench Verified: FailFast saves 14.6%–20.4% execution tokens at a target 5% false-positive rate across four policies. For Qwen3.6-27B, the 20.4% saving exceeds the 12.5% from AgentStop. At a target 25% false-positive rate, RestartSmart raises Qwen3.6-27B resolution from 66.6% to 71.8%, while cold restart only reaches 66.8%. FailFast transfers successfully from Qwen3.6-27B trajectories to three other policies.

Conclusion: The results support early termination with sequential same-policy recovery as an effective strategy: FailFast reliably detects impending failures across diverse policies, and RestartSmart leverages partial progress from interrupted trajectories to improve overall resolution rates, outperforming naive cold restart.

Abstract: Software engineering (SWE) agents resolve repository-level issues through long trajectories that grow increasingly expensive as context accumulates. Failed runs tend to be longer and exhibit redundant exploration or looping, suggesting that some failures may be detectable before completion. Early termination, however, risks interrupting trajectories that would otherwise succeed; conversely, an unsuccessful trajectory may still contain useful repository edits. We present FailFast-RestartSmart, a two-stage controller for a single active trajectory. FailFast is a lightweight 0.6B monitor trained with terminal and dense fail-to-pass supervision to predict failure from observable prefixes without policy logits or hidden states. Upon an alarm, RestartSmart launches a fresh same-policy rollout without prior prompt history and offers the interrupted repository diff as an optional overlay that the agent may inspect, apply, or discard. On SWE-bench Verified, a monitor trained solely on Qwen3.6-27B trajectories transfers to three other policies, including a closed-API model, and saves 14.6%-20.4% of execution tokens at a target 5% false-positive rate; on Qwen3.6-27B, its 20.4% saving exceeds the 12.5% achieved by our per-step AgentStop adaptation. At a target 25% false-positive rate, RestartSmart raises Qwen3.6-27B resolution from 66.6% to 71.8%, whereas cold restart reaches only 66.8%. Together, these results support early termination with sequential same-policy recovery.

</details>


### [134] [NotDec: WebAssembly Decompilation With Inter-Procedural Type Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03286)
*Jikai Wang,Ningyu He,Tianming Liu,Junhai Wang,Haoyu Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: NotDec is a WebAssembly decompilation framework that lifts bytecode to SSA-based IR, uses inter-procedural type recovery (Retypd) with pointer/numeric differentiation, and applies Memory SSA with structured control-flow analysis to generate readable C code. It achieves 100% recompilation success (vs. Ghidra's 45.95%) and recovers 85.33% of struct member accesses (vs. Ghidra's 9.24%), though the full version faces scalability issues on large binaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: WebAssembly's widespread adoption as a universal low-level bytecode standard across browsers, containers, IoT, and serverless platforms creates an urgent need for effective auditing tools. Existing decompilers produce verbose, poorly readable output with limited type recovery, hindering security analysis and understanding of binary behavior.

Method: NotDec operates in four stages: (1) extends WebAssembly's type checking to lift bytecode into SSA-based IR; (2) applies the inter-procedural type recovery algorithm Retypd with pointer/value differentiation to recover complex data structures; (3) employs Memory SSA for memory operation analysis; (4) uses semantics-preserving structured control-flow analysis to emit readable, semantically consistent C code. An intra-procedural variant (NotDec_F) is provided for scalability.

Result: NotDec achieves 100% recompilation success on all 5,241 Juliet test suite samples and the entire Howard dataset, dramatically outperforming Ghidra (45.95%). On type recovery, it recovers 85.33% of struct member accesses in real-world programs vs. Ghidra's 9.24%. The intra-procedural NotDec_F variant uses less than half of Ghidra's memory and up to 97% less execution time on unoptimized binaries, though the full inter-procedural version struggles with large binaries.

Conclusion: NotDec significantly advances the state of the art in WebAssembly decompilation, offering superior recompilation success, type recovery accuracy, and output readability. The intra-procedural variant provides a practical, efficient alternative when scalability is paramount, while the full version sets a new benchmark for decompilation quality.

Abstract: With WebAssembly widely supported in browsers, containers, IoT devices, and serverless platforms and increasingly adopted as a universal low-level bytecode standard, auditing its hidden vulnerabilities and malicious intentions has become critical. Decompiling existing WebAssembly modules can help security researchers and end users understand binary behavior, but current tools suffer from verbose result, poor readability, and limited type recovery.
  We present NotDec, an advanced WebAssembly decompilation framework. NotDec extends the WebAssembly type checking algorithm to lift bytecode into an SSA-based IR, applies the inter-procedural type recovery algorithm Retypd with pointer and numeric value differentiation methods to recover complex data structures, and leverages Memory SSA alongside semantics-preserving structured control-flow analysis to emit readable, semantically consistent C code.
  NotDec achieves 100% recompilation success rate on all 5,241 Juliet samples and all Howard dataset programs, significantly outperforming baselines including Ghidra (45.95% success rate). On type recovery accuracy, NotDec recovers 85.33% of struct member accesses in real-world programs, vastly exceeding Ghidra's 9.24%. While the full inter-procedural version faces scalability challenges on large binaries, the intra-procedural variant NotDec_F demonstrates superior efficiency, consuming less than half of Ghidra's memory and up to 97% less execution time on unoptimized binaries.

</details>


### [135] [Evaluating LLM Trade-offs for Enterprise Automation: Lessons from Workflow Generation in a Production Enterprise Platform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03311)
*Xavier Wrenn,Radoslav Raykov,Aleksandar Angelov,Hirokuni Kitahara,Yuji Watanabe,Anca Sailer*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Evaluates six LLMs for generating enterprise compliance automation workflows, finding that a piecewise (decomposed) generation pipeline dramatically improves structural success rates (74.1–97.8%) over monolithic generation (31.5–82.8%), enabling smaller, cheaper models to achieve production-grade performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional static orchestration fails in hybrid cloud environments where regulatory compliance (DORA, AI RMF, FedRAMP) demands rapid, event-driven adaptation. The authors seek to determine whether LLMs can generate valid automation workflows reliably enough for production use, and whether cost-efficient smaller models can substitute for expensive frontier models.

Method: Six LLMs were benchmarked across 29 real-world IT automation scenarios using two pipeline architectures: (1) monolithic workflow generation and (2) piecewise decomposition (variable scaffolding → base block assembly → nested block generation). Each prompt-model-pipeline configuration ran 8 times, yielding 2,784 total runs. Evaluation metrics included structural success (JSON schema validity, correct UI rendering), cost, and latency.

Result: Monolithic generation achieved 31.5–82.8% structural success. Piecewise decomposition raised this to 74.1–97.8%. Mistral-small reached 95.7% structural success at $0.01/workflow, while the best performers (mistral-medium-2505: 96.1%, gpt-oss-120b: 97.8%) carried up to 19× cost premiums. All pipelines maintained interactive-grade latency (under 50s).

Conclusion: Piecewise decomposition is a critical architectural decision that makes LLM-driven workflow generation production-viable. It decouples structural validity from semantic correctness and enables smaller, cost-effective models to replace expensive frontier models, providing a model-agnostic, scalable solution for enterprise compliance automation.

Abstract: Enterprise compliance management requires rapid adaptation to evolving regulatory frameworks (e.g., DORA, AI RMF, FedRAMP) and tight remediation SLAs. Traditional static orchestrators often fail in hybrid cloud environments where event-driven assessments demand that automation code adapt to runtime context in seconds. This paper presents lessons learned from evaluating six large language models for AI-driven workflow generation in a production enterprise platform, benchmarked across 29 real-world IT automation scenarios, two generation pipeline architectures, and eight independent runs per prompt-model-pipeline configuration (2,784 runs total).
  Our initial pipeline used monolithic workflow generation, achieving 31.5-82.8% structural success rates (JSON schema validity and correct UI rendering), with most models struggling on complex JSON generation. We developed a redesigned piecewise pipeline that decomposes workflow construction into variable scaffolding, base block assembly, and nested block generation, raising structural success to 74.1-97.8% across all models.
  We analyze production tradeoffs including cost (USD 0.008-0.20 per workflow), latency (under 50s for interactive use), and model selection. Piecewise decomposition enables smaller models (e.g., mistral-small at 95.7% structural success and USD 0.01 per workflow) to reach production viability, removing dependency on expensive frontier models.
