While mistral-medium-2505 and gpt-oss-120b achieved the highest structural success (96.1% and 97.8%), mistral-medium-2505 carries a 19x cost premium versus mistral-small. Our deployment lessons highlight the need to separate structural validity from semantic correctness (logical fulfillment of user intent) and provide a solution for model-agnostic, scalable automation in cloud engineering.

</details>


### [136] [Making AI Visible, Not Vanished: How AI Policies Reshape Developer Experience on GitHub](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03329)
*Yunqi Chen,Thomas Zimmermann,Bianca Trinkenreich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: First large-scale empirical study of AI governance policies in OSS, analyzing 29,624 GitHub repos to identify 385 with AI policies. Derives the TRACE framework (Transparency, Responsibility, Attribution, Constraints, Enforcement), classifies policies into five governance families, and uses causal inference methods (propensity-score matching, difference-in-differences) to show that governance regulates rather than prohibits AI use, improving maintainer engagement, disclosure, review quality, and code quality — with transparency/responsibility-focused policies outperforming purely restrictive ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI is rapidly transforming OSS development, yet little is known about how AI governance policies differ across projects or whether they tangibly influence developer experience and project outcomes. There is a gap in empirical evidence to guide OSS communities in designing effective AI policies.

Method: Large-scale empirical study analyzing 29,624 GitHub repositories. Identified 385 projects with AI policies. Derived the TRACE governance framework capturing five dimensions. Classified policies into five governance families. Estimated causal effects using propensity-score matching and longitudinal difference-in-differences analysis.

Result: AI governance primarily regulates rather than prohibits AI-assisted development. Policy adoption leads to increased maintainer engagement, greater AI disclosure, richer review interactions, and improved code quality, while AI-assisted contributions continue to grow. Policies emphasizing transparency and responsibility yield stronger community and quality outcomes than restrictive-only approaches.

Conclusion: AI governance design matters significantly. Transparency- and responsibility-oriented policies produce superior outcomes compared to purely restrictive ones. The findings provide actionable evidence to help OSS communities craft effective AI governance strategies that balance AI adoption with quality and community health.

Abstract: Generative AI is rapidly reshaping Open Source Software (OSS) software development,prompting projects to introduce policies governing AI-assisted contributions. However, little is known about how these policies differ or whether they influence developer experience. We present the first large-scale empirical study of AI governance policies in OSS. Analyzing 29,624 GitHub repositories, we identify 385 projects that adopted AI policies and derive TRACE, a framework capturing five governance dimensions: Transparency, Responsibility, Attribution, Constraints, and Enforcement. We further classify policies into five governance families and estimate their effects using propensity-score matching and longitudinal difference-in-differences analysis. Our results show that AI governance primarily regulates rather than prohibits AI-assisted development. Policy adoption brings maintainer engagement, increased AI disclosure, richer review interactions, and improved code quality while AI-assisted contributions continue to grow. Governance design matters: policies emphasizing transparency and responsibility produced stronger community and quality outcomes than restrictive approaches alone. Our findings show how different AI governance strategies shape developer experience and provide evidence to help OSS communities design effective AI policies.

</details>


### [137] [Assessing Behavioral Validation in UI Component Test Suites Using Inferred Metamorphic Relations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03337)
*Yu Pei,Cunming Zhang,Jeongju Sohn,Mike Papadakis*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a metamorphic relation (MR)-based framework for assessing UI component test suites. It infers component-specific MRs using a UI taxonomy, aligns tests with those relations via deterministic and semantic analysis, and computes MR coverage metrics. Evaluation shows existing tests exercise many relations but explicitly validate far fewer, with MR coverage revealing behavioral gaps that execution-based metrics miss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Execution-based metrics like statement and branch coverage do not reveal whether tests actually verify the behavioral relations implied by UI component APIs and documentation. There is a need for coverage metrics that capture behavioral validation, not just code execution.

Method: The framework takes a component's source code, documentation, and tests as input. It infers component-specific metamorphic relations using a UI-specific taxonomy, aligns tests with inferred relations through a hybrid of deterministic and semantic analysis, and computes MR coverage metrics at the relation level. Manual validation is performed on both the inferred MR space and test-MR alignment. The approach also includes issue-description mapping, oracle strengthening analysis, and MR-relevant fault injection to assess practical relevance.

Result: MR Cover remains between 42.5% and 47.6% across three LLM configurations and consistently below MR Touch. Most uncovered relations are weak-oracle cases — behaviors are exercised but lack explicit behavioral validation. MR coverage reveals behavioral gaps not captured by statement or branch coverage. Most reported issue descriptions map to inferred MR types; weak-oracle relations expose missing validation evidence; and MR labels show a trend in detecting MR-relevant injected faults.

Conclusion: MR coverage provides a complementary, relation-level perspective for assessing behavioral validation in modern UI component testing. It highlights gaps that execution-based metrics miss, particularly around weak-oracle relations where behavior is triggered but not explicitly verified.

Abstract: UI component libraries are commonly assessed using execution-based metrics such as statement and branch coverage, yet these metrics provide limited insight into whether tests verify the behavioral relations implied by component APIs and documentation. This paper presents an MR-based framework that uses inferred metamorphic relations (MRs) as an empirical behavioral reference, rather than a complete specification, for assessing UI component test suites. Given a component's source, documentation, and tests, the framework infers component-specific MRs using a UI-specific taxonomy, aligns tests with the inferred relations through hybrid deterministic and semantic analysis, and computes relation-level MR coverage metrics. We manually validate both the inferred MR space and the test--MR alignment. Our evaluation shows that existing test suites exercise substantially more behavioral relations than they explicitly validate: MR Cover remains between 42.5% and 47.6% across three LLM configurations and consistently below MR Touch. Most uncovered relations are weak-oracle cases, where behaviors are exercised but lack explicit behavioral validation. MR coverage also complements execution-based coverage by revealing behavioral gaps not reflected by statement or branch coverage alone. We further assess practical relevance through issue-description mapping, oracle strengthening, and MR-relevant injected faults. Most reported issue descriptions can be mapped to inferred MR relation types; weak-oracle relations often expose missing validation evidence; and MR labels show a trend in MR-relevant fault detection. Overall, MR coverage provides a complementary relation-level perspective for assessing behavioral validation in modern UI component testing.

</details>


### [138] [Route-Align-Verify for Functional Correctness in Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03341)
*Erxue Zhou,Jingxiang Meng,Aofan Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: RAV is a three-stage framework (Route, Align, Verify) that improves LLM code generation correctness without modifying the backbone model, achieving +6.35pp on MBPP Sanitized and +9.92pp on MBPP Full over the base model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single prompting strategies and single-shot generation are often insufficient for heterogeneous programming tasks. There is a need to improve functional correctness in code generation without altering the backbone LLM architecture.

Method: RAV consists of three coordinated stages: (1) Route — task-aware prompt routing that selects an appropriate prompting strategy before generation; (2) Align — LoRA-based adaptation that reduces mismatch between fine-tuning prompts and inference-time prompts; (3) Verify — execution-based verification that runs multiple candidate outputs against visible public tests to select the best final output.

Result: RAV achieves 0.8911 on MBPP Sanitized and 0.8520 on MBPP Full, representing improvements of 6.35 and 9.92 percentage points over the base model. Ablation studies show routing and adaptation are significantly more effective when combined with execution-based verification. Robustness and contamination analyses support result reliability.

Conclusion: Functional correctness in code generation can be meaningfully improved by jointly optimizing prompt strategies, model adaptation, and output selection, without modifying the backbone architecture.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have substantially improved code generation, yet achieving strong functional correctness remains difficult, especially for heterogeneous programming tasks where a single prompting strategy and a single directly generated output are often insufficient. In this paper, we present RAV, a lightweight and modular framework that improves code generation with a fixed backbone model through three coordinated stages: Route, which applies task-aware prompt routing before generation; Align, which reduces the mismatch between fine-tuning prompts and inference-time prompts through aligned LoRA adaptation; and Verify, which selects the final output by executing multiple candidates against visible public tests.
  We evaluate RAV on the MBPP benchmark under both the sanitized and full settings. The complete RAV pipeline achieves the best performance among all evaluated configurations, reaching 0.8911 on MBPP Sanitized and 0.8520 on MBPP Full. Compared with the base model, these results represent improvements of 6.35 and 9.92 percentage points, respectively. Component-wise ablation experiments further show that task-aware routing and aligned adaptation become substantially more effective when combined with execution-based verification. Additional robustness and contamination analyses support the reliability of the observed improvements. Overall, the results indicate that functional correctness in code generation can be meaningfully improved without modifying the backbone architecture, by jointly optimizing how tasks are prompted, how the model is adapted, and how final outputs are selected.

</details>


### [139] [Self-Evolving Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03392)
*Hao Zhou,Haichuan Hu,Ye Shang,Quanjun Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A systematic survey defining and taxonomizing self-evolving coding agents — AI coding assistants that improve themselves over time from prior coding interactions — and analyzing what evolves, when it evolves, and what software-specific evidence drives evolution, while highlighting key challenges like feedback reliability, safety, cost, and generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most deployed coding agents remain static after deployment, conflicting with the inherently dynamic, feedback-rich nature of software development where repositories, dependencies, tests, and repair attempts continuously change. This gap motivates the survey to synthesize the growing but fragmented body of work on self-evolving coding agents.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic literature survey, proposing an object-centered taxonomy that categorizes what evolves (framework, memory, skills, tools, models, or collaboration structures), complemented by two orthogonal dimensions: when evolution occurs and what software-specific evidence (executable feedback, repository context, coding trajectories) drives it.

Result: The survey finds that software engineering provides a uniquely suitable domain for agent self-evolution due to executable feedback and rich repository-level context, but also surfaces critical challenges: feedback reliability, benchmark overfitting, safety, maintainability, cost, and generalization across diverse software tasks.

Conclusion: The paper clarifies the conceptual boundaries of self-evolving coding agents, distinguishes them from conventional coding agents and general self-evolving agents, and provides a structured foundation for designing more adaptive, reliable, and software-aware agentic systems.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly embedded in software engineering workflows as coding agents that can inspect repositories, invoke tools, execute tests, debug failures, and generate patches. Yet most existing agents remain largely static after deployment, even though software development is a dynamic, feedback-rich process in which repositories evolve, dependencies change, tests fail, and repair attempts leave reusable experience. This tension has motivated a growing body of work on self-evolving coding agents, where the agent improves its future behavior by updating its framework, memory, skills, tools, models, or collaboration structures from prior coding interactions. In this survey, we provide a systematic synthesis of this emerging area. We first define self-evolving coding agents and distinguish them from conventional coding agents and general self-evolving agents. We then develop an object-centered taxonomy that characterizes what evolves in these systems, and complement it with two orthogonal perspectives: when evolution occurs and what software-specific evidence drives it. Across the literature, we find that executable feedback, repository-level context, and coding trajectories give software engineering a distinctive role as a natural domain for agent self-evolution, but also introduce new challenges in feedback reliability, benchmark overfitting, safety, maintainability, cost, and generalization. By organizing existing work around these dimensions, this survey aims to clarify the conceptual boundaries of self-evolving coding agents and provide a foundation for designing more adaptive, reliable, and software-aware agentic systems. The papers we collect can be found at https://github.com/zhouhao1024/Awesome-Self-Evolving-Coding-Agents.

</details>


### [140] [Leveraging System-Level Observations to Inform Bayesian Learning of Model Parameters for Quantitative Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03489)
*Simos Gerasimou,Xingyu Zhao*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: EPIK is an approach that elicits prior knowledge (PK) at the system-level (observable properties) rather than on low-level model transition parameters, formulates a twofold optimisation to infer transition parameter distributions, and embeds them into Bayesian quantitative verification for more accurate analysis of elusive system properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bayesian quantitative verification depends heavily on prior knowledge (PK) about transition probabilities, but obtaining accurate PK at the transition level is difficult and often requires domain expertise. Inaccurate or uninformative PK can compromise verification accuracy. There is a need to leverage more accessible, system-level observable properties as a source of PK.

Method: EPIK elicits PK in the form of system-level properties (directly observable with real-world semantics) rather than low-level transition parameters. It then formulates a twofold optimisation problem: (1) deriving distributions of unknown transition parameters consistent with the elicited system-level PK, and (2) embedding these derived distributions into Bayesian estimators for quantitative verification of elusive (new or hard-to-measure) properties.

Result: Experimental evaluation using multiple variants of real-world case studies with diverse EPIK instantiations demonstrates the approach's effectiveness, flexibility, and generality in improving quantitative verification outcomes compared to existing approaches.

Conclusion: EPIK provides a practical and general framework for incorporating accessible domain knowledge into Bayesian quantitative verification, overcoming the limitations of requiring low-level transition priors and enabling more robust analysis of software system properties such as reliability and response time.

Abstract: Combining Bayesian learning and quantitative verification is a powerful toolset for analysing key quantitative properties of software systems, like reliability and response time. However, the accuracy and robustness of verification results strongly depend on the prior knowledge (PK) underlying Bayesian inference. This knowledge reflects original beliefs about the probability of events and typically depends on domain expertise. Using inaccurate or uninformative PK can negatively affect quantitative analysis, yielding incorrect verification results. Our EPIK approach tackles this important challenge by eliciting and embedding PK in quantitative verification equipped with Bayesian estimators. Unlike existing approaches that require PK on formal model transition parameters, EPIK leverages system-level properties that are directly observable and are linked to real-world semantics. EPIK formulates a twofold optimisation problem to derive the distributions of unknown transition parameters and then embeds these distributions to verify new or difficult-to-measure (elusive) properties. The detailed experimental evaluation using multiple variants of real-world case studies and diverse EPIK instantiations shows its effectiveness, flexibility and generality.

</details>


### [141] [CodeAssay: A Multi-Metric Benchmark with Audited Ground Truth for LLM Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03535)
*Shahbaz Siddeeq,Muhammad Waseem,Umar Subhan Malhi,Pekka Abrahamsson*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CodeAssay is a taxonomy-driven benchmark of 185 Python tasks with audited ground truth, hidden tests, and mutation-based validation. An audit corrected 9% of labels and widened the model performance spread. Evaluation of seven proprietary LLMs revealed significant inter-model differences, no single model excelled across all code properties, and security-focused prompting increased code complexity without consistent security gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing test-based benchmarks for LLM code generation suffer from unreliable references and tests, and they capture only test-passing correctness while ignoring other observable code properties. There is a need for a more rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation framework.

Method: The authors constructed CodeAssay, a benchmark of 185 Python tasks spanning ten software-engineering categories. It features manually audited ground truth, public tests for generation/repair, hidden tests for grading, mutation-based test-suite validation, and selected code-property measures. Seven proprietary LLMs were evaluated under standard and security-focused prompts, with statistical comparison across model pairs and analysis of multiple code properties.

Result: The audit changed 170 of 1,890 correctness labels (9.0%) and increased the best-to-worst model spread from 11.9 to 23.7 percentage points. Mutation scores were 82.6% (complete) and 74.8% (hidden). Correctness ranged from 77.3% to 98.9% across models, with significant differences in 12 of 21 pairs. No model ranked best on all code properties for the 120 tasks all configurations solved. Security prompting did not significantly alter correctness or reduce static-analysis findings, yet it increased program length and cyclomatic complexity universally.

Conclusion: Reliable evaluation of LLM-generated code demands validated ground truth, protected (hidden) tests, and multiple explicitly interpreted measures beyond mere test-passing. CodeAssay offers a reproducible foundation for evidence-based assessment of LLMs in software development.

Abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly evaluated for code generation using test-based benchmarks. The validity of such evaluations depends on the reliability of their references and tests, while test-based correctness captures only part of the observable properties of generated code. We present CodeAssay, a taxonomy-first benchmark of 185 Python tasks across ten software-engineering categories. It combines audited ground truth, public tests for generation and repair, hidden tests for grading, mutation-based test-suite validation, and selected code-property measures. Regrading fixed model outputs after the audit changed 170 of 1,890 correctness labels (9.0%) and increased the measured best-to-worst model spread from 11.9 to 23.7 percentage points, although aggregate correctness remained nearly unchanged. The complete and hidden test suites achieved mutation scores of 82.6% and 74.8%, respectively. Across seven proprietary LLMs, standard-prompt correctness ranged from 77.3% to 98.9%, with significant differences in 12 of 21 model pairs. On the 120 tasks solved by all 14 model-prompt configurations, no model performed best across all selected code properties. A security-focused prompt produced no significant change in correctness or consistent reduction in the selected static-analysis findings, while increasing program length and cyclomatic complexity across all models. These findings show that reliable evaluation of LLM-generated code requires validated ground truth, protected tests, and multiple explicitly interpreted measures. CodeAssay provides a reproducible basis for evidence-based model evaluation in AI-augmented software development.

</details>


### [142] [EffiHolmes: Differential Profiling-Guided Repository Level Time Inefficiency Fix Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03558)
*Haowen Yang,Yun Peng,Zishuo Ding*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: EffiHolmes is an LLM-based framework for localizing time inefficiency fix locations in large software systems. It uses differential profiling under varied workloads, extracts compact execution paths, and applies domain-guided LLM reasoning to bridge the semantic gap between profiling hotspots and actual fix locations, outperforming existing baselines on the newly introduced RepoEffi-Bench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time inefficiencies in large software systems are hard to localize because they produce neither test failures nor stack traces, rendering traditional and LLM-based fault localization ineffective. Existing profiling-based approaches suffer from execution noise, irrelevant background execution, and a semantic gap between observed hotspots and fix locations.

Method: EffiHolmes employs three key components: (1) differential profiling under default and scaled workloads to distinguish true inefficiency hotspots from noise; (2) compact execution path extraction connecting hotspots to the reported inefficient function, filtering out background noise; and (3) domain-guided LLM reasoning to bridge the semantic gap and localize root-cause inefficiency logic. The paper also introduces RepoEffi-Bench, a benchmark of 140 issues from popular Python repositories.

Result: EffiHolmes outperforms state-of-the-art retrieval-, agent-, and profiling-based baselines, achieving a 4.29 percentage point improvement in file-level Acc@3 with GPT-5.1 and a 15.00 percentage point improvement in function-level Acc@5 with qwen3-4b. The framework maintains robustness across different model capacities.

Conclusion: EffiHolmes effectively addresses the unique challenges of repository-level time inefficiency localization by combining workload-aware differential profiling, targeted execution path extraction, and semantically grounded LLM reasoning, establishing a strong baseline on the RepoEffi-Bench benchmark.

Abstract: Large software systems often suffer from time inefficiencies that cause excessive execution time despite functional correctness. Localizing their fix locations is difficult because, unlike functional bugs, they produce neither test failures nor stack-trace clues, making traditional and recent LLM-based fault localization methods unsuitable. Runtime profiling provides alternative evidence but faces three challenges in repository-level settings: single-run profiling cannot reliably distinguish inefficiency hotspots from execution noise; existing profilers struggle to extract relevant execution paths from extensive background execution; and a semantic gap remains between observed hotspots and actual fix locations. We propose EffiHolmes, an LLM-based framework for repository-level time inefficiency fix localization. EffiHolmes uses differential profiling under default and scaled workloads to identify inefficiency hotspots, extracts compact execution paths connecting these hotspots to the reported inefficient function, and employs domain-guided LLM reasoning to locate the underlying inefficiency logic. We also introduce RepoEffi-Bench, the first benchmark for repository-level inefficiency localization, containing 140 high-quality issues collected from popular Python repositories. Experiments show that EffiHolmes consistently outperforms state-of-the-art retrieval-, agent-, and profiling-based baselines, improving file-level Acc@3 by 4.29 percentage points with GPT-5.1 and function-level Acc@5 by 15.00 percentage points with qwen3-4b. It also remains robust across model capacities.

</details>


### [143] [From Bug Reports to Browser-Executable Procedures: An LLM-Driven Agent for Web GUI Bug Reproduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03598)
*Cunming Zhang,Yu Pei,Michail Papadakis*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ReBug is a context-aware agent system that reconstructs missing prerequisites from natural-language web GUI bug reports, then executes and validates browser-level reproduction procedures by driving a real browser. Evaluated on 667 real-world bugs across four open-source web apps, it achieves ~50% reproduction success rate, outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reproducing web GUI bugs from bug reports is critical for software maintenance but difficult because reports often omit prerequisites (dependencies, input files). Existing techniques focus on code units or mobile apps and lack end-to-end visual browser execution and validation for web GUIs.

Method: ReBug is a two-stage agent system: (1) Preparation stage — reconstructs missing prerequisites from the report and available artifacts, producing a high-level reproduction plan; (2) Execution stage — performs tool-mediated browser interactions, maintains structured summaries of page state and action history, and validates final state against report-derived expectations.

Result: On 667 real-world bug reports from four open-source web applications, ReBug achieves an average Reproduction Success Rate (RSR) of 49.96%, mean task completion rate of 74.96%, and mean action execution success rate of 86.54%, outperforming both baselines. Historical replay shows successful procedures often expose original bug-present behavior on restored buggy versions.

Conclusion: Explicit context reconstruction and state-aware browser execution effectively support report-derived browser reproduction. ReBug demonstrates that bridging missing prerequisites and maintaining execution-state awareness are key to automating web GUI bug reproduction from natural-language reports.

Abstract: Reproducing web GUI bugs from natural-language bug reports is critical for software maintenance, but remains difficult because reports often lack prerequisites such as dependencies and input files. Existing bug reproduction techniques mainly target code units or mobile applications and lack end-to-end visual execution and validation for web GUIs. We present ReBug, a context-aware agent system that reconstructs, executes, and validates browser-level reproduction procedures from web GUI bug reports by driving a real browser. ReBug separates reproduction into two stages. In the preparation stage, ReBug reconstructs missing prerequisites from the report and available artifacts, and it produces a high-level reproduction plan. In the execution stage, it performs tool-mediated interactions in the browser, maintains structured summaries of page state and action history, and validates the final state against expectations derived from the report. We evaluate ReBug on 667 real-world bug reports from four open-source web applications. On controlled current deployments, ReBug outperforms both baselines, achieving an average RSR of 49.96%, a mean task completion rate of 74.96%, and a mean action execution success rate of 86.54%. Our results show that explicit context reconstruction and state-aware browser execution effectively support report-derived browser reproduction, while historical replay shows that successful procedures often expose the original bug-present behavior on restored buggy versions.

</details>


### [144] [Pattern over Pixels: Measuring Pattern Completion Bias in Multimodal Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03691)
*Khai-Nguyen Nguyen,Oscar Chaparro,Antonio Mastropaolo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MLLMs translating webpage screenshots to code exhibit strong "pattern-completion bias," where repeated UI patterns cause models to ignore visual perturbations and output pattern-consistent (but incorrect) values. Benchmarking 5 frontier MLLMs across 1,440 screenshots, bias rates reached ~70% (card-width) and ~80% (text font-size), with accuracy at only ~21% and ~8% respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs are increasingly deployed for screenshot-to-code generation, yet repeated UI patterns—common in modern web design—may induce a harmful bias where models default to pattern-consistent outputs even when visual evidence contradicts them. This failure mode lacks systematic investigation.

Method: The authors construct the first benchmark for visual pattern-completion bias using a fill-in-the-blank task. From 30 webpages in the Design2Code dataset, they generate 1,440 evaluated screenshots with localized perturbations (masked width or font-size values) within repeated card and text-style patterns. Conditions include standard and noise-overlaid variants, varying perturbation subtlety and boundary positions. Five frontier MLLMs (including Codex-5.3 and Flash-3.0) are evaluated. Reasoning analysis examines the relationship between chain-of-thought effort and bias.

Result: All models show strong bias toward the repeated baseline. Mean bias rate: 69.78% (card-width) and 80.22% (text font-size); mean accuracy: 21.17% and 7.89%. Codex-5.3 performs best but drops from 68.61% (cards) to 13.89% (text). Flash-3.0 reaches 96.11% bias on text. Noise, subtler perturbations, and boundary positions amplify bias. Greater reasoning effort correlates with lower bias, but models can identify anomalous elements yet still output pattern-consistent (incorrect) answers.

Conclusion: Pattern-completion bias is a concrete and severe failure mode in multimodal code generation. Its severity is strongly associated with visual saliency—text-style patterns, being less visually salient than card structures, yield worse performance. This highlights a critical vulnerability in deploying MLLMs for front-end code generation from screenshots.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to translate webpage screenshots into front-end code, but repeated UI patterns may sway them toward visually incorrect yet pattern-consistent outputs. In this work, we test how repeated webpage patterns hurt MLLM accuracy on an objective screenshot-to-code fill-in-the-blank task. We introduce the first benchmark for visual pattern-completion bias, where one localized element in a repeated UI pattern is perturbed and the model must recover the masked width or font-size value from the screenshot and HTML context. Starting from 30 webpages curated from the Design2Code dataset, we build 1,440 evaluated screenshots spanning structural card and text-style patterns under standard and noise-overlaid conditions. We evaluate five frontier MLLMs and find that all are strongly biased toward the repeated baseline. Mean bias rate reaches 69.78% on card-width perturbations and 80.22% on text font-size perturbations, while mean accuracy is only 21.17% and 7.89%, respectively. Codex-5.3 performs best but still drops from 68.61% accuracy on cards to 13.89% on text, while Flash-3.0 reaches 96.11% bias on text. Noise, subtler perturbations, and boundary positions further increase bias rate. Reasoning analysis further shows that greater reasoning effort correlates with lower bias, yet qualitative evidence reveals that models can identify the anomalous element and still override it with the pattern-consistent answer. Our results identify a concrete failure mode in multimodal code generation and show that its severity is strongly associated with visual saliency

</details>


### [145] [We Must Have Missed This Comment: Detecting and Repairing Stale Function References in Linux Kernel Comments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03734)
*Kexin Sun,Yunbo Lyu,Xutong Ma,Hongyu Kuang,Ratnadira Widyasari,He Zhang,Xiaoxing Ma,Julia Lawall,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ReCite is a three-stage approach to detect and repair stale function references in Linux kernel comments by identifying unresolved symbols, tracing their Git evolution history, and generating LLM-based repair suggestions, achieving 89% useful repair guidance and 50 accepted patches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Linux kernel comments can become outdated when referenced functions are refactored or removed without updating the comments. Such stale references mislead maintainers and hinder code comprehension. Prior work on code-comment inconsistency focused on semantic misalignment in Javadoc-style annotations, making them inapplicable to externally induced staleness in the Linux kernel.

Method: ReCite employs a three-stage approach: (1) detecting unresolved function-form symbols—symbols in comments that appear to reference functions but lack matching functions in the current codebase; (2) tracing each unresolved symbol's evolution through Git history; (3) generating LLM-based repair suggestions grounded in evolution history and current code context.

Result: On Linux kernel v6.18-rc1, ReCite detected 869 stale references with repair suggestions. Manual evaluation of 200 sampled repairs showed 178 (89.0%) provided useful repair guidance and 85 (42.5%) were directly applicable. Of 75 submitted patches, 50 were accepted.

Conclusion: ReCite effectively identifies and repairs stale function references in the Linux kernel, with high practical utility evidenced by both manual evaluation and real-world patch acceptance. The approach addresses a gap left by prior work that focused only on Javadoc-annotated function mismatches.

Abstract: As the Linux kernel evolves, code comments may become outdated, as the functions they reference can be refactored or removed independently without corresponding updates to the comments. Such stale function references can mislead maintainers and thus hinder code comprehension. Prior work on detecting code-comment inconsistency mainly focused on addressing semantic misalignment between Javadoc comments and their directly annotated functions, making them inapplicable to this type of externally induced staleness in the Linux kernel. Therefore, we propose ReCite, a three-stage approach to identify and repair such stale references: (1) detecting unresolved function-form symbols -- symbols in comments that appear to reference functions but for which no matching function can be found in the current codebase, (2) tracing the evolution history of each unresolved symbol through the Git history, and (3) generating LLM-based repair suggestions grounded in the evolution history and current code context. On Linux kernel v6.18-rc1, ReCite detects 869 stale references with generated repair suggestions. A manual evaluation on 200 sampled repairs shows that 178 (89.0%) provide useful repair guidance, with 85 (42.5%) directly applicable. Of our 75 submitted patches, 50 have been accepted. We also empirically study all unresolved function-form symbols.

</details>


### [146] [Can LLMs Test Terminal User Interfaces?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03743)
*Chao Peng,Ruida Hu,Ajitha Rajan,Tegawendé F Bissyandé,Jacques Klein,Cuiyun Gao*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Terminal User Interfaces (TUIs) lack dedicated testing practices. The authors survey 197 real-world TUI apps, finding minimal and often ineffective testing. They build a headless benchmark across four languages/frameworks and evaluate four frontier LLMs against random exploration for automated TUI testing. Key findings: no single LLM dominates, random is a strong baseline due to throughput, but LLMs more efficiently find input-gated crashes. Launch input derivation yields the biggest practical gain, and line coverage poorly predicts crash discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TUIs have become prevalent in developer tools but lack a dedicated testing methodology. Existing testing practices are sparse, and no systematic evaluation exists for automated TUI testing — particularly comparing modern LLM-based approaches against simpler baselines like random exploration.

Method: The authors surveyed 197 real-world TUI applications to quantify current testing practices. They then constructed a headless benchmark spanning four frameworks (ratatui/Rust, bubbletea/Go, textual/Python, ink/TypeScript), packaging each as an instrumented Docker image. They recorded line coverage, widget coverage, rendered terminal states, and crashes. Under equal wall-clock budgets, they compared four frontier LLMs with random exploration, and also evaluated the impact of automatically deriving launch inputs.

Result: Only 12% of test code in the surveyed apps exercises the TUI, and 45% of those tests never send input. No LLM dominates across the board. Random exploration is a strong time-budgeted baseline due to higher interaction throughput, but LLMs are more efficient per interaction and uniquely reach input-gated faults. Automatically deriving launch inputs provides the largest practical gain, enabling apps that otherwise would not start. Line coverage is a poor predictor of crash discovery.

Conclusion: Automated TUI testing is feasible but far from solved. Honest baselines matter more than model choice. The authors release tuicov (coverage tool) and tuibot (testing framework) as open-source contributions.

Abstract: Terminal User Interfaces (TUIs) combine the stateful, screen-oriented behaviour of GUIs with terminal deployment and are now common in developer tools. Yet they lack a dedicated testing methodology. We survey 197 real-world TUI applications: only 12% of test code exercises the interface, and 45% of those tests never send input, checking a static frame instead. We turn these applications into a headless benchmark spanning ratatui/Rust, bubbletea/Go, textual/Python, and ink/TypeScript, packaging each as an instrumented Docker image. We record line and widget coverage where reliable, rendered terminal states, and crashes. Under equal wall-clock budgets, we compare four frontier LLMs with random exploration. No model dominates. Random is a strong time-budgeted baseline, but its crash advantage comes from higher throughput: per interaction, LLM guidance is more efficient and uniquely reaches input-gated faults. Automatically deriving launch inputs yields the largest practical gain, enabling applications that otherwise never start. Line coverage poorly predicts crash discovery, weakening it as a proxy for test effectiveness. Automated TUI testing is feasible but far from solved, and honest baselines matter more than model choice. We release the coverage tool tuicov at https://github.com/tui-testing/tuicov and the testing framework tuibot at https://github.com/tui-testing/tuibot.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [147] [Deep Divide-and-Reduce in Symbolic Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02628)
*Yusong Deng,Yanjie Li,Weijun Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DDRSR proposes a mathematically rigorous approach to symbolic regression that broadens expression decomposition, eliminates brute-force sub-expression search, and guarantees theoretical correctness, outperforming prior methods like AI Feynman on both decomposition and regression tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ML-based symbolic regression methods lack deep understanding of the mathematical/physical principles behind expressions. The AI Feynman method, despite leveraging such principles, has a narrow scope of applicability, fails on complex equations, and relies heavily on brute-force sub-expression search, limiting practical utility.

Method: Through rigorous mathematical deduction and proofs, DDRSR fundamentally broadens the scope of expression decomposition and reduction. It circumvents brute-force sub-structure searches by employing principled divide-and-reduce strategies that ensure strict theoretical correctness.

Result: Empirical evaluations show DDRSR yields significant advantages in both expression decomposition and numerical regression tasks compared to existing approaches.

Conclusion: The DDRSR paradigm offers wider versatility and theoretical guarantees for symbolic regression. The authors also discuss applicable scenarios, inherent limitations, and future research directions.

Abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is the task of discovering underlying patterns from data and representing them using mathematical expressions. Current machine learning approaches to SR often lack a profound understanding of the intrinsic mathematical and physical principles governing these expressions. While the pioneering AI Feynman method leverages the mathematical properties underlying the data, its expression simplification mechanism suffers from a narrow scope of applicability and is prone to failure on complex equations. Furthermore, its underlying mechanisms rely heavily on brute-force searches for sub-expressions, severely limiting its practical utility. Through rigorous mathematical deduction and proofs, we propose our method, Deep Divide and Reduce in Symbolic Regression (DDRSR). DDRSR fundamentally broadens the applicability of expression decomposition and reduction, circumvents the need for brute-force sub-structure searches, and ensures both wider versatility and strict theoretical correctness. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that these theoretical principles yield significant advantages in both expression decomposition and numerical regression tasks. Finally, we discuss the applicable scenarios and inherent limitations of this paradigm, alongside promising directions for future research.

</details>


### [148] [Multimodal Auto-regressive Transformer Surrogate for Modeling Variable Operations and Quantifying Uncertainty in Geological Carbon Storage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02629)
*Yifu Han,Louis J. Durlofsky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multimodal auto-regressive transformer surrogate is developed for geological carbon storage, trained on 4000 simulations to predict saturation, pressure, and CO2 mass quantities. It achieves median saturation MAE of 0.028 and is used within hierarchical MCMC for data assimilation, enabling substantial uncertainty reduction in fault permeabilities under variable well injection strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Variable well perforation and injection strategies can improve geological carbon storage efficiency, but simulating these operations under geological uncertainty is computationally expensive. A fast, accurate surrogate model is needed to enable uncertainty quantification and data assimilation for such complex operational strategies.

Method: A multimodal auto-regressive transformer architecture is developed. Three separate encoders process: (1) the 3D geomodel, (2) scalar relative permeability parameters, and (3) control variables (stage durations, injection rates). These modalities are fused via self-attention in a transformer encoder, and a temporal decoder generates predictions auto-regressively through encoder-decoder cross-attention. Training uses 4000 GEOS flow simulations on a modified SEAM CO2 model (faulted system, three stacked aquifers, two injection wells perforated bottom-to-top). The surrogate predicts saturation/pressure at monitoring locations, total injected and mobile CO2 mass, and saturation footprints. The trained surrogate is embedded in a hierarchical Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) data assimilation framework applied to a synthetic true model under three operational strategies.

Result: On a test set with randomly sampled geomodels and control variables, the surrogate achieves median saturation MAE of 0.028 and median relative errors of 0.2–5% for other quantities of interest. It successfully captures the switch from rate-controlled to bottom-hole-pressure-controlled injection. In the hierarchical MCMC data assimilation, substantial uncertainty reduction is achieved for key metaparameters, especially fault permeabilities. Posterior predictions for saturation footprints and total injected/mobile CO2 mass are generally consistent with true model results.

Conclusion: The multimodal auto-regressive transformer surrogate provides accurate and efficient emulation of complex geological carbon storage operations involving variable well controls. Its integration with hierarchical MCMC enables effective data assimilation and uncertainty reduction, particularly for fault permeability characterization, demonstrating practical utility for geological CO2 storage management under uncertainty.

Abstract: The use of variable well perforation and injection strategies can improve the efficiency of geological carbon storage operations. We develop a new multimodal auto-regressive transformer surrogate to model these operations under geological uncertainty. A modified SEAM CO2 geomodel, which involves a faulted system with three stacked aquifers, is considered. The two injection wells are perforated in stages, from bottom to top, with the stage durations and individual well injection rates treated as control variables. The surrogate model processes three input modalities - the 3D geomodel, scalar parameters characterizing relative permeability functions, and control variables - through separate encoders. These are fused via self-attention in a transformer encoder, and a temporal decoder generates predictions auto-regressively through encoder-decoder cross-attention. The surrogate is trained, using 4000 GEOS flow simulations, to predict saturation and pressure at monitoring locations, total injected and mobile CO2 mass, and saturation footprints. For a new test set, involving randomly sampled geomodels and control variables, the surrogate achieves a median saturation MAE of 0.028 and median relative errors of 0.2-5% for the other quantities of interest. Importantly, it captures the switch from rate to bottom-hole-pressure control. The surrogate model is used within a hierarchical Markov chain Monte Carlo data assimilation procedure for a synthetic true model under three operational strategies. Substantial uncertainty reduction is achieved for key metaparameters, particularly the fault permeabilities. Posterior predictions for saturation footprints and total injected and mobile CO2 mass are also shown to be generally consistent with true model results.

</details>


### [149] [LLMs Can Annotate Attribution Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02632)
*Ameen Patel,Max Zhang,Nathan Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a simple automated pipeline that uses language models to group individual features or MLP neurons into supernodes for circuit tracing, eliminating the time-intensive manual annotation step. The pipeline produces supernodes as interpretable as human-generated ones, successfully recovers known intermediate representations, and enables open-ended exploration of attribution graphs at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Circuit tracing reveals internal computation in language models but requires a laborious manual step of grouping individual features/neurons into semantically meaningful supernodes. Automating this grouping step would dramatically accelerate circuit analysis and enable large-scale exploration.

Method: The authors propose a straightforward pipeline: present textual feature descriptions directly to a language model and prompt it to group related features into supernodes. They validate this using automated interpretability metrics, test it on a controlled two-hop Capitals task, and apply it to 1000 Wikipedia prompt completions for open-ended exploration, using an LLM judge to flag interesting attribution graphs.

Result: Automated supernodes match human-annotator interpretability. On the two-hop Capitals task, the pipeline recovers the intermediate-hop supernode in 97/100 prompts. The open-ended exploration on Wikipedia completions successfully identifies attribution graphs worthy of human review.

Conclusion: Even simple automation can produce meaningful attribution graph annotations, demonstrating that automated circuit tracing is feasible and should motivate further research in this direction.

Abstract: Circuit tracing is an exciting technique for revealing the internal computation of language models, but it requires a time-intensive manual step of grouping individual features or MLP neurons into supernodes. We present a simple pipeline for automating this step: directly presenting feature descriptions to a language model that groups them into supernodes. Using automated interpretability metrics, we confirm that supernodes generated by our pipeline are as interpretable as those generated by human annotators. On a two-hop Capitals task, our pipeline recovers a supernode corresponding to the intermediate hop in 97 of 100 prompts. Finally, we present a simple proof of concept using our pipeline for open-ended exploration, where we automatically annotate 1000 attribution graphs from Wikipedia prompt completions and then use an LLM judge to flag interesting graphs worth human review. We hope this work demonstrates that even simple automation can produce meaningful attribution graph annotations, motivating further work on automated circuit tracing.

</details>


### [150] [GeoID-PINN: Identifiability-Aware Regional Epidemic Inference with Geographic Coupling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02633)
*Weixiong Hua,Fan Bu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GeoID-PINN is a physics-informed neural network for SIRD dynamics that uses a row-stochastic source-composition matrix regularized toward spatial priors; simulations show trajectory accuracy does not guarantee recovery of true spatial dependence, and Louisiana COVID-19 evaluation reveals improved point forecasts over a baseline but cautions that edge recovery is not unique without prior-sensitivity checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Regional surveillance data conflate local transmission, reporting, seeding, and external infection pressure—factors that are hard to disentangle. Existing models struggle to separately identify spatial dependence structure from transmission dynamics, motivating a method that can incorporate spatial priors while jointly learning both.

Method: GeoID-PINN embeds a row-stochastic source-composition matrix within a SIRD compartmental model implemented as a physics-informed neural network. The matrix is regularized toward a spatial prior (distance, adjacency, commuting, or lead-lag). The framework is tested via a four-region simulation with known ground truth and a retrospective analysis using COVID-19 data from 64 Louisiana counties, compared against an autoregressive negative-binomial baseline.

Result: In simulation, a compatible distance prior yields source-composition error of 0.099 (vs. 0.159 unregularized, 0.577 under misspecification), while trajectory fit remains similar across conditions. On Louisiana data, GeoID-PINN reduces MSE from 32,957 to 11,468 and MAE from 70.60 to 57.73 relative to baseline, though baseline achieves lower NLL (5.158 vs. 5.346). A 15-county comparison shows adjacency priors reduce MSE by 6.85% and MAE by 3.1%. Similar performance across priors suggests structured regularization helps but does not uniquely recover edges.

Conclusion: Accurate trajectory fitting does not imply reliable recovery of spatial dependence structure. Structured spatial regularization improves point forecasts, but prior-sensitivity analysis and observation-model checks are essential before interpreting inferred regional connectivity. Edge recovery remains non-unique across plausible priors.

Abstract: Regional surveillance data reflect local transmission, reporting, seeding, and external infection pressure, which are difficult to identify separately. We introduce GeoID-PINN, a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for susceptible-infectious-recovered-deceased (SIRD) dynamics. The model represents spatial dependence with a row-stochastic source-composition matrix whose rows assign nonnegative source weights that sum to one. We regularize this matrix toward a spatial prior constructed from distance, adjacency, commuting, or lead-lag information. In a four-region simulation with known truth, a compatible distance prior gives source-composition error 0.099. The error rises to 0.159 without regularization and 0.577 under a strongly misspecified prior, while trajectory fit and transmission-scale estimates remain similar. Accurate trajectories therefore do not guarantee recovery of the regional dependence structure. We also evaluate GeoID-PINN retrospectively using COVID-19 data from 64 Louisiana counties. Relative to an autoregressive negative-binomial baseline, Forecast-Trained Geo-PINN reduces mean squared error (MSE) from 32,957 to 11,468 and mean absolute error (MAE) from 70.60 to 57.73. The baseline has lower negative log likelihood (NLL), 5.158 versus 5.346, indicating better distributional fit but worse point accuracy. In a controlled 15-county comparison, county adjacency reduces MSE by 6.85 percent and MAE by 3.1 percent. Similar performance across plausible priors supports structured regularization but not unique edge recovery. These results require prior-sensitivity and observation-model checks before interpretation.

</details>


### [151] [Verifier-Guided Model Discovery for Physical Dynamical Systems with Pretrained Symbolic Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02662)
*Farbod Faraji,Francesco Belardinelli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ODEFormer, a pretrained transformer for symbolic equation discovery from trajectories, is enhanced with a verifier-guided workflow that uses dynamical and physical-admissibility criteria to select from candidate equations. The method transfers successfully from synthetic ODEs to high-dimensional physical data, recovering vortex shedding dynamics without domain-specific priors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-fidelity simulations are prohibitively expensive, and ML surrogates often lack interpretability and generalizability. While pretrained transformers can discover symbolic equations from synthetic ODE trajectories without system-specific knowledge, reliably transferring them to high-dimensional real-world physical data remains an unsolved challenge.

Method: A verifier-guided (VG) workflow built around ODEFormer as a symbolic backbone. The method pools candidate equations from multiple trajectories and selects among them using dynamical and physical-admissibility criteria. For high-dimensional systems (e.g., vortex shedding), coordinate reduction is applied before symbolic discovery. The approach is tested at both fixed and varying Reynolds numbers.

Result: On Van der Pol oscillators, VG outperforms the original ODEFormer on held-out initial conditions. For vortex shedding, VG discovers reduced-order equations that recover the fundamental shedding oscillator and higher harmonics without requiring a wake-specific candidate library or prescribed Navier-Stokes structure. The cross-parameter model generalizes to withheld Reynolds number regimes. Reconstruction fidelity alone did not predict symbolic discoverability.

Conclusion: The verifier-guided neural-to-symbolic methodology enables interpretable, physically auditable forecasting for nonlinear physical systems. Success depends critically on the compatibility between latent dynamics and the backbone model's pretraining distribution, not merely on reconstruction accuracy.

Abstract: Reliable forecasting of nonlinear physical systems underpins scientific discovery and engineering decision-making. Yet high-fidelity simulations are prohibitively costly, and machine-learning surrogates can be opaque and encode assumptions about system dynamics, limiting generalizability. Pretrained transformers mapping synthetic ODE trajectories to equations offer interpretable alternatives, promising transfer without system-specific equation knowledge. Transferring them reliably to high-dimensional physical data, however, remains an open challenge. We develop a verifier-guided (VG) workflow around ODEFormer as a symbolic backbone, using dynamical and physical-admissibility criteria to select from a multi-trajectory candidate equation pool, enabling transfer. On canonical Van der Pol oscillators, VG outperforms the original ODEFormer workflow across held-out initial conditions. We then address vortex shedding, a phenomenon occurring in atmospheric and plasma systems of societal relevance, through coordinate reduction and symbolic discovery at fixed and varying Reynolds numbers. VG discovers fixed-parameter reduced-order equations that recover the fundamental shedding oscillator and higher harmonics without a wake-specific candidate library or prescribed Navier-Stokes structure, while the cross-parameter model generalizes to withheld regimes. Reconstruction fidelity alone did not determine symbolic discoverability, highlighting the importance of compatibility between latent dynamics and the backbone's pretraining distribution. This work establishes a verifier-guided neural-to-symbolic methodology for interpretable and physically auditable forecasting in the natural sciences.

</details>


### [152] [CT-HEG: A Bidirectional, Timestamp-Attributed Event Graph for ICU In-Hospital Mortality Prediction - An Architectural Ablation Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02663)
*Mohammad Nasir Uddin,Rahnuma Tabassum Orpita,Asaduzzaman Anik,Eklachur Rahman Bhuiyan,Marjahan Risalat,SM Wali Ullah,Asif Ahamed*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes CT-HEG, a continuous-time heterogeneous graph schema for ICU mortality prediction that models typed, timestamped clinical events without imputation. The GATv2Conv instantiation (CHIRP-Net) achieves AUROC 0.8449 on MIMIC-IV, with bidirectional edges proving essential and time-attentive features providing modest gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sequence models (e.g., GRU-D, mTAND, Transformers) handle irregularly sampled clinical time series but ignore typed relational structure among heterogeneous entity types (visits, vitals, labs). Graph-based models capture relational structure but typically assume fixed-interval inputs. The gap is a unified representation that jointly models irregular timing and typed heterogeneity.

Method: CT-HEG schema encodes each ICU stay as a heterogeneous graph with three node types (visit, vital, lab_event) and 2D edge attributes (t_hours/48, value_norm) encoding relative timing and normalized values without imputation. CHIRP-Net instantiates this as a 4-layer heterogeneous GATv2Conv network. Evaluated on MIMIC-IV v3.1 (31,142 ICU stays, LOS ≥48h, 13.4% mortality) with five seeds, bootstrapped CIs, and ablation of reverse edges, edge features, and edge type collapsing. Compared against logistic regression, mTAND, Transformer, and GRU-D baselines. Post-hoc temperature scaling for calibration.

Result: CHIRP-Net: 5-seed mean AUROC 0.8449±0.0071, AUPRC 0.4958±0.0209; ensemble AUROC 0.8618 (95% CI: 0.8485–0.8745). Removing reverse edges disconnected observation nodes from the visit readout, dropping AUROC by 0.1968±0.0073. Time-attentive edge features contributed +0.0247±0.0093 AUROC. Collapsing heterogeneous edge types into one relation (7× fewer parameters) surprisingly outperformed the full typed model. Post-calibration ECE: 0.0307.

Conclusion: Bidirectional connectivity is necessary for the model to use its inputs at all. CT-HEG is reasonably well calibrated after temperature scaling. Results support CT-HEG for irregular EHR data, but external validation, pre-specified temporal evaluation, and demographic fairness audits remain required before robustness claims.

Abstract: Accurate ICU mortality prediction requires modeling irregular clinical observations across heterogeneous entity types. Existing sequence models handle irregular sampling but ignore typed relational structure; existing graph models assume fixed-interval inputs. We introduce the Continuous-Time Heterogeneous EHR Graph (CT-HEG) schema and evaluate which architectural choices drive predictive performance. CT-HEG encodes each ICU stay as a typed, timestamped graph with three node types (visit, vital, lab_event) and 2D edge attributes (t_hours/48, value_norm) encoding timing and value without imputation. We instantiate CT-HEG as CHIRP-Net, a four-layer heterogeneous GATv2Conv network, evaluated on MIMIC-IV v3.1 (31,142 ICU stays, LOS>=48h, 13.4% mortality) with five seeds and bootstrapped confidence intervals, against logistic regression, mTAND, a Transformer, and GRU-D, plus an ablation study. CHIRP-Net achieved 5-seed mean AUROC 0.8449+/-0.0071 (AUPRC 0.4958+/-0.0209); the ensemble achieved AUROC 0.8618 (95% CI: 0.8485-0.8745). Removing reverse edges disconnected observation nodes from the visit readout, cutting AUROC by 0.1968+/-0.0073. Time-attentive edge features contributed 0.0247+/-0.0093 AUROC. Collapsing heterogeneous edge types into one relation (7x fewer parameters) outperformed the full model on all seeds. Post-calibration ECE was 0.0307. Temporal and demographic subgroup analyses were explored but not reported here, pending follow-up work. Bidirectional connectivity was necessary for the model to use its inputs at all, and CT-HEG was reasonably well calibrated after validation-fitted temperature scaling. These results support CT-HEG for irregular EHR data, while external validation, a pre-specified temporal evaluation, and a demographic fairness audit remain necessary before any claim of robustness. Code: https://github.com/nasiruddinstudents-ctrl/chirp-net-mimic-iv.

</details>


### [153] [Sphere Retraction Normalizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02668)
*Jie Zhang,Cheng-Fang Su,Yi-Jui Huang,Min-Te Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GeoNorm confines residual streams to a hypersphere via the exponential map, but the authors show all retractions on the hypersphere differ only in how update magnitude maps to rotation angle. They unify Euclidean residuals and GeoNorm within one framework, introduce a one-parameter family called $p$-SpheretNorm (with Proj- and Cay-SpheretNorm as special cases at $p=1$ and $p=2$), and demonstrate on nanoGPT that finite $p$ outperforms the exponential map limit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Residual connections are essential for stable deep network training. GeoNorm recently reinterpreted them on a Riemannian manifold, but its reliance on the exponential map raises the question: is the exponential map the optimal retraction, or could simpler algebraic retractions perform better? The authors aim to unify and generalize spherical residual streams under a broader retraction framework.

Method: The authors prove that on the hypersphere, all retractions collapse to a single scalar choice: how an update's magnitude is converted into a rotation angle within the plane spanned by the hidden state and the update. They propose $p$-SpheretNorm, a one-parameter family of angular retractions whose rotation angle saturates (rather than growing unbounded). The metric projection retraction ($p=1$) and Cayley retraction ($p=2$) yield Proj-SpheretNorm and Cay-SpheretNorm, both norm-preserving with only algebraic operations. Euclidean residuals and GeoNorm emerge as limiting cases.

Result: On nanoGPT experiments, Proj-SpheretNorm, Cay-SpheretNorm, and general $p$-SpheretNorm all outperform existing lightweight deep connection schemes. The best validation loss is achieved at finite $p$, not at the exponential map limit (GeoNorm), indicating the exponential map is not the preferred retraction for spherical residual streams.

Conclusion: The exponential map is merely one end of a spectrum of retractions on the hypersphere. Simpler, algebraically computed retractions (Proj- and Cay-SpheretNorm) not only preserve norms exactly but also empirically outperform GeoNorm. The $p$-SpheretNorm family provides a principled way to tune spherical residual stream dynamics, with saturation of rotation angle being a beneficial property.

Abstract: Residual connections are the de facto mechanism for training deep neural networks stably. Geodesic Normalization (GeoNorm) recasts them on a Riemannian manifold, orthogonalizing each layer output against the current hidden state and applying the resulting update through the Riemannian exponential map. Every hidden state thus keeps a constant $\ell_{2}$-norm, confining the residual stream to a hypersphere. The exponential map, however, is only one member of a broad family of retraction maps. We show that on the hypersphere this entire family collapses to a single scalar design choice. What distinguishes one retraction from another is only how the magnitude of an update is converted into a rotation angle within the plane spanned by the hidden state and the update. This view places Euclidean residual connections and GeoNorm in one framework. Instantiating it with the metric projection retraction and the Cayley retraction yields Proj-SpheretNorm and Cay-SpheretNorm, which are exactly norm-preserving yet require only algebraic operations. Both prove to be members of a one-parameter family of angular retractions, $p$-SpheretNorm, whose rotation angle saturates rather than growing without bound. The two methods above are recovered exactly at $p = 1$ and $p = 2$, while the identity map and GeoNorm arise only as limits at either end. On nanoGPT, all three methods outperform existing lightweight deep connection schemes, and the best validation loss is attained at finite $p$, indicating that the exponential map is not the preferred retraction for spherical residual streams but merely one end of a spectrum.

</details>


### [154] [Learning Molecular Representations from Cellular Phenotypes with Structure Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02688)
*Xuan Lin,Jingyu Sheng,Tengfei Ma,Li Sun,Dapeng Xiong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PhenMol is a structure-preserving multimodal framework that disentangles molecular and cellular representations into shared and private components, enabling phenotype-guided alignment without distorting chemical neighborhoods, leading to improved performance on molecular property prediction, retrieval, and clinical trial outcome tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal representation learning methods for phenotypic drug discovery optimize cross-modal alignment between molecular structures and cellular responses but neglect the intrinsic organization of chemical space, causing distorted molecular representations and loss of structural information.

Method: PhenMol disentangles molecular and cellular representations into shared (cross-modal) and private (modality-specific) components. A dedicated molecular branch preserves chemical structure, while phenotype-guided alignment integrates cellular phenotype information without disrupting molecular neighborhood organization.

Result: On ~30,400 molecule–cell morphology pairs, PhenMol outperforms baselines on 270 bioactivity prediction tasks, molecule–phenotype retrieval, and clinical trial outcome prediction. ECFP4-based structural analysis confirms better preservation of molecular neighborhoods and reduced embedding distortion.

Conclusion: Structure-aware constraints are critical in multimodal molecular representation learning. PhenMol provides an effective approach for integrating cellular phenotypes with chemical knowledge, advancing drug discovery applications.

Abstract: Phenotypic drug discovery enables the discovery of functional relationships between molecular structures and cellular responses. However, existing multimodal representation learning methods often optimize cross-modal alignment without considering the intrinsic organization of chemical space, resulting in distorted molecular representations and loss of structural information. We propose \textbf{PhenMol}, a structure-preserving framework for phenotype-aware molecular representation learning. PhenMol disentangles molecular and cellular representations into shared and private components, enabling phenotype-guided alignment while preserving chemical structures through a dedicated molecular branch. This design integrates cellular phenotype information without disrupting molecular neighborhood organization. Experiments on approximately $3.04 \times 10^{4}$ molecule--cell morphology pairs demonstrate that PhenMol improves molecular property prediction across 270 bioactivity tasks, molecule--phenotype retrieval, and clinical trial outcome prediction. Moreover, ECFP4-based structural analysis shows that PhenMol better preserves molecular neighborhoods and reduces embedding distortion compared with existing multimodal alignment methods. These results highlight the importance of structure-aware constraints in multimodal molecular representation learning and provide an effective approach for integrating cellular phenotypes with chemical knowledge for drug discovery.

</details>


### [155] [GLOBE: Trajectory-Aligned Gradient Matching with Structured SparseOptimization for Coreset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02690)
*Hetian Liu,Jin Cui,Mengcheng Shi,Yanbin Hu,Xinyue Long,Boran Zhao,Pengju Pen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GLOBE proposes a trajectory-aligned coreset selection method that uses gradient trajectories across multiple checkpoints and multi-order moment matching, combined with structured sparse regularization, to select compact subsets that outperform existing methods, especially at low retention ratios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing gradient-based coreset methods rely on single-snapshot gradients and greedy selection, failing to capture evolving optimization dynamics or handle strongly correlated samples, which limits their effectiveness for on-device training with constrained resources.

Method: GLOBE represents each sample as a gradient trajectory across multiple training checkpoints. It formulates selection as a globally optimized sparse weighting problem with a multi-order matching objective that aligns first-order mean and projected uncentered second-order moments. Group LASSO, Elastic Net regularization, and nonnegative budget constraints induce group- and sample-level sparsity, followed by class-balanced Top-K selection.

Result: Experiments across six benchmarks and five architectures show GLOBE consistently outperforms existing coreset selection methods in downstream test accuracy, with particularly strong gains at low retention ratios.

Conclusion: Combining dynamic gradient information, multi-order distribution matching, and structured sparsity is highly effective for data-efficient learning, enabling robust coreset selection that better preserves full-dataset training behavior.

Abstract: On-device training of deep neural networks is fundamentally constrained by the computational and memory costs of large-scale datasets. Coreset selection offers a practical solution by retaining only a compact subset of real training samples. However, existing gradient-based methods commonly rely on gradients computed at a single model snapshot and employ greedy or pursuit-based selection procedures, limiting their ability to capture evolving optimization dynamics and handle strongly correlated samples. We propose GLOBE (Gradient Local-Balanced Extraction), a trajectory-aligned coreset selection framework that formulates sample selection as a globally optimized sparse weighting problem. GLOBE represents each sample by a gradient trajectory constructed across multiple training checkpoints, thereby capturing its influence throughout different stages of optimization. To preserve the training behavior of the full dataset, we introduce a multi-order matching objective that jointly aligns the first-order mean and projected uncentered second-order moments of gradient trajectories. GLOBE further combines Group LASSO, Elastic Net regularization, and nonnegative budget constraints to induce group- and sample-level sparsity while stabilizing the weights of correlated trajectories. Finally, class-balanced Top-K selection maintains adequate category coverage under limited sampling budgets. Experiments across six benchmarks and five evaluation architectures demonstrate that GLOBE consistently outperforms existing coreset selection methods in downstream test accuracy, particularly at low retention ratios. These results highlight the effectiveness of combining dynamic gradient information, multi-order distribution matching, and structured sparsity for data-efficient learning.

</details>


### [156] [Output-Aware Rotation for INT2 KV-Cache Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02691)
*Vincent-Daniel Yun,Woosang Lim,Minsoo Cheong,Sunwoo Lee,Murali Annavaram,Sai Praneeth Karimireddy,Sungjoo Yoo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OptR is an output-aware rotation method for INT2 KV-cache quantization that minimizes post-output-projection attention error by learning per-head orthogonal corrections through the full quantization and attention path, improving long-context LLM inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing rotation-based INT2 KV-cache quantization methods optimize cache statistics or proxy errors before the complete attention readout, but model performance is ultimately determined by error propagated through both attention and the output projection W_O. This mismatch between optimization objective and actual downstream error motivates an output-aware approach.

Method: OptR decomposes the post-W_O attention-output error into key-induced and value-induced terms. It learns per-head orthogonal rotation corrections by minimizing this error through the full INT2 quantization and attention pathway. Additionally, it employs an attention-equivalent key reparameterization that reduces large channel-wise offsets without altering the softmax distribution, preserving the paged KV-cache format.

Result: Across three models and five reasoning and coding benchmarks, OptR consistently improves over both QuaRot and OSCAR baselines. It also strengthens long-context retrieval performance while maintaining negligible inference overhead.

Conclusion: Output-aware rotation via OptR effectively bridges the gap between INT2 quantization optimization and actual model behavior, yielding superior KV-cache compression with practical deployment characteristics.

Abstract: The key-value (KV) cache has become a major memory and bandwidth bottleneck in long-context large language model inference, making ultra-low-bit quantization increasingly important. However, existing rotation-based INT2 methods optimize cache statistics or proxy errors before the complete attention readout, even though the model is ultimately affected by the error propagated through attention and the output projection $W_O$. To address this mismatch, we propose \textit{OptR}, an output-aware rotation method that minimizes post-$W_O$ attention-output error. OptR decomposes the post-$W_O$ attention-output error into key- and value-induced terms and learns per-head orthogonal corrections through the full INT2 quantization and attention path. OptR further applies an attention-equivalent key reparameterization to reduce large channel-wise offsets without changing the softmax distribution. Across three models and five reasoning and coding benchmarks, OptR consistently improves both QuaRot and OSCAR and strengthens long-context retrieval, while preserving the paged KV-cache format with negligible inference overhead.

</details>


### [157] [PatTree: a novel approach for automated creation of multimodal, graph-based patient representations for medical classification tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02692)
*Julia Gehrmann,Lars Quakulinski,Hamza Naseem,Oya Beyan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PatTree introduces a graph-based patient representation that automatically structures heterogeneous, multimodal clinical real-world data into a unified knowledge graph, enabling early-stage data integration without pre-standardization. Evaluated on ADNI-1 (n=763) for Alzheimer's disease classification, it achieves 98.5% balanced accuracy and 0.987 F1 score, demonstrating that assumption-free, automated structuring can bypass tedious data harmonization for clinical AI pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Holistic, multimodal data improves medical AI classification, but clinical real-world data is plagued by heterogeneity: missing values, multiple time points, diverse modalities, and inconsistent formats/semantics. Existing data harmonization approaches are resource-intensive, error-prone, and limit scalability and reproducibility. There is a need for automated, assumption-free methods to structure and integrate multimodal clinical data without relying on pre-standardized inputs.

Method: The authors propose PatTree, a graph-based holistic patient representation derived through automated structuring of multimodal clinical data. PatTree encodes heterogeneous clinical data into a unified knowledge graph while preserving semantic relationships between data elements across modalities and data sources. This enables early-stage data integration and machine-interpretable data access without requiring pre-standardized inputs.

Result: On a subset of the ADNI-1 cohort (n=763), PatTree achieved a balanced accuracy of 98.5% and an F1 score of 0.987 on the held-out test set for the three-class classification task (Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, cognitively normal), demonstrating state-of-the-art performance.
