Conclusion: Assumption-free, automated structuring of multimodal medical data via graph-based representations like PatTree can serve as a scalable foundation for clinical AI pipelines, eliminating the need for tedious data preparation and standardization while maintaining high classification performance.

Abstract: Access to holistic, multimodal data improves the performance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in medical classification tasks compared to utilizing single modalities or data sources. However, the inherent heterogeneity and complexity of clinical real-world data pose significant challenges to structured data analysis and AI application. This heterogeneity includes missing values, multiple time points, diverse modalities, and inconsistent formats and semantics. Data harmonization prior to data integration tackles this challenge but remains resource-intensive and error-prone, limiting the scalability and reproducibility of holistic, AI-driven decision support on clinical real-world data. We therefore propose PatTree, a graph-based, holistic representation of patients that can be derived from real-world clinical data through the automated structuring of multimodal clinical data. PatTree enables early-stage data integration without relying on pre-standardized inputs. While representing heterogeneous clinical data within a unified knowledge graph, PatTree preserves the semantic relationships between data elements across modalities and data sources, facilitating interoperability and machine-interpretable data access. Using a subset of the ADNI-1 cohort (n = 763), we demonstrate that classification of patients is directly feasible on PatTree reaching state-of-the-art classification performance. In the three-class classification task distinguishing Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, and cognitively normal individuals, we achieve a balanced accuracy of 98.5% and an F$_1$ score of 0.987 on the held-out test set. Our results show that assumption-free, automated structuring of multimodal medical data can serve as a scalable foundation for clinical AI pipelines bypassing tedious data preparation and standardization.

</details>


### [158] [Measuring Explainer Stability via Attribution Separability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02697)
*Eddie Conti,Álvaro Parafita,Axel Brando*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a distribution-based framework to quantify the stability of attribution methods by assessing the separability of ranked feature importance scores and determining up to which rank index the ranking remains reliable; also extends to comparing explainer robustness across datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most attribution methods produce variable scores due to inherent stochasticity, yet existing evaluation focuses primarily on fidelity/faithfulness rather than stability. A principled way to assess whether feature rankings are reliable and separable is lacking.

Method: A distribution-based framework that models the variability of attribution scores to measure separability in the ranked attribution vector. It identifies the largest index (rank position) for which the feature ranking remains statistically reliable. The framework is extended to compare attribution methods based on ranking robustness across entire datasets.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method effectively evaluates explainer stability, revealing how different attribution methods vary in ranking reliability. The approach successfully identifies the threshold beyond which feature rankings become unreliable.

Conclusion: The framework offers a complementary criterion — stability — for evaluating attribution methods, supplementing traditional fidelity metrics and enabling practitioners to select more reliable explainers.

Abstract: Attribution methods (AMs) assign an importance score to each feature and are widely adopted to explain black-box models. However, most methods can produce variable attribution scores due to stochastic components in their definition. In this paper, we propose a distribution-based framework to capture the stability of attribution scores. In particular, our approach allows to understand the degree of separability in the ranked attribution vector and obtain the largest index for which a feature ranking remains reliable. We further extend this framework to compare AMs based on the robustness of their rankings across a dataset. Through experiments, we demonstrate how to apply our method to evaluate explainer stability. Overall, our approach provides a complementary criterion for evaluating the stability of AMs.

</details>


### [159] [NANQ: Noise-Floor-Aware Mixed-Precision Non-Uniform Quantization for Analog Compute-in-Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02700)
*Yizhe Chen,Wenshuai Yao,Saiya Wang,Yuannuo Feng,Wenbo Qi,Kechao Tang,Ngai Wong,Wenyong Zhou,Wang Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NANQ is a noise-aware mixed-precision non-uniform quantization framework for analog CIM that adapts quantization density based on measured hardware noise profiles, achieving significant accuracy gains on an eFlash CIM SoC with only 3.2–3.8 equivalent bits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CIM-oriented quantization methods minimize ideal quantization error while ignoring hardware noise (device variation, read noise), leading to inefficient precision allocation. Precision is wasted in noise-dominated regions while noise-sensitive regions remain under-protected.

Method: NANQ models magnitude-dependent weight noise from measured eFlash CIM array responses. It converts the noise profile into an adaptive non-uniform quantization density function that allocates finer resolution to low-noise regions and coarser resolution to noise-dominated regions. Layer-wise mixed-precision bit-widths are assigned by detecting each layer's precision saturation point under hardware noise using a unified threshold.

Result: On an eFlash CIM SoC with 2-bit weight-magnitude quantization, NANQ improves vision-model accuracy by 8.05 percentage points and reduces language-model perplexity by 54.7% on average compared to PowerQuant. Mixed-precision NANQ captures most gains from additional quantization resources using only 3.2–3.8 equivalent bits.

Conclusion: Noise-aware non-uniform quantization is essential for analog CIM; modeling hardware noise and adaptively allocating precision yields substantial accuracy improvements with minimal effective bit-width overhead.

Abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) enables energy-efficient neural network inference, but device variation and read noise can severely degrade low-bit quantized models. Existing CIM-oriented quantization methods mainly minimize ideal quantization error, ignoring the hardware noise floor and thus causing inefficient precision allocation. We propose NANQ, a noise-aware mixed-precision non-uniform quantization framework for analog CIM. NANQ models magnitude-dependent weight noise from measured responses of an eFlash CIM array and converts the noise profile into an adaptive quantization density, assigning finer resolution to low-noise regions while avoiding ineffective precision in noise-dominated regions. It further assigns layer-wise bit-widths by identifying each layer's precision saturation point under hardware noise using a unified threshold. On-chip experiments on an eFlash CIM SoC show that, under 2-bit weight-magnitude quantization, NANQ improves vision-model accuracy by 8.05 percentage points and reduces language-model PPL by 54.7% on average over PowerQuant. Mixed-precision NANQ captures most of the gains obtainable from additional quantization resources with only 3.2-3.8 equivalent bits.

</details>


### [160] [Can Training Logs Make Model Comparisons More Precise?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02705)
*Wei-Jung Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training logs from stochastic model runs can improve precision of model comparisons via arm-specific covariate adjustment, but covariate selection must avoid overfitting to noise; early-log statistics often help reduce uncertainty when selected carefully.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Comparing stochastically trained models requires estimating performance differences along with uncertainty from repeated runs. The authors investigate whether training logs — covariates generated during training — can make these comparisons more precise than using only final performance metrics.

Method: The paper proposes arm-specific covariate adjustment: each model (arm) is adjusted using only statistics from its own training runs, preserving the raw mean difference as the reported effect. The method is evaluated across three architectures and three datasets in a vision study, using early training log statistics as covariates to reduce variance in model comparison estimates.

Result: Simple adjustments based on early training logs often reduce uncertainty in model comparisons. However, the main limitation is covariate selection: broadly searching the log pool for the most correlated statistic typically adds more noise than it removes, even when genuinely useful statistics exist in hindsight.

Conclusion: Training logs are useful for more precise model comparisons, but only when the adjustment procedure avoids large selection noise. Careful covariate selection is essential to realizing the precision gains.

Abstract: Comparing stochastically trained models requires estimating both a performance difference and its uncertainty from repeated runs. We study whether training logs from those same runs can make such comparisons more precise. Because training-log covariates are produced during training rather than measured before it, we use arm-specific covariate adjustment: each model is adjusted only with statistics from its own runs, and the raw mean difference remains the reported effect. In a vision study spanning three architectures and three datasets, simple adjustments based on early training logs often reduce uncertainty in model comparisons. The main limitation is covariate selection. Broadly searching the log pool for the most correlated statistic often adds more noise than it removes, even when useful statistics exist in hindsight. Training logs therefore appear useful for more precise model comparisons, but only when the adjustment avoids large selection noise.

</details>


### [161] [Designing a Good Virtual Node: Addressable and Cardinality-Preserving Global Memory for Message Passing Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02709)
*Félix Marcoccia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Virtual nodes in MPNNs suffer from an information bottleneck due to homogeneous broadcasting. The paper proposes factorizing global memory into addressable cross-attention slots with private key/value anchors to preserve cardinality/multiplicity, achieving injective multiset representations capable of 1-WL refinement at O(nMd) cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard virtual nodes compress the entire graph into a single homogeneous state and broadcast it identically to all nodes, creating a finite-capacity bottleneck. The authors aim to relieve this bottleneck without self-attention by designing auxiliary virtual memory that can (1) be factorized into independently writable/readable states and (2) preserve multiplicity/cardinality information, which standard softmax attention loses due to uniform replication invariance.

Method: The method introduces addressable cross-attention slots as factorized virtual memory, where each slot can be independently written to and read from. To recover the multiplicity information lost by softmax attention's invariance to uniform replication, each slot query is inserted as a private key/value anchor, which captures the discarded normalization mass. This yields an injective multiset representation on bounded color domains, provably capable of implementing 1-WL refinement.

Result: Experiments on multiplicity-aware Two-Radius tasks, motif counting, and constrained link-set prediction demonstrate that the proposed addressable and cardinality-preserving virtual memory outperforms standard virtual node approaches. The method achieves this with O(nMd) arithmetic cost, where n is the number of nodes, M the number of memory slots, and d the feature dimension.

Conclusion: Factorizing virtual node memory into addressable slots with cardinality-preserving anchors effectively relieves the information bottleneck in MPNNs without resorting to self-attention. The approach is both theoretically grounded (1-WL expressivity) and empirically effective across tasks requiring multiplicity awareness.

Abstract: Virtual nodes give message-passing neural networks a simple global communication route, but the standard node--VN--node pipeline compresses the graph into one homogeneous state and broadcasts it identically to every node. Building on the Two-Radius analysis of Mishayev et al., we ask how auxiliary virtual memory can relieve this finite-capacity bottleneck without self-attention. We identify two requirements. First, the global memory should be factorized into independently writable and readable states: this can be achieved using addressable cross-attention slots. Second, addressability alone does not preserve multiplicity, because softmax attention is invariant to uniform replication. Inserting each slot query as a private key/value anchor recovers the discarded normalization mass and yields, on bounded color domains, an injective multiset representation able to implement a 1-WL refinement. Experiments on multiplicity-aware Two-Radius, motif counting, and constrained link-set prediction support this addressable and cardinality-preserving virtual memory at (O(nMd)) arithmetic cost.

</details>


### [162] [FedCritic-MIMO: Communication-Efficient Serverless Federated Critic Learning for Massive-MIMO Resource Control in Open and Disaggregated 6G RANs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03852)
*Amin Farajzadeh,Melike Erol-Kantarci*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedCritic-MIMO is a communication-efficient, serverless federated multi-agent RL framework for 6G RANs where cell-level controllers exchange only compressed, sparse critic parameters peer-to-peer over an interference-aware graph, achieving superior performance-communication tradeoffs with 76% lower overhead than uncompressed exchange.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open and disaggregated 6G RANs require independently deployable cell-level controllers that must coordinate for multi-cell resource management (scheduling, power allocation, beamforming, interference) without centralized training, shared actors, or parameter-server aggregation, while minimizing inter-controller communication overhead.

Method: FedCritic-MIMO employs a serverless peer-to-peer architecture where controllers retain local actors and personalized critic components, exchanging only compatible shared critic parameters. Key techniques include: (1) wireless-aware event triggering, (2) adaptive layer-wise top-k sparse critic exchange with error feedback, (3) balanced interference-aware fusion over an interference graph. Theoretical analysis provides conditional finite-time stationarity and consensus guarantees for the compressed peer-to-peer critic recursion under a fixed-policy, frozen-target critic-regression model.

Result: In strongly interference-coupled reuse-1 simulations, FedCritic-MIMO achieves: best performance-communication tradeoff among all baselines; highest held-out throughput; improved user-rate distribution and mean SINR; increased QoS satisfaction; lowest interference cost per delivered bit; 76% reduction in critic-communication overhead versus uncompressed distributed critic exchange.

Conclusion: Serverless exchange of compatible shared critic parameters can effectively coordinate RAN controllers without centralized trajectory collection or parameter-server aggregation, enabling practical federated MARL for disaggregated 6G RAN deployments.

Abstract: This paper proposes FedCritic-MIMO, a communication-efficient serverless federated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for AI-native resource control across independently deployable cell-level controllers in open and disaggregated 6G RANs. Controllers share no trainer, retain local actors and personalized critic components, and exchange only compatible shared critic parameters. FedCritic-MIMO targets reuse-$1$ multi-cell massive-MIMO OFDMA deployments, where RAN controllers jointly manage user scheduling, per-stream power allocation, beamforming, interference, and long-term QoS with limited inter-controller signaling. Each base station locally executes its actor without centralized training or actor federation, while critic knowledge is exchanged peer-to-peer over an interference-aware graph. It enables this collaboration through wireless-aware event triggering, adaptive layer-wise top-$k$ sparse critic exchange with error feedback, and balanced interference-aware fusion. We establish conditional finite-time stationarity and consensus guarantees for the balanced, compressed peer-to-peer critic recursion under a fixed-policy, frozen-target critic-regression model. In strongly interference-coupled reuse-$1$ simulations, FedCritic-MIMO achieves the best performance-communication tradeoff among heuristic, independent-learning, centralized-training, and communication-ablation baselines. It achieves the highest held-out throughput, improves user-rate distribution and mean SINR, increases QoS satisfaction, and attains the lowest interference cost per delivered bit among learning baselines. It reduces critic-communication overhead by $76\%$ relative to uncompressed distributed critic exchange. These results demonstrate that serverless exchange of compatible shared critic parameters can coordinate RAN controllers without centralized trajectory collection or parameter-server aggregation.

</details>


### [163] [Neural Networks with Local Converging Inputs for Efficient Options Pricing Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02778)
*Harris Cobb,Wenbo Hao,Yingjie Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NNLCI uses neural networks to locally correct coarse-to-refined mesh numerical PDE solutions for option pricing, achieving 4-12× RMSE reduction with minimal high-fidelity training data across Black-Scholes (1D–3D) and Heston stochastic volatility models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-dimensional option pricing PDEs are computationally expensive for real-time trading and risk management. Existing numerical methods require fine meshes that are prohibitively costly, motivating a hybrid approach that combines cheap coarse solutions with learned local corrections to achieve high accuracy at low computational cost.

Method: NNLCI (Neural Networks with Local Converging Inputs) takes solutions from a coarse mesh and a refined mesh as inputs to a neural network that predicts local corrections. Only a small subset of high-fidelity training data is needed. The method uses a concise input format and is applied to cash-or-nothing options under Black-Scholes (1D, 2D, 3D) and down-and-out barrier call options under the Heston model (2D PDE in S and v).

Result: NNLCI reduces the RMSE of refined-mesh numerical solutions by a factor of approximately 4–12 across test sets, even when trained on only a small subset of parameter combinations, demonstrating strong generalization and low training data requirements.

Conclusion: NNLCI significantly reduces computational requirements for high-dimensional option pricing problems, offering low training costs and strong generalization, making it well-suited for real-time options trading and risk management applications.

Abstract: We present a novel application of Neural Networks with Local Converging Inputs (NNLCI) to improve the efficiency of existing numerical methods for pricing multi-asset options. The most concise input format for NNLCI has been introduced, offering substantial convenience and efficiency. NNLCI uses a neural network to locally correct solutions from a coarse mesh and a refined mesh (relative to the coarse one), requiring only a minimal amount of high-fidelity training data. We demonstrate this approach on cash-or-nothing options under the Black-Scholes equation in one, two, and three spatial dimensions, and on single-asset down-and-out barrier call options under the Heston stochastic-volatility model (whose pricing PDE is two-dimensional in the spot price $S$ and the instantaneous variance $v$). In each case, NNLCI reduces the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of the refined-mesh numerical solution by a factor of approximately 4-12 on test sets, even when the neural network is trained on only a small subset of parameter combinations. These results demonstrate that NNLCI significantly reduces computational requirements for high-dimensional problems in real-time options trading and risk management, offering low training costs and strong generalization ability.

</details>


### [164] [Evaluation Blindness: How Silent Measurement Failures Corrupt AI Systems from Training to Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02786)
*Priyanka Bajaj*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces "evaluation blindness," where AI measurement systems fail to detect failures despite producing normal readings. It unifies training-time and deployment-time failure detection under a formal framework, catalogs real-world silent failures across a six-class taxonomy, and proposes a failure budget framework tied to risk class.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI systems can fail silently, with measurement pipelines showing healthy signals while failures propagate undetected. This problem spans both training and deployment but has been treated separately in prior literature. The authors aim to formalize and unify these phenomena to make measurement infrastructure a first-class correctness concern across the entire AI lifecycle.

Method: The paper (1) formally defines a detectability predicate for evaluation blindness, (2) conducts four training-time case studies including a real implementation bug in TRL PR #6594 where loss decreases normally despite corrupted gradients, (3) develops a six-class failure taxonomy validated against 50 real-world incidents from court documents and regulatory filings, and (4) proposes a failure budget framework that maps acceptable failure rates to use-case risk classes.

Result: 53% of verifiable public failures were found to be silent. An Operational failure category was identified as 100% silent by structural definition. The TRL PR #6594 case demonstrated corrupted gradients with normally decreasing loss, confirming evaluation blindness at training time. The taxonomy provides systematic coverage of six production failure classes.

Conclusion: Measurement infrastructure must be treated as a correctness concern throughout the AI lifecycle — not only at evaluation time. Current monitoring and evaluation practices are structurally insufficient to catch silent failures, requiring both formal detectability analysis and risk-calibrated failure budgets.

Abstract: AI systems can fail silently. The failure propagates through training loops, evaluation pipelines, and production monitoring stacks until downstream harm makes it visible. This paper introduces evaluation blindness: a measurement function M exhibits evaluation blindness with respect to failure class F when it produces readings indistinguishable from a healthy state while the system is actually failing, with no auxiliary signal flagging the gap.
  The problem surfaces at two lifecycle stages the literature has treated separately. At training time, reward models are gamed, importance-sampling corrections are silently miscalculated, and benchmark contamination inflates fine-tuning evaluations, all while loss curves look healthy and gradient updates proceed normally. At deployment time, monitoring fails to catch six classes of production failure, including an Operational category that is 100% silent by structural definition.
  We provide a formal detectability predicate unifying both stages. Four training-time case studies trace concrete breakdowns, including a real implementation bug in TRL PR #6594 where gradients are corrupted as loss decreases normally. A six-class taxonomy validated against 50 real-world incidents from court documents and regulatory filings finds that 53% of verifiable public failures were silent. A failure budget framework ties acceptable failure rates to use-case risk class.
  The implication is direct: measurement infrastructure is a correctness concern across the full AI lifecycle, not just at evaluation time. Data, code, and taxonomy schema are at https://github.com/priyanka25aug/llm-failure-taxonomy.

</details>


### [165] [Topological Simplification in Predictive Coding Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02816)
*Adam Shaw,Jiayu Li,Michael Sperling,Michael Kim,Alvin Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper uses persistent homology to analyze how predictive coding networks (PCNs) compress representations layer-by-layer, finding that larger PCNs delay topological simplification, that later simplification correlates with better reconstruction, and that PCNs consistently simplify later than feedforward MLPs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the compression–reconstruction tradeoff in predictive coding networks through a quantitative topological lens, addressing a gap in how recurrent, bidirectional architectures shape the geometry of learned representations across layers.

Method: Layer-wise persistent homology analysis (0D homology for connected components) applied to trained PCNs and matched MLPs on synthetic and MNIST datasets, with Spearman correlation, bootstrap comparisons, and comparisons across model sizes and activation functions.

Result: Smaller PCNs collapse connected components earlier (ρ ∈ [0.72, 0.79]); a strong negative correlation (ρ = −0.58) exists between simplification depth and reconstruction error; PCNs collapse components later than MLPs by ~3.6 layers on average.

Conclusion: Persistent homology provides a principled quantitative framework for studying representational compression in PCNs, revealing that both model capacity and recurrent predictive coding dynamics govern when the compression–reconstruction tradeoff is resolved across layers.

Abstract: We study the topology of learned representations in predictive coding networks (PCNs), a neuro-inspired bidirectional architecture, using a quantitative layer-wise persistent homology analysis. We train well-performing PCNs on a synthetic classification dataset ($\geq 99.9\%$ test accuracy) and on MNIST ($\geq 95\%$ test accuracy), and measure how topological features change across layers for different architectures and activation functions. We find that smaller PCNs collapse connected components across layers earlier than larger models (Spearman $\unicode{x1D70C} \in [0.72, 0.79]$ across activations), with model size measured as the sum of hidden-layer widths. We also observe a strong negative correlation ($\unicode{x1D70C} = -0.58$) between the depth at which simplification occurs and reconstruction error; i.e., architectures that simplify later reconstruct better. Finally, a seed-level bootstrap comparison across architectures and activations shows that PCNs consistently collapse connected components later than matched MLPs, with an average difference of $3.6$ layers. These results suggest that persistent homology offers a useful quantitative lens on the compression--reconstruction tradeoff in PCNs, and that both model capacity and the recurrent, bidirectional dynamics of predictive coding inference shape when this tradeoff is resolved across layers.

</details>


### [166] [Wiring Beats Blending: What Transfers Between Transformer Sizes -- and What Doesn't](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02829)
*Ravi Satya Durga Prasad Yenugula*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether a large pretrained model can be cost-effectively converted into a smaller, performant model. Studying the Pythia family (1.4B→410M), it finds that while internal representations align well, direct weight projection fails. Two independent levers—least-squares compensation and variance-preserving rescaling—enable efficient conversion that beats training from scratch, especially at low token budgets, though the method has scaling limits at ~5x donor size ratio.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training large language models from scratch is computationally expensive. The authors ask a practical question: can an already-pretrained large model be converted into a smaller model, bypassing the cost of training every size independently? This would enable efficient model family creation by deriving smaller siblings from a single large pretrained donor.

Method: The authors characterize the 1.4B→410M conversion in the Pythia family through four empirical analyses: (1) measuring cross-size representation alignment via ridge regression (R²=0.84); (2) demonstrating that dense weight projection is destructive due to breaking rotary embeddings, per-head structure, GELU, and LayerNorm; (3) showing weight residuals after best-fit linear operators are noise-like under shuffle controls; (4) isolating two independent conversion levers—least-squares compensation (for function/zero-shot quality) and variance-preserving rescaling (for training dynamics/endpoints). These are tested in matched-budget continued pretraining across width-reduced and depth-reduced pairs at varying token budgets (30M to ~1B tokens) and at larger scale (6.9B→1.4B).

Result: At a 30M-token budget, the compensation lever beats the strongest subcloning baseline on width-reduced pairs (84.0 vs. 89.7, lower is better) and depth-reduced pairs (109.3 vs. 117.9). Both levers together match the best method. At a 33× larger budget (~1B tokens), conversion methods converge to parity with the best baseline (40.0 vs. 40.0), while all transfer methods consistently beat from-scratch training—by up to 18× at low budgets. At ~5× donor scale (6.9B→1.4B), stacking both levers over-corrects due to ill-conditioning of the least-squares solve at large width ratios, suggesting dimension-aware regularization is needed.

Conclusion: Model conversion is viable and valuable primarily through initialization transfer. Least-squares compensation provides a token-efficient, low-budget win but is not universally superior—it converges to parity with baselines at scale. Variance-preserving rescaling governs training dynamics. The method has a boundary at large width gaps (~5× scale ratio), where ill-conditioning requires dimension-aware regularization. Transfer initialization always beats from-scratch, with the largest margin at low budgets.

Abstract: Model families train every size from scratch. Can a pretrained large model be converted into a smaller sibling? We characterize the 1.4B->410M conversion in the Pythia family end-to-end: (i) representations align strongly across sizes (ridge R^2=0.84) while parameters align weakly; (ii) dense weight projection is functionally destructive -- provably not an assembly artifact -- because basis mixing breaks rotary, per-head, GELU, and LayerNorm structure; (iii) after the best-fit linear operator, weight residuals are statistically indistinguishable from noise under shuffle controls; (iv) conversion value therefore lives in initialization. In matched-budget continued pre-training we decompose conversion into two independent levers -- least-squares compensation (function: best zero-shot) and variance-preserving rescale (dynamics: best endpoints). Compensation is a token-efficient, low-budget win rather than a universal one: at 30M tokens it beats the strongest subcloning variant on both a width-reduced pair (84.0 +/- 1.8 vs. 89.7 +/- 3.7, 3/3 seeds) and a held-out depth-reduced pair (109.3 vs. 117.9, 3/3 seeds), reaching a given quality with fewer tokens; at a 33x larger budget the two converge to parity (40.0 vs. 40.0), both far ahead of from-scratch, which transfer initialization always beats -- by up to 18x at low budget, the margin narrowing at convergence and at the largest scale. We further map the method's boundary: at ~5x the donor scale (6.9B->1.4B) stacking both levers over-corrects, which we trace to ill-conditioning of the compensation solve at large width, pointing to dimension-aware regularization as the fix. Code, checkpoints, and the frozen evaluation corpus are released.

</details>


### [167] [NOMADD: Numerical Optimization of Models Adapting to Data Drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02845)
*Swapn Shah,Keith Burghardt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A post-hoc, model-agnostic method to mitigate concept drift in tabular models by factorizing parameter evolution across time periods, compressing via low-rank factorization, and extrapolating latent factors forward with damped, regularized forecasts — achieving competitive drift resilience with negligible training cost compared to bespoke pre-trained solutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabular models suffer performance degradation from data drift and concept drift, yet real-time mitigation is hampered by unavailable labels, impractical retraining, and existing drift-reduction tools being tied to specific neural architectures. Users often face constraints (accuracy, inference latency, model size) requiring model selection across families, motivating a general post-hoc drift-correction method applicable across model types.

Method: The algorithm (1) fits the base model separately on each labeled training period, (2) measures parameter evolution against a single anchor model pooled across all periods, (3) compresses parameter changes via low-rank factorization, and (4) extrapolates each latent factor forward using a damped, regularized forecast. This yields drift-corrected parameters for deployment.

Result: Evaluated on the 18-dataset Drift-Resilient TabPFN benchmark under its own protocol and metric, the extrapolation method improves every base model family it is applied to and achieves performance competitive with the state-of-the-art Drift-Resilient TabPFN, while requiring only seconds of training versus ~1,300 GPU-hours for the baseline and being orders of magnitude faster at inference.

Conclusion: The proposed post-hoc drift correction is effective, efficient, and broadly applicable across model families, offering a practical alternative to expensive pre-training-based drift mitigation. The paper also discusses extending the approach to other modalities, highlighting both promise and challenges.

Abstract: Tabular model performance degrades when feature distributions change over time or the relationship between features and outcome variables change over time, known as data drift and concept drift, respectively. These issues are challenging to mitigate in real time because labeled data may not be immediately available, or re-training a model could be impractical. While tools exist to reduce drift, they are typically bespoke to neural network architectures and adapt how models are trained. In this paper, we offer an alternative post-hoc method to reduce concept drift, which is applicable to a variety of models, from trees to neural networks to tabular foundation models. This new tool is especially useful when constraints, such as high model accuracy, bounded inference time, or model size requires users to choose between different models for their specific use-cases. Our algorithm fits the base model separately on each labeled training period, measures how its parameters evolve against a single anchor model pooled over all of those periods, compresses those changes with a low-rank factorization, and extrapolates each latent factor forward with a damped, regularized forecast. On the 18-dataset Drift-Resilient TabPFN benchmark, evaluated under that benchmark's own protocol and metric, the extrapolation improves every base family it is applied to, and achieves performance competitive with the state-of-the-art Drift-Resilient TabPFN with seconds of training. In contrast, Drift-Resilient TabPFN requires pre-training on millions of synthetic datasets over approximately 1,300 GPU-hours, and is orders of magnitude slower in inference (depending on the model). In the discussion, we explore the promise and challenges of extending this tool to other modalities.

</details>


### [168] [Adaptive Sampling for Automated Post-Disaster Rapid Damage Assessment via Level-Set Cost-Aware Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02868)
*Boyang Xu,Mostafa Reisi Gahrooei,Mohammad Ilbeigi,Hao Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A cost-aware Bayesian optimization framework with level-set estimation guides autonomous data collectors (e.g., UAVs) to efficiently map post-disaster damage by dynamically targeting the most informative regions, reducing uncertainty while minimizing operational costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional post-disaster damage assessment relies on static, labor-intensive, and expensive data collection that cannot adapt to dynamic conditions. There is a need for rapid, reliable, cost-effective methods that actively guide data collection toward regions of highest uncertainty.

Method: A cost-aware Bayesian optimization framework integrated with level-set estimation that continuously guides autonomous agents (e.g., UAVs) toward the most informative geographic zones. The method dynamically updates damage estimates, traces damage boundaries, and reduces predictive uncertainty while accounting for operational costs.

Result: The framework was validated on a synthetic toy study (demonstrating efficient boundary tracing, damage map recovery, and uncertainty reduction) and on high-fidelity disaster data from the R2D software, providing accurate and timely damage estimates.

Conclusion: The proposed approach delivers accurate, timely damage estimates that support informative and rapid emergency response, demonstrating its potential for real-world post-disaster assessment applications.

Abstract: Natural disasters frequently inflict severe damage to the built environment, which demands a rapid, reliable, and cost-effective damage assessment for emergency response. However, traditional methods for post-disaster damage assessment often rely on static, labor-intensive data collection strategies that can be prohibitively expensive and struggle to adapt to dynamic post-disaster conditions. In this study, we propose a cost-aware Bayesian optimization framework combined with level-set estimation that continuously guides autonomous data collectors, e.g., an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), toward the most informative regions. By dynamically updating damage estimates across different geographic zones, our approach systematically reduces uncertainty while minimizing operational costs. The proposed framework is first validated using a controlled synthetic toy study, demonstrating the agent's ability to efficiently trace damage boundaries, recover the underlying damage map, and rapidly reduce predictive uncertainty. Furthermore, the approach is evaluated using high-fidelity disaster data generated by the Regional Resilience Determination (R2D) software. The results of the algorithm provide accurate and timely damage estimates that support informative and fast emergency response.

</details>


### [169] [Contrast-invariant deep ptychography neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02869)
*Albert Vong,Steven Henke,Oliver Hoidn,Hanna Ruth,Junjing Deng,Apurva Mehta,David Shapiro,Alexander Hexemer,Nicholas Schwarz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper tackles ptychography neural networks' poor out-of-distribution generalization by introducing (1) a factorization strategy that decouples object texture from measurement scaling using real/imaginary representation instead of amplitude/phase, and (2) a synthetic object sampling strategy to reduce phase distribution mismatch. These yield up to 5× Fourier error reduction over PtychoPINN-torch across five experimental datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ptychography neural networks exhibit scaling inconsistencies when generalizing out of distribution, which severely limits their practical real-world deployment. The core issue is a mismatch between how the network learns object representations and how measurements scale under varying illumination conditions, preventing a single trained model from producing measurement-consistent reconstructions across diverse experimental settings.

Method: Two key innovations: (1) A factorization strategy that decouples learned object texture from measurement scaling by predicting the object in real and imaginary units rather than the conventional amplitude and phase representation. This allows a single trained network to maintain measurement consistency under varying illumination. (2) A synthetic object sampling strategy designed to minimize the phase distribution mismatch between synthetic training data and experimental targets, improving sim-to-real transfer.

Result: The proposed improvements achieve up to a 5× reduction in Fourier error compared to the previous PtychoPINN-torch baseline, validated across five experimental datasets spanning multiple beamlines and facilities.

Conclusion: Representing the object in real/imaginary units and aligning synthetic training distributions with experimental phase statistics are effective strategies for overcoming scaling inconsistencies in ptychography neural networks, enabling robust, measurement-consistent reconstructions across diverse real-world conditions from a single trained model.

Abstract: Ptychography neural networks suffer from scaling inconsistencies when generalizing out of distribution, limiting their real world viability. We address this scaling mismatch using a factorization strategy which decouples the learned object texture from measurement scaling, enabling a single trained network to produce measurement-consistent reconstructions across varying illumination conditions. This requires predicting the learned object in real and imaginary units instead of the canonical amplitude and phase representation. We additionally introduce a synthetic object sampling strategy that minimizes phase distribution mismatch between synthetic training data and experimental targets. These improvements yield up to a 5x reduction in Fourier error over the previous PtychoPINN-torch baseline across 5 experimental datasets spanning multiple beamlines and facilities.

</details>


### [170] [Maglev: Sliding Recurrent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02870)
*Bo Liu,Qiang Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a recurrent Transformer architecture with fixed-size memory that generalizes sliding-window attention. It uses two coupled models — a prefiller and a decoder — trained with a memory consistency loss, enabling efficient inference with the decoder alone while outperforming sliding-window and latent recurrent baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Transformers scale quadratically with sequence length, while sliding-window attention reduces this cost but loses access to long-range context. Latent recurrent models offer fixed-size memory but are typically harder to train. The authors aim to combine the efficiency of sliding-window attention with the expressive power of full-context models, while maintaining parallel trainability.

Method: The proposed architecture comprises a prefiller Q (using full or interleaved full/sliding-window attention) that produces memory targets m'_t, and a decoder P (using only sliding-window attention with recurrent K/V injection) that produces decoder memories m_t. A memory consistency loss aligns m_t with m'_t during training. At inference, only P is used, operating with fixed-size memory. Parameter sharing between P and Q is also explored.

Result: The architecture improves validation loss and downstream pretraining benchmarks over both sliding-window and latent recurrent Transformer baselines. Parameter sharing between P and Q reduces memory footprint while preserving most performance gains.

Conclusion: The proposed recurrent Transformer with memory consistency training successfully bridges the gap between efficient sliding-window attention and expressive full-context models, offering a practical architecture that is both parallel-trainable and memory-efficient at inference.

Abstract: We introduce \ours{}, a recurrent Transformer architecture with fixed-size memory that generalizes sliding-window attention while remaining parallelizable during training. \ours{} consists of two coupled models: a prefiller $Q$, which leverages full attention\footnote{In practice, we use interleaved full and sliding-window attention for $Q$, as this yields stronger performance. The essential requirement is that $Q$ be more expressive than $P$, with access to the full history.} to produce memory targets $m'_t$, and a decoder $P$, which uses only sliding-window attention and recurrent K/V injection to produce decoder memories $m_t$ for next-token prediction. We train \ours{} with a memory consistency loss that aligns $m_t$ with $m'_t$, allowing inference to use $P$ alone. Empirically, \ours{} improves validation loss and downstream pretraining benchmarks over sliding-window and latent recurrent transformer baselines. Moreover, sharing parameters between $P$ and $Q$ reduces parameter memory while preserving most of the gains.

</details>


### [171] [GoT-CD: Graph-of-Thoughts Causal Discovery and the Fragility of Post-hoc Path-Specific Fairness Audits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02877)
*Nitish Nagesh,Elahe Khatibi,Thomas Dean Hughes,Mahdi Bagheri,Pratik Gajane,Amir M. Rahmani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces GoT-CD, a Graph-of-Thoughts causal discovery method that generates DAGs via parallel candidate edge set reasoning with hard validity constraints. It demonstrates that structural metrics alone are insufficient for fairness audits — path-specific counterfactual fairness analyses can report null effects when discovery fails to recover the specific pathway of interest, even when aggregate structural scores are competitive.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing causal discovery evaluation relies on aggregate structural metrics that weight all edges equally, ignoring whether the specific pathway needed for a downstream fairness audit is recovered. When discovery misses an unfair pathway, path-specific counterfactual fairness audits can erroneously report null effects, undermining their reliability in clinical and high-stakes settings.

Method: GoT-CD treats the reasoning unit as a complete candidate edge set: multiple candidate graphs are generated in parallel, scored by a deterministic validity function, and merged under a hard union constraint that prohibits invented edges. Greedy projection enforces DAG structure before commitment. The method is compared against LLM-based baselines on five benchmarks (Asia, Alzheimer's, COVID-Respiratory, and others). A post-hoc path-specific fairness audit is conducted on an Alzheimer's benchmark with a known unfair pathway.

Result: GoT-CD returns a valid DAG on all five benchmarks and achieves the best DAG-valid F1 among LLM methods on Asia, Alzheimer's, and COVID-Respiratory datasets. However, on the Alzheimer's fairness benchmark, five of eight discovered graphs fail to recover a path from the sensitive attribute to the outcome, yielding a null overall effect while mediated effects persist — demonstrating that structural fidelity does not guarantee faithfulness of downstream fairness audits.

Conclusion: Structural fidelity alone does not guarantee fairness-faithful audits. Path-specific counterfactual fairness analysis must be performed alongside structural discovery, as missing pathways can produce misleading null results. GoT-CD provides a competitive DAG-discovery approach, but the broader implication is that evaluation protocols for causal discovery in fairness contexts must incorporate pathway-level auditing.

Abstract: Causal discovery recovers directed structure from observational data and is increasingly used in clinical settings to support mechanism reasoning and fairness audits of predictive models. Path-specific counterfactual fairness asks whether a protected attribute influences an outcome through illegitimate pathways, but these estimands are defined relative to a supplied causal graph and therefore inherit whatever errors the discovery step introduces. Discovery methods are routinely scored on aggregate structural metrics that weight all edges equally, and no established evaluation asks whether the specific pathway an audit depends on survives discovery---or what the audit reports when that pathway is missing. Here we show that full-graph Graph-of-Thoughts reasoning yields acyclic discovered graphs that are structurally competitive with large language model (LLM) baselines, yet that structural fidelity alone does not guarantee fairness-faithful audits. We introduce GoT-CD, in which the reasoning unit is a complete candidate edge set: multiple graphs are generated in parallel, scored by a deterministic validity function, and merged under a hard union constraint that forbids invented edges, with greedy projection enforcing a DAG before commitment. GoT-CD returns a valid DAG on all five reported benchmarks and achieves the best DAG-valid F1 score among LLM methods on Asia, Alzheimer's, and COVID-Respiratory datasets. On an Alzheimer's benchmark with known unfair path, a post-hoc path-specific audit shows that five of eight discovered graphs recover no path from the sensitive attribute to the outcome and therefore report a null overall effect while mediated effects persist, necessitating downstream path-specific fairness analysis along with structural discovery.

</details>


### [172] [Population-Robust Feature Selection via Generalized Welfare Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02887)
*Ruiqi Lyu,Alistair Turcan,Bryan Wilder*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PopFS is a feature selection method that learns one shared, deployable feature set robust to population heterogeneity. It uses a tunable welfare objective to balance overall predictive performance against protection for the worst-off populations, employing multitask sparse learning for candidate reduction followed by direct hard-feature-set search. Evaluated on six prediction tasks with eight population splits, it achieves strong average and worst-population performance and scales to thousands of features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feature collection is a deployment-level decision where a single limited set of features (e.g., questionnaire, sensors) must serve multiple heterogeneous populations. Standard feature selection optimizes for a single large population, while robust approaches learn one shared model per population. Neither paradigm addresses the practical need: one fixed feature set that permits population-specific models while ensuring equitable performance across groups, including protecting the worst-off populations.

Method: PopFS formulates a tunable welfare objective (balancing average vs. worst-population predictive benefit) for learning a single shared feature set. To scale to thousands of candidates, it employs a two-stage approach: (1) multitask sparse learning to reduce the candidate feature pool, then (2) direct combinatorial search over hard feature subsets by ranking promising feature additions and swaps, with full model refitting only on a shortlist of candidates.

Result: Across eight population splits from six prediction tasks on five tabular and public-health datasets, PopFS consistently achieves strong average and worst-population performance while scaling to thousands of features. A 43-state COVID-19 nowcasting study demonstrates that varying the welfare objective improves performance for the least-served states with minimal degradation in average performance, and yields interpretable changes in selected symptom signals.

Conclusion: PopFS provides a practical, scalable solution for deploying a single feature set across heterogeneous populations with tunable equity-efficiency trade-offs. The welfare objective offers practitioners meaningful control over how much to protect disadvantaged subgroups, and the two-stage search makes the approach viable for real-world, high-dimensional feature spaces.

Abstract: Choosing which features to collect is a deployment decision: the same limited questionnaire, test panel, or sensor set may need to serve several heterogeneous populations. Standard feature-selection methods typically optimize for one large population, while existing robust approaches tend to learn one shared model for every population. We introduce PopFS, a method for learning one shared, deployable feature set that is robust to population differences while letting each pop- ulation train its own model. PopFS uses a tunable welfare objective that lets practitioners balance overall predictive ben- efit against stronger protection of the populations that benefit least. To make this objective practical at scale, PopFS first uses multitask sparse learning to reduce the candidate pool, then searches directly over hard feature sets by ranking promising additions and swaps and fully refitting only a shortlist. Across eight population splits from six prediction tasks drawn from five tabular and public-health datasets, PopFS consistently achieves strong average and worst-population performance while scaling to thousands of candidate features. A 43-state COVID-19 nowcasting study further shows that changing the welfare objective can improve the least-served states with lit- tle change in average performance and yields an interpretable change in the selected symptom signals. Our code is available at https://github.com/Rachel-Lyu/PopFS.

</details>


### [173] [Robust Counterfactual Policy Optimisation via Nondeterministic Causal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02893)
*Jessica Lally,Milad Kazemi,Nicola Paoletti,David Watson,Sander Beckers*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper formalizes counterfactual policy optimization under probabilistic causal models that separate latent confounding from irreducible stochasticity, proposes a sensitivity analysis framework for identifying robust counterfactual policies, and validates the approach on a sepsis treatment simulator with hidden confounding (diabetes status).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing counterfactual inference methods for sequential decision-making assume deterministic causal models where all randomness comes from latent variables, but MDPs are inherently stochastic. This mismatch means current approaches cannot properly distinguish between randomness due to unobserved confounding and irreducible environmental stochasticity, limiting their practical applicability.

Method: The authors formalize counterfactual policy optimization under probabilistic nondeterministic causal models, which explicitly separate latent confounding from irreducible stochasticity. They then propose a practical optimization problem for identifying robust counterfactual policies within a sensitivity analysis framework that accounts for the strength of hidden confounding.

Result: The proposed approach is validated on a sepsis treatment simulator where diabetes status serves as a hidden global confounder. The sensitivity analysis framework successfully identifies policies that are robust to varying degrees of unobserved confounding.

Conclusion: Properly accounting for both latent confounding and irreducible stochasticity in causal models enables more robust counterfactual policy optimization in sequential decision-making settings, offering a practical pathway for applying counterfactual reasoning to inherently stochastic environments like healthcare.

Abstract: Counterfactual inference approaches for sequential decision-making typically assume deterministic causal models, where all randomness stems from latent variables. However, Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are inherently stochastic. We address this by formalising counterfactual policy optimisation under probabilistic nondeterministic causal models, which properly separates latent confounding from irreducible stochasticity, and here propose a first practical optimisation problem for identifying robust counterfactual policies under a sensitivity analysis framework. We validate our approach on a sepsis treatment simulator, where diabetes status acts as a hidden global confounder.

</details>


### [174] [AnchorKV: Anchor-Residual KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02901)
*Malik Khalaf,Yara Shamshoum,Nitzan Hodos,Yuval Sieradzki,Assaf Schuster*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AnchorKV achieves 20× KV cache compression without token eviction by using exact anchor tokens and similarity-based approximation, selectively refining critical tokens to maintain 99% of full-cache accuracy at 70B scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The KV cache is the primary memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference. Existing solutions trade off between two extremes: eviction methods permanently discard tokens (risking information loss when discarded tokens become essential), and quantization methods retain all tokens at low precision but achieve limited compression. A method is needed that achieves high compression without discarding information.

Method: AnchorKV compresses the KV cache by (1) storing a small set of "anchor" tokens at full precision, (2) approximating all remaining tokens by referencing their most similar anchor, and (3) identifying and refining only those approximated tokens whose reconstruction error most significantly impacts the model's output, thereby preserving critical information while maintaining high compression.

Result: AnchorKV achieves 20× cache compression, retains 99% of the full-cache performance score at the 70B model scale, and consistently preserves accuracy across multiple models and datasets.

Conclusion: AnchorKV offers a compelling middle ground between eviction and quantization, enabling high-compression KV cache reduction without discarding tokens, making long-context LLM inference significantly more memory-efficient while preserving accuracy.

Abstract: The key-value (KV) cache is the primary memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference. Existing approaches attack it from opposite ends: eviction methods permanently discard tokens, degrading performance whenever a discarded token later proves essential, while quantization methods retain all tokens at low precision but offer limited compression. We propose AnchorKV, a compression scheme that shrinks the cache by $20\times$ without discarding a single token. AnchorKV represents the cache using a small set of anchors stored exactly, expresses every other token through its most similar anchor, and refines only those whose approximation most affects the model's output. AnchorKV consistently preserves accuracy across models and datasets, retaining 99% of the full-cache score at the 70B scale, while keeping the entire context at a fraction of its cost.

</details>


### [175] [Bayesian Data Reweighting Improves Multimodal Retrieval for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02907)
*Jingchen Sun,Shaobo Han,Ruiyi Zhang,Naresh Kumar Devulapally,Ming Liu,Yitao Long,Vishnu Suresh Lokhande,Changyou Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Bayesian Data Reweighting, a probabilistic framework that adaptively reweights negative samples in contrastive learning for multimodal retrieval, mitigating the issue of false negatives and improving performance on knowledge-based VQA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard contrastive training for multimodal retrievers treats all unmatched query-document pairs as equally negative, ignoring that many unmatched documents are semantically relevant (false negatives), which harms retrieval quality.

Method: Bayesian Data Reweighting models query-document importance as latent variables with conjugate priors. Posterior weights are inferred via closed-form updates within a stochastic EM optimization framework, downweighting likely false negatives during training.

Result: The method consistently improves retrieval accuracy across three different retriever architectures and seven knowledge-based VQA benchmarks.

Conclusion: Adaptively reweighting negatives through Bayesian inference effectively addresses the false negative problem in contrastive learning, yielding robust improvements without requiring architectural modifications.

Abstract: Multimodal retrievers are essential for knowledge-based visual question answering, where they retrieve external evidence for image-question pairs. However, existing contrastive training methods typically treat all unmatched query-document pairs as equally informative negatives, which is problematic because many unmatched documents may still be semantically relevant or partially useful. We propose Bayesian Data Reweighting, a probabilistic framework that models query-document importance as latent variables and adaptively infers posterior weights to downweight likely false negatives. With closed-form posterior updates under conjugate priors and stochastic EM optimization, our method consistently improves retrieval accuracy across three retrievers and seven knowledge-based VQA benchmarks.

</details>


### [176] [Forecasting Revenue with its Customer-Base Drivers: When and Why Coordination Helps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02911)
*Kyeongbin Kim,Daniel McCarthy,Dokyun Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces CBMT, a multi-task Transformer that jointly forecasts customer-base primitives (acquisition, repeat purchasing, spending per order) and aligns them with aggregate revenue. CBMT achieves 30% lower total-sales error than established benchmarks, outperforms separately estimated single-task models for 74.3% of firms, but its advantage over a direct-sales Transformer is not statistically significant. Gains are larger when primitives co-move strongly; accuracy degrades under high volatility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aggregate revenue forecasts fail to decompose whether change stems from acquisition, repeat purchasing, or spending per order. Managers need primitive-level forecasts for acquisition budgeting, demand planning, and customer-based valuations, but existing approaches either forecast revenue directly or estimate primitives separately, missing shared structure and co-movement among primitives.

Method: The authors develop the Customer-Based Multi-task Transformer (CBMT) using weekly transaction panels for 966 companies across 25 industries. CBMT learns shared structure across primitives, retains separate primitive forecasts, and aligns their combination with downstream revenue. It is benchmarked against established customer-base models, a direct-sales Transformer, and separately estimated single-task forecasts. Source-level MAE is compared across 24 benchmark-by-outcome comparisons, and the role of primitive co-movement, volatility, and calibration-period routing rules is examined.

Result: CBMT's mean total-sales error is 30% below the strongest established benchmark. It beats a direct-sales Transformer by 2.65% (not statistically significant, p=.222). It outperforms separately estimated single-task forecasts for 74.3% of firms. Source MAE is lower in 23 of 24 benchmark-by-outcome comparisons. Firms with stronger primitive co-movement benefit more. Accuracy deteriorates under high volatility, narrowing CBMT's advantage. Calibration-period routing rules do not improve average accuracy over always using CBMT.

Conclusion: Coordinated customer-base forecasts via CBMT support revenue planning by decomposing aggregate trends into actionable primitives. The approach is most beneficial when primitives co-move and volatility is moderate. Simple always-deploy-CBMT routing suffices over more complex calibration-based selection rules.

Abstract: Revenue forecasts guide acquisition budgets, demand planning, and customer-based valuations, yet an aggregate forecast does not show whether change reflects acquisition, repeat purchasing, spending per order, or offsetting movements. Using weekly transaction panels for 966 companies in 25 industries, the authors develop the Customer-Based Multi-task Transformer (CBMT), which learns shared structure, retains separate primitive forecasts, and aligns their combination with downstream revenue. CBMT's mean total-sales error is 30% below the strongest representative established customer-base benchmark. It is also 2.65% below a Transformer that forecasts total sales directly, although the paired difference is not statistically significant (p=.222), and it beats separately estimated single-task forecasts for 74.3% of firms. CBMT's source MAE is lower in 23 of 24 benchmark-by-outcome comparisons, with the remaining difference not statistically distinguishable from zero. Firms whose primitives co-move more strongly are more likely to benefit from joint forecasting; selected-family scenario-3 comparisons are consistent with gains from shared representation and revenue alignment but remain diagnostic rather than causal. Accuracy deteriorates for all models when customer-base dynamics are highly volatile, and CBMT's advantage narrows there. Calibration-period routing rules do not improve average accuracy over always deploying CBMT. The results show how coordinated customer-base forecasts support revenue planning and when they warrant greater caution.

</details>


### [177] [When Should Graph Attention Be Sparse? Learning a Per-Edge Tsallis Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02938)
*Kleyton da Costa,Bernardo Modenesi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LTGA proposes a graph attention layer where the Tsallis entropic index q is learned jointly with network weights, allowing continuous interpolation between heavy-tailed, softmax, and compact-support attention. While it doesn't significantly outperform tuned baselines, the learned q provides interpretability by selectively pruning ~42% of wrong edges to exactly zero attention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard graph attention (GAT) uses softmax normalization, which is optimal under Shannon entropy (q=1). However, homophilic and heterophilic graphs benefit from different attention distributions — broader (heavy-tailed) or narrower (compact-support) attention respectively. A single fixed normalization cannot accommodate both types, motivating a learnable, flexible attention mechanism.

Method: LTGA replaces softmax with Tsallis entropy-based normalization, parameterized by the entropic index q. The q parameter is learned jointly with attention weights under a bounded reparameterization (initialized to q=1, i.e., GAT baseline). Four granularities are explored: global scalar, per-layer, per-head, and per-edge. The formulation interpolates between heavy-tailed (q<1), softmax (q=1), and compact-support (q>1) regimes, with q>1 naturally producing sparse attention via exact zeros.

Result: Across 8 benchmarks and 10 seeds, LTGA-Edge achieves the best average rank (2.75), but an omnibus test does not reject the null (p=0.199). Learning q does not outperform grid search: frozen tuned q-grid (61.4%), tuned α-entmax (62.2%), and q≡1 control (62.0%) vs. LTGA-Edge (61.7%). However, where q deviates from 1, ~42% of attention coefficients are pruned to exact zero — and these are selectively the wrong edges. Restoring them costs 7.1 accuracy points, while random pruning at the same rate costs 13.0 points.

Conclusion: Learning the Tsallis index q offers practical convenience (one run vs. grid search) and interpretability rather than a statistically significant accuracy gain. The mechanism's ability to selectively prune incorrect edges to exactly zero is its key contribution, demonstrating that the learned q captures meaningful graph structure.

Abstract: Graph attention normalizes neighborhood scores with softmax, the maximum-entropy choice under Shannon statistics. But homophilic and heterophilic graphs want different attention shapes, and one fixed normalization cannot serve both. We propose \textbf{LTGA} (\textbf{L}earnable \textbf{T}sallis \textbf{G}raph \textbf{A}ttention), a graph attention layer whose Tsallis entropic index $q$ is learned jointly with the weights, interpolating continuously between heavy-tailed ($q\!<\!1$), softmax ($q\!=\!1$) and compact-support ($q\!>\!1$) attention at four granularities from a global scalar to a per-edge index, under a bounded reparameterization that starts every model at the GAT baseline. Across eight benchmarks at ten seeds, LTGA-Edge takes the best average rank ($2.75$), but the omnibus test does not reject ($p\!=\!0.199$) and learning $q$ does not beat searching it: a validation-tuned frozen grid reaches $61.4\%$, tuned $α$-entmax $62.2\%$ and a capacity-matched $q\!\equiv\!1$ control $62.0\%$, against $61.7\%$ for LTGA-Edge. What the learned index buys is one run instead of a grid, and an interpretable mechanism: where $q$ leaves $1$, it prunes $42\%$ of attention coefficients to exactly zero, and those edges are selectively the wrong ones, restoring them costs $7.1$ points, while random pruning at the same rate costs $13.0$ more. Project page: https://kleyt0n.github.io/ltga

</details>


### [178] [Federated generative event models for tokenized electronic health records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02939)
*Michael C. Burkhart,Luke Solo,Inhyeok Lee,S'Khaja Charles,Zewei "Whiskey" Liao,Kaveri Chhikara,Dema Therese,Wan-Ting Liao,Catherine A. Gao,William F. Parker,Brett K. Beaulieu-Jones*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Federated training of generative event models across three health systems nearly matched centralized performance within 5-10 communication rounds, but multi-site data provided only modest gains over local training, with the primary remaining challenge being learning transportable representations from heterogeneous data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EHR foundation models suffer from institutionally siloed data and significant performance degradation when transferred across sites. The authors sought to determine whether federated learning could overcome these barriers while preserving model performance.

Method: Tokenized generative event models (GEMs) were trained on 122,251 ICU hospitalizations from three independent health systems, all harmonized to the Common Longitudinal ICU Data Format. Models were evaluated on 12 clinical prediction tasks at the 24-hour mark, comparing within-site, cross-site, centralized, and federated (FedAvg, FedAvgM) training strategies.

Result: GEMs achieved the highest mean within-site and cross-site ROC-AUC. Their cross-site transportability penalty was substantially lower (0.025 ROC-AUC, 0.027 PR-AUC) than LightGBM (0.079, 0.089). Federated learning approached centralized performance within 5-10 rounds. However, centralized multi-site training offered only modest improvement over local training, with benefits most pronounced when local data were limited.

Conclusion: Federated GEM training is technically feasible and preserves most centralized performance. The key open challenge is not the federation mechanism itself, but learning truly transportable representations that can translate larger, heterogeneous multi-site data into reliable target-site benefits.

Abstract: Electronic health record foundation models are limited by institutionally siloed data and substantial performance degradation under cross-site transfer. We evaluated federated training of tokenized generative event models (GEMs) across 122,251 intensive care hospitalizations from three independent health systems harmonized to the Common Longitudinal ICU Data Format. Models were assessed on 12 post-24-hour clinical prediction tasks using within-site, cross-site, centralized, and federated training configurations. GEMs achieved the highest mean within-site and cross-site ROC-AUC and were substantially more transportable than conventional supervised models: their average cross-site penalties were 0.025 ROC-AUC and 0.027 PR-AUC, compared with 0.079 and 0.089 for LightGBM. Federated Learning (FedAvg and FedAvgM) approached the performance of centralized GEM training, with most gains obtained within 5-10 communication rounds. However, centralized multi-site training provided only modest improvements over complete local training. Multi-site models were most useful when local training data were limited, with their advantage narrowing as institutional data accumulated. These findings show that federated GEM training is technically feasible and preserves most centralized performance, but that the main open challenge is learning transportable representations to translate larger, but heterogeneous data from multiple health systems into a reliable target-site benefit.

</details>


### [179] [Sedentary Behavior Classification for Wearable Sensors with a CNN-BiLSTM Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02946)
*Yuliang Chen,Weiwei Shi,Jingjing Zou,Rong Zablocki,Animesh Kumar,Jordan A. Carlson,Sheri J. Hartman,Mikael Anne Greenwood-Hickman,Paul R. Hibbing,Marta Jankowska,Jay Yang,Arun Kumar,Loki Natarajan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hip-trained CNN-BiLSTM model (CHAP) for sitting classification shows performance degradation when transferred zero-shot to wrist-worn accelerometers, but finetuning with limited wrist data outperforms transformers trained from scratch, supporting hip-based pretraining as a viable starting point for wrist deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sedentary behavior detection is critical for health risk assessment, yet posture-based classification from wearable sensors—particularly wrist-worn accelerometers—remains challenging due to higher signal variability compared to hip-worn sensors. The study explores whether a model pretrained on hip data can effectively transfer to wrist data.

Method: The authors use CHAP, a CNN-BiLSTM architecture originally designed for hip accelerometers, and evaluate it under two transfer paradigms: (1) zero-shot inference on wrist data without any retraining, and (2) finetuning with varying amounts of labeled wrist data. Performance is compared against transformer models trained from scratch. Ground-truth posture labels come from the iWatch dataset using wearable cameras.

Result: The hip-trained model maintains strong accuracy on hip data without retraining but suffers a significant accuracy drop on wrist data in zero-shot conditions due to sensor placement shift. Finetuning CHAP with wrist data consistently outperforms transformer baselines trained from scratch, demonstrating the value of hip-based pretraining.

Conclusion: Hip-based pretraining provides an effective initialization for wrist-worn posture classification, but wrist-specific finetuning is necessary to address the increased signal variability and placement shift. The findings advocate for transfer learning as a practical strategy for adapting activity recognition models across sensor positions.

Abstract: Accurate detection of sedentary behavior is important for studying health risks related to prolonged sitting, but posture-based classification remains challenging with wearable sensors, especially at the wrist. We study whether a deep learning model trained on hip-worn accelerometer data can transfer to wrist-worn accelerometer data for sitting versus non-sitting classification. We use CHAP, a CNN-BiLSTM model originally developed for hip accelerometers, and evaluate its zero-shot performance on wrist data as well as its adaptation through finetuning with varying amounts of labeled wrist data. Experiments are conducted on the iWatch dataset with ground-truth posture labels derived from wearable cameras. The hip-trained model performs strongly on hip data without retraining, but accuracy drops on wrist data due to sensor placement shift. Finetuning CHAP provides consistent advantages over transformer models trained from scratch. These findings suggest that hip-based pretraining provides a useful starting point for wrist deployment, while highlighting the need for wrist-specific adaptation to handle higher signal variability.

</details>


### [180] [ATFlash: Per-RoPE-Wavelength Attention Windows for Compute/Memory-Efficient LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02947)
*Shun-ichiro Hayashi,Daichi Mukunoki,Tetsuya Hoshino,Takahiro Katagiri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a per-RoPE-wavelength distance window that deterministically prunes query-key inner-product terms in attention based on each 2D-rotation frequency pair's wavelength, achieving 37–48% term reduction with minimal quality loss (96–98% top-1 match rate) and up to 1.31× speedup at 1M-token contexts, with simple integration into FlashAttention and FlashInfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) decompose attention scores as a sum over frequency pairs, where each pair's wavelength limits its positional discrimination range. High-frequency pairs can only discriminate nearby tokens, making their contributions to distant token interactions redundant. This structural insight motivates pruning those terms, but existing sparse attention methods rely on dynamic, input-dependent token selection — the authors instead exploit the frequency-level structure for deterministic, input-independent pruning that is orthogonal and complementary to token-level sparsity.

Method: The method defines a distance window per RoPE frequency pair: for each 2D-rotation frequency, query-key inner-product terms are pruned when the positional distance exceeds a threshold proportional to that frequency's wavelength. Unlike a sliding window, low-frequency pairs retain global reach. The pruning is input-independent with a closed-form logarithmic reduction rate in sequence length N. Implementation is a simple slice on the query-key contraction axis, preserving online-softmax recurrences, and is ported into FlashAttention-4 (prefill) and FlashInfer (decode) with minimal code diffs.

Result: On Qwen2.5-0.5B and Llama-3.2-3B, 37–48% of inner-product terms are pruned within native context length. Top-1 match rate vs. full attention is 96–98%, with mean output-distribution KL divergence at ~10⁻³ nats on LongBench-v2. Long-context benchmarks (RULER, OpenAI-MRCR, LongCodeQA, ∞Bench) show broadly preserved scores. On RTX PRO 6000 with Llama, FlashAttention-4 prefill and FlashInfer decode ports outperform stock, with gains growing with context length (up to 1.29× at 128K). End-to-end on Qwen2.5-7B-1M with 57% terms pruned, speedup reaches 1.31× at 1M-token context.

Conclusion: The per-RoPE-wavelength distance window is a lightweight, principled pruning method that exploits the frequency structure of RoPE to reduce attention computation deterministically. It preserves model quality, integrates easily into existing optimized attention kernels, and delivers meaningful speedups that scale with context length, making it a practical acceleration technique for long-context Transformers.
