Abstract: The attention score with rotary position embeddings (RoPE) decomposes exactly into a sum over its 2D-rotation frequency pairs, and each pair's wavelength limits how far it can discriminate position. Aligned with this structure, we propose the per-RoPE-wavelength distance window: it prunes the query--key inner-product terms beyond a wavelength-proportional distance. Unlike a sliding window, every key remains reachable, at least through the low-frequency pairs. The reduction rate is input-independent, with a closed form logarithmic in the sequence length $N$, in contrast to dynamic-sparse methods like MInference. Such token-level selection is orthogonal to our frequency-level pruning. The window can therefore be applied on top of those methods. On Qwen2.5-0.5B and Llama-3.2-3B, the window prunes 37--48\% of the query--key inner-product terms within each model's native context length. Relative to full attention, the top-1 match rate stays at 96--98\% and the mean output-distribution KL at the $10^{-3}$-nat level on LongBench-v2 contexts. We examine absolute scores on long-context benchmarks such as RULER, OpenAI-MRCR, LongCodeQA, and $\infty$Bench: they are broadly preserved. We implement the window as a slice of the query--key contraction axis, leaving the online-softmax recurrences untouched, and port it with minimal diffs into the released FlashAttention-4 prefill and FlashInfer decode. On RTX PRO 6000 with Llama, both ports outpace stock with gains growing with context length, up to $1.29\times$ at 128K. End to end on Qwen2.5-7B-1M, with 57\% of the inner-product terms pruned, the speedup reaches $1.31\times$ at a 1M-token context.

</details>


### [181] [Rubrics as Privileged Information for Open-Ended Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02948)
*Deepika Bablani,Ajay Gupta,Wanming Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper extends on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) from math domains to open-ended generation by using soft privileged information in the form of rubrics instead of hard ground-truth answers. Rubrics provide dense token-level supervision that outperforms both reference-completion distillation and rubric-as-reward RL across multiple model families and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPSD has succeeded in verifiable domains (e.g., math) where ground-truth answers provide hard privileged information (PI) that structurally constrains valid outputs. However, open-ended generation lacks such hard PI — many valid responses exist. The authors investigate whether soft PI (rubrics specifying preference structures) can serve as effective PI for distillation, hypothesizing that rubrics provide richer signal than either scalar RL rewards or single reference completions.

Method: The authors propose using rubrics as privileged information (RuPI) for on-policy self-distillation in open-ended generation. A single model acts as both student and teacher: the student generates roll-outs, and the teacher (same model conditioned on rubric PI) provides dense token-level supervision by specifying the preference structure shared across valid responses. This is contrasted with (1) reference-PI distillation (distilling toward a single reference completion) and (2) rubric-as-reward (RaR) RL, where rubrics provide only scalar rewards. Experiments use Qwen and Llama model families, evaluated on HealthBench (physician-created rubrics for health responses) and ResearchQA (science domain), with matched training recipes and KL constraints.

Result: On HealthBench, RuPI beats RaR RL by up to +0.10 absolute score and reference-PI distillation by +0.034 to +0.079 across three models under matched conditions. On the science domain (RubricHub Science → ResearchQA), RuPI achieves 66.6% vs. 64.2% for reference-PI distillation and 57.6% for RaR RL.

Conclusion: Soft rubric PI provides substantially richer and more effective training signal than hard reference completions or scalar rubric rewards for open-ended generation. Distilling toward a single reference over-constrains the student, whereas rubrics capture the preference structure across the set of valid responses. The findings generalize across model families and domains, establishing rubric-based self-distillation as a superior approach for open-ended tasks.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD), where a single model acts as both student and teacher with different contexts, has shown promise in verifiable domains like math, where hard privileged information (PI) in the form of ground-truth answers structurally constrains valid continuations. We extend OPSD to open-ended generation using soft PI in the form of rubrics that guide preferences but admit many valid responses. Rubrics have served as scalar rewards for reinforcement learning (RL); we show that they provide substantially richer signal as dense PI for distillation, and contrary to intuition, soft rubric PI provides a larger and more effective training signal on student roll-outs than hard reference completion PI in this regime. A reference completion is one point in a set of valid responses, so distilling towards it over-constrains the student, while rubrics specify the preference structure shared across the set of valid responses. We show the effectiveness of using rubrics as PI for open-ended generation across Qwen and Llama model families and show that it outperforms rubric-as-reward (RaR) RL using HealthBench, a benchmark that grades open-ended health responses against physician-created rubrics, providing dense token-level supervision for open-ended tasks; RuPI beats RaR RL by up to +0.10 absolute score and, under matched recipe and KL direction, beats reference-PI by +0.034 to +0.079 absolute score across three models. We further show that these findings generalize to training on the RubricHub Science corpus and evaluating on ResearchQA: soft rubric PI outperforms both reference-PI distillation and RaR RL (66.6% vs. 64.2% and 57.6%).

</details>


### [182] [Schedule-Informed Temporal Fusion Forecasting of Hourly Airport Security-Checkpoint Throughput](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02950)
*Yinxiao Zhang,Sen Wang,Yi Gao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Converts flight departure schedules into passenger arrival signals using truncated Poisson kernels, then feeds these into a Temporal Fusion Transformer to forecast hourly airport security checkpoint throughput, achieving a 9.33% WMAPE (vs. 11.37–12.16% for LSTM/RNN baselines).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Airport checkpoint staffing requires accurate forecasts of when passengers arrive at security, but flight schedules only record departure times — not arrival times. There is no direct passenger-to-flight matching available, creating a gap between schedulable information and operational demand signals needed for staffing, lane-opening, and multiday planning.

Method: Domestic and international seat capacity from Cirium Diio schedules (Atlanta/ATL, 2023–2024) is distributed across pre-departure hours using truncated Poisson kernels to generate arrival-intensity signals. These derived signals are combined with historical TSA throughput, scheduled activity, and temporal variables as inputs to a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT). Models are trained chronologically, tested on July–December 2024, and benchmarked against RNN and LSTM models across five random seeds. Both direct six-hour forecasts and recursively updated 24–96 hour horizons are evaluated.

Result: The TFT model achieved a WMAPE of 9.33% for direct six-hour forecasts, outperforming RNN (12.16%) and LSTM (11.37%), with lowest errors during peak periods. For recursive multi-horizon forecasts, errors remained between 10.60% and 11.04% across 24–96 hour horizons, though longer horizons had fewer valid forecast origins.

Conclusion: Transforming scheduled departures into pre-departure screening-load signals — without requiring passenger-flight matching — provides an interpretable and effective input for TFT-based checkpoint throughput forecasting. This supports advance staffing and capacity planning. However, because observed throughput reflects realized processing rather than unconstrained demand, forecasts should be interpreted alongside local staffing, capacity, queue, and wait-time data.

Abstract: Checkpoint staffing requires accurate forecasts of when screening demand will occur, yet flight schedules record departure times rather than passenger arrival times at security checkpoints. This study develops a framework that converts known flight schedules into temporally aligned signals for forecasting hourly checkpoint throughput. Using 2023-2024 Transportation Security Administration throughput data and Cirium Diio flight schedules for Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, domestic and international seat capacity was distributed across pre-departure hours using truncated Poisson kernels. A Temporal Fusion Transformer then combined these schedule-derived arrival-intensity signals with historical throughput, scheduled activity, and temporal variables. Models were trained chronologically, with July-December 2024 reserved for testing, and evaluated against recurrent neural network and long short-term memory models across five random seeds. For direct six-hour forecasts, the proposed model achieved a weighted mean absolute percentage error of 9.33%, compared with 12.16% for the recurrent neural network and 11.37% for long short-term memory, while also producing the lowest errors during peak periods. With six-hour recursive updates, errors remained between 10.60% and 11.04% across 24-96 hour horizons, although longer horizons contained fewer valid forecast origins. By transforming scheduled departures into interpretable pre-departure screening-load signals without requiring passenger-flight matching, the framework supports advance staffing, lane-opening, and multiday checkpoint planning. Because observed throughput reflects realized processing rather than unconstrained arrivals, the forecasts should be interpreted together with local staffing, capacity, queue, and wait-time information.

</details>


### [183] [SP3O: Reinforcement Learning from Segment Preferences without Reward Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02951)
*Evan Assmus,Qining Zhang,Lei Ying*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SP3O introduces a novel reward-model-free, critic-free, gradient-based PbRL algorithm that uses segment-level (rather than trajectory-level) preference feedback. It constructs a policy value difference estimator via off-policy importance sampling and optimizes using a PPO-type loss, offering theoretical guarantees and improved performance on long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reward-model-free PbRL methods are limited to bandits/deterministic MDPs or use slower zeroth-order optimization. Additionally, most methods rely on trajectory-level feedback, which is burdensome for human evaluators on long trajectories. Segment-level feedback is easier to provide but lacks compatible gradient-based, reward-model-free algorithms.

Method: SP3O uses segment-level pairwise preferences to build a policy value difference estimator via off-policy importance sampling. This estimator feeds into a PPO-type surrogate loss to compute policy gradients. The algorithm is both reward-model-free and critic-free, relying purely on segment preference data and importance weighting.

Result: SP3O demonstrates improved performance over existing PbRL/RLHF algorithms in both robotic control and LLM finetuning experiments, particularly excelling in long-horizon tasks where trajectory-level feedback becomes impractical.

Conclusion: Segment-level preference feedback combined with gradient-based, reward-model-free optimization (SP3O) offers a practical and theoretically grounded approach to PbRL, especially for long-horizon problems where trajectory-level evaluation is costly.

Abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) for general stochastic MDPs often requires training a reward model. Existing reward-model-free methods are either restricted to bandits or deterministic MDPs, such as DPO or P3O, or use zeroth-order, gradient-free optimization, which in general exhibits a slower convergence rate than gradient-based algorithms. Furthermore, existing reward-model-free preference-based RL algorithms almost exclusively use trajectory-level feedback, which can require significant effort from a human evaluator when trajectories are long. On the other hand, segments are much shorter, so they are easier to compare and evaluate. In this paper, we introduce a novel reward-model-free, critic-free, and gradient-based PbRL algorithm compatible with segment preferences named Segment Pairwise Proximal Policy Optimization (SP3O). SP3O utilizes segment-level preference feedback to construct an accurate policy value difference estimator via off-policy importance sampling, and then uses the estimator to compute the policy gradient via a PPO-type loss function. We provide a theoretical basis for the algorithm and analyze the tradeoff in choosing the segment length. We also evaluate it experimentally against other PbRL/RLHF algorithms in robotic control and LLM finetuning settings to show its improved performance, especially in long-horizon tasks.

</details>


### [184] [Inverted Detection and Control in Steering Vectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02957)
*Max Torop,Aria Masoomi,Jennifer Dy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Some steering vectors that are highly discriminative (well-aligned with positive concept representations) paradoxically promote the opposite behavior. The authors call these "inverted-steering vectors" (ISVs), provide a geometric explanation, and propose a method to detect and correct them without generation, improving ITI-based steering by up to +138% across 27/30 experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core assumption behind steering vectors is linear discriminability: vectors aligned with concept-positive representations should promote that concept when steered toward. The authors challenge this by revealing that some highly discriminative SVs consistently produce inverted (opposite) effects, undermining the reliability of detection-based steering pipelines.

Method: The authors (1) empirically identify ISVs by measuring the discrepancy between discriminability and actual steering effect, (2) provide a geometric characterization showing ISVs push representations in downstream attention heads toward "concept-absent" states even before decoding, and (3) propose a generation-free method to distinguish ISVs from normal SVs using only internal representations, enabling targeted sign flips. This is integrated into the Inference Time Intervention (ITI) pipeline.

Result: The proposed approach improves steering performance in 27 out of 30 experiments across Gemma 3 12B, Qwen 2.5 14B, and Olmo 3 7B on 5 concepts, with gains ranging from +0.9% to +138%.

Conclusion: Highly discriminative steering vectors can be deceptively inverted in their actual effects. The inverted-steering phenomenon is geometrically predictable and can be detected without generation, enabling simple sign-flip corrections that substantially improve detection-based steering methods like ITI.

Abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are widely used to influence the expression of concepts (e.g., truthfulness) in large language model outputs. A key assumption underpinning SVs is that they are linearly discriminative with respect to the concept: representations of texts that exhibit the concept are more aligned with the SV than those that do not, motivating shifts along the positive or negative SV direction to respectively promote or suppress the concept. In this work, we identify an inverted detection-control phenomenon in which some highly discriminative SVs that are aligned with positive representations can consistently promote the opposite behavior. We refer to such vectors as inverted-steering vectors (ISVs). We provide a geometric characterization of ISVs' effects, finding that steering along these directions systematically pushes representations in discriminative downstream heads as if the concept were absent, even prior to decoding. Motivated by this analysis, we propose an approach for distinguishing ISVs without requiring generation or associated response scoring. This enables targeted sign flips, which we use to improve a foundational detection-based steering pipeline via Inference Time Intervention (ITI). Our approach improves results in 27/30 experiments, ranging from +0.9% to +138%. We evaluate our findings on Gemma 3 12B, Qwen 2.5 14B, and Olmo 3 7B across 5 concepts.

</details>


### [185] [Scaling an Autoregressive Transformer for Single-Cell Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02961)
*Aleksandr Sharipov,Yusif Mukhtarov,Igor Molybog*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A self-supervised generative model for single-cell gene expression is proposed, using a causal transformer with a quantized VAE tokenizer. The study evaluates biological fidelity of generated vectors and discovers a two-exponent scaling law and compute-optimal frontier for single-cell foundation models, with potential finetuning for perturbation response prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a generative model capable of producing biologically faithful gene expression vectors for a given cell type, and to systematically characterize the scaling behavior of pretraining loss in single-cell foundation models.

Method: A causal transformer paired with a learned quantized VAE tokenizer, trained via cross-entropy loss on single-cell gene expression vectors. Evaluation is performed by conditioning on held-out vectors of a cell type, generating new vectors, and comparing the generated distribution against the ground truth distribution. Scaling properties are assessed by varying parameter count and training data volume.

Result: The model generates biologically faithful gene expression vectors matching the ground truth distribution of the target cell type. The authors report the first jointly-fit two-exponent scaling law and compute-optimal frontier for a single-cell foundation model.

Conclusion: The proposed architecture effectively models single-cell gene expression distributions with well-characterized scaling behavior, and holds promise for downstream tasks such as perturbation response prediction via finetuning.

Abstract: We study a self-supervised generation task for single-cell gene expression vectors: given a set of vectors from a cell type, we aim to generate additional gene expression vectors of that cell type. For this task we characterize both the biological fidelity of the generated gene expression vectors and the scaling behavior of the pretraining loss. The model is a causal transformer paired with a learned quantized VAE tokenizer, trained with a cross-entropy loss. To evaluate the model, we condition it on held-out gene expression vectors of a cell type and generate vectors of gene expression, comparing the resulting distribution over gene expression vectors to the ground truth distribution of that cell type. We study the scaling properties of the proposed architecture by varying the number of trained parameters and the amount of training data. To our knowledge, we find the first jointly-fit two-exponent scaling law and compute-optimal frontier for a single-cell foundation model. Finally, we discuss how this pretrained model could be finetuned for perturbation response prediction.

</details>


### [186] [A Physics-Informed Hybrid Neural Operator for Transient Magnetization Prediction in Power Magnetics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02965)
*Yachao Zhu,Qiujie Huang,Sinan Li,Yang Li,Gang Lei,Jianguo Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PI-HNO is a compact neural operator that predicts transient B-H magnetization trajectories in ferrite cores under non-sinusoidal excitation, achieving ~2% mean energy consistency error with only ~4,800 parameters through a dual-branch architecture combining local recurrence and Preisach-inspired global hysteresis context, regularized by physics-informed energy constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-frequency power converters expose magnetic cores to complex flux-density waveforms (fast transitions, minor loops, DC bias, temperature swings). Existing steady-state core-loss formulas and single-valued material curves cannot capture the transient B-H magnetization dynamics under these conditions, creating a need for accurate, compact, material-specific transient models.

Method: PI-HNO employs a dual-branch architecture: (1) a local recurrent branch that learns boundary-state representations and rate-dependent response evolution from recent B(t)-H(t) history, and (2) a Preisach-inspired global branch that extracts waveform-level hysteresis context. The model takes measured B(t)-H(t) history, future B(t) sequence, and operating-condition metadata as inputs, and predicts the H(t) series and reconstructed B-H loop trajectory. A physics-informed energy-consistency regularization enforces thermodynamic admissibility of the predicted hysteresis. Evaluation uses material-specific models on the MagNetX transient database across 14 ferrite materials.

Result: PI-HNO achieves a mean B-H energy consistency error of 1.92% and a 95th-percentile error of 7.60% with only 4,777 trainable parameters per material-specific model. Ablation studies confirm that the local branch, global branch, and energy-aware regularization each contribute distinctly to transient magnetization prediction accuracy.

Conclusion: PI-HNO provides a highly compact yet accurate solution for transient magnetization modeling in ferrite cores under realistic converter operating conditions. The dual-branch design with physics-informed regularization effectively balances sequence prediction accuracy and thermodynamic energy consistency, making it suitable for integration into high-frequency power converter design workflows.

Abstract: Magnetic components in high-frequency, high-power-density converters are increasingly driven by non-sinusoidal flux-density waveforms with fast transitions, minor-loop operation, dc bias, and temperature variation. Under these conditions, steady-state core-loss formulas and single-valued material curves cannot fully capture transient magnetization responses. This work proposes the Physics-Informed Hybrid Neural Operator (PI-HNO), a compact material-specific neural model with B-H energy-consistency regularization for core-loss-oriented transient magnetization prediction. Given the measured B(t)-H(t) history, the input B(t) series over the prediction interval and operating-condition information, PI-HNO predicts the H(t) series and the corresponding reconstructed B-H trajectory. The model integrates a local recurrent branch for boundary-state representation and rate-dependent response evolution with a Preisach-inspired global branch that extracts waveform-level hysteresis context. Evaluation on the MagNetX transient database using material-specific models for 14 ferrite materials demonstrates that PI-HNO achieves a compact trade-off between sequence accuracy and B(t)-H(t) energy consistency, with the mean and 95th percentile B(t)-H(t) energy consistency errors of 1.92% and 7.60%, respectively, using only 4777 trainable parameters per model. Ablation studies further demonstrate that the local, global, and energy-aware regularized components provide distinct contributions to transient magnetization prediction.

</details>


### [187] [Temporal Leakage in LLM Backtesting: Measurement, Validation, and Adjusted Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02985)
*Zeyu Zhang,Bradly C. Stadie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Standard temporal cutoff checks for LLM contamination are structurally uninformative because recency bias mimics leakage. The authors propose two estimators—a boundary discontinuity test and a matched clean control—to separate genuine knowledge from contamination, validated via planted leakage experiments on twin models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current backtests for detecting training data contamination in LLMs rely on comparing performance before vs. after a training cutoff date. The authors demonstrate this approach is fundamentally flawed: models naturally perform better on questions closer to their cutoff (recency bias), making it impossible to distinguish contamination from legitimate temporal knowledge using passive backtests alone.

Method: The authors develop two estimation approaches that require external information beyond the backtest: (1) a known cutoff date detects leakage as a discontinuity at the boundary between train and test periods; (2) a matched clean control set identifies leakage globally and yields a leakage-adjusted performance score. They also characterize where leakage concentrates—on surprising outcomes with heavy training coverage—and show that partial memorization is disproportionately rewarded. Validation uses twin models with deliberately injected contamination to confirm the estimators recover the true leakage dose and return null results on clean data.

Result: Four flagship models fail the standard backtest on questions resolved entirely after their cutoffs, which they cannot have memorized, proving the standard check is uninformative. The proposed estimators successfully recover injected contamination doses in validation experiments. When deployed on frontier models, one cutoff-localized leakage signature is detected; at the audit's power floor, five models whose apparent advantages were driven solely by recency are cleared of contamination.

Conclusion: Backtests remain useful but require at least one defensible external reference—either a known cutoff for boundary detection or a matched clean control for global estimation—to meaningfully separate contamination from genuine model knowledge. The standard before/after cutoff comparison alone is insufficient.

Abstract: The standard check for contamination in LLM backtests is simple: compare scores before and after the training cutoff. We show this check is uninformative. Four flagship models fail it on questions they cannot have memorized: every scored question resolved after their cutoffs. The reason is structural. Models legitimately know more about times near their cutoff, so recency mimics leakage, and we prove no passive backtest can separate the two from genuine skill. Measurement, not just detection, requires information from outside the backtest. We supply it in two forms. A known cutoff identifies leakage at the boundary; a matched clean control identifies it globally and yields a leakage-adjusted score. We also derive where leakage hides: it concentrates on outcomes that surprised the crowd and were well covered in training, and partial memorization is disproportionately rewarded. We validate the estimators against ground truth by planting leakage in twin models, where they recover the injected dose and return null on clean questions. Deployed on frontier models, they detect one cutoff-localized signature and, at the audit's power floor, clear five models whose apparent advantages were recency alone. Backtests need not be discarded; they need one defensible reference.

</details>


### [188] [AcceptMoE: Commitment-Weighted Self-Sizing Verifier Expert Sets for Efficient MoE Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02989)
*Shuang Liang,Hao,Chen,Zhiwen Mo,Qianzhou Wang,Guoyu Li,Lingxiao Ma,Wayne Luk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AcceptMoE is a verifier-side expert selector for speculative decoding with MoE targets that dynamically adjusts eligible experts per verification block using router scores and commitment probabilities, eliminating manual expert budgets. It achieves 1.29× throughput with all weights on GPU and 2.06× under offloading while reducing host-to-device traffic by ~75%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In MoE speculative decoding, parallel draft-tree verification activates the union of all experts across tree nodes, but only a small subset of nodes contribute to the final accepted output. This creates a mismatch between token count, activated-expert count, and expert-weight traffic. Under expert offloading, cache residency further complicates efficiency. The authors aim to reduce this wasted expert activation and data movement without requiring manual expert budget tuning.

Method: AcceptMoE integrates target-router scores with offline-estimated commitment probabilities to dynamically select a subset of eligible experts for each verification block. Under offloading, it conditions expert eligibility on cache residency rather than predicting natural routes and prefetching weights. The approach is implemented within the SGLang serving framework and evaluated against EAGLE-3 speculative decoding.

Result: Across 12 model-task pairs (3 MoE targets, 4 benchmarks), AcceptMoE's mean accuracy is only 0.27 percentage points below EAGLE-3 with natural routing. It achieves 1.290× throughput at batch size 1 with all expert weights in GPU memory, and 2.06× throughput under physical expert offloading, while reducing host-to-device traffic by 73.6%–77.1%.

Conclusion: AcceptMoE demonstrates that dynamically constraining expert eligibility during verification significantly improves MoE speculative decoding throughput, especially under offloading, with negligible accuracy loss and without requiring manual expert budget specification.

Abstract: Speculative decoding verifies a tree of draft tokens in one target-model forward pass. For a mixture-of-experts (MoE) target, however, parallel verification can activate the union of the experts selected by all tree nodes, even though only a small subset of those nodes reaches the accepted output. Token count, activated-expert union size, and expert-weight traffic are therefore distinct cost measures: reducing the token workload need not shrink the expert union proportionally, and under offloading, transfer traffic also depends on cache residency. We introduce AcceptMoE, a verifier-side expert selector that combines target-router scores with offline-estimated commitment probabilities and automatically adjusts the number of eligible experts for each verification block, eliminating the need for a user-specified expert budget. Under offloading, AcceptMoE conditions expert eligibility on cache residency instead of predicting natural routes and prefetching the corresponding expert weights. Although constraining target-expert eligibility changes the model distribution, across 12 model-task pairs spanning three MoE targets and four benchmarks, AcceptMoE's mean accuracy is 0.27 percentage points lower than that of EAGLE-3 speculative decoding with natural routing. Served with SGLang at batch size one, it reaches 1.290 times the throughput of this baseline with all expert weights in GPU memory, and 2.06 times under physical expert offloading, while reducing host-to-device traffic by 73.6 percent to 77.1 percent.

</details>


### [189] [Joint Affine Spectral Shaping: Coupling Weight and Bias Updates Beyond Weight-Only Muon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02991)
*Gongyue Zhang,Honghai Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether biases in neural network affine layers should be treated jointly with weights under spectral optimization. The proposed Joint Regularized Inverse (JRI) method applies a capped regularized-inverse spectral map to a joint momentum matrix incorporating both weights and biases, yielding small but consistent improvements over weight-only spectral optimization on a BERT-mini text classification benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing spectral optimizers (like Muon) reshape weight-update spectra but delegate bias updates to a separate, independent optimizer (e.g., Adam). The paper questions whether this separation is theoretically neutral and investigates whether jointly spectrally transforming weights and biases within affine layers yields measurable performance gains.

Method: Each affine layer is formulated as a joint momentum matrix A = [M_W, αm_b], where M_W is the weight momentum and m_b is a scaled bias momentum. A capped regularized-inverse spectral map (akin to Muon's Newton-Schulz iteration) is applied to the full joint matrix via exact SVD, producing both weight and physical bias updates simultaneously. Ablation experiments compare: (1) exact-SVD Muon (weight-only), (2) weight-only inverse shaping, (3) affine-probe inverse shaping (bias influences SVD but retains independent Adam update), and (4) the proposed JRI. Evaluation uses a four-layer BERT-mini trained from scratch on IMDb with strict five-seed and 22-seed replications.

Result: Weight-only inverse shaping improves validation-loss-selected test accuracy from 84.903±0.242% to 85.562±0.308% and lowers test loss from 0.3479 to 0.3345. Affine-probe shaping (bias alters SVD only) yields no improvement. JRI further raises accuracy to 85.738±0.180% and lowers loss to 0.3291, with all five seeds improving. JRI reduces bias-update norm from 0.02095 to 0.00301, lowers boundary-function share from 86.58% to 78.97%, and shifts the cosine between weight-induced boundary motion and explicit bias from +0.030 to -0.137. A 22-seed replication yields 85.743±0.203%.

Conclusion: Joint affine spectral allocation is a small but consistent extension to weight-only spectral optimization. Incorporating biases into the spectral transform yields statistically reliable improvements in both accuracy and loss, suggesting that the weight-bias separation in current spectral optimizers is not entirely neutral and that joint treatment merits further investigation.

Abstract: Matrix spectral optimizers reshape weight-update spectra but usually delegate vector-valued biases to a separate optimizer. We study whether this separation is neutral. We formulate each affine layer as a joint momentum matrix $A=[M_W,αm_b]$ and apply a capped regularized-inverse spectral map to the complete matrix, producing both the weight and physical bias updates. A strict five-seed ablation on a four-layer BERT-mini trained from scratch on IMDb compares exact-SVD Muon, weight-only inverse shaping, affine-probe inverse shaping, and the proposed joint regularized inverse (JRI). Weight-only inverse shaping raises validation-loss-selected test accuracy from $84.903\pm0.242\%$ to $85.562\pm0.308\%$ and lowers selected test loss from $0.3479$ to $0.3345$. Allowing bias to alter the joint SVD while retaining an independent Adam bias update does not improve over weight-only inverse shaping. Using the transformed bias jointly raises selected test accuracy to $85.738\pm0.180\%$ and lowers test loss to $0.3291$, with all five seeds improving relative to the probe baseline. During the peak-performance window, JRI preserves the eligible weight-update norm while reducing the bias-update norm from $0.02095$ to $0.00301$, lowers boundary-function share from $86.58\%$ to $78.97\%$, and changes the cosine between weight-induced boundary motion and explicit bias from $+0.030$ to $-0.137$. An independent 22-seed replication yields $85.743\pm0.203\%$ selected test accuracy. These results identify joint affine spectral allocation as a small but consistent extension to weight-only spectral optimization.

</details>


### [190] [A Graph Signal Processing Perspective on Numerical Sequence Representations in LLM In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03015)
*Jiajun Bao,Zihao Qi,Toni J. B. Liu,Gurbir Arora,Raphaël Sarfati,Nicolas Boullé,Christopher J. Earls*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Using graph signal processing, this paper reveals that LLM internal representations during numerical in-context learning become systematically organized by input complexity: simpler inputs yield smoother, globally-connected token graphs while complex inputs produce localized graphs with richer high-frequency components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work has only characterized numerical ICL via output-level metrics (e.g., prediction error), leaving the internal organization of numerical information within LLM representations largely unexplored.

Method: The authors adopt a graph signal processing framework: attention weights define a weighted graph over tokens, and token hidden states serve as graph signals. They apply quantitative graph-spectral diagnostics and qualitative token-graph visualizations to analyze how representations evolve with context length across varying input dynamical complexity.

Result: Representations become increasingly differentiated by input complexity as context length grows. Simpler inputs produce token graphs with stronger global connectivity and spectrally concentrated (smoother) hidden-state signals. More complex inputs yield localized graphs with broader spectral support and greater high-frequency energy. These signatures are conserved across model families.

Conclusion: There exist systematic, context-dependent internal representational signatures for numerical ICL that generalize across LLM architectures, offering a new lens for understanding how transformers internally organize structured reasoning.

Abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated in-context learning (ICL) capabilities for numerical inference over sequences serialized as text. Prior work has identified and characterized this form of numerical inference primarily through output-level evaluations such as prediction error. However, how numerical information is organized within LLM representations remains much less understood. To study this internal organization, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective in which attention induces a weighted graph over tokens, while token hidden states define signals on its nodes. Quantitative graph-spectral diagnostics and qualitative token-graph visualizations reveal that representations become more clearly differentiated by input dynamical complexity as context length increases. Simpler inputs produce attention-induced token graphs with stronger global connectivity and smoother, spectrally concentrated hidden-state signals, whereas more complex inputs produce more localized graphs and hidden-state signals with broader spectral support and greater high-frequency energy. Together, these findings point to systematic, context-dependent internal signatures associated with numerical ICL that are conserved across model families.

</details>


### [191] [Paired Recipient-based Evaluation of Survival Prediction for Deceased Donor Kidney Transplants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03017)
*Misaki Matsuura,Mohammadreza Nemati,Dulat Bekbolsynov,Stanislaw Stepkowski,Kevin S. Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a novel paired recipient-based evaluation framework for kidney transplant survival prediction models, finding that models of varying complexity achieve ~60% accuracy when comparing which of two recipients would have better graft survival from the same donor. The authors argue this metric is more clinically relevant than the traditional C-index.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing survival prediction models for kidney transplant outcomes are typically evaluated using the concordance index (C-index), which the authors argue is poorly suited for assessing real-world donor-recipient matching decisions. There is a need for evaluation metrics that reflect the counterfactual nature of allocation — namely, determining which recipient would benefit more from a given donor kidney.

Method: The authors use deceased donor kidney transplant data from the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR). They train five survival prediction models spanning linear to deep learning approaches. They propose a paired recipient-based evaluation framework: for each deceased donor who donated two kidneys, they compare predicted graft survival between the two recipients and assess whether the model correctly identifies which recipient had longer graft survival. This is further translated into estimated post-transplant years gained.

Result: All five survival prediction models achieve approximately 60% paired recipient-based accuracy. The authors translate this accuracy into an interpretable estimate of post-transplant years gained. They also demonstrate that the C-index is a misleading metric in this context, as it does not adequately capture the clinically relevant decision-making scenario of selecting between potential recipients for a given donor.

Conclusion: The paired recipient-based accuracy metric provides a more clinically meaningful and interpretable evaluation of survival prediction models for kidney transplantation than the commonly used C-index. The ~60% accuracy across models suggests room for improvement in donor-recipient matching algorithms, and the proposed framework enables better assessment of the practical utility of such models in real-world allocation settings.

Abstract: There has been significant interest in using machine learning algorithms to predict kidney transplant outcomes, such as the number of years until a graft inevitably fails. These prediction algorithms could possibly be used for pre-transplant donor-recipient matching to identify more compatible donors and recipients and thus improve post-transplant outcomes. In this study, we explore the use of survival prediction models trained on deceased donor kidney transplant data from the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR). We propose a novel paired recipient-based evaluation framework that compares graft outcomes between two recipients who received kidneys from the same deceased donor, allowing us to evaluate the counterfactual benefit of changing the recipient for a certain donor. We find that five different survival prediction models, ranging in complexity from linear to deep learning-based models, all result in ~60% paired recipient-based accuracy. We further translate this accuracy into an interpretable quantity of post-transplant years gained. We also highlight major limitations of the commonly used concordance index (C-index) metric for evaluating survival prediction accuracy in this setting and demonstrate that our proposed paired recipient-based accuracy metric is more clinically relevant and better reflects real-world allocation settings.

</details>


### [192] [Resume Means Resume: A Machine-Checked Conformance Contract for Checkpoint, Interrupt, and Resume Semantics in Workflow Persistence Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03836)
*Sajjad Khan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper audits five agent workflow frameworks for crash-resume behavior, finds all violate even their own stated contracts, formalizes the RESUME CONTRACT with six properties in TLA+, empirically measures failures (e.g., exactly-once violations, concurrent consume-once breaks), and presents REMIT—a verified recovery sequencer that repairs the identified faults.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent workflow frameworks must persist execution state to survive crashes and resume, but existing systems lack machine-checkable contracts for what resumption means regarding already-fired effects. The paper reveals that five widely-deployed frameworks exhibit undocumented, inconsistent, and often incorrect resume semantics, motivating a formal specification and verified repair.

Method: The authors define the RESUME CONTRACT with six formal properties (prefix continuation, effect exactly-once, fork determinism, checkpoint validity, consume-once, recovery determinism) plus fork-intent and liveness obligations. They build a TLA+ model for exhaustive model checking (7.4M states), construct a 39-cell fault matrix to establish property independence, and implement a deterministic, LLM-free harness to measure pinned releases of LangGraph, CrewAI, pydantic-graph, and others. They develop REMIT, a reference sequencer with a Verus-verified recovery core (line-identical to shipped executable), and an opt-in consumption gate using a shared store for cross-process repair.

Result: LangGraph 1.2.9 durably records a second resume value but never consults it, persists schema-invalid state silently, and re-executes durably recorded work after SIGKILL (exactly-once across interrupts, at-least-once across crashes). CrewAI 1.15.2 re-executes completed effect-bearing methods contrary to its claims. Pydantic-graph 1.x cannot resume after a mid-node crash. No two frameworks share a conformance profile. Consume-once holds sequentially but fails under concurrent delivery: k processes resuming one parked interrupt fire the gated effect k times, with saturation 1.0 in 36 of 40 cells across hosts. REMIT repairs the fork and validity cells; the cross-process cell is repaired at the read path and ships.

Conclusion: Current agent workflow frameworks lack coherent, verifiable resume semantics, with failures spanning both sequential and concurrent scenarios. The RESUME CONTRACT provides a precise, machine-checkable specification, and REMIT demonstrates that verified, line-identical recovery logic can systematically repair these faults, including a practical opt-in gate for cross-process consume-once.

Abstract: A framework that persists execution state so a run can be interrupted, survive a crash, and continue must decide what a resume means for effects that already fired. Five widely deployed agent workflow frameworks answer differently, none exposes a machine-checkable contract, and behavior violates even the fragments they state. The RESUME CONTRACT states six properties over the persistence API (prefix continuation, effect exactly-once, fork determinism, checkpoint validity, consume-once, recovery determinism), plus fork-intent and liveness obligations. A TLA+ model checks a reference semantics exhaustively, unchanged at scaled bounds (7.4 million states); a 39-cell fault matrix yields the separating models independence requires, and consume-once splits, its consumption clause independent of all six others. A deterministic, LLM-free harness measures them at pinned releases. LangGraph 1.2.9 durably records a second resume value and never consults it, persists schema-invalid state silently, and re-executes durably recorded work after a real SIGKILL: exactly-once across interrupts, at-least-once across crashes, on one API. CrewAI 1.15.2 re-executes completed effect-bearing methods against its written claim; pydantic-graph 1.x cannot resume after a mid-node crash; no two probed frameworks share a conformance profile. Consume-once holds sequentially and fails under concurrent delivery: k processes resuming one parked interrupt fire the gated effect k times, saturation 1.0 in 36 of 40 cells, and the failure crosses hosts. REMIT, a reference sequencer whose Verus-verified recovery core is line-identical to the shipped executable, repairs the fork and validity cells. The cross-process cell is repaired at the read path, and that repair ships: an opt-in gate claims consumption in the shared store, serving one racer and refusing the rest before any node executes.

</details>


### [193] [PLAN: Parallel Liquid-Inspired Approximation Network for Efficient Representation Learning in Flexible Job Shop Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03041)
*Dhivya Dharshini Kannan,Wei Zhang,Jieyi Bi,Yingpeng Du,Tianjun Wei,Jie Zhang,Zuming Liu,Anupam Trivedi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PLAN reformulates liquid neural network dynamics into a parallelizable framework for flexible job shop scheduling, achieving superior makespan and major reductions in parameters and inference latency across deterministic, stochastic, and dynamic FJSP variants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep RL for FJSP relies on attention-based architectures that are parameter-heavy and suffer from high inference latency as problem scales grow. Liquid neural networks are parameter-efficient but suffer from inherently sequential computation that bottlenecks speed. The paper aims to resolve this trade-off between parameter efficiency and computational efficiency.

Method: PLAN (Parallel Liquid-inspired Approximation Network) discretizes continuous liquid-state dynamics into a parallelizable formulation. It structurally decouples state evolution (handled by liquid-inspired updates for the primary evolving state) from context aggregation (handled by a lightweight module for global context). The framework is plug-and-play: it pairs with a compact stochastic module for stochastic FJSP and replaces heavy heterogeneous graph transformers in multi-faceted dynamic FJSP.

Result: Across deterministic, stochastic, and multi-faceted dynamic FJSP benchmarks, PLAN reduces average makespan by 1.2%, 1.4%, and 2.3% respectively (up to 10.2% in one setting). Inference latency drops by 13.2%, 31.7%, and 26.9% (up to 69.2% on largest instances), while using only 22–47% of baseline parameters.

Conclusion: PLAN successfully navigates the parameter-efficiency vs. computational-efficiency trade-off, offering a lightweight, parallelizable alternative to both attention-heavy and sequential liquid architectures for DRL-based FJSP and its variants.

Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches for flexible job shop scheduling (FJSP) heavily rely on attention-centric architectures to achieve state-of-the-art performance. However, these models suffer from excessive parameter counts and prohibitive inference latency as problem scales expand. While liquid neural networks (LNNs) offer a parameter-efficient alternative for modeling adaptive state evolution, their inherently sequential dynamics bottleneck computational efficiency. To resolve this trade-off, we propose PLAN (Parallel Liquid-inspired Approximation Network), a lightweight representation learning framework that reformulates continuous liquid-state dynamics into a discretized and parallelizable formulation. PLAN structurally decouples state evolution from context aggregation, where liquid-inspired updates handle the primary evolving state representation, and a lightweight context aggregation module provides complementary global context. Furthermore, PLAN acts as a versatile, plug-and-play backbone that generalizes to complex FJSP variants, pairing with a compact stochastic module for stochastic FJSP and replacing heavy heterogeneous graph transformers in multi-faceted dynamic FJSP. Extensive evaluations across deterministic, stochastic, and multi-faceted dynamic FJSP benchmarks show that PLAN reduces the average makespan by 1.2%, 1.4%, and 2.3%, respectively, compared with the corresponding state-of-the-art baselines, with the improvement reaching 10.2% in one benchmark setting. PLAN also reduces average inference latency by 13.2%, 31.7%, and 26.9%, respectively, with a maximum reduction of 69.2% on the largest instances, while using only 22$-$47% of the baseline parameters.

</details>


### [194] [Exploiting Separability in Multi-Scale Grey-Box Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03045)
*Joshua E. Hammond,Tyler A. Soderstrom,Brian A. Korgel,Michael Baldea*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A bilevel Bayesian optimization framework for grey-box problems separates black-box variables (optimized via outer BO) from white-box variables (solved via inner global optimization), yielding lower regret, fewer iterations, and faster wall-clock time across 13 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grey-box optimization problems contain both expensive black-box functions and explicit white-box equations, yet standard BO treats all variables uniformly, leading to inefficiency. The authors aim to exploit this natural separability to improve sample efficiency and constraint satisfaction.

Method: The problem is reformulated as a bilevel optimization: an outer BO loop models the scalar objective as a function of black-box variables only, using a Gaussian process surrogate; an inner global optimization solves the white-box subproblem exactly. This avoids penalty functions, chance constraints, or moment approximations for handling white-box constraints.

Result: Bilevel BO achieves lower regret with fewer iterations and reduced wall-clock time on 13 benchmark problems. The advantage is robust to initialization set size, exploration parameters, and the choice of inner solver.

Conclusion: Exploiting the natural partition between black-box and white-box variables via bilevel BO yields significant improvements in efficiency and robustness for grey-box optimization, without requiring constraint relaxations.

Abstract: We consider grey-box optimization problems where the decision variables naturally partition into black-box variables (as arguments to an expensive black-box function) and white-box variables, governed by a set of explicit, closed-form equations that also depend on the output of the black-box function. We exploit this separability through a bilevel reformulation: an outer Bayesian optimization (BO) to optimize the scalar objective as a function of black-box variables alone, while an inner problem solves the white-box subproblem via global optimization. The Gaussian process surrogate used in BO is therefore defined rather than and white-box constraints are satisfied exactly whenever the inner optimizer converges to a feasible point---without penalty functions, chance constraints, or moment approximations. On a suite of 13 benchmark problems, bilevel BO achieves lower regret, with fewer iterations and wall clock time. This advantage is robust to initialization set size, exploration parameters, and inner-solver choice.

</details>


### [195] [Revisiting TD Target Aggregation under Uncertainty in Q-Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03069)
*Lipeng Zu,Xiaonan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SADQ modifies the TD target in Q-learning by using one-step rollout predictions from a learned dynamics model to regularize action aggregation, reducing overestimation bias while preserving the standard fixed point. It improves training stability across control tasks, vector-based environments, and Atari benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard DQN bootstrapped TD updates use greedy maximization over next-state action values, which is sensitive to estimation noise — the max operator blindly favors the largest Q-value regardless of its reliability, amplifying errors through bootstrapping. There is a need for a more robust aggregation rule that attenuates unreliable maxima.

Method: SADQ introduces a mixed Bellman update where one-step rollout predictions from a learned dynamics model guide comparisons among candidate next-state actions. This regularization mechanism adds structure to the aggregation step, attenuating unreliable maxima while maintaining the standard fixed point as model error diminishes, all without altering the underlying Q-learning framework.

Result: Theoretical analysis demonstrates that SADQ reduces bootstrap-induced overestimation in a pointwise manner. Empirically, SADQ consistently improves training stability across classical control tasks, real-world vector-based environments, and Atari benchmarks compared to strong DQN variants.

Conclusion: SADQ offers a simple yet effective modification to Q-learning that addresses the fundamental overestimation problem by leveraging model-based rollouts to regularize TD target formation, yielding more stable and reliable value function learning.

Abstract: Deep Q-Networks (DQNs) learn value functions through bootstrapped temporal-difference updates, where future returns are approximated using a greedy maximization over next-state action values. While effective, this aggregation rule is inherently sensitive to estimation noise: when Q-values are uncertain, the maximization operator deterministically favors the largest estimate, regardless of its reliability, leading to amplified errors through bootstrapping. In this work, we propose the \textbf{S}uccessor Rollout \textbf{A}ggregation \textbf{D}eep \textbf{Q}-Network (SADQ), a simple modification to Q-learning that regularizes how the TD target is formed. SADQ uses one-step rollout predictions from a learned dynamics model to guide the comparison among candidate next-state actions, introducing additional structure into the aggregation step without altering the underlying learning framework. The resulting mixed Bellman update attenuates unreliable maxima while preserving the standard fixed point under diminishing model error. We provide theoretical analysis showing that SADQ reduces bootstrap-induced overestimation in a pointwise manner. Empirically, SADQ consistently improves training stability across classical control tasks, real-world vector-based environments, and Atari benchmarks when compared to strong DQN variants.

</details>


### [196] [SynEnergy: Anomaly Semantic-Guided Diffusion for Synthetic Energy Data Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03087)
*Lin Jiang,Dahai Yu,Ravikumar Gelli,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SynEnergy is a two-stage diffusion-based framework for generating synthetic energy consumption data that preserves anomalous events. It uses Heterogeneous Graph-based Anomaly Semantic Learning (HG-ASL) to extract anomaly semantics from sparse residuals, and Anomaly Semantic-guided Diffusion (AS-Diff) to inject these semantics into the generation process. Evaluated on four real-world datasets against 11 baselines, it improves anomaly preservation fidelity by 12.21% and downstream quality by 2.96%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing synthetic energy data generation methods reproduce overall consumption distributions and regular patterns but fail to preserve anomalous events (caused by extreme weather, infrastructure failures, behavioral shifts). These anomalies are sparse, spatiotemporally localized, and depend on heterogeneous geographical and regional dependencies, making them difficult to model.

Method: A two-stage diffusion-based framework: (1) HG-ASL — Heterogeneous Graph-based Anomaly Semantic Learning extracts region-specific anomaly semantics by jointly modeling spatial proximity and regional attribute dependencies on sparse residual structures; (2) AS-Diff — Anomaly Semantic-guided Diffusion injects learned anomaly semantics into the denoising process for controllable, anomaly-preserving sequence generation, scaling from individual regions to city-wide settings.

Result: On four real-world energy consumption datasets against 11 baselines (both general-purpose and energy-specific), SynEnergy improves anomaly preservation fidelity by an average of 12.21% and downstream task quality by 2.96%, while maintaining competitive overall generation fidelity.

Conclusion: SynEnergy effectively addresses the gap in anomaly-preserving synthetic energy data generation by leveraging heterogeneous graph modeling and semantic-guided diffusion, demonstrating significant improvements in anomaly fidelity and downstream utility without sacrificing overall generation quality.

Abstract: Fine-grained energy consumption data are essential for applications such as demand forecasting, demand response planning, and grid reliability assessment. However, access to such data is often restricted by privacy concerns and data-sharing constraints, motivating growing interest in synthetic energy data generation. Although existing methods can reproduce overall consumption distributions and recurring temporal patterns, they often smooth out or underrepresent anomalous events caused by extreme weather, infrastructure failures, and behavioral shifts. Preserving these events is challenging because they are sparse, localized in time and space, and shaped by heterogeneous dependencies across geographical proximity and regional attributes. To address these challenges, we propose SynEnergy, a two-stage diffusion-based framework for anomaly-preserving energy consumption data generation. The first stage, Heterogeneous Graph-based Anomaly Semantic Learning (HG-ASL), extracts region-specific anomaly semantics from sparse residual structures by jointly modeling spatial and attribute dependencies across urban regions. The second stage, Anomaly Semantic-guided Diffusion (AS-Diff), injects the learned anomaly semantics into the denoising process to generate realistic consumption sequences while preserving anomalous patterns. This design enables controllable generation for individual regions and scales naturally to city-wide settings. We evaluate SynEnergy on four real-world energy consumption datasets against 11 general-purpose and energy-specific generation baselines. Experimental results show that SynEnergy improves anomaly preservation fidelity by an average of 12.21% and downstream quality by 2.96%, while maintaining competitive overall generation fidelity compared to baselines.

</details>


### [197] [SMOPD: Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning via Specialize-and-Merge Online Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03092)
*Wen Wang,Jiahua Bao,Tu Yongsiqi,Yihao Liu,Haotian Zhou,Haoxuan Ma,Mengyu Zhou,Wenkui Fan,Junwei He,Xiaoxi Jiang,Guanjun Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SMOPD is a two-stage method (Specialize then Merge) that addresses the limitation of GDPO in handling multi-reward RL training with disparate reward granularities (dense vs. sparse). It first trains reward-specialized teacher policies, then distills them into a single student via online policy distillation, outperforming GDPO on 1.5B-7B models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GDPO normalizes each reward dimension separately before aggregation, but still fails when rewards have different granularities — e.g., a dense reward (0.1–1.0) alongside a sparse binary reward (0/1). The sparse reward provides insufficient optimization signal, so its corresponding capability is not effectively reinforced. The core challenge: strengthening the sparse reward's signal without degrading capabilities already learned from the fine-grained reward.

Method: SMOPD operates in two stages. Stage 1 (Specialize): Multiple teacher policies are trained using reward-priority configurations, where each teacher specializes in one reward dimension under conditions that allow that reward's signal to drive optimization effectively. Stage 2 (Merge): Online policy distillation combines the specialized capabilities of all teachers into a single student policy, maintaining balanced task-level optimization throughout the distillation process.

Result: SMOPD outperforms GDPO across two multi-reward settings — complementary rewards (tool-calling accuracy and format) and conflicting rewards (helpfulness and harmlessness) — on backbone models of 1.5B, 3B, and 7B parameters.

Conclusion: The two-stage specialize-and-merge paradigm effectively resolves the granularity mismatch problem in multi-reward RL, enabling sparse rewards to contribute meaningful optimization signals without compromising dense-reward capabilities.

Abstract: We aim to improve model performance in multi-reward reinforcement learning training process. Existing Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO) has mitigated the issue of reward signals masking one another during direct scalarization by normalizing each reward dimension separately before aggregation. However, our experiments show that GDPO still struggles to balance reward signals with different granularities. Specifically, in some particular training tasks, the model may receive a dense reward that assigns fine-grained scores ranging from 0.1 to 1.0, together with a sparse reward that provides only binary feedback of either 0 or 1. In such cases, we find that the sparse reward may provide an insufficient optimization signal, preventing its corresponding capability from being effectively reinforced. Therefore, how can we strengthen the optimization signal from the sparse reward without sacrificing the capability already learned from the fine-grained reward? To overcome this limitation, we propose Specialize-and-Merge Online Policy Distillation (SMOPD), a two-stage training method for multi-reward optimization. Stage1-Specialize: SMOPD first employs reward-priority configurations to train multiple reward-specialized teachers, allowing each reward to be learned under conditions where its signal can effectively drive optimization. Stage2-Merge: SMOPD then utilizes online policy distillation to combine the reward-specialized capabilities of these teachers into a single student policy, while maintaining balanced task-level optimization. To validate our method, we conduct experiments on two multi-reward settings: complementary rewards(tool-calling accuracy and format) and conflicting rewards (helpful and harmless rewards). Based on above settings, SMOPD outperforms GDPO across 1.5B, 3B and 7B backbones.

</details>


### [198] [Convex-Hull-Neighborhood Smooth Dual Generalization: Controlling Local Correction Propagation in Offline RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03108)
*Yi Yang,Zhennan Chen,Mingfeng Lv,Hanlei Li,Zhengsen Ruan,Lvqing Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CSDG reformulates the Bellman backup as an in-sample target plus a Convex Hull Neighborhood (CHN) local correction, explicitly separating the generalized (OOD) contribution from the in-sample reference path. It uses dual candidate smoothing at different perturbation radii with a mixture coefficient λ, provides theoretical bounds, and achieves strong offline RL performance without explicit OOD penalties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline RL suffers from bootstrapping amplification of estimation errors at out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Existing methods control either the admissible OOD region or the influence of generalized targets via separate mechanisms. The authors aim to unify these aspects by making the OOD generalization contribution explicit and controllable within the Bellman backup itself.

Method: CSDG expresses the Bellman backup as an in-sample value target plus a CHN-local correction term. The correction is computed by smoothing both in-sample-oriented and OOD-oriented candidates sampled at different perturbation radii, blended via a mixture coefficient λ. The practical algorithm uses asymmetric bounded noise and expectile regression to approximate the theoretical quantities, avoiding exact support classification or explicit pessimistic OOD penalties. Theoretical contributions include an exact one-step correction identity, time-varying iterate bounds, a fixed-point bound depending only on branch discrepancy, characterization of induced implicit policies, and a conditional non-degradation criterion.

Result: Experiments on Gym-MuJoCo and AntMaze benchmarks demonstrate strong aggregate performance and stable value estimation, outperforming or matching existing offline RL methods.

Conclusion: CSDG provides a theoretically grounded framework that cleanly separates in-sample and OOD generalization in offline RL Bellman backups, enabling stable value learning without explicit pessimistic penalties, and achieves competitive empirical results.

Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (offline RL) can benefit from nearby out-of-distribution (OOD) actions, but estimation errors at these actions may be amplified by bootstrapping. Existing regularization and local-generalization methods control either the admissible OOD region or the influence of generalized targets, often through separate mechanisms. We propose Convex Hull Neighborhood Smooth Dual Generalization (CSDG), which expresses the Bellman backup as an in-sample value target plus a CHN-local correction. This formulation makes the generalized contribution explicit and separates it from the in-sample reference path. The correction is obtained by smoothing in-sample-oriented and OOD-oriented candidates sampled at different perturbation radii. A mixture coefficient lambda scales its contribution to each backup, while the recursive discount remains gamma. Under boundedness and fixed perturbation kernels, we derive an exact one-step correction identity, a time-varying iterate bound, and a fixed-point bound that depends only on the branch discrepancy at the fixed point. We further characterize the implicit policies induced by the idealized operators and give a conditional non-degradation criterion. The practical algorithm approximates these quantities using asymmetric bounded noise and expectile regression, without exact support classification or an additional pessimistic OOD penalty. Experiments on Gym-MuJoCo and AntMaze show strong aggregate performance and stable value estimation. Code is available at: https://github.com/YOUNG-fnxm/CSDG

</details>


### [199] [Double Descent in Gradient Boosting Decision Trees via Split-Candidate Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03111)
*Ryuichi Kanoh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes "number of split candidates" as a single-axis capacity parameter for studying double descent in gradient boosting decision trees (GBDTs). As split-candidate budgets increase, test error exhibits a double descent pattern. An empirical tree-kernel diagnostic reveals that the peak arises from noise-sensitive directions when the kernel rank approaches sample size. Predictions about tree depth, training set size, and label noise are experimentally validated across XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Double descent is well-studied in neural networks via explicit capacity parameters like width, but GBDTs lack an analogous single-axis capacity control. Existing GBDT hyperparameters (tree depth, number of trees, learning rate) do not individually produce a clean double descent curve. The authors seek to identify a unified capacity parameter for GBDTs that reveals double descent and explains its mechanism.

Method: The authors propose "number of split candidates" as the capacity parameter: fixing all other controls, increasing split-candidate budget refines the feature-quantization grid and expands the dictionary of root-to-leaf paths available to boosting. They construct an empirical tree-kernel diagnostic — a kernel matrix derived from indicator vectors of which training examples share the same leaf — and analyze its rank and eigenvalue spectrum as split candidates increase. This connects candidate-induced path geometry to model capacity and noise sensitivity.

Result: Test error exhibits a double descent peak at intermediate split-candidate budgets across XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. The empirical kernel rank grows with split candidates toward sample size; when very small positive eigenvalues emerge, noise-sensitive directions cause the error peak. Three predictions are validated: deeper trees reach the critical regime with fewer split candidates; larger training sets require finer grids; label noise amplifies the peak. Random forests do not exhibit this double descent under the same sweep.

Conclusion: Split-candidate scaling serves as a valid single-axis capacity intervention for studying GBDTs. The observed double descent stems from an interaction between candidate-induced geometry (via the tree-kernel spectrum) and boosting dynamics, rather than from standard bias-variance tradeoff. The kernel diagnostic provides a mechanistic explanation linking discretization granularity to generalization.

Abstract: Double descent is commonly studied by scaling an explicit capacity parameter, such as neural-network width. For gradient boosting decision trees (GBDTs), however, an analogous single-axis capacity parameter has not been established. We propose the number of split candidates as an operational capacity parameter for GBDTs. Holding other training controls fixed, increasing the split-candidate budget refines the feature-quantization grid and expands the dictionary of root-to-leaf paths from which boosting selects its updates. To analyze this expansion, we construct an empirical tree-kernel diagnostic that summarizes how candidate-induced paths group the training examples. A regime in which the empirical kernel rank grows toward the sample size and very small positive eigenvalues emerge exposes noise-sensitive directions; in this regime, test error peaks before decreasing again at larger split-candidate budgets. This perspective predicts that deeper trees should reach the regime with fewer split candidates, larger training sets should require finer grids, and label noise should make the peak more pronounced. Experiments support these predictions and show test-error peaks at intermediate split-candidate budgets across XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, whereas a random-forest control improves monotonically under the same split-candidate sweep. Taken together, our analysis and experiments support split-candidate scaling as a single-axis capacity intervention for studying GBDTs and suggest that the observed double descent arises from an interaction between candidate-induced geometry and boosting dynamics.

</details>


### [200] [Simulation-free and finite-time diffusion model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03117)
*Kentaro Kaba,Masayuki Ohzeki,Yuki Sughiyama*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a framework for designing reference diffusion processes that simultaneously enable simulation-free training and finite-time generation, by prescribing tractable time-dependent conditional distributions and constructing the reference process to realize them as marginals. Score matching emerges naturally from process reversal, and conditional flow matching appears as a small-noise limit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional diffusion models face a trade-off: simulation-free training versus finite-time generation. The choice of reference diffusion process is critical to performance, but existing approaches cannot achieve both desirable properties simultaneously.

Method: The authors prescribe tractable time-dependent conditional distributions and construct a reference diffusion process whose marginals realize these distributions. This reverses the conventional design paradigm — rather than starting from a stochastic process and deriving marginals, they start from desired marginals and construct the process.

Result: Score matching is shown not to be fundamental but rather a natural consequence of reversing the reference process. Conditional flow matching emerges as the small-noise limit of the proposed framework, unifying diffusion and flow-based generative approaches.

Conclusion: The framework unifies and generalizes existing generative modeling paradigms, demonstrating that both score-based diffusion and flow matching are manifestations of the same underlying principle when the reference process is designed through prescribed conditional distributions.

Abstract: The performance of generative diffusion models is determined by the choice of the reference diffusion process connecting the empirical and prior distributions. Conventional approaches typically trade off simulation-free training against finite-time generation. We propose a framework for designing the reference process that achieves both simultaneously. The key idea is to prescribe tractable time-dependent conditional distributions and then construct the reference process realizing them as its marginals. This framework reveals that score matching is not fundamental to diffusion-model training but instead emerges naturally through reversal of the reference process. We further show that conditional flow matching arises as the small-noise limit of the proposed framework.

</details>


### [201] [Trajectory-Guided Forget-Recover Network for Continual LLM Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03123)
*Zezheng Wu,Xinghe Cheng,Qinggang Zhang,Haoran Luo,Jiapu Wang,Qing Yang,Jingwei Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TFR-Net addresses continual machine unlearning by tracking channel-level risk to distinguish persistent from transient target-related channels, suppressing only persistent ones, and reactivating dormant channels to recover model capacity — achieving better trade-offs between unlearning effectiveness and retained utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continual unlearning requests introduce two underexplored challenges: (1) unlearning interventions can shift computation to remaining pathways, causing forgotten knowledge to re-emerge; (2) repeated interventions progressively degrade model capacity, harming retained utility.

Method: TFR-Net (Trajectory-guided Forget-Recover Network) tracks channel-level forget risk over time across requests, separating persistent target-related channels from transient hotspots and suppressing only persistent ones. It recovers capacity by reactivating dormant channels that strongly contribute to retained utility and exhibit low forget risk (both current and historical). Recovery is gated by a predefined tolerance on retained-utility degradation.

Result: Experiments on four datasets demonstrate that TFR-Net consistently achieves a more favorable trade-off between unlearning effectiveness and retained utility compared to representative baselines.

Conclusion: Channel-level risk tracking with targeted suppression and capacity recovery effectively handles the twin challenges of knowledge re-emergence and capacity degradation in continual machine unlearning.

Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to eliminate the influence of sensitive data on a model. In the real world, unlearning requests arrive continually, which gives rise to two challenges. First, an unlearning intervention may redistribute target-related computation across remaining pathways, allowing previously forgotten knowledge to re-emerge. Second, repeated unlearning interventions may progressively reduce the model capacity needed to preserve retained utility. To address these challenges, we propose the Trajectory-guided Forget-Recover Network (TFR-Net). TFR-Net tracks channel-level risk across requests. It separates persistent target-related channels from transient hotspots and suppresses only the persistent ones. TFR-Net also recovers model capacity by reactivating dormant channels. These channels make strong contributions to retained utility and show low current and historical forget risk. The recovery is accepted only when retained-utility degradation remains within a predefined tolerance. Experiments on four datasets show that TFR-Net consistently achieves a more favorable trade-off between unlearning effectiveness and retained utility than representative baselines.

</details>


<div id='cs.MA'></div>

# cs.MA [[Back]](#toc)

### [202] [Everyone Conforms, No One Believes: Pluralistic Ignorance in LLM Agent Populations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02758)
*Yashwanth YS*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: LLM agents robustly exhibit pluralistic ignorance—publicly conforming to norms they privately reject—across 100 scenarios and 8 models. A single dissenter rarely triggers norm cascades (under 26% for most models, except GPT-4o at 48%). Conformity is emergent, not instruction-driven, and model choice critically shapes simulation outcomes, suggesting LLM-based social simulations may overestimate norm stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether LLM-based multi-agent systems can reproduce pluralistic ignorance—a well-documented social phenomenon where individuals privately reject a norm but publicly conform under the false belief that others accept it—and to assess whether such systems capture the tipping-point dynamics (via norm entrepreneurs) that drive real-world norm change.
