Method: The authors constructed a benchmark of 100 scenarios spanning 10 domains and 5 authority levels, grounded in human pluralistic ignorance literature. They evaluated 8 LLMs from 6 organizations, measuring public conformity vs. private opposition rates. They tested whether a single dissenting "norm entrepreneur" agent could trigger cascades of public dissent. An ablation study removed false-consensus framing and fit-in goals to distinguish emergent behavior from instruction-driven conformity.

Result: Public conformity rates ranged from 64–94% despite private opposition. Conformity was domain-sensitive (workplace and social relationships near-universal) and model-dependent but uncorrelated with capability. Norm entrepreneur cascades succeeded <26% for 7 of 8 models; one model showed zero cascades; GPT-4o was an outlier at 48%. Ablation reduced but did not eliminate conformity (52–92% minimal condition), confirming emergent behavior.

Conclusion: Pluralistic ignorance emerges robustly in LLM agent populations. Model selection is a critical, unacknowledged degree of freedom shaping simulation outcomes. The near-absence of cascades suggests LLM simulations systematically overestimate norm stability and may miss the fragile tipping-point dynamics characteristic of real-world social change.

Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly used to simulate social dynamics, from opinion formation to collective decision-making. These simulations can reproduce certain social phenomena, but it is unknown whether they capture pluralistic ignorance, a state where a majority privately rejects a norm yet publicly conforms, each believing they are alone in dissenting. This phenomenon drives norm persistence, social movements, and political revolutions. We show that pluralistic ignorance emerges robustly in LLM agent populations. We construct a benchmark of 100 scenarios across 10 domains and 5 authority levels, grounded in the human pluralistic ignorance literature, and evaluate 8 models from 6 organizations. Agents publicly conform at rates of 64 to 94% despite privately opposing the norm. Conformity is domain-sensitive (workplace and social relationship scenarios produce near-universal compliance) and highly model-dependent, though uncorrelated with capability. We test whether a single "norm entrepreneur" can break the false consensus by publicly dissenting. For 7 of 8 models, cascades succeed less than 26% of the time, with one model showing zero cascades across all scenarios. GPT-4o is a notable outlier at 48%, revealing qualitatively distinct dynamics across model families. A prompt component ablation across all 8 models establishes that conformity is emergent rather than instruction-driven: removing both the false-consensus framing and fit-in goal reduces conformity but does not eliminate it (52 to 92% in the minimal condition). Our findings identify model selection as an unacknowledged degree of freedom that fundamentally shapes simulation outcomes. More broadly, the near-absence of cascades suggests LLM simulations may systematically overestimate the stability of social norms, missing the fragile tipping-point dynamics that drive real-world norm change in human societies.

</details>


### [203] [Stateful Governance for Concurrent Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02764)
*Yuxiang Peng,Xiaodi Wu*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper identifies "stale authorization" as a critical failure mode in AI agent governance, where authorization decisions made at request time become invalid by the time effects execute due to changing state. The authors propose Provenact, a runtime architecture that enforces policy-state serializability—ensuring all committed effects are authorized against the policy state immediately before execution—and demonstrate its effectiveness against baselines in concurrent, resource-constrained workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents transition from advisory roles to executing high-stakes operations (refunds, inventory reservations, financial transfers), governance must shift from controlling model outputs to controlling effects on shared stateful resources. Existing safeguards evaluate authorization at request time using potentially stale state—budgets, inventory levels, approval statuses, and risk signals can all change before the effect materializes, rendering prior authorization invalid. This "stale authorization" problem is especially acute in concurrent agentic systems where multiple agents operate on shared resources, yet no prior work has formally addressed stateful governance for such settings.

Method: The authors formally define "policy-state serializability" as a correctness condition: every committed effect must be explainable as authorized against the policy state immediately prior to the effect's occurrence. They then present Provenact, a runtime architecture that treats policies as reviewable programs while coordinating policy state and effects to preserve authorization validity. Provenact tracks policy-relevant state changes, re-evaluates authorization at effect-commit time rather than request time, handles delayed approvals without blocking unrelated work, and keeps policy logic in policy text (not buried in trusted provider code). A PostgreSQL-backed prototype is evaluated against baselines that naïvely pass policy state as ordinary request context.

Result: In experiments with the Provenact prototype, the system successfully prevents stale authorizations that baselines miss when policy state is passed as ordinary request context. It preserves delayed approvals while allowing unrelated concurrent work to proceed. Policy evolution remains largely in policy text rather than requiring changes in trusted provider code. In a scripted, LLM-free procurement workflow with shared budgets and inventory, Provenact avoids policy violations that agent-governance baselines produce through stale authorizations.

Conclusion: Provenact demonstrates a viable architecture for integrating stateful governance boundaries into agent frameworks and provider-backed domains where agents act on shared resources. The work suggests a broader path toward principled effect-level governance in concurrent agentic systems, moving beyond per-request authorization toward correctness conditions grounded in the actual state at the time of effect commitment.

Abstract: AI agents are moving from advisory interfaces into systems that execute consequential operations: issuing refunds, reserving scarce inventory, provisioning cloud resources, and initiating financial transfers. These workflows require governance over effects, not only over model outputs. Existing safeguards often decide whether an action is allowed from the information available when the action is requested. For stateful policies, that request-time view may be incomplete: budgets, inventory, approval status, and risk signals can change before the effect occurs, making an earlier authorization or approval stale.
  This paper studies stateful governance for concurrent agentic systems. We identify stale authorization as the core failure mode and define policy-state serializability, a correctness condition requiring committed effects to be explainable as authorized against the policy state immediately before they occur. We present Provenact, a runtime architecture that keeps policies as reviewable programs while coordinating the state and effects needed to preserve their decisions. In experiments with a PostgreSQL-backed prototype of Provenact, the system prevents stale authorizations missed by baselines that pass policy state as ordinary request context, preserves delayed approvals while unrelated work proceeds, keeps policy evolution mostly in policy text rather than trusted provider code, and avoids policy violations in a scripted, LLM-free procurement workflow where agent-governance baselines produce stale authorizations over shared budgets and inventory. More broadly, Provenact suggests a path for integrating stateful governance boundaries into agent frameworks and provider-backed domains where agents act on shared resources.

</details>


### [204] [Emergence of Biased Consensus in Multi-Agent LLM Debates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02827)
*Maya Okawa*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Multi-agent LLM debates can amplify individual biases into collective norms through a phase transition driven by conformity and noise; agent heterogeneity suppresses this emergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While multi-agent LLM debates improve decision-making and problem-solving, their safety and fairness implications are underexplored. The authors aim to understand how and why collective biased norms emerge from interactions among individually biased LLMs.

Method: The authors propose an analytical framework based on physics-inspired models of social dynamics. They model debate dynamics to predict a phase transition to collective bias when conformity exceeds a critical threshold (determined by initial LLM bias and debate noise). They validate predictions through controlled experiments, observing finite-size crossover behavior, and test generalization on realistic tasks (investment decisions, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation).

Result: A phase transition to collective biased norms occurs when conformity surpasses a critical threshold. Finite-size crossover consistent with this transition is observed empirically. Agent heterogeneity smooths/rounds the transition, suppressing collective bias emergence. Results generalize to realistic decision-making tasks.

Conclusion: Collective bias in multi-agent LLM debates emerges via a phase transition modulated by conformity, noise, and heterogeneity. These insights offer a theoretical foundation for designing safer, fairer multi-agent LLM systems.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM debates achieve strong performance on decision-making tasks as well as problem-solving benchmarks, yet their safety and fairness risks remain poorly understood. Notably, interaction can amplify the biases of single LLMs, raising concerns for real-world deployment. We identify the emergence of collective (often biased) norms in multi-agent LLM debates and show that noise (e.g., LLM sampling temperature) is a key driver. To explain this, we propose an analytical framework drawing on physics-inspired theoretical models of social dynamics. We predict a phase transition to collective bias when conformity surpasses a critical threshold given the LLMs' initial bias and debate noise. We test the theoretical predictions through controlled experiments and observe a finite-size crossover consistent with an underlying phase transition. We further find that agent heterogeneity suppresses emergence by smoothing (rounding) this transition. Finally, we show that these insights generalize to realistic decision-making tasks, including investment decisions and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.

</details>


### [205] [SABRE: A Multi-Agent Approach for Selecting Out-of-Distribution Detectors Under a Budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02959)
*Mary Wisell,Salimeh Sekeh*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Post-hoc OOD detection for vision-language models fails across domains because the best detector varies and can invert. SABRE uses three LLM agents (Selector, Reporter, Analyst) with a bounded query budget to dynamically select and aggregate detectors per input, recovering reliability without prior domain knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing post-hoc OOD detection methods assume that a detector chosen based on benchmark performance remains reliable after deployment. The authors demonstrate this assumption fails across domains: a detector that performs best in one domain can invert in another (scoring in-distribution inputs as more anomalous than genuine outliers), and no single fixed detector is reliable across all domains.

Method: SABRE (Selective Agentic Budgeted Reliability Ensemble) employs three LLM agents operating under a bounded query budget: (1) a Selector that chooses which detector from a library to consult next for a given input, (2) a Reporter that consolidates evidence across detector calls into a final OOD score, and (3) an Analyst that calibrates detector reliability using a small labeled sample held out from the deployment domain (disjoint from test data), weighting selection and aggregation without observing any scored input's label. The library includes four newly proposed multimodal density detectors. The approach infers the operating regime from data and dynamically tracks the strongest detector per domain.

Result: SABRE recovers reliable detection where conventional detectors invert (scoring inliers as outliers) and converges to the best detector where it is sound. Ablation shows the agents are complementary: the Reporter's feedback yields consistent gains, and the Analyst's calibration is decisive against inversion by ruling out unreliable detectors so that aggregation does not cancel sound ones.

Conclusion: Since no fixed detector can be trusted across domains, reliability must be established at deployment rather than assumed from benchmarks. SABRE demonstrates this can be done automatically through per-regime agentic selection and calibration.

Abstract: Post-hoc out-of-distribution (OOD) detection for vision-language models assumes that a detector chosen on a benchmark stays reliable once deployed. We show this fails across domains: on a single frozen encoder, a detector that leads in one domain can invert in another, scoring in-distribution inputs as more anomalous than genuine outliers, and the best detector changes from domain to domain, so no fixed choice is reliable throughout. We introduce SABRE (Selective Agentic Budgeted Reliability Ensemble,) which replaces this fixed choice with per-regime selection at inference. Three language-model agents reason over a library of post-hoc detectors under a bounded query budget: a Selector chooses which detector to consult next, a Reporter consolidates the evidence for each input, and an Analyst calibrates detector reliability on a small labeled sample held out from the deployment domain and disjoint from the test data, weighting selection and aggregation without ever observing a scored input's label. The library includes four multimodal density detectors we propose. Inferring the operating regime from data, SABRE tracks the strongest detector in each domain without prior knowledge of it, recovering reliable detection where a conventional detector inverts and converging to that detector where it is sound. A component analysis shows the agents are complementary: the Reporter's feedback yields consistent gains, and the Analyst's calibration is decisive against inversion, ruling out unreliable detectors so that aggregation no longer cancels the sound ones. Since no fixed rule can be trusted across domains, reliability must be established at deployment rather than assumed from a benchmark, and SABRE shows this can be done automatically.

</details>


### [206] [When Truth Is Distributed: Misinformation Derails Collective Fact Recovery in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03421)
*Chenfei Yan,Zeyang Yue,Feifei Zhao,Erliang Lin,Lu Jia,Haibo Tong,Mingyang Lyu,Chengyi Sun,Yi Zeng*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Hi-Agreement is a controlled evaluation framework that reveals how false testimony from a single deceiving agent propagates through multi-agent LLM systems, causing aggregate truth recovery to plummet from 72.5% to 14.17%. False testimony is adopted more readily than truthful testimony, propagates further, and persists even after the deceiver exits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based multi-agent systems focus on final outcomes, leaving the reliability and propagation dynamics of distributed information aggregation unclear. The authors aim to understand how communication can amplify local errors into collective risks, specifically how deception by a single evidence holder affects the collaborative reasoning process.

Method: The authors introduce Hi-Agreement, a controlled evaluation framework using 120 five-agent object-movement environments with partial observations that jointly determine a unique endpoint. They strictly pair all-honest collaboration with a condition where one key evidence holder deceives. Analysis proceeds through multi-stage voting, testimony adoption, and evidence-root lineage propagation. They evaluate three homogeneous LLM-based multi-agent systems and use process tracing plus exit ablations (removing the deceiver after initial communication).

Result: Aggregate truth recovery drops from 72.50% (all-honest) to 14.17% (with deceiver), with significant declines across all three systems. False testimony is adopted more readily than truthful testimony and propagates to higher orders. After the deceiver exits, false testimony persists through honest agents. Observers without first-hand evidence suppress incorrect consensus but do not improve truth recovery.

Conclusion: Distributed fact recovery in LLM-based multi-agent systems is fragile. The underlying mechanism is that false evidence gains collective influence through its adoption and continued propagation by other agents after entering communication, even when the original deceiver is removed.

Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems promise effective collaborative reasoning, but communication may amplify local errors into collective risks. Existing evaluations emphasize final outcomes, leaving the reliability and propagation dynamics of distributed information aggregation unclear. We introduce Hi-Agreement, a controlled evaluation framework that strictly pairs all-honest collaboration with controlled deception by a key evidence holder and analyzes the aggregation process through multi-stage voting, testimony adoption, and evidence-root lineage propagation. Using 120 five-agent object-movement environments where partial observations jointly determine a unique endpoint, we evaluate 3 homogeneous LLM-based multi-agent systems. Across these paired conditions, aggregate truth recovery falls from 72.50% to 14.17%, with significant declines for every system. Process tracing and exit ablations show that a single false testimony is adopted more readily than truthful testimony, propagates to higher orders, and persists through honest agents after the deceiver exits. Observers without first-hand evidence suppress incorrect consensus but do not improve truth recovery. Together, these findings reveal both the fragility of distributed fact recovery and its underlying mechanism: false evidence gains collective influence through its adoption and continued propagation by other agents after entering communication.

</details>


### [207] [Group Perspective Matters: Regulating Debate Relationships Can Mitigate Blind Conformity in Multi-Agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03648)
*Hao Wu,Shoucheng Song,Chang Yao,Haoyu Wang,Huaiyu Wan,Youfang Lin,Kai Lv*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: DEAR is a framework that dynamically regulates debate relationships among LLMs to mitigate blind conformity in multi-agent debate, using group evidence and dual RL agents (Selection and Behavior) optimized jointly via multi-agent reinforcement learning, achieving superior performance with lower token consumption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) suffers from blind conformity, where LLMs blindly agree with others. Individual evaluation methods (confidence/perplexity-based) fail to reflect reasoning correctness and can worsen this problem. The key insight is that regulating debate relationships (mutual referencing patterns among agents) from a group interaction perspective is essential to mitigating blind conformity.

Method: The DEAR framework first quantifies consensus and divergence as "group evidence" to capture the debate state. It then operates in three stages: (1) What: perceiving group consultation tendency and uncertainty; (2) Who: a Selection RL-Agent dynamically selects reference peers; (3) How: a Behavior RL-Agent adaptively adjusts generation behaviors. The two RL agents are formulated as a sequential decision-making process and jointly optimized via multi-agent reinforcement learning.

Result: Extensive experiments show DEAR achieves superior performance while significantly reducing token consumption compared to existing MAD approaches.

Conclusion: Shifting from individual evaluation to group interaction and dynamically regulating debate relationships via reinforcement learning is an effective strategy for improving multi-agent debate, both in reasoning quality and efficiency.

Abstract: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) improves the reasoning performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) through multi-round interaction. However, LLMs in MAD are highly susceptible to blind conformity. Existing individual evaluation methods, typically based on confidence or perplexity, fail to reflect the correctness of reasoning and may even exacerbate blind conformity. To address this, we shift the perspective from individual evaluation to group interaction. We define mutual referencing among LLMs as \textbf{Debate Relationships} and recognize that regulating these relationships is the key to mitigating blind conformity. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for \textbf{D}ynamically r\textbf{E}gulating deb\textbf{A}te \textbf{R}elationships (DEAR) from the group perspective. At first, DEAR quantifies consensus and divergence as \textit{group evidence} to capture the debate state. Then, DEAR operates through three stages: 1) What: perceiving group consultation tendency and uncertainty; 2) Who: introducing a Selection RL-Agent to dynamically select reference peers; and 3) How: adopting a Behavior RL-Agent to adaptively adjust generation behaviors. Notably, we formulate the execution of the two RL-Agents as a sequential decision-making process, jointly optimizing via multi-agent reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DEAR achieves superior performance while significantly reducing token consumption.

</details>


### [208] [An Actionable Diagnosis of Multilingual, Multi-Agent Planning Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03735)
*Vikas Pahuja,Jonathan Brokman,Omer Hofman,Tamir Nizri,Daniel Vishna,Seraphina Goldfarb-Tarrant,Kelly Marchisio,Hisashi Kojima,Roman Vainshtein*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Multilingual multi-agent systems fail significantly in non-English languages due to planning-grounding failures. The authors derive a taxonomy of these failures and introduce TART, a representation that makes planning constraints explicit, yielding consistent performance improvements across languages, with a 5.6 pp average gain on multilingual GAIA across 11 languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual multi-agent systems degrade substantially beyond English, but prior work fails to identify how task-critical information is lost when converting user requests into executable plans. Understanding and mitigating these planning-grounding failures is essential for building robust multilingual agentic systems.

Method: The authors (1) study the planner as the request-to-action interface in multi-agent systems, (2) derive an actionable taxonomy of planning-grounding failures from failed real-world task executions using LLM-based analysis, and (3) introduce TART (Taxonomy-Guided Actionable Representation), which explicitly surfaces the taxonomy's key aspects to both the planner and downstream sub-agents.

Result: LLM-based analysis reveals that planning-grounding failures constitute an increasing share of unsuccessful executions as language-resource availability declines, with strongest effects in low-resource languages. TART consistently improves performance across multiple languages, three LLM backbones, two datasets, and two agentic configurations. On multilingual GAIA, TART raises a state-of-the-art system's accuracy by 5.6 percentage points averaged across eleven low- to high-resource languages.

Conclusion: Planning-grounding failures are a critical bottleneck in multilingual multi-agent systems, disproportionately affecting low-resource languages. The proposed taxonomy and TART representation offer an effective mitigation strategy, demonstrating that making planning constraints explicit significantly improves cross-lingual agentic performance.

Abstract: Multilingual multi-agent systems exhibit substantial degradation beyond English, yet prior work rarely identifies how task-critical information is lost when user requests are converted into executable plans. We study the planner in a multi-agent system as the request-to-action interface and derive an actionable taxonomy of planning-grounding failures from failed real-world task executions. LLM-based analysis shows that these failures constitute an increasing share of unsuccessful executions as language-resource availability declines, with the strongest effects in low-resource languages. To test whether the taxonomy supports mitigation, we introduce TART, Taxonomy-Guided Actionable Representation, that makes the taxonomy's key aspects explicit to the planner and downstream sub-agents. Across multiple languages, three LLM backbones, two datasets, and two agentic configurations, TART consistently improves performance. On multilingual GAIA, it raises a state-of-the-art system's accuracy by 5.6 percentage points averaged across eleven languages spanning low- to high-resource settings.

</details>


### [209] [History Matters: Meta-policy Delegation with Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03833)
*Ziqing Lu,Avinash Reddy Mudireddy,Sarra Alqahtani,Weiyu Xu*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper studies delegation in heterogeneous multi-agent systems where agents with different capabilities and costs collaborate on research tasks. The authors develop MARL-based delegation training, extend it to prescribed topologies, and introduce two new frameworks: history-dependent policies for improved coordination and a multi-dimensional monetary mechanism to facilitate collaboration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents will play a critical role in future decision-making systems, but heterogeneous multi-agent systems face resource constraints due to differing member capabilities and operating costs. Effective task delegation is essential for completing research tasks under these constraints, yet conventional MARL methods typically restrict policies to the current state, limiting coordination potential.

Method: The authors develop a MARL-based delegation training approach enabling sequential delegation decisions while minimizing total execution cost. This is extended to scenarios with prescribed delegation topologies. Two novel frameworks are introduced: (1) history-dependent policies where agent decisions depend on both the current MDP state and interaction history (including prior joint actions), and (2) a multi-dimensional monetary mechanism to facilitate collaboration and delegation in MAS.

Result: The paper proposes frameworks showing that history-dependent policy formulations can improve coordination even in fully observable environments where conventional MARL restricts policies to the current state. The multi-dimensional monetary mechanism provides a novel approach for facilitating collaboration and delegation.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous MAS can achieve effective task delegation under resource constraints through MARL-based training with history-dependent policies and monetary mechanisms. The history-dependent formulation notably improves coordination beyond what current-state-only MARL methods can achieve, even in fully observable settings.

Abstract: AI agents are expected to play an increasingly important role in future decision-making systems. In this paper, we consider collaborative systems composed of heterogeneous multi-agent systems (MAS), where their members have different capabilities and operating costs. We study how agents can delegate tasks to one another so that certain research tasks can be completed effectively under resource-constrained scenarios. We first develop a multi-agent reinforcement learning-based (MARL) delegation training that enables agents to make sequential delegation decisions while minimizing the total execution cost. We then extend this approach to MARL with prescribed delegation topologies. Furthermore, we introduce two new frameworks for collaboration and delegation in multi-agent systems. The first framework proposes that an agent's policy depends not only on the current state of the underlying Markov decision process but also on the interaction history, including previous joint actions. This history-dependent formulation can improve coordination even in fully observable environments, where conventional MARL methods typically restrict policies to depend only on the current state. The second framework proposes a novel, potentially multi-dimensional monetary mechanism to facilitate the collaboration and delegation for MAS.

</details>


<div id='cs.IR'></div>

# cs.IR [[Back]](#toc)

### [210] [Knowledge-Geometry Decoupling: Refreshable Pretrained Transfer for Streaming Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02738)
*Zixuan Wang,Yuhong Chen,Yuxuan Zhu,Guidong Lei,Zhiluohan Guo,Yu Zhao,Kun Wang,Bangyang Hong,Kangle Wu,Yabo Ni,Anxiang Zeng,Cong Fu,Hui Li*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: KGD decouples behavioral knowledge (what to learn) from task-specific geometry (how to transfer) in pretrain-transfer recommenders. BMTP replaces next-token prediction with multi-token supervision from related items, while decoupled parameter ownership via cross-attention and ACR enables continual encoder refresh without task-gradient interference. Achieves 4-12% gains on public benchmarks, sustains advantage over production stream, and yields +1.75% GMV and +1.53% ad revenue in Shopee's live A/B test.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial recommenders using pretrain-then-transfer face two underexplored problems: (1) what to learn from behavior sequences when next-token prediction may encode spurious cross-session transitions, and (2) how to transfer knowledge when the pretrained model is continually refreshed, since pretrained knowledge and task-specific geometry impose conflicting optimization demands on shared parameters.

Method: Knowledge-Geometry Decoupling (KGD) addresses both questions: (1) Behavioral Multi-Token Prediction (BMTP) replaces conventional next-token prediction by retaining only collaboratively or semantically related future items as supervision targets, yielding cleaner behavioral knowledge. (2) KGD assigns pretrained knowledge and task-specific geometry to separate parameter sets — a refreshable encoder holds behavioral knowledge, while a task learner reads encoder states via read-only cross-attention and writes task-specific geometry through Anchored Calibration Residual (ACR), which is orthogonal to the pretrained embedding. This decoupled ownership allows continual encoder refresh without task-gradient interference or invalidating downstream adaptation.

Result: KGD improves over strong pretrain-transfer baselines by 4-12% across eight public benchmarks. Over a 90-day production stream, KGD sustains its advantage while baselines show no gains. Fully deployed in Shopee, a live A/B test on Homepage Search yields +1.75% GMV per user and +1.53% advertising revenue.

Conclusion: KGD provides a principled solution to the dual challenges of knowledge extraction from behavior sequences and conflict-free transfer under continual pretrained model refresh. The decoupled architecture proves both theoretically sound and practically valuable, as evidenced by strong offline results and significant online business gains at Shopee scale.

Abstract: Industrial recommenders increasingly adopt the pretrain-then-transfer paradigm, yet behavioral distribution drift raises two questions: what to learn from behavior sequences, and how to transfer the learned knowledge while the pretrained model is continually refreshed. To resolve them, we propose Knowledge-Geometry Decoupling (KGD). For what to learn, conventional next-token prediction treats adjacency as dependency and may encode spurious transitions across unrelated sessions. We introduce Behavioral Multi-Token Prediction (BMTP) to retain only collaboratively or semantically related future items as supervision, yielding cleaner and more transferable behavioral knowledge. For how to transfer, pretrained knowledge and task-specific geometry impose conflicting optimization demands on shared parameters. To handle it, KGD assigns them to separate parameter sets: a refreshable encoder owns behavioral knowledge, while a task learner reads contextualized encoder states through read-only cross-attention and writes task-specific geometry through Anchored Calibration Residual (ACR) orthogonal to the pretrained embedding. The decoupled ownership enables continual knowledge refresh without task-gradient interference or invalidating downstream adaptation. KGD improves over strong pretrain-transfer baselines by 4-12% on eight public benchmarks and sustains its advantage over a 90-day production stream where baselines show no gains. KGD has been fully deployed in Shopee. In a live A/B test on Shopee Homepage Search, it increases GMV per user by 1.75% and advertising revenue by 1.53%, demonstrating its high practical value. We provide the core implementation of KGD at https://github.com/FuCongResearchSquad/KGD4REC.

</details>


### [211] [Search, Inspect, Fetch: Exploiting Boolean Retrieval for Deep-Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02751)
*Shuai Wang,Haodong Chen,Yu Yin,Shengyao Zhuang,Bevan Koopman,Guido Zuccon*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SIEVE is a search-inspect-fetch agent that uses fielded Boolean retrieval (BQL) to filter and rank web documents by their structure (titles, headings, sections), then fetches only selected sections, achieving higher QA accuracy than conventional search-visit agents while using 20.7–50.6% fewer tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep-research agents employ a naive search-visit workflow that retrieves and reads entire web pages without leveraging the addressable structure (titles, headings, sections, metadata) that web sources expose. This results in irrelevant content being carried into the agent's context, wasting tokens and reducing accuracy.

Method: SIEVE introduces a three-phase interface: (1) Search — uses fielded Boolean retrieval (BQL) to filter candidates over specific document fields; (2) Inspect — ranks the admitted set and presents structure-rich result cards showing titles, headings, and metadata; (3) Fetch — retrieves only selected sections rather than whole pages. BQL filtering is applied across all stages to maintain precision.

Result: Across three QA collections, SIEVE outperforms the most accurate conventional Search-Visit configuration on each collection while using 20.7–50.6% fewer tokens. BQL filtering improves all tested rankers, and the accuracy-context advantage holds across different retriever choices and agent backbones.

Conclusion: Exploiting the addressable structure of web documents via fielded Boolean retrieval yields both higher accuracy and greater token efficiency for deep-research agents compared to the standard whole-page search-visit paradigm. Code and data are publicly released.

Abstract: Existing deep-research agents use a search-visit workflow that retrieves and reads whole pages, without considering the addressable structure that web sources expose through titles, headings, sections, and metadata. This prevents agents from directly constraining retrieval to document fields and often carries irrelevant page content into their context. We introduce SIEVE, a search-inspect-fetch interface driven by fielded Boolean retrieval (BQL). SIEVE filters candidates over document fields, ranks the admitted set, presents structure-rich result cards for inspection, and fetches only selected sections. Across three QA collections, SIEVE achieves higher accuracy than the most accurate conventional Search-Visit configuration on each collection while using 20.7-50.6% fewer tokens. Further analyses show that BQL filtering improves all tested rankers and that the accuracy-context advantage persists across retriever choices and agent backbones. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ielab/skim-search-agent.

</details>


### [212] [Field Aware Agent Skill Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02880)
*Paimon Goulart,Liang Wu,Kelly Wan,Evangelos E. Papalexakis,Liangjie Hong*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether preserving the inherent multi-field structure of skills (name, description, body, etc.) improves skill retrieval for lifelong learning agents. By computing sparse and dense similarities per field and combining them via a learned MLP, the field-aware approach consistently outperforms flat concatenation baselines, especially as the skill bank grows larger.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As lifelong learning agents accumulate large skill banks, retrieving the correct skill becomes a critical bottleneck. Current methods concatenate all skill fields into a flat document, ignoring the natural multi-field structure where each field (name, description, body) signals different information about when and how a skill should be used. The authors hypothesize that preserving this structure can improve retrieval performance.

Method: Skills are represented as separate field-level components. Sparse (e.g., BM25) and dense (embedding-based) similarities are computed independently for each field, yielding a tensorized, field-aware representation of the skill bank. Field-level scores are then aggregated either via uniform weighting or a small learned MLP. This is evaluated against concatenated baselines on two benchmarks: SkillRet and SRA-Bench.

Result: Field-aware hybrid retrieval outperforms concatenated baselines. The field-aware MLP achieves 77.95 Recall@10 on SkillRet and 83.78 Recall@10 on SRA-Bench, surpassing learned concatenated baselines. The performance advantage grows as the skill bank size increases, indicating field-aware retrieval is most beneficial in the hardest retrieval settings.

Conclusion: Skill representation matters: simply preserving the natural multi-field structure already present in skill files yields substantial retrieval improvements. Field-aware methods provide stronger and more consistent results, especially at scale, suggesting this approach is particularly valuable for large, lifelong skill banks.

Abstract: As lifelong learning agents accumulate lifelong growing skill banks, retrieving the correct skill becomes an increasingly important bottleneck. Most current skill retrieval methods treat each skill as one flat document by concatenating fields such as the name, description, and body. However, skills are naturally structured, multi-field objects, where each field provides different information about when and how the skill should be used. In this work, we study whether preserving this structure improves skill retrieval. We represent each skill as its separate components, and compute sparse and dense similarities for each field independently, exposing a naturally tensorized, field-aware representation of the skill bank. We then combine these field-level scores either with uniform weights or with a small learned MLP. Across two different skill retrieval benchmarks, SkillRet and SRA-Bench, we find that keeping fields separate improves hybrid retrieval, and learning over the field-level scores gives the strongest and most consistent results. Our field-aware MLP reaches $77.95$ Recall@10 on SkillRet and $83.78$ Recall@10 on SRA-Bench, outperforming the corresponding concatenated learned baselines. We also find that the advantage grows as the skill bank becomes larger, suggesting that field-aware skill retrieval becomes especially useful in the setting where retrieval is most difficult. Our results show that skill representation itself matters, and that simply preserving the structure already present in skill files can substantially improve retrieval.

</details>


### [213] [Coverage Matters: MarginMerge for Compressing Multi-Vector Visual Document Retrievers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02969)
*Ailar Mahdizadeh,Aria Salari,Sohail Rajabi,Shahriar Mirabbasi,Panos Nasiopoulos,Alireza Morsali*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: MarginMerge compresses multi-vector visual document retrieval indexes by selecting query-relevant coverage-aware anchors and synthesizing cluster representatives, achieving 90–95% vector reduction while retaining 97–99% of nDCG@5 compared to uncompressed indexes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-vector visual document retrievers (ColPali, ColQwen) produce prohibitively large indexes due to fine-grained patch embeddings and incur costly late-interaction scoring. Existing compression methods select patches independently by salience, but effective compression should instead preserve query-relevant coverage — the diverse document regions that may serve as the strongest MaxSim match across different queries.

Method: MarginMerge is a compression method operating on frozen multi-vector retrievers during indexing. It selects coverage-aware anchors, clusters document patches, and employs a lightweight shared network to synthesize one representative embedding per cluster. The standard MaxSim retrieval interface is preserved unchanged.

Result: Across six datasets on ColQwen2.5 and ColPali, MarginMerge achieves the highest matched query-agnostic average at 5% and 10% vector retention. It preserves 97–99% of average nDCG@5 while reducing stored vectors by 90–95%. At 5% retention, it reduces ranking flips by ~41% on average compared to geometric merging across all ColQwen2.5 datasets. The model transfers to unseen datasets and retention ratios without retraining.

Conclusion: Coverage-aware compression via MarginMerge substantially outperforms salience-based patch selection for multi-vector visual document retrieval, maintaining near-uncompressed retrieval quality at a fraction of the index size, with strong generalization properties.

Abstract: Multi-vector visual document retrievers such as ColPali and ColQwen achieve strong retrieval by storing fine-grained patch embeddings, but this produces large indexes and costly late-interaction scoring. We argue that effective compression should preserve query-relevant coverage, meaning the diverse document regions that may become the strongest MaxSim match across queries, rather than selecting patches independently by salience. This view also explains why dense rendered pages are easier to compress than natural images. We introduce MarginMerge, a compression method for frozen multi-vector retrievers. It selects coverage-aware anchors, clusters document patches, and uses a lightweight shared network to synthesize one representative per cluster. Compression is performed once during indexing, while retrieval keeps the standard MaxSim interface. Across six datasets on both ColQwen2.5 and ColPali, MarginMerge achieves the highest matched query-agnostic average at 5% and 10% vector retention. Compared with the uncompressed index using the same backbone, it preserves between 97% and 99% of average nDCG@5 while reducing stored document vectors by between 90% and 95%. At 5% retention, it also reduces ranking flips relative to geometric merging on all six ColQwen2.5 datasets by approximately 41% on average. The same model transfers to unseen datasets and retention ratios without retraining.

</details>


### [214] [Position Bias Undermines Preference Consistency in Listwise LLM-Based Reranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03091)
*Ethan Bito,Yongli Ren,Estrid He*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper studies position bias in LLM-based listwise rerankers for recommender systems, finding that candidate ordering affects pairwise preferences, global preference structures, and ranked outputs. The authors introduce a multi-level evaluation framework and demonstrate that mitigating exposure bias alone does not guarantee ranking consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based rerankers process recommendation candidates as serialized lists, but candidates form an unordered set. The arbitrary serialization order should not affect ranking outcomes. However, decoder-only LLMs exhibit position bias, and it is unclear how deeply this bias penetrates the induced ranking process—beyond final list changes—at pairwise, global structural, and output levels.

Method: The authors treat rankings produced under equivalent candidate permutations as observations of an induced preference system and introduce a three-level evaluation framework: (1) pairwise preference instability, (2) global preference inconsistency (e.g., Condorcet cycles), and (3) listwise output consistency. Experiments span multiple LLMs, datasets, and list lengths, comparing these consistency measures against recommendation effectiveness and marginal position-exposure bias.

Result: The three consistency measures are closely aligned across settings but can diverge from recommendation effectiveness and marginal position-exposure bias. Improving relevance or flattening exposure across positions does not necessarily restore stable pairwise preferences, globally coherent preference structures, or consistent ranked outputs. Reducing marginal exposure skew is insufficient to establish ranking-function validity.

Conclusion: Position bias in LLM-based rerankers manifests as fundamental preference instability and structural inconsistency, not merely marginal exposure skew. Mitigating exposure bias is insufficient; ensuring ranking-function validity requires addressing deeper preference coherence. This motivates future work on permutation-invariant LLM ranking mechanisms.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising listwise rerankers for recommender systems, but their reliability under equivalent candidate permutations remains unclear. Since recommendation candidates form an unordered set, a reranker should not depend on the arbitrary order used to serialize them. However, decoder-only LLM rerankers can allow input order to affect model scores, pairwise preferences, and rankings. We study how position bias affects the ranking process induced by LLM-based rerankers. Instead of measuring only changes in final ranked lists, we treat rankings produced under equivalent candidate permutations as observations of an induced preference system. We introduce an evaluation framework measuring pairwise preference instability, global preference inconsistency, and listwise output consistency. This framework characterizes candidate-order sensitivity at the pairwise, global, and output levels. Experiments across multiple LLMs, datasets, and list lengths show that these consistency measures are closely aligned, but can diverge from recommendation effectiveness and marginal position-exposure bias. Improving relevance or flattening exposure across positions does not necessarily restore stable pairwise preferences, globally coherent preference structures, or consistent ranked outputs. These results show that reducing marginal exposure skew is insufficient to establish ranking-function validity in LLM-based reranking. Code is available at https://github.com/ejbito/InvariRank .

</details>


### [215] [Attacking and Defending Multi-Agent Collaborative Filtering Systems Through Connectivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03272)
*Anjun Hu,Hanting Xie,Saranya Govindan,Jas Kandola,Kurt Cutajar*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper adapts multi-agent system (MAS) attacks and defenses to LLM-powered agent-based collaborative filtering (CF), systematically evaluating how two connectivity axes—candidate count and catalog concentration—shape attack/defense outcomes in the AgentCF framework, revealing role asymmetries, non-monotonic temporal dynamics, and potential for epidemic-inspired metrics in robustness assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent CF systems inherit vulnerabilities from both data-driven recommendation and multi-agent interactions, but how connectivity modulates these vulnerabilities is poorly understood. Understanding this relationship could enable more robust recommendation pipelines.

Method: The authors adapt attacks and defenses from general MAS literature to the agent-based CF setting and systematically evaluate them under varied connectivity within the AgentCF framework. Connectivity is characterized along two axes: (i) candidate count (items per turn per user) and (ii) catalog concentration (item catalog overlap across users). Epidemic-inspired static metrics are also explored for ranking CF configurations by expected attack outcomes.

Result: Partial transferability of MAS attacks/defenses to agentic CF is confirmed. Connectivity strongly shapes outcomes, with asymmetries between user and item agent roles, non-monotonic temporal dynamics in attack efficacy, and divergent patterns across dissemination vs. extraction attack goals. Epidemic-inspired static metrics show preliminary promise for cost-efficient robustness ranking.

Conclusion: Connectivity is a critical modulating factor for vulnerability in multi-agent CF systems. Characterizing its influence across attack types and agent roles provides a foundation for developing more robust, connectivity-aware recommendation pipelines, with static epidemic metrics offering a potential path toward efficient robustness assessment.

Abstract: Multi-agent collaborative filtering (CF) systems coordinate autonomous LLM-powered user and item agents through natural-language interaction to refine preferences and generate recommendations. These systems inherit vulnerabilities from both their data-driven nature and their multi-agent interactions, which manifest in distinct ways. Understanding how connectivity modulates vulnerability in these systems could facilitate the development of more robust recommendation pipelines.
  In this work, we adapt attacks and defenses from the general multi-agent systems (MAS) literature to the agent-based CF setting, evaluating them under systematically varied connectivity in the AgentCF framework, where CF connectivity is characterized along two axes: (i) candidate count (the number of item candidates per turn per user, measuring user-side interaction density) and (ii) catalog concentration (the degree of item catalog overlap across users).
  Our contributions include: (1) Adaptation: we reproduce MAS-inspired attacks and defenses in the agentic CF domain, confirming partial transferability of original observations. (2) Characterization: we characterize how the two aspects of connectivity shape attack and defense outcomes, revealing role asymmetries between user and item agents, non-monotonic temporal dynamics in attack efficacy, and divergent patterns across dissemination and extraction attack goals. Additionally, as an exploratory extension, we assess the applicability of epidemic-inspired static metrics in ranking CF configurations by expected attack outcome, potentially enabling cost-efficient robustness assessment. Implementation is available at https://github.com/anjunhu/ConnACF

</details>


### [216] [LLM-Derived Priors for Thompson Sampling in Cold-Start Comment Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03382)
*Eugene Lee,Oseong Choi,Byungsoo Kang,Taeyeong Jang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper proposes using LLMs to extract semantic signals from user-generated text comments, converting them into informative Bayesian priors to warm-start Thompson sampling for online recommendation, addressing cold-start problems. A/B/C testing shows LLM-based priors yield largest gains in sparse-feedback regimes, with distinct funnel-level effects and demographic heterogeneity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-armed bandit algorithms like Thompson sampling suffer from cold-start limitations when new arms lack interaction history. The authors recognize that in text-rich recommendation settings (user-generated comments), semantic content can reveal appeal before sufficient feedback accumulates, motivating the use of LLMs to bridge this gap.

Method: The authors use LLMs to extract semantic signals from comment text and convert them into informative Bayesian priors for Thompson sampling. They design two prior types: a Gender Prior capturing demographic-affinity cues and a Content Prior capturing title-specific identity cues. Posteriors are maintained and updated separately for each gender-age segment. A real-world online A/B/C test compares these against a uniform prior baseline.

Result: LLM-based priors prove most beneficial in sparse-feedback regimes, with the largest gains emerging after a small amount of interaction evidence has accumulated. Prior design leads to distinct funnel-level effects. Click-oriented alignment is strongest for the Gender Prior. Treatment effects vary substantially across demographic segments.

Conclusion: LLM-derived priors serve as a practical warm-start mechanism for text-rich bandit recommendation, though deployment involves trade-offs. The work demonstrates that semantic signals from LLMs can effectively mitigate cold-start problems while revealing nuanced effects across prior designs and demographic groups.

Abstract: Multi-armed bandit algorithms, especially Thompson sampling, are widely used in online recommendation. Despite their ability to adapt from online feedback, these methods often suffer from cold-start limitations when newly introduced arms have little or no interaction history. In our setting, the candidate arms are user-generated textual comments, whose semantic content can reveal a title's appeal before sufficient interaction feedback is available. We therefore use large language models (LLMs) to extract semantic signals from comment text and convert them into informative Bayesian priors that warm-start Thompson sampling under sparse early-stage feedback. To account for aggregate segment-level differences in response patterns, we maintain and update posteriors separately for each gender-age segment. In a real-world online A/B/C test, we compare a uniform prior with two LLM-based designs: a Gender Prior for demographic-affinity cues and a Content Prior for title-specific identity cues. The results show that LLM-based priors are most beneficial in sparse-feedback regimes -- with the largest gains emerging once a small amount of interaction evidence has accumulated -- and that prior design leads to distinct funnel-level effects. We further analyze prior-reward alignment and demographic heterogeneity, finding that click-oriented alignment is strongest for the Gender Prior and that treatment effects vary substantially across demographic segments. These findings suggest that LLM-derived priors can serve as a practical warm-start mechanism for text-rich bandit recommendation, while also revealing deployment trade-offs.

</details>


### [217] [Training Documents Reranker with Search Rubrics for Deep Research Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03527)
*Wenhan Liu,Yu Lu,Qiaolin Xia,Hui Xu,Tong Zhao,Jian Xi,Yutao Zhu,Haijin Liang,Haibo Shi,Hao Wang,Zhicheng Dou*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Proposes search-oriented rubrics to define high-quality document set requirements for agent queries, and trains RubricRanker via a two-stage framework (SFT + RL) to select optimal subsets, outperforming baselines on deep research and RAG benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrievers select documents individually via relevance matching, but top-k documents that are individually relevant may not collectively satisfy an agent query's complex needs (e.g., diversity, conciseness, authority). There is a gap between per-document relevance and set-level quality.

Method: Hierarchical search rubrics are synthesized by an LLM to explicitly define set-level requirements per query. RubricRanker, a document reranker, is trained with a two-stage framework: (1) rubrics-guided supervised fine-tuning, and (2) rubric-based reinforcement learning, to select high-quality document subsets from retrieved candidates.

Result: RubricRanker outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.6 points on four deep research benchmarks and demonstrates strong generalization on five RAG benchmarks.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling set-level quality criteria via search rubrics and training a reranker accordingly significantly improves document selection for both deep research agents and general RAG systems.

Abstract: Retrieval systems help deep research agents generate high-quality answers by providing relevant documents. However, existing retrievers typically select documents through relevance matching, while individually well-matched top-$k$ documents may not form a \textit{set} that satisfies the complex information needs of an agent query (\eg, diverse, concise and authoritative documents). In this paper, we propose search-oriented rubrics that \textit{explicitly} define the requirements that high-quality document sets should satisfy for each agent query. Our search rubrics are organized into a hierarchical structure and synthesized using a powerful LLM. Based on these search rubrics, we further train a document reranker \textbf{RubricRanker} to select a high-quality subset from retrieved documents. We design a two-stage training framework that consists of rubrics-guided supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RubricRanker outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.6 points on four deep research benchmarks and generalizes well to five RAG benchmarks.

</details>


### [218] [Conditionally Identifiable Latent-Environment Modeling for Out-of-Distribution Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03647)
*Qianqian Wang,Wenwu Gong,Yunshan Li,Zhenqing Wu,Ruili Wang,Lili Yang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: CILER is a recommendation framework that models latent environments using user-conditioned exponential families and feature-indexed polynomials to achieve conditionally identifiable OOD recommendation, with theoretical guarantees on identifiability and excess risk bounds, empirically improving OOD ranking across three datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OOD recommendation suffers from preference shifts driven by latent environments, but existing methods lack statistical grounding—the meaning of the latent environment and its causal effect on preferences remain underdetermined. This motivates a formal identifiability framework.

Method: CILER formulates the problem as Conditionally Identifiable Risk-Aware Recommendation (CI-RR). It models the latent environment via a user-conditioned exponential family distribution and captures environment-to-preference effects using feature-indexed polynomials. Prediction proceeds by marginalizing item probabilities over the inferred posterior environment distribution. Identifiability is established under three conditions: sufficient variation, correct specification, and decoder regularity. An excess risk bound is derived linking deployment log-risk to environment-inference error.

Result: Controlled studies validate the observable consequences of sufficient variation and model specification. On three real-world datasets, CILER improves all twelve OOD ranking metrics under feature, temporal, and geographical distribution shifts within shared support.

Conclusion: CILER provides a statistically principled, identifiable approach to OOD recommendation by explicitly modeling latent environments, offering both theoretical guarantees (identifiability up to equivalence class, excess risk bounds) and consistent empirical gains across diverse shift types.

Abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) recommendation is vulnerable to preference shifts induced by a latent environment. Existing methods can infer latent states from logged interactions, yet the statistical meaning of the latent environment and its effect on preference remain underdetermined. We formulate this task as conditionally identifiable risk-aware recommendation (CI-RR) and propose Conditionally Identifiable Latent-Environment Recommendation (CILER). CILER uses a user-conditioned exponential family to model the latent environment and a feature-indexed polynomial to specify how it changes preference. It predicts by marginalizing item probabilities over the inferred environment distribution. Under sufficient variation, correct specification, and decoder regularity, CILER identifies the environment-sensitive representation up to the stated equivalence class. We further bound excess deployment log-risk by environment-inference error. Controlled studies test the observable consequences of sufficient variation and model specification. Experiments on three datasets show that CILER improves all twelve OOD ranking metrics under feature, temporal, and geographical shifts within shared support.

</details>


### [219] [SITA: Semantic Interest Tokens for Target-Aware Compression in Long-Sequence Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03692)
*Rui Zhou,Bo Chen,Qinglin Jia,Jiezhou Ji,Chaoyi Ma,Ruiming Tang,Hao Wang,Enhong Chen*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SITA proposes a target-aware compression framework for long-sequence recommendation that organizes compressed user interests into semantic structures using learned semantic identifiers, enabling adaptive, target-specific user representations without sacrificing inference efficiency or scalability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-sequence user behavior modeling methods face a trade-off: target-aware retrieval methods require expensive target-dependent inference, while target-independent compression methods sacrifice personalization. The key challenge is achieving target-aware modeling while maintaining the efficiency and scalability of compressed representations.

Method: SITA organizes compressed user interests into semantic structures via parallel semantic quantization, assigning semantic identifiers. During inference, conditioned on the target item's semantic identifier, SITA adaptively aggregates corresponding structured interests to construct a target-specific user representation.

Result: Extensive experiments on public datasets and a large-scale industrial dataset show SITA consistently outperforms representative baselines while maintaining strong scalability.

Conclusion: SITA effectively bridges the gap between target-aware modeling and compressed representation efficiency, demonstrating strong potential for real-world recommender systems.

Abstract: As user behavior histories continue to grow on modern Internet platforms, effectively modeling long behavior sequences has become crucial for predicting user interests in candidate items. Existing methods have evolved along two directions. One line dynamically retrieves target-relevant behaviors from long histories, enabling target-aware modeling but requiring target-dependent computation during inference. The other line compresses entire behavior sequences into compact user representations, achieving high efficiency and scalability but sacrificing target-specific adaptation due to target-independent encoding. The key challenge is therefore to enable target-aware modeling while preserving the efficiency and scalability of compressed user representations. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{SITA}, a target-aware compression framework for long-sequence recommendation. SITA enables target-aware compression by organizing compressed interests into semantic structures through semantic identifiers learned via parallel semantic quantization. Conditioned on the semantic identifier of the target item, SITA adaptively aggregates the corresponding structured interests to construct the target-specific user representation. Extensive experiments on public datasets and a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate that SITA consistently outperforms representative baselines while maintaining strong scalability, highlighting its strong potential for real-world recommender systems.

</details>


### [220] [LegalPincite: Multi-level Legal Information Retrieval Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03756)
*Theresia Veronika Rampisela,Henrik Palmer Olsen,Giovanni Colavizza*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper introduces a large-scale legal IR dataset from CJEU judgments featuring masked queries, a complete paragraph corpus, and paragraph-level citation ground truth with human validation, addressing data leakage and oversimplified retrieval settings in prior datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing legal IR datasets either lack paragraph-level citation annotations or, when they do include them, suffer from two critical flaws: (1) data leakage from citation information present in query text, and (2) artificial removal of non-cited/non-citing paragraphs from the corpus. These issues create unrealistic retrieval settings and inflate performance metrics, undermining rigorous evaluation of legal IR methods.

Method: The authors construct a dataset from CJEU judgments, featuring masked case/paragraph queries with citation information removed, a complete corpus containing all paragraphs (not just cited/citing ones), and both case-level and paragraph-level ground-truth citations. Partial human expert validation is performed to ensure annotation quality. The dataset supports three retrieval granularities: case-to-case, paragraph-to-case, and paragraph-to-paragraph.

Result: The resulting dataset, hosted on HuggingFace, is a large-scale, publicly available resource for legal IR that enables realistic evaluation across multiple query-document levels without the data leakage and corpus truncation issues of prior datasets.

Conclusion: By providing a realistic, multi-level legal IR benchmark with masked queries, a complete corpus, and validated paragraph-level ground truth, this dataset enables both more robust method development and more trustworthy evaluation in legal information retrieval, particularly for pinpoint citation tasks.

Abstract: A common task in legal Information Retrieval (IR) is to find relevant legal sources from case-law collections. While legal practice often requires pinpoint citations (pincites) to specific case paragraphs, most existing public legal IR datasets lack paragraph-level citation annotations. Yet, publicly available datasets with such information contain data leakage in the query text and exclude paragraphs that are neither citing nor cited from the corpora, creating an unrealistic and oversimplified retrieval setting, potentially leading to inflated performance. To address these limitations, we contribute a large-scale legal IR dataset constructed from Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) judgments. The dataset contains: (i) masked case/paragraph queries, with removed citation information; (ii) a corpus that includes all paragraphs; and (iii) case- and paragraph-level ground-truth citations, with partial human expert validation. Our dataset supports both the development and rigorous evaluation of legal IR methods, at multiple query-document levels (case-to-case, paragraph-to-case, and paragraph-to-paragraph retrieval). Link to dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/theresiavr/legalpincite

</details>


### [221] [ATLAS: Learning to Recommend Across Unseen Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03899)
*Pervez Shaik,Prosenjit Biswas,Abhinav Thorat,Ravi Kolla,Niranjan Pedanekar*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: ATLAS is a multi-source domain generalization framework for recommender systems that learns domain-invariant user-item representations from multiple heterogeneous source domains, enabling zero-shot recommendation on entirely unseen target domains without retraining or LLM pretraining. It combines Gromov-Wasserstein alignment, adversarial training, and residual vector quantization to outperform state-of-the-art baselines by 24% average HitRate gain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recommender systems are inherently domain-bound — a model trained on one domain cannot be directly deployed to recommend items from an unseen domain (e.g., movies → groceries). Existing solutions require target-domain adaptation, restricted knowledge transfer, or leverage LLMs. The authors challenge this paradigm by asking whether recommendation knowledge from multiple heterogeneous source domains alone can generalize zero-shot to unseen domains.

Method: ATLAS (multi-source Recommendation Domain Generalization framework) integrates three key components: (1) Gromov-Wasserstein alignment to preserve relational structure among users across domains; (2) an adversarial objective that renders item representations domain-indistinguishable; and (3) Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) codebooks that compress user/item embeddings into a discrete latent space, capturing hierarchical interaction patterns while suppressing domain-specific variation. The model is trained on multiple disjoint source domains simultaneously.

Result: Trained on five Amazon domains and evaluated on ten unseen domains, ATLAS outperforms sequential, graph-based, cross-domain, quantization-based, and LLM-based baselines on most target domains, achieving an average relative HitRate improvement of 24%. Ablation studies validate each component, and analysis reveals a strong source-domain diversity effect — increasing source heterogeneity significantly boosts zero-shot transfer performance.

Conclusion: Recommendation domain generalization is established as a viable and promising paradigm for zero-shot recommendation. ATLAS demonstrates that purely structural knowledge distilled from diverse source domains can transfer effectively to unseen domains without relying on target-domain adaptation or language-model pretraining.

Abstract: Recommender systems remain domain-bound: a model trained on one interaction environment typically requires retraining or target-domain adaptation before it can operate on a new catalogue. A recommender trained on movies cannot be directly deployed to recommend groceries or video games. Existing approaches mitigate this by transferring restricted forms of recommendation knowledge, adapting to the target domain, or leveraging large language models (LLMs) for transferable representations. We instead ask whether recommendation-specific knowledge learned solely from multiple heterogeneous domains can generalize to entirely unseen domains without target-domain adaptation or language-model pretraining. We introduce ATLAS, a multi-source recommendation domain generalization framework that learns a shared, domain-invariant user-item representation from disjoint source domains, enabling zero-shot recommendation on unseen domains. ATLAS combines a Gromov-Wasserstein alignment that preserves how users relate to one another across domains, an adversarial objective that makes item representations indistinguishable across domains, and residual vector quantization (RVQ) codebooks that compress user and item embeddings into a discrete latent space, capturing hierarchical interaction patterns while suppressing domain-specific variation. Trained on five Amazon domains and applied directly to ten unseen domains, ATLAS outperforms state-of-the-art sequential, graph-based, cross-domain, quantization-based, and LLM-based baselines on most unseen domains, with an average relative gain in HitRate of 24%. Ablations and representation analyses validate each component, and we identify a pronounced source-domain diversity effect: increasing source heterogeneity substantially improves zero-shot transfer. ATLAS establishes recommendation domain generalization as a promising paradigm for zero-shot recommendation.

</details>
