To address these limitations, we propose Causal Context-based Agentic Reasoning (CLEAR), a novel multi-agent vulnerability detection framework integrated with a causal knowledge graph. CLEAR systematically constructs a Vulnerability Causal Knowledge Graph (VCKG) that models the causal chains between entrypoints, preconditions, root causes, and fix intents across vulnerability instances. Leveraging this structured knowledge, four specialized agents, including the Collector, Claim, Critic, and Judge, collaboratively verify vulnerability hypotheses through retrieved causal contexts. Experimental results on C/C++ and Java vulnerability benchmarks demonstrate that CLEAR improves Pair-Correct (P-C) performance by 130.7% and 71.56% over state-of-the-art approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of causal knowledge graph-guided reasoning for automated vulnerability detection.

</details>


### [266] [SpreadMark: Robust Image Watermarking via Spread-Spectrum Embedding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03165)
*Wei Song,Yuxin Cao,Zhenchang Xing,Liming Zhu,Jin Song Dong,Yulei Sui,Jingling Xue*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SpreadMark revisits classical spread-spectrum watermarking within a neural post-hoc architecture, spreading each message bit as a dense pseudo-random codeword across the entire image. This dense spreading increases the budget required for removal, making SpreadMark the only method retaining high detection under both regeneration and latent-space sparsification attacks, while maintaining competitive robustness to JPEG compression and additive noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Invisible watermarks for deepfake detection and provenance tracking must resist both incidental distortions and deliberate removal. Existing neural encoder-decoder watermarking schemes suffer from fragility because each message bit occupies only a small fraction of the image, meaning an attacker only needs to disturb that narrow region. A more resilient approach is needed that raises the removal cost.

Method: SpreadMark spreads each message bit as a dense pseudo-random codeword over the entire image, then recovers it via matched-filtering of a learned cover-suppressed chip representation. It employs a parallel convolutional decoding path and sparsification-aware training. A conditional chip-space analysis under a codeword-independent perturbation model formally demonstrates that dense spreading increases the perturbation budget required to disrupt matched-filter recovery.

Result: Evaluated on COCO and DIV2K against nine competing schemes, SpreadMark was the only method retaining high detection performance under both regeneration and latent-space sparsification settings. It also exhibited competitive robustness against JPEG compression and additive noise, while maintaining imperceptible watermarking with high perceptual quality on both datasets.

Conclusion: Dense spreading of watermarks via spread-spectrum principles, when combined with modern neural architectures and matched-filter recovery, provides a significantly more robust post-hoc watermarking solution that withstands both regeneration-based and sparsification-based removal attempts without sacrificing image quality.

Abstract: Invisible image watermarks are increasingly used for deepfake detection and provenance tracking, where they must survive not only incidental distortions but also deliberate removal. We revisit spread-spectrum embedding, a classical watermarking principle, inside a modern neural post-hoc watermarking architecture. Our starting point is a measurement: in existing encoder-decoder schemes each message bit occupies only a small fraction of the image, a shared contributing factor to their fragility, since removal then need only disturb the region a bit occupies. SpreadMark instead spreads each bit as a dense pseudo-random codeword over the whole image and recovers it by matched-filtering a learned cover-suppressed chip representation, with a parallel convolutional decoding path and sparsification-aware training. A conditional chip-space analysis shows that, under a codeword-independent perturbation model, dense spreading increases the budget required to disrupt matched-filter recovery. Evaluated on COCO and DIV2K against nine schemes, SpreadMark is the only evaluated method retaining high detection under both the regeneration and the latent-space sparsification settings we test, with competitive JPEG and additive-noise robustness. It keeps the embedded watermark imperceptible, maintaining high perceptual quality on both COCO and DIV2K.

</details>


### [267] [Test-time reasoning effort and unauthorized tool use in language-model agents: a prespecified equivalence study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03169)
*Xiaonan Xu,Wenjing Wu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This study tests whether varying the reasoning-effort parameter in GPT-5.6 affects the rate of unauthorized (policy-prohibited) tool use by language-model agents. Across 840 trajectories under two model tiers and 14 TRIO-20 scenarios, no unauthorized tool calls occurred. Higher reasoning effort increased rule-probing behavior but did not induce policy violations, with equivalence testing confirming effort does not meaningfully change violation rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-model agents executing multi-step tool-calling workflows are subject to access-control policies, yet it is unknown whether the reasoning-effort parameter — which operators routinely adjust for cost/latency trade-offs — also alters the likelihood of unauthorized tool use. No prior study had tested this via direct manipulation within a single model, motivating a rigorous, preregistered experiment.

Method: The authors used GPT-5.6 across two tiers (Terra, Sol) and manipulated reasoning effort (low vs. max) within the TRIO-20 benchmark — 14 confirmatory scenarios of matched workplace triads where a prohibited tool call is either (a) effective with stated metric impact, (b) effective but discoverable only via rule inspection, or (c) ineffective. All three conditions share one code base, differing only in two configuration fields; prompts and tool sets were identical. Analyses were fully prespecified in a frozen plan. Exact one-sided 95% confidence limits and an interaction estimand with simultaneous exact 95% interval were computed, with equivalence tested against a ±7.01 percentage-point margin.

Result: Across 840 trajectories, zero unauthorized tool calls occurred. One-sided 95% upper limits placed violation rates below 3.50% (Terra, n=84) and 5.21% (Sol, n=56). The interaction estimand's simultaneous exact 95% interval of ±4.34 pp on Terra fell within the ±7.01 pp equivalence margin. Raising effort did increase rule-probing rates in all conditions, most notably where probing yielded no instrumental payoff — a pattern inconsistent with targeted-search hypotheses (−14.3 pp, 95% CI −27.4 to +1.2).

Conclusion: Increasing reasoning effort in GPT-5.6 does not elevate unauthorized tool-use rates, as confirmed by equivalence testing. However, effort does alter agent behavior by increasing rule-inspection (probing), especially in conditions where such inspection lacks practical utility. This dissociation suggests that higher reasoning effort makes agents more inquisitive without making them more likely to violate access-control policies.

Abstract: Language-model agents that execute multi-step workflows through tool calls operate under access-control policies that restrict which operations each role may perform. The APIs serving these agents expose a reasoning-effort parameter that operators adjust for cost and latency. Whether this parameter also changes the rate of unauthorized tool use has not been tested by direct manipulation within a single model. We vary reasoning effort (low, max) inside GPT-5.6 across the 14 confirmatory scenarios of TRIO-20, a suite of 20 matched workplace triads in which a policy-prohibited tool call is effective and its effect on the target metric is stated in the environment, effective but discoverable only through rule inspection, or ineffective. The three conditions derive from one code base and differ in two configuration fields, with identical prompts and tool sets. All analyses were prespecified in a frozen plan before confirmatory collection. Across 840 trajectories and two model tiers, no unauthorized tool call occurred. Exact one-sided 95% limits place each arm's violation rate below 3.50% (Terra, n = 84) and 5.21% (Sol, n = 56). The interaction estimand, with a simultaneous exact 95% interval of $\pm 4.34$ percentage points on Terra, lies inside the $\pm 7.01$-point equivalence margin. Raising effort did change behaviour, but only in inspection: rule-probe rates rose in all conditions, most where probing carried no instrumental payoff, a pattern inconsistent with the hypothesis of targeted search ($-14.3$ points, 95% CI $-27.4$ to $+1.2$). Raw trajectories are released at https://github.com/WenJing95/trio-20.

</details>


### [268] [Attribute-based Undetectable Watermarking for Generative AI Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03174)
*Miryam Mi-Ying Huang,Chung-Wei Lee,Max Raffel,Er-Cheng Tang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces attribute-based watermarking for generative AI, enabling fine-grained, policy-controlled watermark detection. Detection keys are constrained by policies over attributes, preventing misuse like sanitization, scope abuse, and user profiling. The scheme is formally proven secure and empirically validated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cryptographic watermarking methods provide undetectability but lack safe delegation of detection capabilities — unrestricted detection keys enable malicious detectors to sanitize watermarks, abuse detection scope, or profile users.

Method: The authors construct an attribute-based watermarking scheme integrating constrained pseudorandom functions (CPRFs), pseudorandom error-correcting codes, and randomness recovery procedures. Each output is tagged with attributes; detection keys are policy-constrained so they only detect outputs whose attributes satisfy the key's policy.

Result: The scheme is formalized with security properties (consistency, adaptive robustness to bounded corruptions, undetectability, soundness) and proven secure under standard cryptographic assumptions. A prototype implementation and empirical evaluation demonstrate practicality and effectiveness.

Conclusion: Attribute-based watermarking is the first approach to provide fine-grained, policy-controlled detection for generative AI, effectively mitigating delegation-related security risks while remaining practical.

Abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly produce content whose provenance is difficult to verify, motivating watermarking techniques for identifying model-generated outputs. Existing cryptographic watermarking methods provide strong undetectability guarantees: without a detection key, watermarked outputs are computationally indistinguishable from unwatermarked ones. However, these approaches do not address the crucial deployment challenge of how to safely delegate detection capabilities. With an unrestricted detection key, a malicious detector may use the detection key beyond its intended scope, enabling watermark sanitization, scope abuse, and user profiling.
  To mitigate this safety concern, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first \emph{attribute-based watermarking} for generative AI models, providing fine-grained, policy-controlled watermark detection. In our approach, each generated output is associated with attributes, and each detection key is \emph{constrained by a policy} on potential attributes. A detection key can only be used to detect watermarked outputs whose attributes satisfy the corresponding policy, while watermarked outputs that fall outside the policy remain computationally indistinguishable from unwatermarked ones. We construct such an attribute-based watermarking scheme and formalize its security properties, including consistency, adaptive robustness to bounded corruptions, undetectability, and soundness, along with a security proof under standard cryptographic assumptions. Our construction integrates constrained pseudorandom functions, pseudorandom error-correcting codes, and randomness recovery procedures with generative AI models. Finally, we implement a prototype and an empirical evaluation, demonstrating that attribute-based watermarking is both effective and practical.

</details>


### [269] [MalTotal: Cost-Effective and Language-Agnostic Malicious Code Poisoning Detection for Millions of Repositories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03232)
*Jian Zhao,Shenao Wang,Qingyang Wu,Yanjie Zhao,Xiao Cheng,Haoyu Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MalTotal is a scalable, cost-effective, language-agnostic framework for detecting malicious code in open-source software. It uses LLM-assisted semantic reasoning and hybrid semantic slicing to identify malicious behavior while drastically reducing token consumption. It achieves 93.1% F1 across 5 languages, cuts analysis costs by ~94%, and discovered 564 previously unknown malicious repositories in a 120K-repo GitHub study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current malicious code detection methods (heuristic, learning-based, LLM-based) are language-specific, generalize poorly, and incur high analysis costs, making them impractical for large-scale, multi-language OSS ecosystem monitoring.

Method: MalTotal employs three core components: (1) LLM-assisted semantic reasoning to identify sensitive APIs across languages, (2) hybrid semantic slicing that combines static and semantic analysis to isolate malicious code contexts, and (3) behavioral reconstruction that synthesizes these slices into a coherent malicious behavior representation for classification, significantly reducing the input size fed to LLMs.

Result: MalTotal outperforms 8 SOTA baselines with an average F1 of 93.1% across Java, Python, JavaScript, Go, and Ruby. Hybrid slicing reduces LLM token consumption by 94.0%, lowering analysis cost from $86.25 to $5.19 on 2,168 repositories. In a large-scale scan of 120K GitHub repos (7.3M+ files), it uncovered 564 unknown malicious repositories across multiple languages at a total cost of $338.

Conclusion: MalTotal demonstrates that language-agnostic, LLM-assisted semantic reasoning combined with hybrid slicing is a practical and highly cost-effective approach for large-scale malicious code detection, significantly outperforming existing methods while dramatically reducing operational costs.

Abstract: The widespread adoption of open source software (OSS) has introduced significant security risks, with malicious code poisoning attacks increasingly targeting public package registries and open-source platforms. Existing detection approaches, including heuristic-, learning-, and LLM-based methods, suffer from language-specific designs, limited generalization, and high analysis costs, making them unsuitable for large-scale multi-language analysis. To address these challenges, we propose MalTotal, a scalable and cost-effective framework for language-agnostic malicious code detection. MalTotal leverages LLM-assisted semantic reasoning to identify sensitive APIs, perform hybrid semantic slicing, and reconstruct malicious behavior contexts while reducing analysis overhead. Our evaluations show that MalTotal outperforms 8 state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average F1-score of 93.1% across 5 mainstream languages. Its hybrid slicing reduces LLM token consumption by 94.0%, lowering the analysis cost from \$86.25 to \$5.19 on 2,168 repositories. In a large-scale study of 120K GitHub repositories containing over 7.3 million files, MalTotal discovered 564 previously unknown malicious repositories across multiple languages at a total cost of \$338. These results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and cost-efficiency of MalTotal in mitigating large-scale code poisoning attacks.

</details>


### [270] [ShielDroid: A Hybrid Approach Integrating Machine and Deep Learning for Android Malware Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03250)
*Md Faisal Ahmed,Zarin Tasnim Biash,Abu Raihan Shakil,Ahmed Ann Noor Ryen,Arman Hossain,Faisal Bin Ashraf,Muhammad Iqbal Hossain*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A hybrid dynamic analysis framework combining Random Forest and Multilayer Perceptron achieves 97.5% accuracy for real-time Android malware detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many malicious Android apps evade pre-publication screening by activating malicious behaviors only at runtime, making static analysis insufficient. Undetected malware can cause irreversible damage post-installation, motivating the need for real-time, behavior-based detection.

Method: A hybrid dynamic analysis technique is employed to capture runtime application behavior. After dataset preprocessing and filtering, multiple machine learning classifiers are trained and evaluated. The winning approach fuses Random Forest with a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) in a hybrid ensemble model.

Result: The hybrid Random Forest + MLP model achieves 97.5% detection accuracy with an execution time of 22.945 seconds, outperforming other classifiers in the comparative evaluation.

Conclusion: The proposed real-time Android malware detection framework effectively distinguishes malicious from benign applications using hybrid dynamic analysis, enhancing mobile security by enabling timely threat detection and reducing cyberattack risk.

Abstract: The rapid advancement of modern technology has led to a significant increase in the use of smart devices, such as smartphones and tablets, resulting in the widespread adoption of mobile applications. Although applications are required to undergo malware screening before being published on official app stores, many malicious applications successfully evade detection by concealing sophisticated malware variants. These malicious behaviors are often activated only during runtime, making them difficult to identify through conventional static analysis. As a result, malware may remain undetected until after installation, potentially causing irreversible damage to users and their devices. This study presents a real-time Android malware detection framework that analyzes application behavior to accurately identify and classify complex malware. The proposed approach employs a hybrid dynamic analysis technique to distinguish malicious applications from benign ones. After preprocessing and filtering the collected dataset, the applications are classified using multiple machine learning algorithms. A comprehensive performance evaluation is conducted to compare the effectiveness of different classification techniques in terms of detection accuracy and execution time. Experimental results demonstrate that a hybrid model combining Random Forest and a Multilayer Perceptron achieves the best overall performance, attaining an accuracy of 97.5% with an execution time of 22.945 seconds. The proposed framework can enhance mobile device security by enabling timely detection of malicious applications and reducing the risk of cyberattacks.

</details>


### [271] [FedGSA: Geometry-Consistent Subspace Aggregation for Differentially Private Federated LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03267)
*Lele Zheng,Ruijie Hu,Tao Zhang,Ke Cheng,Yulong Shen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: FedGSA proposes a geometry-consistent aggregation framework for differentially private federated LoRA that operates on the Grassmann manifold, using subspace representations to avoid basis misalignment and noise distortion, achieving significant accuracy gains over existing baselines under various privacy budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Integrating DP into federated LoRA faces two key issues: (1) independent perturbation of two low-rank matrices causes aggregation mismatch and quadratic noise; (2) existing solutions that freeze one matrix still use Euclidean aggregation, which is basis-dependent and can distort the global update due to misalignment across clients. A geometry-aware approach is needed to resolve these fundamental limitations.

Method: FedGSA represents each privatized client update as a basis-invariant subspace on the Grassmann manifold. Clients extract low-dimensional subspaces capturing dominant update directions and encode them as projection matrices. The server aggregates these projection matrices to estimate a geometry-consistent global update subspace, then reconstructs global LoRA factors within that subspace, reducing distortion from basis misalignment, privacy noise, and data heterogeneity.

Result: On four GLUE tasks and a language generation benchmark, FedGSA consistently outperforms baselines across different privacy budgets and data heterogeneity levels. It improves average accuracy over the strongest baseline by 2.17% (ε=6) and 2.27% (ε=3). The method provably incurs no additional privacy loss beyond client-side DP training and enjoys formal convergence guarantees.

Conclusion: FedGSA effectively addresses the basis-misalignment and noise-distortion problems in DP federated LoRA through Grassmann manifold aggregation, yielding substantial and consistent accuracy improvements while maintaining the same privacy guarantees as client-side DP training.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables communication-efficient federated fine-tuning of pretrained language models. However, integrating differential privacy (DP) into federated LoRA remains challenging: independently perturbing and aggregating its two low-rank matrices can cause aggregation mismatch and the quadratic noise term. Existing methods mitigate these issues by freezing one low-rank matrix but still rely on Euclidean aggregation, which is basis-dependent and may distort the global update. To address this limitation, we propose FedGSA, a geometry-consistent aggregation framework for differentially private federated LoRA. FedGSA represents each privatized client update as a basis-invariant subspace on the Grassmann manifold. In each communication round, clients extract low-dimensional subspaces capturing dominant update directions and encode them as projection matrices. The server aggregates these representations to estimate a geometry-consistent global update subspace and reconstructs the global LoRA factors within it, reducing distortion caused by basis misalignment, privacy noise, and heterogeneous client updates. We prove that FedGSA incurs no additional privacy loss beyond client-side DP training and establish its convergence under standard assumptions. Experiments on four GLUE tasks and a language generation benchmark demonstrate consistent improvements across privacy budgets and degrees of data heterogeneity. In particular, FedGSA improves average accuracy over the strongest baseline by 2.17% and 2.27% under $ε=6$ and $ε=3$, respectively.

</details>


### [272] [Breaking ACDGV MinRank Gabidulin encryption schemes over matrix codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03328)
*Thai Hung Le*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper presents a cryptanalysis of Enhanced Gabidulin Matrix Codes (EGMC) that breaks all 16 proposed parameter sets by combining combinatorial and algebraic techniques to recover an equivalent secret key, reducing claimed 128-bit security to 35 bits with key recovery in under 10 minutes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EGMC was proposed at Asiacrypt 2024 as a way to hide the algebraic structure of Gabidulin matrix codes for compact post-quantum encryption schemes (ciphertexts as small as 65 bytes at 128-bit security). The authors aim to test whether the "enhanced" masking construction truly eliminates the structural leakage that enables key recovery.

Method: The attack combines combinatorial and algebraic techniques in a two-stage process: first, a combinatorial-algebraic hybrid recovers a Gabidulin-equivalent compressed code from the masked public code; second, this compressed code is extended to a full-length equivalent secret key in polynomial time. The attack yields both a distinguisher and a complete key-recovery attack.

Result: All 16 EGMC parameter sets are broken by large margins. For the flagship 128-bit parameter set (2,17,37,4,0), the security level drops from 186 bits to 35 bits. The equivalent secret key is recovered in less than 10 minutes in the authors' implementation.

Conclusion: The EGMC construction retains enough algebraic structure to be vulnerable to key recovery, and the enhanced masking is insufficient to prevent structural attacks. The proposed encryption schemes are fully broken.

Abstract: Enhanced Gabidulin Matrix Codes (EGMC), introduced by Aragon, Couvreur, Dyseryn, Gaborit, and Vincotte at Asiacrypt 2024, were designed to hide the algebraic structure of Gabidulin matrix codes while enabling very compact McEliece- and Niederreiter-type encryption schemes, with ciphertexts as small as $65$ bytes at the claimed 128-bit security level. Their security relies on the assumption that a masked EGMC code is hard to distinguish from a random matrix code. We show that this enhanced construction leaves enough structure for an equivalent code of the secret key to be recovered. Unlike previous cryptanalysis, our attack combines combinatorial and algebraic techniques to recover a Gabidulin-equivalent compressed code. This code can then be extended to a full-length equivalent secret key in polynomial time. As a result, the attack provides both a distinguisher and a key-recovery attack against the EGMC encryption schemes. The attack breaks all 16 proposed EGMC parameter sets by large margins. For example, for the claimed 128-bit parameter set $(2,17,37,4,0)$, it reduces the security level from 186 bits to 35 bits. In our implementation, the equivalent secret key is recovered in less than 10 minutes.

</details>


### [273] [SkillSentry: Adaptive Honey Worlds for Dynamic Safety Testing of Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03485)
*Nizhang Li,Zonghao Ying,Xiangfan Wu,Zonglei Jing,Xixun Lin,Hao Zhang,Wenxin Zhang,Jiaye Lin,Quanchen Zou,Xiangzheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SkillSentry is a dynamic safety-testing framework that uses adaptive honey worlds — LLM-simulated environments with decoy resources — to detect conditionally harmful agent skills that evade static analysis. It achieves 99.50% recall and 96.26% F1 on benchmarks, and 92.95% F1 under evasion attacks, significantly outperforming existing scanners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: External skills extend LLM agent capabilities but introduce a subtle attack surface: malicious skills can conceal harmful behavior behind conditional triggers (specific environment states, resources, or interaction histories). Existing scanners relying on static analysis, predefined rules, or one-shot semantic judgments fail to reliably elicit and attribute such conditional malicious behavior.

Method: SkillSentry employs three core mechanisms: (1) it infers a skill's intended capability boundary; (2) it constructs an LLM-simulated "honey world" with controlled decoy resources and adaptively generates tasks to explore the skill's behavioral states across diverse execution conditions; (3) it compares skill-enabled trajectories against matched no-skill executions, grounding any suspicious behaviors in source code and verified execution traces before rendering a final safety decision.

Result: Against seven scanner configurations, SkillSentry achieves 99.50% Recall and 96.26% average F1 on standard benchmarks. Under semantics-preserving evasion attacks, it maintains 92.95% average F1, compared to 80.07% for the strongest baselines.

Conclusion: Adaptive honey-world testing with trajectory comparison and source-level attribution significantly improves detection of conditionally harmful agent skills, advancing the state of the art in LLM agent safety.

Abstract: External skills extend the capabilities of large language model agents, but also introduce an execution-time attack surface: a skill that appears benign under inspection may reveal harmful behavior only after particular environmental states, resources, or interaction histories are encountered. Existing scanners primarily rely on static analysis, predefined rules, or one-shot semantic judgments, making such conditional behavior difficult to elicit and attribute. We present SkillSentry, a dynamic safety-testing framework based on adaptive honey worlds. SkillSentry infers the intended capability boundary of a skill, constructs an LLM-simulated environment with controlled decoy resources, and adaptively generates tasks to explore its behavioral states. It then compares skill-enabled trajectories with matched no-skill executions, grounding suspicious behaviors in source code and verified execution traces before making a final decision. We evaluate SkillSentry against seven scanner configurations. SkillSentry achieves 99.50% Recall and 96.26% average F1 on standard benchmarks. Under semantics-preserving evasion, it reaches 92.95% average F1, compared with 80.07% for the strongest baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/nizhangli062-jpg/SkillSentry-Adaptive-Honey-Worlds-for-Dynamic-Safety-Testing-of-Agent-Skills.

</details>


### [274] [SkillJack: Persistent Skill Backdoors in Self-Evolving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03509)
*Zonghao Ying,Xiangfan Wu,Huiyu Wu,Xing Zheng,Huangsheng Cheng,Xiaorong Shi,Jing Guo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SkillJack is the first attack targeting the experience-to-skill pipeline in self-evolving agents, where poisoned interaction histories are transformed into durable, reusable malicious skills that evade detection, persist after source deletion, and can activate unintentionally on benign queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work only addresses memory/retrieval poisoning where attacks require poisoned records in runtime context. The authors identify a more fundamental risk: self-evolving agents autonomously convert experiences into reusable skills, creating a new attack surface where poisoning can survive beyond individual tasks and become persistent behavioral artifacts.

Method: SkillJack exploits the agent's own skill extraction pipeline by injecting poisoned trajectories that, during skill extraction, undergo "sanitization whitewashing" (malicious intent obscured), "cross-layer promotion" (transient→persistent), and "persistence isolation" (survives source deletion). Evaluated on SkillX and Anything2Skill using 150 trajectories across four policy-risk categories.

Result: Safety detection drops from 98.5% (poisoned trajectories) to 11.4% (extracted skills) in SkillX; similar effect in Anything2Skill. Attack success rates: 56.2% (SkillX) and 89.2% (Anything2Skill). 80.0% of skill-mediated attacks persist after deleting original poisoned records. Some skills unintentionally activate on benign queries.

Conclusion: Skill evolution constitutes a critical new attack surface. The authors call for provenance-aware skill lifecycle protection mechanisms to defend against this class of attacks.

Abstract: Self-evolving agents increasingly convert interaction histories into reusable skills that persist beyond individual tasks. While prior work studies memory and retrieval poisoning, such attacks only affect agents when poisoned records are retrieved as context. We uncover a new and more fundamental risk: poisoned experiences can be transformed by the agent itself into durable behavioral artifacts. We present \textbf{SkillJack}, the first attack that exploits the experience-to-skill pipeline of self-evolving agents. Instead of directly manipulating runtime context, SkillJack hijacks the agent's own learning process to implant malicious behaviors into its reusable skill repertoire. We identify three key properties of this transformation: \emph{sanitization whitewashing}, where malicious intent is obscured during skill extraction; \emph{cross-layer promotion}, where transient experiences become persistent capabilities; and \emph{persistence isolation}, where the attack survives removal of its original source records. We evaluate SkillJack on two representative systems, SkillX and Anything2Skill, using a shared dataset of 150 trajectories across four policy-risk categories. Results show that skill extraction substantially reduces attack detectability: in SkillX, safety detection drops from 98.5\% for poisoned trajectories to 11.4\% for extracted skills, while Anything2Skill shows a similar effect. Meanwhile, the implanted skills remain effective, achieving attack success rates of 56.2\% and 89.2\% on the two systems, respectively. Furthermore, 80.0\% of skill-mediated attacks persist after deleting the original poisoned records, and some skills unintentionally activate on benign queries. Our findings reveal skill evolution as a new attack surface and motivate provenance-aware skill lifecycle protection. Our code is available at https://github.com/Tencent/AI-Infra-Guard/research/skilljack.

</details>


### [275] [AI Forensics Across White-, Grey-, and Black-Box Access: A Process Model and Research Agenda for Post-Incident Investigation of AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03520)
*Ali Dehghantanha,Sajad Homayoun*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes organizing AI forensics around investigator access levels (white/grey/black box), introduces a four-phase process model matrix and an order of volatility for AI artifacts, and derives an access-conditioned examination framework with open research challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI systems increasingly make consequential decisions requiring post-incident investigation, yet existing AI forensics work is fragmented across specific system types, artifacts, and techniques. A unifying organizational framework is needed to systematize the field.

Method: The authors distinguish three access levels — white box (full internal access), grey box (partial/log access), and black box (input-output only) — and map each to the four forensic phases (collection, preservation, analysis, reporting). They propose an order of volatility for AI system artifacts (runtime state → context windows → logs → retrieval stores → model artifacts → training lineage) and construct an access-conditioned examination framework from this matrix.

Result: The resulting framework shows how each access level constrains forensic capabilities across all phases. The order of volatility guides prioritization during evidence collection. Key open problems identified include black box preservation, model version attestation, uncertainty quantification for surrogate-based analysis, and chain of custody for mutable AI artifacts.

Conclusion: Investigator access level provides an effective organizing principle for AI forensics. The proposed matrix and volatility ordering offer practical guidance for practitioners while surfacing foundational research gaps that must be addressed as AI forensics matures into a coherent discipline.

Abstract: AI systems are increasingly involved in decisions and actions that may later require investigation. When an AI related incident occurs, investigators need to reconstruct what the system did, why it behaved that way, and which part of the system or supply chain contributed to the outcome. Existing work on AI forensics remains fragmented, often focusing on a specific system type, artifact, or analysis technique. This paper argues that investigator access is a useful starting point for organizing the field. We distinguish white box, grey box, and black box access and show how each access level changes what can be collected, preserved, analyzed, and reported. Based on this distinction, we propose a process model matrix for AI forensics across four phases: collection, preservation, analysis, and reporting. We also introduce an order of volatility for AI systems, covering runtime state, context windows, logs, retrieval stores, model artifacts, and training lineage. From this matrix, we derive an access conditioned examination framework and identify open research problems, including black box preservation, model version attestation, uncertainty quantification for surrogate based analysis, and chain of custody for mutable AI artifacts.

</details>


### [276] [A Challenge-Nonce Freshness Gap in Project Veraison's TPM Reference Schemes, Found by Appraising Application-Layer Action Evidence End-to-End](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03534)
*Anton Sokolov*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates end-to-end RATS-based attestation of AI agent actions using TPM quotes, integrating with a conformant Veraison Verifier. It uncovers and fixes a critical nonce-replay vulnerability where replayed quotes still appraise as affirming, and provides a reproducible two-part fix that ensures quote freshness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When automated agents take consequential actions, the integrity of the software stack producing the audit record is itself suspect. Signed logs only prove which key wrote a record, not whether the runtime was trustworthy. Prior work proposed Action Evidence Packages (AEPs) bound into TPM quotes under the RATS architecture, but only validated against a minimal stand-in Verifier — leaving a gap in real-world conformance.

Method: The authors drive an AEP quote end-to-end through a conformant Project Veraison RATS Verifier: they generate an EC P-256 attestation key, measure the AEP outcome digest into a PCR, pack the quote into Veraison's tpm-enacttrust format, provision a Concise Reference Integrity Manifest (trust anchor + golden reference value), and obtain a signed EAT Attestation Result (EAR). They test both valid evidence (expecting affirming) and tampered evidence (outcome-swap, signature byte-flip, expecting contraindicated). They also test quote replay across sessions.

Result: Valid AEP quotes yield affirming EAR; outcome-swapped or signature-tampered quotes yield contraindicated EAR. However, the reference scheme fails to enforce challenge-nonce freshness — a replayed quote still appraises as affirming. The authors disclose this finding, provide an upstreamable two-part fix, and validate that with the fix active, the same valid quote flips from affirming (in its own session) to contraindicated when replayed to a fresh session.

Conclusion: The pipeline is fully reproducible and demonstrates that AEP-backed RATS attestation can be integrated with a conformant Verifier. The discovered nonce-replay vulnerability and its fix constitute a security-relevant contribution to the reference implementation. The Attester remains an emulated swtpm, so hardware-backed guarantees are left for future work.

Abstract: When an automated agent (an AI agent, say) takes a consequential action, the record it leaves behind is produced by the very software stack whose integrity is in question. A signed log proves which key wrote the record, not what the runtime was. Prior work proposed treating that record (an Action Evidence Package, AEP: a signed append-only record of an action, its authorising principal, and its outcome) as application-layer Evidence under the IETF Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) architecture (RFC 9334), binding the outcome into a hardware-rooted TPM quote so that swapping it invalidates the quote. But that prior work appraised the result only against a minimal Verifier stand-in. This article closes that gap. We drive an AEP quote, produced on an emulated software TPM, end-to-end through a conformant Project Veraison RATS Verifier. We generate an EC P-256 attestation key, measure the AEP outcome digest into a PCR, pack a genuine quote into Veraison's tpm-enacttrust format, provision a Concise Reference Integrity Manifest (trust anchor plus golden reference value), and obtain a signed EAT Attestation Result (EAR). Good evidence yields affirming; an outcome-swap or a one-byte signature tamper yields contraindicated. Along the way we uncover, responsibly disclose, and fix a security-relevant finding: the reference scheme does not enforce challenge-nonce freshness, so a replayed quote still appraises as affirming. We give an exact, upstreamable two-part fix and validate it end-to-end. With the fix active, the same valid quote that is affirming in its own session flips to contraindicated when replayed to a fresh one. The pipeline is fully reproducible; the Attester remains an emulated swtpm, not a hardware guarantee.

</details>


### [277] [ReputationChain: Robust Trust Updating for Blockchain-Enabled Supply Chains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03554)
*Adnan Iftekhar,Chengliang Zheng,Xiaohui Cui,Mir Hassan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper presents a participant trust framework for supply-chain blockchains that computes reputation off-chain using bounded on-chain evidence, incorporating decay based on verified interaction volume, counterparty diversity penalties, repeated-interaction discounting, and governance-supplied identity confidence. Simulations show reduced collusive gain, limited Sybil inflation, and fairer scores for honest newcomers with sparse histories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing blockchain-based reputation systems suffer from three underexplored problems: (1) repeated bilateral inflation, where colluding parties artificially boost each other's scores through repeated interactions; (2) identity multiplicity (Sybil attacks), where a single controller operates multiple identities to inflate reputation; and (3) unfair decay that penalizes honest participants with sparse but legitimate interaction histories. The authors argue that ledger integrity alone is insufficient for trust decisions in risk-sensitive supply-chain transactions.

Method: The proposed framework, called RC, treats blockchain as an evidence and provenance layer rather than the trust source. Governed interaction outcomes are converted into bounded evidence. Key mechanisms include: (a) discounting repeated same-pair interactions, (b) penalizing low counterparty diversity, (c) weighting positive evidence by governance-supplied identity confidence, and (d) decaying scores toward a neutral prior proportionally to verified interaction volume (volume-aware decay). Reputation computation is performed off-chain with nonlinear functions, while on-chain verification ensures admissibility. Identity, contract, outcome, and update provenance remain on-chain.

Result: In controlled simulations over 30 seeded runs with matched interaction traces: (1) mean collusive gain dropped to 0.1443 vs. 0.3688 (naive mean evidence) and 0.3585 (static decay); (2) with ten Sybil identities under one controller, the reputation inflation ratio fell to 0.8723, while three baselines exceeded 1.08; (3) volume-aware decay raised mean newcomer reputation from 0.6626 to 0.7589 and reduced the false low-trust rate from 0.3633 to 0.1683. Paired analysis confirmed consistency across runs.

Conclusion: The framework achieves bounded reduction in reputation distortion rather than attacker detection. The authors acknowledge that deployment evaluation and calibration with operational data are required before production use. The approach demonstrates that nonlinear, volume-aware reputation mechanisms computed off-chain but verifiable on-chain can meaningfully mitigate collusion, Sybil inflation, and unfair decay in supply-chain trust systems.

Abstract: Blockchain can preserve supply-chain records, but ledger integrity alone does not show whether a participant should be trusted in a future risk-sensitive transaction. Existing reputation systems mainly address product evidence, global feedback aggregation, or review authenticity, while giving less attention to repeated bilateral inflation, identity multiplicity, and unfair decay for honest participants with sparse histories. We present \RC, a participant trust framework that uses blockchain as an evidence and provenance layer rather than as the source of trust. Governed interaction outcomes are converted into bounded evidence. Repeated interactions between the same pair are discounted, low counterparty diversity is penalized, governance-supplied identity confidence weights positive evidence, and scores decay toward a neutral prior according to verified interaction volume. Identity, contract, outcome, and update provenance remain on chain, while nonlinear reputation computation is performed off chain and checked on chain for admissibility. In controlled simulations with 30 seeded runs and matched interaction traces, the full model reduces mean collusive gain to 0.1443, compared with 0.3688 for naive mean evidence and 0.3585 for static decay. With ten identities under one controller, the reputation inflation ratio falls to 0.8723, while three comparison baselines remain above 1.08. On identical newcomer traces, volume-aware decay increases mean newcomer reputation from 0.6626 to 0.7589 and reduces the false low-trust rate from 0.3633 to 0.1683. Paired analysis confirms these improvements across runs. The results support a bounded reduction in reputation distortion, not attacker detection. Deployment evaluation and calibration with operational data are still required before production use.

</details>


### [278] [CAN Disabler: Hardware-based Prevention method of Unauthorized Transmission in CAN and CAN-FD networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03567)
*Ryo Kurachi,T. David Pyun,Shinya Honda,Hiroaki Takada,Hiroshi Ueda,Satoshi Horihata*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a modified CAN controller that blocks unauthorized bus access by detecting and preventing ECUs from transmitting messages at abnormal frequencies, and demonstrates its effectiveness on both standard CAN and CAN-FD buses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite numerous reported security attacks against CAN in recent years, current in-vehicle control networks lack built-in security functions in ECUs. There is a pressing need for cost-effective security features that can be deployed in automotive environments without prohibitive overhead.

Method: The authors propose modifying the CAN controller hardware to incorporate a transmission-rate monitoring mechanism. When an ECU attempts to transmit messages at an abnormal (excessively high) frequency — indicative of a compromised or malicious node — the modified CAN controller blocks those transmissions, effectively acting as a "disabler" that prevents unauthorized CAN-bus access.

Result: The proposed method successfully blocks unauthorized message transmissions on both standard CAN and CAN with flexible data-rate (CAN-FD) buses, demonstrating the disabler's effectiveness across both legacy and next-generation in-vehicle network protocols.

Conclusion: A lightweight, cost-effective CAN controller modification can serve as an effective countermeasure against CAN-bus attacks by enforcing per-ECU transmission frequency limits, providing a practical security enhancement suitable for resource-constrained in-vehicle networks.

Abstract: There have been a quite number of security attack cases against Controller Area Network (CAN) reported in recent years, but in the meantime no security function is included in the ECU in the current in-vehicle control network. Thus, in-vehicle control networks particularly require cost-effective security features. In this paper, therefore, we propose a method to block unauthorized CAN-bus access using a CAN controller that is modified to prevent the ECU from transmitting messages to the CAN-bus at abnormal frequency. Then, we have also demonstrated the effectiveness of the disabler on CAN with flexible data-rate (CAN-FD) buses.

</details>


### [279] [Secure Long-Range Autonomous Valet Parking: A Reservation Scheme With Three-Factor Authentication and Key Agreement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03590)
*Di Wang,Yue Cao,Fei Yan,Yining Liu,Daxin Tian,Yuan Zhuang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SecLAVP is a three-factor authentication and key agreement protocol for long-range autonomous valet parking reservation services, combining passwords, biometrics, and smart cards to secure passenger-AV communication at drop-off/pick-up points, with formal security proofs and practical performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LAVP reservation schemes focus narrowly on parking request verification and check-in, neglecting identity legitimacy and communication security during passenger drop-off and pick-up phases. This gap motivates a comprehensive authentication protocol covering the full LAVP service lifecycle.

Method: The authors design SecLAVP, a three-factor (password, biometric, smart card) mutual authentication and key agreement protocol between passengers and autonomous vehicles, mediated by a drop-off/pick-up point (DP). Security is formally proven using the Real-Or-Random (ROR) model for session-key security and verified via AVISPA simulations against man-in-the-middle attacks. Informal analysis covers 15 security goals. Performance is benchmarked on communication overhead, computational overhead, and scheduling.

Result: SecLAVP is formally proven secure under the ROR model, resists man-in-the-middle attacks in AVISPA simulations, and satisfies all 15 defined security goals. Performance evaluation shows feasible communication and computational overhead for real-world LAVP deployment.

Conclusion: SecLAVP fills a critical security gap in LAVP reservation systems by protecting identity and communication during drop-off/pick-up, and its provable security combined with practical performance makes it suitable for real-world deployment.

Abstract: Long-range autonomous valet parking (LAVP) is increasingly adopted to alleviate traffic congestion and parking difficulties. For large-scale parking demand, reservation can improve parking management. However, existing schemes mainly focus on parking request verification and parking check-in, and do not adequately protect identity legitimacy and communication security during passenger drop-off and pick-up. To address this problem, we propose SecLAVP, a provably secure three-factor authentication and key agreement protocol for LAVP reservation services. SecLAVP combines passwords, biometrics, and smart cards. With assistance from the drop-off/pick-up point (DP), the passenger and the autonomous vehicle (AV) achieve mutual authentication and establish a session key for secure communication. In the Real-Or-Random (ROR) model, we formally prove that SecLAVP provides session-key security. AVISPA simulations show that SecLAVP resists man-in-the-middle attacks, while informal analysis demonstrates that it satisfies 15 defined security goals. Finally, performance evaluation in terms of communication overhead, computational overhead, and scheduling shows that SecLAVP is feasible for practical deployment.

</details>


### [280] [DiagChain: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents on Evidence-Grounded Attack Chain Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03591)
*Xuyang Liu,Yibin Han,Zhenwei Zhang,Kai Chang,Zhiwei Xu,Tian Qiu,Weixian Deng,Jiabao Gao,Xiaolin Peng,Hai Wan,Xibin Zhao*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: DiagChain is a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on evidence-grounded attack chain reconstruction. It features 69 multi-OS scenarios (MAIN-69), a novel Evidence-Centric RAG approach (ECRAG), and five stage-wise metrics. Evaluation across 6 LLMs reveals that even the best model succeeds on only 39.6% of reference steps, with smaller models failing at evidence incorporation and larger models bottlenecked by action ordering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based attack chain reconstruction evaluate only final outputs or aggregate accuracy, obscuring how and where errors emerge at intermediate reasoning stages. There is a need for fine-grained, stage-wise diagnostic evaluation to understand failure modes and guide improvements in evidence-grounded cybersecurity agents.

Method: The authors introduce DiagChain, comprising: (1) MAIN-69, a benchmark of 69 attack scenarios varying by OS, evidence noise levels, and chain lengths; (2) Evidence-Centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ECRAG), which pairs evidence retrieval with an evolving structured representation of the reconstructed attack chain; and (3) five complementary metrics that evaluate distinct stages of the reconstruction pipeline for systematic failure diagnosis. Six LLMs are evaluated under this framework.

Result: Even the strongest LLM configuration succeeds on only 39.6% of the 849 reference steps in MAIN-69. Smaller models primarily fail at incorporating retrieved evidence into outputs, while larger models progress further but are bottlenecked by correctly ordering the evidence into a coherent attack chain.

Conclusion: Diagnostic, stage-wise evaluation beyond end-to-end accuracy is essential for understanding LLM agent failures in attack chain reconstruction. The findings highlight actionable directions: improving evidence incorporation for smaller models and enhancing sequential reasoning (ordering) for larger models.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents offer a promising approach to attack chain reconstruction by retrieving and interpreting heterogeneous telemetry to infer ordered attacker actions. However, existing benchmarks mainly evaluate final outputs or aggregate accuracy, providing limited insight into how errors arise and propagate across intermediate reasoning stages. We present DiagChain, a diagnostic benchmark for evidence-grounded attack chain reconstruction that enables stage-wise evaluation of LLM agents. DiagChain includes MAIN-69, a suite of 69 scenarios spanning multiple operating systems, evidence noise levels, and chain lengths. It further introduces Evidence-Centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ECRAG), which couples evidence retrieval with an evolving structured representation of the reconstructed chain. Five complementary metrics are introduced to assess distinct stages of the reconstruction process and support systematic failure diagnosis. Based on evaluations using 6 LLMs, DiagChain reveals that even the strongest configuration succeeds on only 39.6% of the 849 reference steps in MAIN-69. Our analysis further shows that smaller models struggle with the more basic task of incorporating retrieved evidence into their outputs, whereas larger models can proceed to later steps, where correctly ordering that evidence becomes the main bottleneck. These results validate the importance of diagnostic evaluation beyond end-to-end accuracy and provide actionable insights for improving evidence-grounded cybersecurity agents.

</details>


### [281] [A Security-Oriented Lifecycle Model for Large Language Model Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03626)
*Eleftherios Batzolis,George Drosatos,Vassilis Katsouros,Konstantinos Rantos*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new security-oriented lifecycle model for LLM systems comprising 32 stages across four pipeline layers, a 12-stage LLMOps pillar, and a 9-category governance pillar. It reveals that governance oversight concentrates on deployment-facing stages while the most consequential decisions occur at development-facing stages with minimal regulatory visibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM lifecycle frameworks prioritize operational efficiency over security analysis, leaving critical security activities (data provenance, artifact signing, permission control, decommissioning) implicit. Governance frameworks like NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001 organize requirements around risk levels but fail to map them to specific lifecycle stages, creating gaps in both security and regulatory coverage.

Method: The authors construct a lifecycle model structured around security-relevant boundaries rather than workflow optimization. The model spans 32 stages across four core pipeline layers (Data, Model, Distribution, Application), supplemented by a 12-stage LLMOps pillar and a 9-category governance pillar. Thirteen novel stages are introduced to capture security concerns that existing frameworks fail to distinguish. A governance mapping is performed by synthesizing requirements from NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001 against the proposed lifecycle stages.

Result: The governance mapping reveals a structural asymmetry: governance evidence and regulatory visibility concentrate at deployment-facing stages (where systems are externally observable), while the most consequential decisions — data selection, alignment strategy, and capability boundary definition — occur at development-facing stages, where regulatory visibility is lowest. Thirteen security-relevant stages were identified that existing frameworks do not clearly distinguish.

Conclusion: Current LLM lifecycle and governance frameworks suffer from a structural mismatch: security activities are under-specified in operational frameworks, and governance requirements lack lifecycle-stage anchoring. The proposed model addresses both deficiencies and exposes a critical regulatory blind spot — high-impact design decisions are made where oversight is weakest.

Abstract: Large language models are being integrated into critical infrastructure and enterprise workflows at unprecedented scale,yet the lifecycle frameworks governing their development and operations were designed for operational efficiency rather than security analysis. As a result, security-relevant activities such as data provenance verification, artifact signing, agentic permission control, and decommissioning are often left implicit or assumed to receive due care. Governance frameworks, in turn, organise requirements around risk levels or management processes without clearly linking them to the lifecycle stages where they apply. This paper addresses both deficiencies. We propose a lifecycle model for LLM systems that supports security analysis by structuring it around security-relevant boundaries rather than workflow optimisation. The model comprises 32 stages across four core pipeline layers (Data, Model, Distribution, Application), supported by a 12-stage LLMOps pillar and a 9-category governance pillar. Thirteen stages are introduced here as separate units because they expose distinct security concerns that existing frameworks do not clearly distinguish. A governance mapping synthesising the NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001 reveals a structural property of the current regulatory landscape: governance evidence concentrates at deployment-facing stages, where systems are visible to regulators, while the most consequential decisions, data selection, alignment strategy, and capability boundaries, are made at development-facing stages, where regulatory visibility is lowest.

</details>


### [282] [Empirical Analysis of Evasion and Poisoning Against Malware Data Drift Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03642)
*Mingyue Yang,David Lie,Nicolas Papernot*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper investigates how evasion and poisoning attacks—traditionally aimed at malware classifiers—affect machine learning-based data drift detectors, revealing that drift detectors respond differently to these attacks due to their distinct design and operational characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While concept drift from malware evolution is a known challenge, and data drift detectors are deployed alongside malware classifiers to address it, the combined vulnerability of these two components to adversarial attacks (evasion and poisoning) remains unexplored. Understanding this interaction is critical for robust malware detection pipelines.

Method: The authors systematically examine evasion and poisoning attacks against an integrated pipeline consisting of a malware classifier and a data drift detector. They analyze how the unique design goals, feature spaces, and decision logic of drift detectors cause adversarial perturbations crafted for classifiers to produce different, potentially unintended effects on drift detection.

Result: The study demonstrates that evasion and poisoning attacks affect data drift detectors differently than malware classifiers, owing to the structural and functional differences between the two systems. Specific attack outcomes on drift detection behavior are characterized.

Conclusion: Adversarial attacks against malware classifiers do not straightforwardly translate to data drift detectors. Security evaluations of ML-based malware detection pipelines must consider both components jointly, as their interplay introduces novel attack surfaces and failure modes.

Abstract: As concept drift due to malware evolution presents challenges for malware classification, machine learning-based data drift detection tools are developed to mitigate this problem. These data drift detector tools are designed for a different purpose and built with different techniques compared to malware classifiers. Although evasion and poisoning attacks against machine learning-based malware classifiers can cause misclassification of malware samples, it is not clear how these attacks work against data drift detectors and malware classifiers in combination. This work investigates the effect of evasion and poisoning attacks on the data drift detector along with the malware classifier. We demonstrate how unique characteristics of data drift detectors cause attacks against malware classifiers to work differently against them.

</details>


### [283] [When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03700)
*Yongli Xiang,Zhifang Zhang,Bojun Yang,Ziming Hong,Lei Feng,Miao Xu,Tongliang Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AntiSkillBench is a benchmark for evaluating privacy and safety risks in persona-skill pipelines. It includes 7,500 dialogue traces from 50 profiles, measures skill-level privacy leakage and agent-level impersonation, and tests defenses. Experiments show risks persist across agents and distillation methods, with existing defenses proving inadequate and distillation-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persona skills—condensed, reusable artifacts from personal interaction histories—amplify privacy risks by concentrating fragmented personal signals and enabling their repeated use. Existing defenses designed for individual records or retrieval-based memory are insufficient for this new threat surface, yet no systematic benchmark exists to evaluate safety across the full persona-skill pipeline.

Method: The authors introduce AntiSkillBench with three components: (1) a dataset of 7,500 persona-grounded dialogues from 50 behaviorally rich profiles spanning diverse tasks; (2) an evaluation suite measuring skill-level privacy leakage, agent-level attribute disclosure, and behavioral impersonation across three skill-distillation strategies; and (3) a defense suite covering four configurations of online and post-hoc interventions (active risk suppression and passive provenance protection). Three frontier agents are evaluated.

Result: Persona-skill risks persist across all tested agent backbones and distillation protocols, extending from explicit attributes to communication styles and personality traits. Existing defenses show limited, distillation-dependent effectiveness and fail to generalize across different risk types and distillation strategies.

Conclusion: AntiSkillBench represents a challenging and necessary benchmark for advancing privacy-preserving and authenticity-aware persona skills. Current defenses are insufficient, highlighting the need for more robust, generalizable protection mechanisms in persona-skill pipelines.

Abstract: Persona skills distill personal interaction histories into portable and executable artifacts for downstream agents. While enabling flexible personalization, this process concentrates fragmented personal signals, amplifies their impact through reuse, and challenges defenses designed for individual records or retrieval-based memory. To systematically investigate the safety of the persona-skill pipeline, we introduce AntiSkillBench, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating risks and defenses across the persona-skill pipeline. It comprises: (i) a dataset of 7,500 persona-grounded dialogue traces, constructed from 50 behaviorally rich profiles spanning diverse task scenarios; (ii) an evaluation suite that measures skill-level privacy leakage and agent-level attribute disclosure and behavioral impersonation across three skill-distillation strategies; and (iii) a defense evaluation covering four configurations across online and post-hoc interventions, including active risk suppression and passive provenance protection. Experiments across three frontier agents show that persona-skill risks persist across agent backbones and distillation protocols, extending from explicit attributes to communication styles and personality traits. Existing defenses exhibit limited and distillation-dependent effectiveness, failing to generalize across risk and distillation strategies. These results highlight AntiSkillBench as a challenging benchmark for developing privacy-preserving and authenticity-aware persona skills.

</details>


### [284] [Dependency Triad: A Metric to Quantify the Dependencies Between Attributes for Local Differential Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03737)
*Sandaru Jayawardana,Sennur Ulukus,Ming Ding,Kanchana Thilakarathna*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces "Dependency Triad" (DT), a constant-time conservative estimator for correlation-induced privacy leakage (CPL) in Local Differential Privacy settings. DT summarizes pairwise dependency using three parameters, handles uncertainty in prior knowledge, and scales effectively to high-cardinality attributes and multidimensional data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CPL analysis methods either demand accurate prior knowledge or fail to scale with many attributes and high cardinalities, limiting real-world applicability. A practical, scalable, and robust CPL estimator is needed that can operate without precise prior information.

Method: The authors propose the Dependency Triad (DT) metric, which captures pairwise dependency information relevant to CPL through three parameters. It provides a constant-time conservative estimate of pairwise CPL, explicitly models uncertainty in prior distributional knowledge, and leverages pairwise formulation as a building block for total leakage assessment in multidimensional settings.

Result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that DT consistently estimates CPL across diverse dependency regimes and prior uncertainties, demonstrating robustness particularly for high-cardinality attributes and sparse distributions.

Conclusion: DT offers a practical, scalable solution for estimating correlation-induced privacy leakage without requiring precise prior knowledge, making it suitable for real-world multidimensional LDP data collection with inter-attribute dependencies.

Abstract: Collecting multidimensional user data is essential for extracting rich insights across various applications. Local Differential Privacy (LDP) has emerged as a de facto standard for mitigating privacy risks in such scenarios. A key challenge in privacy-preserving multidimensional data collection lies in inter-attribute dependencies, as they can inadvertently reveal correlated information and increase privacy vulnerabilities. Therefore, accurately measuring correlation-induced privacy leakage (CPL) is essential for privacy analysis and privacy-utility trade-off. However, existing CPL analysis solutions either require accurate prior knowledge or face scalability challenges for large numbers of attributes and high-cardinality attributes. These limit their practical applicability in real data. To address this research gap, we propose a novel metric, ``Dependency Triad'' (DT), which summarizes the pairwise dependency information relevant to CPL using three parameters and yields a \emph{constant-time} conservative estimator of pairwise CPL. DT explicitly models uncertainty in prior distributional knowledge through its parameters, delivering robust leakage estimates. Moreover, its robustness to sparse distributions makes it particularly suitable for high-cardinality attributes, while the pairwise formulation serves as a tractable building block for assessing total leakage in multidimensional settings. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that DT consistently estimates CPL across diverse dependency regimes and prior uncertainties.

</details>


### [285] [Delay Attacks on the German Smart Metering Infrastructure: A Security Analysis of CLS Channel Timing Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03751)
*Fabio Stoll,Benjamin Pottkamp,Heiko Lorenz,Shalaka Kale,Jessica Rövekamp,Joachim Gerlach*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper investigates delay attacks on control signals in Germany's Smart Metering Infrastructure, finding that an on-path WAN attacker can delay signals up to ~48 hours. Scaling this to hundreds of thousands of CLS devices could induce grid frequency deviations severe enough to trigger load shedding. Mitigation proposals include configuration restrictions, implementation fixes, and novel TLS 1.3 protocol extensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The increasing deployment of smart metering infrastructure for grid control creates new attack surfaces. The CLS channel of the German SMI is used to transmit control signals (e.g., for load management, distributed energy resource control), yet its resilience against delay attacks — where an adversary intentionally postpones time-sensitive commands — had not been systematically evaluated under the formal threat model of the Common Criteria Protection Profile for the SMGW.

Method: The authors combine theoretical analysis with experimental validation. They model an on-path attacker in the WAN with sufficient contextual knowledge about target implementations and protocol configurations. The upper bound of delay feasibility is derived analytically from protocol timeout and retransmission parameters. Impact projection scales a single-CLS delay to several hundred thousand CLS devices, estimating the resulting frequency deviation in the power grid. Mitigation strategies are categorized into SMGW configuration restrictions, manufacturer-level implementation changes for FNN Steuerbox and CLS.EEDI, and backward-compatible TLS 1.3 extensions to enforce application-data time limitations.

Result: The theoretical maximum delay is approximately 48 hours for certain deployed protocol configurations. An on-path WAN attacker can feasibly execute such delays. Scaled to hundreds of thousands of CLS devices, the resulting aggregate effect could produce frequency deviations significant enough to necessitate load shedding. The feasibility of scaling the attack depends on contextual knowledge per implementation; standardization may inadvertently simplify acquiring this knowledge. Time-restricted transmissions in FNN Steuerbox and CLS.EEDI are implementation-specific and fixable by manufacturers, whereas TLS 1.3 requires protocol extensions to enforce application-level time bounds.

Conclusion: Delay attacks on the CLS channel represent a credible threat to grid stability, particularly when coordinated across many devices. Mitigation requires a multi-layered approach: SMGW configuration hardening, implementation fixes by manufacturers, and the proposed TLS 1.3 extensions for application-data time enforcement. Other out-of-scope control channels (e.g., proprietary RTUs) may be similarly or more vulnerable and warrant future investigation.

Abstract: This work analyzes the feasibility of delay attacks on control signals transmitted via the Controllable Local System (CLS) channel of the German Smart Metering Infrastructure (SMI). It combines theoretical analysis with experimental validation under a threat model aligned to the Common Criteria Protection Profile for the Smart Meter Gateway (SMGW) and assess the potential impact on the power grid if the identified attack vector is exploited across multiple CLS channels simultaneously. We also outline mitigation strategies, including SMGW configuration restrictions, implementation-level changes, and protocol extensions.
  Our results show that an on-path attacker in the Wide Area Network (WAN) with sufficient contextual knowledge can feasibly execute delay attacks, with a theoretical upper bound of roughly 48 hours for some deployed protocol configurations. Projecting from a single CLS to several hundred thousand CLS devices indicates such an adversary could cause a significant frequency deviation potentially resulting in load shedding. Scaling the attack requires contextual knowledge for each targeted implementation and configuration; whether this knowledge can be broadly reused across CLS channels is uncertain but may become easier to obtain as standardization progresses.
  Time restricted transmissions in the FNN Steuerbox and in applications using CLS.EEDI are implementation-specific and can therefore be addressed by manufacturers. By contrast, ensuring application-data time limitations in TLS~1.3 requires protocol-level extensions. The TLS extensions proposed here offer a sustainable mitigation while preserving backward compatibility.
  Other communication channels outside the SMI (for example, proprietary remote terminal units used to control a CLS) are outside this work's scope and may exhibit similar or worse vulnerabilities.
